blocks.text: A Glosso program is one source file handed to the compiler. Execution begins at the procedure named `main`, which every hosted program must declare. The smallest complete program declares it and nothing else.
main :: () {}

`::` binds a name to a compile-time constant, and the constant here is a procedure: an empty parameter list, no return type, an empty body. Compiling that file links an executable that starts, returns immediately, and reports status 0. Nothing is printed because nothing asked for output.
Printing

`print` is an ordinary procedure, not a statement or a keyword, and it is not one of the names the implicit prelude supplies. It comes from the `Io` module, so a program that prints begins with an import. The Implicit Prelude lists what does arrive with no import at all.

$ glosso --run hello.glo
glosso: compile hello.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
glosso: link hello.exe (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
glosso: done hello.exe  (backend=llvm, target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
hello, world

Omitting the import is the first mistake a new program makes. The checker does not know `print`, and the name it suggests instead is `tprint`, the temp-allocated formatting helper `Format` supplies. That one is not in scope either; the suggestion reaches it because the Prelude imports `Format` for its own use.
What the build prints

Every line the driver writes about its own progress goes to stderr and is prefixed `glosso: `. Stdout belongs to the program and to compile-time execution, so the two streams can be separated without filtering text. A default build prints three lines; the rest of the vocabulary appears only for particular backends and options.

blocks.text:
$ glosso --run hello.glo 2>/dev/null
hello, world
The signature of `main`

`main` takes no parameters. There is no argument-vector form of the declaration on a hosted target; command-line arguments are read with `get_cmdline_args()`, which the prelude supplies. The one exception is the freestanding WebAssembly entry point, described in Freestanding, Bare Metal, UEFI, and WebAssembly.

// main :: (args: []string) {}
error: main must not take parameters; use get_cmdline_args() for command-line arguments

The return type is optional. A `main` with no return type, or with an explicit `-> void`, always reports status 0. Any other return type is accepted only if it implements the `Termination` typeclass, which is the protocol that turns a returned value into a process status.
That instance is why every integer type works as a return type directly. The value is narrowed to `s32` and handed to the host, which then applies its own rules for what a status may be.

$ glosso -o status.exe status.glo
glosso: compile status.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
glosso: link status.exe (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
glosso: done status.exe  (backend=llvm, target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
$ ./status.exe
working
$ echo $?
3

The protocol is open. Declaring an instance for an application's own result type makes it a legal return type for `main` and centralizes the conversion to a process status. `Termination` is exported through the Prelude; the class itself requires no explicit import.

$ ./reason.exe
checking input
$ echo $?
64

The prelude also gives `E!void` a `Termination` instance for every error type `E` that implements `Error`. `.Ok` is status 0; `.Err` calls `report_error` on the payload and then reports status 1. A `main` declared that way can use `?` on any failing call in its body. The reporting protocol itself belongs to `Error`, `Termination`, and `main`.

$ ./apperr.exe
app: step failed
$ echo $?
1

rows: `main :: () -> ssize { … }` and any other integer type
`main :: () -> T { … }` for any `T` with a `Termination` instance
Rejected while checking, for example `error: main return type bool does not implement Termination`.

blocks.text: `--run` reports the program's status but does not adopt it. A program that exits 3 makes the compiler print `glosso: program exited with status exit code: 3` and then exit 1 itself. An exact status is observable only by building the executable and running it directly.

`exit(status)` ends the process immediately from anywhere in the program. It is also supplied by the prelude, so it needs no import, and unlike a `return` from `main` it does not run the remaining `defer` statements.

$ ./exitp.exe
before exit
$ echo $?
9

A file with no `main` is not a compile error. Checking succeeds, the backend emits a module with no entry point, and the platform linker is the component that complains. Building a library rather than a program is what `--backend static-lib`, `--backend shared-lib`, and `--no-main` are for; they are covered in Using the Compiler and in Backends, Artifacts, and Optimization Levels.

$ glosso helper.glo
glosso: compile helper.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
glosso: link helper.exe (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
error: lld-link: error: undefined symbol: wmain

The driver compiles exactly one source file: `glosso [options] <file.glo>`. There is no project file, no source list, and no separate link step. Everything else a program needs enters through `#import` and `#load` from inside that one file, and the whole graph reached that way is a single compilation unit.

$ glosso --run app.glo
glosso: compile app.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
glosso: link app.exe (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
glosso: done app.exe  (backend=llvm, target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
area = 42

`parts/geometry.glo` is part of the program but is not a program: naming it on the command line instead compiles it on its own, and it then has no `main` to link against. Which file is named therefore decides what is built. If more than one positional argument is given the last one silently wins; `glosso a.glo b.glo` builds `b.exe` from `b.glo` and never mentions `a.glo`.
The option list

`glosso --help` prints the complete list and exits 0. It is printed before the backend, the target, and the source file are validated, so it works alongside otherwise invalid options. There is no `--version` option: `glosso --version` is `glosso: unknown option --version`.

Every option that takes a value accepts both the separated and the `=`-joined spelling, so `--backend=object`, `--color=never`, `--std=<dir>`, `--target=wasm32-wasi`, `--cache-dir=<dir>`, `--linker-arg=<arg>`, and `--temp-allocator-size=8192` are equivalent to the two-token forms. `-o` is the exception: it has no `=` form, and `-o=out.obj` is rejected with `glosso: unknown option -o=out.obj`.

blocks.text: Without `-o` the output name is derived from the source file's stem and the chosen backend and target; the full set of default names is in Backends, Artifacts, and Optimization Levels. `-o` with a path whose parent directory does not exist creates the directory. `-o ""` is not an error; the empty string falls back to the backend default.
`--std`

`--std <dir>` names the standard-library root. The directory must contain either a `Prelude.glo` file or a `Prelude/` directory, and anything else is `glosso: --std directory must contain Prelude.glo or Prelude/`. Without the option the driver searches, in order, `$GLOSSO_STD`, `<cwd>/std`, and then `std` beside the compiler executable and one and two directories above it, followed by the per-user install locations; the first candidate that holds a prelude wins. Finding none is `glosso: could not find the project-local or installed Glosso standard library`.
`--use-std`

`--use-std` loads every top-level single-file module and every directory module marked by `module.glo`, unqualified, after the Prelude. It is a conformance convenience rather than the normal import model. Namespace-only directories such as `File_System` are not bulk modules, so their components still need explicit imports.
`--run`

`--run` builds the program and then executes it with no arguments, inheriting stdout and stderr. It is accepted only for the default `llvm` backend, because no other backend produces something that can be executed, and the target must be the host.

$ glosso --run --backend object hello.glo
glosso: --run is available only for --backend llvm

$ glosso --run --target x86_64-linux-musl hello.glo
glosso: --run can only execute the host target (got x86_64-pc-linux-musl)

The first of those two is a command-line error and exits 2; the second is discovered after the options parse and exits 1. `--run` never adopts the program's own status either, so it is a convenience for development rather than a way to script a build.
`--no-main`

Reachability normally starts at `main`. `--no-main` starts it at every `#c_call` function that has a body instead, which is what a library wants; the `static-lib` and `shared-lib` backends do this on their own and do not need the flag. The effect is visible in the emitted module: with the flag, the allocators, the formatters, and the hosted entry wrapper are all gone.

add  :: (a: s32, b: s32) -> s32 #c_call { return a + b; }
main :: () #c_call { }

$ glosso --no-main --backend llvm-ir -o roots.ll roots.glo
$ grep '^define' roots.ll
define i32 @glo_add(i32 %0, i32 %1) {
define void @glo_main() {

$ glosso --backend llvm-ir -o roots2.ll roots.glo
$ grep -c '^define' roots2.ll
28

Combining `--no-main` with the executable backend on a hosted target is a mistake: the flag suppresses the platform entry wrapper as well, so the link fails with `error: lld-link: error: undefined symbol: wmain` on Windows and the equivalent elsewhere. The flag belongs with an object, library, or bare-metal build.
`--color`

`--color auto` is the default and enables colored diagnostics only when stderr is a terminal. `--color always` and `--color never` force the choice, and any other value is `glosso: --color must be auto, always, or never`. Setting `NO_COLOR` in the environment turns color off whatever the flag says, including `--color always`.
Compile-time arguments after `--`

`get_cmdline_args()` returns the process argument vector when the program runs, and the arguments written after `--` when the same call is made during compile-time execution. That is how a build script written in Glosso is parameterized without an extra configuration file.

$ glosso -o cmdargs.exe cmdargs.glo -- build --release "two words"
glosso: compile cmdargs.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
[comptime] count = 3
[comptime]   build
[comptime]   --release
[comptime]   two words
glosso: link cmdargs.exe (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
glosso: done cmdargs.exe  (backend=llvm, target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
$ ./cmdargs.exe
[runtime]  count = 1
[runtime]    C:\Users\almag\...\cmdargs.exe

The two vectors differ in more than their contents: the runtime vector begins with the executable path, and the compile-time one does not. `--` also swallows the whole rest of the command line, so the source file and every driver option have to appear before it. For a nested `add_build_file` or `add_build_string` call, the elements of `Build_Options.compile_time_command_line` occupy this same tail, one argument per element and after an implicit `--`.
Exit codes

`-O` accepts a single digit 0 through 3 and nothing else. `-O4` is not a clamped level, it is `glosso: unknown option -O4`.

The size modes -Os, -Oz, and -Ozz produce runnable artifacts. They combine LLVM optimization with optsize/minsize attributes and target-specific linker size policies. Runtime checks are disabled in these modes; use -O0 or -O1 for checked builds. -Ozz also strips symbols and metadata.
`--memory-sanitizer` and `--thread-sanitizer` are mutually exclusive rather than last-wins; asking for both is a command-line error.

blocks.text: `--backend` chooses what a build produces. All five backends go through LLVM, and the one that produces an executable is spelled `llvm`; `llvm-ir` is the one that stops at textual IR instead of generating machine code.

blocks.text: `exe` and `executable` are not spellings of the first one. An unrecognized name is a command-line error, reported before the source file is read: `glosso: unknown backend 'exe' (choose llvm, object, static-lib, shared-lib, or llvm-ir)`. The library backends root reachability at the defined `#c_call` functions on their own, so they do not need `--no-main`.

$ glosso --backend object lib.glo
glosso: compile lib.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
glosso: wrote lib.obj  (backend=object, target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)

glosso: compile lib.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
glosso: link lib.lib (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
glosso: done lib.lib  (backend=static-lib, target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)

glosso: link lib.dll (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
glosso: wrote import library lib.dll.lib
glosso: done lib.dll  (backend=shared-lib, target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)

glosso: compile lib.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
glosso: wrote lib.ll  (backend=llvm-ir, target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
Default artifact names

Without `-o`, the output name is the source file's stem plus whatever naming convention the target uses for that kind of artifact. The stem is taken from the file, not from any declaration inside it, so `lib.glo` gives the names below.

rows: `lib.exe` on Windows, `lib.wasm` on a WebAssembly target, `lib` with no extension on ELF and Mach-O targets.
`lib.obj` on `*-windows-msvc`, `lib.o` on every other target including `*-windows-gnu`.
`lib.lib` on Windows targets that are not `-gnu`, `liblib.a` everywhere else.
`lib.dll` on Windows, `liblib.dylib` on Darwin, `liblib.wasm` on WebAssembly, `liblib.so` elsewhere.

blocks.text: A Windows `shared-lib` build writes a second file, the import library that a consumer links against: `lib.dll.lib` under the MSVC ABI and `liblib.dll.a` under the GNU one. It is announced by its own progress line, and it is the file to name in a `#library` declaration on the consuming side, not the `.dll` itself.

# all four library backends, one target per line
x86_64-windows-msvc:  lib.obj  lib.lib   lib.dll  lib.dll.lib   lib.ll
x86_64-windows-gnu:   lib.o    liblib.a  lib.dll  liblib.dll.a  lib.ll
x86_64-linux-gnu:     lib.o    liblib.a  liblib.so             lib.ll
wasm32-wasi:          lib.o    liblib.a  liblib.wasm           lib.ll

Only `llvm`, `object`, and `static-lib` participate in the native artifact cache; a `shared-lib` or `llvm-ir` build recompiles every time. Building the same `llvm-ir` file twice therefore prints `glosso: wrote lib.ll` twice, where the object build prints `glosso: restored lib.obj from the native artifact cache` the second time. The cache itself is described in The Build Cache and Generated Sources.
Optimization levels

The size modes -Os, -Oz, and -Ozz produce runnable artifacts. They combine LLVM optimization with optsize/minsize attributes and target-specific linker size policies. Runtime checks are disabled in these modes; use -O0 or -O1 for checked builds. -Ozz also strips symbols and metadata.

rows: builds; runtime checks on; the default allocator remains the heap allocator
LLVM O2 with `optsize`; removes unused sections
LLVM O3 with `optsize` and `minsize`; folds identical code when supported
the `-Oz` size request plus stripping symbols and metadata

blocks.text: Runtime checks are configured exactly at underlying level 0 or 1. Levels 2 and 3 remove overflow, bounds, tag, and null checks, so the three size modes are configured without them. Today that distinction does not become observable program behaviour because LLVM stops before emitting the object.

The size modes -Os, -Oz, and -Ozz produce runnable artifacts. They combine LLVM optimization with optsize/minsize attributes and target-specific linker size policies. Runtime checks are disabled in these modes; use -O0 or -O1 for checked builds. -Ozz also strips symbols and metadata.
What the checks cover
Signed and unsigned integer overflow on `+`, `-`, and `*`.
Array bounds on any index into something with a known element count. A many-pointer `[*]T` has no count and is never checked.
Union tag mismatch, on the unchecked payload reads that `#enable(allow_union_unwrap)` permits.
A null address when an integer or an enum is converted to `*T`, `[*]T`, or a `#fn_ptr` type.

A failing check writes a category and terminates immediately. Arithmetic and slice failures have labels such as `arithmetic.overflow`; array bounds and union-tag failures also name their source location. Windows and Linux x86-64 use status 134, WASI uses 125, and the remaining targets use their platform `abort()` path. Runtime Safety Checks and Panics covers the complete family.

-O0    runtime check failed: arithmetic.overflow   status 134 on Windows
-O1    runtime check failed: arithmetic.overflow   status 134 on Windows
-O2    sum = -2147483648 / survived      status 0
-O3    sum = -2147483648 / survived      status 0

The wrap-around result at `-O2` is not undefined behaviour; it is the defined two's-complement result of the same instruction, with the trap removed. The bounds check behaves the same way: the read that aborts at `-O1` returns whatever the address held at `-O2`.

$ glosso -O1 -o bounds.exe bounds.glo && ./bounds.exe
in range: 20
<path>:<line>:<column>: runtime check failed: array.bounds
$ echo $?
134

$ glosso -O2 -o bounds.exe bounds.glo && ./bounds.exe
in range: 20
out of range: 0
survived

$ glosso -O1 -o unionfail.exe unionfail.glo && ./unionfail.exe
...\unionfail.glo:6:28: union access: expected .Ok, but the value holds one of .Ok | .Err
$ echo $?
134

$ glosso -O2 -o unionfail.exe unionfail.glo && ./unionfail.exe
value = 4

`4` is the length of `"nope"`: the `.Err` payload is a string descriptor, and reading it as an `s32` picks up the low half of its count field. That is the cost of the missing check stated plainly. At `-O1` the program stops at the line that is wrong; at `-O2` it continues with a value that means nothing.
`GLOSSO_DEBUG_ALLOCATOR`

Optimization no longer selects the default allocator. With `GLOSSO_DEBUG_ALLOCATOR` absent or set to `0`, every optimization level starts with the plain heap allocator. Set it to any other value to install the debug allocator, which records each allocation with its source location and prints a leak report when the process ends. The allocator itself is described in The Debug Allocator.

$ GLOSSO_DEBUG_ALLOCATOR=1 glosso -O1 -o leak.exe leak.glo && ./leak.exe
allocated
glosso debug allocator: leaked 1 allocation(s), 64 byte(s)
  leak: 64 byte(s)
    allocated at:
      ...\leak.glo:5:10

$ glosso -O0 -o leak.exe leak.glo && ./leak.exe
allocated

The environment choice is part of the native artifact-cache identity, so a cached heap build is never restored for a debug-allocator build or the reverse. The switch is independent of the runtime checks: `-O0` and `-O1` still control those exactly as the table above says.
Size optimization

The size modes -Os, -Oz, and -Ozz produce runnable artifacts. They combine LLVM optimization with optsize/minsize attributes and target-specific linker size policies. Runtime checks are disabled in these modes; use -O0 or -O1 for checked builds. -Ozz also strips symbols and metadata.

Size modes apply target-specific linker policies: dead-section removal, identical-code folding where supported, and symbol stripping at -Ozz. These modes produce artifacts with the current installed toolchain.
Nested builds select the same size modes through Optimization.Optimized_Small, Optimized_Very_Small, and Optimized_Tiny. Native_Compile_Output.compile_c_archive accepts the same Optimization enum.
A bare-metal target cannot use `-O0` or `-O1` without supplying an `abort`, because that is what a failing runtime check calls. See Freestanding, Bare Metal, UEFI, and WebAssembly.

A build is one compiler process running a fixed sequence of phases over the whole program. Each phase consumes what the phase before it produced, so every failure is reported in the vocabulary of the phase that found it: the lexer talks about characters, the parser about tokens, the checker about types, the linker about symbols.
The order is not configurable and no option skips a phase. `--backend`, `--target` and the `-O` level change what the last two phases do; everything up to Glosso IR is the same work for every build.

blocks.text: Setting the environment variable `GLOSSO_TIMINGS` to any value prints one line per phase to stderr. It is the cheapest way to see where a build spends its time, and where compile-time output falls relative to the rest of the work.

glosso: compile engines.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
glosso: timing prepare 237.568 ms
[const] evaluated during checking
[const] evaluated during checking
glosso: timing check 570.978 ms
glosso: timing lower 304.605 ms
[vm] evaluated after lowering
glosso: link engines.exe (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
glosso: done engines.exe  (backend=llvm, target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)

The transcript places the two compile-time engines. The `[const]` lines come from the constant evaluator, which folds `CONSTANT` while the checker is running, and which visits the initializer more than once. The `[vm]` line comes from the bytecode VM, which runs top-level `#comptime` exactly once after lowering and before the backend emits. What Runs When treats the difference in full.
Lexing

The lexer turns a file's bytes into tokens. It has no recovery: the first lexical error ends the build, and no diagnostic from any later phase for that file is printed beside it. The file below contains an illegal declaration name on line 1, which is a parse error, and an unterminated literal on line 2, which is a lex error. Only the second is reported.

error: unterminated string literal
  --> …\scan.glo:2:19
  |
2 | main :: () { s := "unterminated
  |                   ^^^^^^^^^^^^^
The operator prescan

Every operator in Glosso is a typeclass method carrying an `#operator` directive, so a token like `<^>` means nothing until such a declaration has been read. Parsing cannot discover the fixity as it goes, because the declaration may come after the use. Before parsing starts, the prescan records the `#operator` modes and levels in the source and its relative `#load` and `#export` dependency graph, starting with the Prelude's operator table.

The declaration sits below its own use and the expression still groups to the right: `2 <^> (3 <^> 2)` is 512. Changing both directives to `#operator(left, 17)` prints 64 instead. An operator declared in a relative `#load`ed dependency can also be used by its loader: the dependency graph is scanned before the loader's expressions are parsed. This does not make private declarations public or give one sibling module another sibling's dependencies. The Operator Prescan gives the complete rules.
Parsing and feature gates
The parser recovers. It records a diagnostic, skips to the next plausible declaration boundary and continues, so one run reports every top-level form it could not read and finishes with a count.

error: bad decl name '1'
  --> …\decls.glo:1:1
  |
1 | 1bad :: 3;
  | ^

error: a top-level constant binding uses '::'; the second ':' is missing
  --> …\decls.glo:2:5
  |
2 | Foo : struct { x: ssize; }
  |     ^

error: aborting due to 2 previous errors

Feature gates are resolved here rather than by the checker. `#enable` and `#disable` are sticky from the directive to the end of the file, and the parser stamps the gates that were active onto each declaration it builds; the checker reads the stamp back when it checks that declaration. That is why wrapping one procedure in `#enable(lossy_numerics)` relaxes conversions in that procedure alone. An unrecognised name is rejected immediately with `error: unknown feature 'bogus_feature'`. Feature Gates: `#enable` and `#disable` lists the three supported gates.
Resolution

Resolution assembles the program: it installs the compiler-owned declarations, loads `std/Prelude`, expands `#load`, resolves `#import`, applies declaration visibility, and appends the root file, producing a single declaration list with no ordering rule inside it. A module that cannot be found is reported here, as is a `#load` path that does not exist. Resolution failures do not stop the checker: both sets of diagnostics are printed in one batch sorted by line and column, so a file with one bad import and one bad conversion reports both and ends with `error: aborting due to 2 previous errors`. Source Files, Imports, and Loads covers what resolution accepts.
Checking and monomorphization

Checking gives every expression a type, selects a typeclass instance for every operator and method call, and checks each generic body once per instantiation. A generic declaration on its own proves nothing: the body is checked against the types it is actually called with, which is why the diagnostic points into the generic body while the reason for it is at the call site.

error: no operator '+' for Pair, Pair
  --> …\twice.glo:5:34
  |
5 | twice :: (x: $T) -> T { return x + x; }
  |                                  ^
A `where` clause moves the check back to the call and names the callee instead: `error: constraint failed for double`. Constraints with `where` explains when to prefer one over the other.
Compile-time execution

Compile-time code runs in two places. Values, which means `X :: #comptime f()`, `#comptime` parameters, `#if`, `#assert` and `#insert`, are produced by the constant evaluator during checking. A top-level `#comptime` block or call is lowered to an IR function and executed by the bytecode VM after lowering, once each and in declaration order, whichever backend was selected.

A VM failure ends the build with the phase named in the message, for example `error: #comptime stopped: VM: unknown #magic intrinsic 'ctx_alloc'`. Calling `exit(n)` from compile time is the one path that hands an arbitrary status to the shell: the compiler stops after this phase, writes no artifact, and exits with `n`.
Lowering, emission, and linking

Lowering turns checked declarations into Glosso IR, and rejects the constructs that survive checking but have no runtime form, such as `error: recursive call to lazy function 'rec' is not supported`. Backend emission then translates IR into an LLVM module; an unregistered intrinsic fails here with `error: native LLVM lowering has no classification for #magic 'no_such_intrinsic'`. The linker is last and speaks only about symbols, which is why a file with no `main` compiles without complaint and then fails.

glosso: compile helper.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
glosso: link helper.exe (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
error: lld-link: error: undefined symbol: wmain
>>> referenced by exe_common.inl:90
>>>               msvcrt.lib(exe_wmain.obj):(int __cdecl invoke_main(void))
Reading a diagnostic by its phase

Matching a message to the phase that produced it says what the compiler already knew when it complained, and therefore what can and cannot be the cause. Every message below is real output from this compiler.

blocks.text: A Glosso source file is a flat sequence of top-level declarations with no ordering rule. `main` may call a procedure declared below it, a type may be used above its declaration, and `#import` and `#load` may sit anywhere in the file, including on the last line.
manhattan = 7

The resolver assembles declarations before ordinary name checking, so forward references in one module work. Each dependency still has its own imports and visibility. Module-level `#if` selects declarations using compile-time conditions; those conditions need already available imports. Top-level `#comptime` steps retain their declaration order.
`#import` and `#load` are declarations, not statements. Written inside a procedure body, `#import "Io";` is `error: unexpected directive 'import'`.
`#import`

`#import` names a module in the standard-library search path and brings its public declarations into the importing file. Five forms are accepted. `only` and `hide` are the only modifiers; anything else is `error: #import modifier must be only or hide`.

rows: Public names enter the importing file's scope unqualified.
Names are reachable through the namespace, such as `M.S32_MAX`.
Exactly the listed public names enter scope.
Everything except the listed names enters scope.

blocks.text: qualified=1 selected=1

A name in an `only` or `hide` list must be a public module-level declaration. A typeclass method is not one, so `#import,only(sqrt) "Math/Core";` fails with `error: #import,only names unknown public declaration 'sqrt' in module "Math/Core"` followed by a `note: public names:` list of what is selectable. Repeating a name is `error: duplicate name 'print' in #import,only`. An empty list, `#import,only() "Io";`, is legal and imports nothing at all.

`hide` removes the selected declaration from this import's unqualified surface. Repeating an import is harmless. Visibility controls selection, not a name's spelling: an explicitly public `_helper` can be named in `only` and `hide`, while a private declaration cannot.

Use the explicit `Math/Core` module name for scalar mathematics and `Math/Constants` for constants. A `Math` compatibility shorthand exists only in full-standard-library conformance mode; ordinary source imports should name the component directly.
How a module name resolves

A module name is a path with `/` separators. It is validated first: `..`, backslashes, absolute paths and empty components are rejected by `error: invalid standard module name`, which then quotes the spelling it refused. The resolver looks for two things in the standard-library directory.

rows: That one file is the module.
That entry file is the module; its `#export` directives select its public components.
`error: cannot find module "Name" (searched: <roots>)`, where the roots are the standard-library directory followed by every `--module-path` directory

blocks.text: Only `module.glo` is loaded automatically. It normally contains `#export "Component.glo";` directives that assemble an umbrella module. A sibling file is included only through an explicit dependency. Nested modules can be named by path or reexported by their parent.

Both shapes coexist in the standard library, and a name may have a file and a same-named directory without being ambiguous when the directory has no `module.glo`. `std/Io.glo` and `std/Io/` are that shape, so `#import "Io"` resolves to the file. `std/File_System/` now has neither a sibling `File_System.glo` nor a marker: it is a namespace only, and each component is imported by its full path.
exists = 1
Namespace-only directories

A directory without `module.glo` is a namespace, not a module. `#import "Container";` is `error: cannot find module "Container" (searched: <std>)`, which lists the standard-library root and every `--module-path` directory. Its contents are imported one component at a time, by path. The six are `Container`, `Crypto`, `File_System`, `Math`, `Net`, and `Serialization`. `Strings` has an umbrella entry point exporting `Memory`, `Utf8`, and `Utf16`.
comp

The same path form also names one file of a real module, so `#import "Io/Core";` imports a single component of the `Io` directory. Each component declares its own dependencies. Umbrella modules expose the components their `#export` directives select; importing a component directly exposes that component's public declarations and reexports.
`#load`

`#load` loads an isolated module by file path. The path is relative to the file containing the directive, not the working directory, and may contain `..`. Public declarations become available in the loading file; an alias makes them available through a namespace. The loaded file resolves names using its own explicit dependencies.
manhattan = 1
Each distinct path is loaded once; a repeated `#load` of the same path is a no-op rather than a redeclaration error.
With an alias the names are reachable only through it: writing `Point` alone gives `error: unknown type 'Point'`.
A missing file is `error: #load: cannot find file "parts/nope.glo" (looked for <absolute path>)`, and the absolute path the compiler tried is printed in full.

Dependencies stay local: loading a helper that imports `Io` does not make `print` available to the caller. The helper also cannot use a dependency loaded only by its caller or by another sibling module.
Declarations are private by default. A loaded file must mark its API `#public`, or use `#public(unit)` for callers in the same ownership unit. Visibility and Ownership Units explains both audiences.

The operator prescan follows relative `#load` and `#export` dependencies, including embedded loads, before parsing expressions. The loader can therefore use an operator declared by its loaded module. Ordinary module visibility still governs whether the owning typeclass and implementation can be used; a spelling in the parser's table is not an implicit import.
`#export`: umbrella modules

`#export "path";` loads a relative module and exposes its public declarations to this module's users. If `A.glo` exports `B.glo`, a file that loads `A.glo` can use `B.glo` too. Reexports are transitive; ordinary loads and imports inside a dependency remain local.
`#load,embed`: shared source fragments

`#load,embed "path";` places a source fragment in its containing logical module and shares the module's dependencies. Each fragment retains its physical source identity, so cross-file declarations still need `#public(unit)` or `#public`. This manual uses unit-visible chapter and UI fragments. Nested paths remain relative to the directive's physical file.

Every compilation begins with names already in scope. Nothing in the program declares them and no import produces them. They arrive in three layers, in this order: type spellings the parser recognises, declarations the compiler injects, and the thirteen public components of `std/Prelude`.
The Prelude is loaded unqualified for every program, before any `#import` in the program is resolved. It is the only module treated this way, and it cannot be turned off.
Built-in type names
A fixed set of names, the `Simd` and `Matrix` type constructors, and two declaration-annotation forms are recognised by the compiler itself. They are not library declarations and need no import.

`ssize` and `usize` are signed and unsigned pointer-width integers: 32 bits on a 32-bit output target and 64 bits on a 64-bit one. An integer literal with no other context defaults to `ssize`; collection counts and indices use it too. The checker additionally accepts `sN` and `uN` for every unpadded decimal width `N` from 1 through 65535. `rune` is a Unicode scalar in four bytes, distinct from integers. An ASCII `#char` literal defaults to `u8`, while a non-ASCII literal defaults to `rune`; there is no built-in `char` type. Primitive Types covers the full primitive set and its representations. `Typeclass(...)` and `Macro(...)` describe explicitly typed declarations; they are not general-purpose type-value constructors.
Declarations the compiler injects

Before the Prelude is read the compiler installs two source fragments of its own, under the pseudo-paths `<builtin:Types>` and `<builtin:Context>`. The first declares the two unions that `?T` and `E!T` resolve to.

Those names are internal and the parser rejects them wherever a program could write one: `Option(ssize)` is `error: the built-in option type is written '?T'; its variants are '.Some(x)' and '.None'`, and `Result(string, ssize)` is `error: the built-in result type is written 'E!T'; its variants are '.Ok(x)' and '.Err(e)'`. They are built in rather than declared in `std` so that a program cannot reshape the type that `?`, `#try` and pattern lowering resolve to. `std/Prelude/Option.glo` and `std/Prelude/Result.glo` supply everything else about them.
The second fragment declares the implicit context's type. Its spelling carries the `#`: a parameter typed `Context` is `error: the built-in Context type is written #Context`.
user_index = 0

The struct is always in scope but its field types are gated. Naming `Allocator`, `Logger` or `Random_Generator` in a program that has not imported `Context` gives `error: 'Allocator' is a #Context field type`, and the rest of the message asks for `#import "Context";`. The Implicit Context and Allocators cover what the fields do.
The thirteen Prelude components
`std/Prelude/module.glo` explicitly assembles the Prelude. Everything its public components declare is in scope for every program.

The default, integer-radix, and character `Formatter` instances. The `Formatter` protocol itself lives in `Format`.
The operator typeclasses and their primitive instances, plus `Indexable`, `Step`, the range classes, and `ToPattern`.
`Try`, `Try_Branch`, and `Propagate`, the protocols behind postfix `?` and residual conversion.
`Termination(T)`, which converts a value returned by `main` into a process status.
`Asm_Constraint`, `Asm_Operand_Flags`, `Asm_Clobber`, the vocabulary `#asm` operands are written in.

The operator typeclasses

Every operator in the language is a method of a typeclass declared in `Primitive_Operators.glo` or `Primitive_Typeclasses.glo`, with its fixity and precedence written on the requirement. That is what the operator prescan reads out of the Prelude, and it is why `a + b` needs no import while a library's own operator does.

rows: `AddAssign` and the rest of the assign family

blocks.text: The wrapping and saturating families (`WrapAdd`, `SaturatingMul` and their assigning forms) follow the same shape, and `Indexable` and `IndexSet` own `[]` and `[]=` without a precedence. The Operator System and Operator Precedence and the 0-20 Scale give the complete table.
`LogicalAnd` and `LogicalOr` declare their right operand `#lazy`, which is the whole mechanism behind short-circuiting `&&` and `||`; Lazy Parameters and Short-Circuit Operators explains it.
The command line and exit
`Utilities.glo` also supplies the two process-level procedures every program can reach without an import.

get_cmdline_args :: () -> []string #magic "get_cmdline_args"
exit :: (status: ssize) -> #Never #magic "exit";

`get_cmdline_args` returns the process argument vector at run time, including the program path at index 0. During compile-time execution it returns the arguments written after `--` on the compiler's own command line, without a leading program path. `exit` ends the process, and called from a top-level `#comptime` it ends the build with that status and writes no artifact.
What is not in the Prelude

`print` is not. It belongs to `Io`, so the smallest program that writes anything needs one import. The help text points at `tprint`, which is no more in scope: it belongs to `Format`, which the Prelude imports for itself, and naming it takes `#import "Format";`.
main :: () { print("hello from glosso\n"); }

error: unknown function print
  --> …\hello.glo:1:14
  |
1 | main :: () { print("hello from glosso\n"); }
  |              ^^^^^
help: did you mean 'tprint'?

Numeric constants are not supplied by the Prelude. `PI`, `S64_MAX`, `F64_MAX`, and the other numeric limits belong to `Math/Constants`. Import that component directly; a dependency's private import does not bring its names into the caller's scope.
