blocks.text: A source file is a sequence of bytes that the compiler reads as UTF-8 text, and nothing else is accepted. A root file whose bytes are not valid UTF-8 is rejected before lexing begins, with `glosso: cannot read` followed by the file name; a file reached through `#load` fails with `could not read`, the path, and `stream did not contain valid UTF-8`. An encoding mistake is therefore always a read failure, never a stray token halfway down the file.

Past that point the scanner works on decoded code points rather than bytes. The line, column and length recorded on every token are counted in code points from the start of the line, which is what keeps a caret span the same width as the token it underlines when the line holds non-Latin text.

That program fails with `error: unbound 'oops'`, reported at `3:17`. Column 17 counts the sixteen code points before `oops`; a byte count would have said 24, because `λ`, `μ` and `ν` occupy two bytes each and `안` and `녕` occupy three.
Whitespace
Exactly four code points are skipped as whitespace. The scanner tests for them before anything else, and only for them.

rows: Ends the line and advances the line counter.
Skipped, which is why a CRLF file lexes exactly like an LF file.
Skipped, and counted as a single column.

blocks.text: Nothing else is whitespace. Any other code point falls through to token dispatch, and one that starts no token becomes a stray-character error whose entire message is the offending character in single quotes. Three invisible characters reach that path often enough to be worth naming.

rows: `error: ''`, with the byte-order mark itself between the quotes, so nothing is visible
A form feed used as a page break
`error: ' '`, which looks exactly like a space

blocks.text: A byte-order mark sits at 1:1, so a BOM-prefixed file does not compile at all: the first thing the scanner sees is a character it cannot use. An editor that offers both `UTF-8 with BOM` and `UTF-8` produces a working file only with the second.

Because a carriage return is whitespace, line endings do not matter to ordinary tokens. Marked multi-line-string lines follow the same rule: their scanner removes a trailing carriage return before storing the line, so LF and CRLF source files produce the same literal text.
Line comments
`//` begins a comment that runs to the next newline, or to the end of input if there is none. Everything after it on that line is invisible to the scanner, including quotes, `/*` and `*/`.

Comments are recognised before token dispatch, so a `/` immediately followed by `/` or by `*` can never begin an operator. A library may declare an operator named with those characters, but no use site can ever spell it; see Reserved Operators and Operator Names.
Block comments

`/*` opens a comment that `*/` closes, and the pair nests. The scanner keeps a depth counter rather than searching for the first `*/`, so a region that already contains comments can be commented out as a whole.

x = 3
[http://example.com /* not a comment */]

Two further facts are visible there. A newline inside a block comment still advances the line counter, so diagnostics after a large commented-out region report the right line. An unterminated `/*` is a lexical error instead: the scanner reports `error: unterminated block comment` at the opening delimiter rather than emitting end-of-input.

The depth counter reacts to `/*` and `*/` everywhere inside the comment, including inside text that looks like a string literal. A comment is scanned as characters, not as tokens, so nothing protects a `*/` written between quotes.

The comment ends at the `*/` inside the quotes. What remains of the line opens a string literal that no quote closes, and the file fails with `error: unterminated string literal`, underlining from that quote to the end of the line.
A `/*` written inside a `//` comment opens nothing; the line comment already owns the rest of the line.
A `//` written inside a block comment does not close it, and neither does a newline.
A `/*` or `*/` written inside a string literal is ordinary text: the scanner looks for comments only where a token could start.
Reading a source position

`#source_location` is an expression whose value has the Prelude type `Source_Location`. It records the position of its own `#` token, with one-based `line` and `column` fields. Columns count Unicode scalars, not UTF-8 bytes, display cells, or tab stops: a tab is one column and a combining mark is another scalar. Comments and whitespace before the directive still contribute to its position.

The `filename` field is the compiler's source path, absolute for loaded source files, or `<unknown>` when no filename is available. On Windows the compiler removes extended-length path prefixes for editor-friendly diagnostics; a path's backslashes remain literal characters, not string escapes. The chapter `#assert` and `#compile_error` shows how to print and pass these values without losing their origin.
An identifier begins with `_` or an alphabetic code point, and continues with `_` or an alphanumeric one. There is no length limit and no restriction to ASCII.

The two classes come from Unicode tables generated into the compiler and built to match CPython's single-character `str.isalpha` and `str.isalnum`. Carrying the tables rather than borrowing the host language's own predicates means the accepted identifier set does not shift when the toolchain that built the compiler updates its Unicode version.

`isalnum` is the union of the alphabetic, decimal, digit and numeric classes, so it is strictly wider than `isalpha`. Some code points can therefore continue an identifier without being able to start one.

`λ`, `Ω` and `Δθ` are Greek letters and `안녕` is Hangul; all are alphabetic and may start a name. `ᵃ` is a modifier letter, which is alphabetic too. `a²` ends in a superscript two, which is a digit but not a letter, so it may appear only after the first character.
Marks, emoji, and superscripts
A combining mark belongs to neither class. An identifier written in decomposed form therefore ends at its base letter, and the mark that follows becomes a stray character.

With `é` written as `e` plus U+0301 that file fails, and the stray-character message quotes the combining mark, which renders on top of whatever precedes it. With `é` written precomposed as U+00E9 the same source compiles: one alphabetic code point, one identifier. No normalisation is performed in either direction, so the two spellings are simply different source text.
Emoji are not alphabetic, and there is no separate rule for them. `🙂 := 1;` fails with `error: '🙂'`, the ordinary stray-character message.

Superscripts and other non-decimal digits satisfy `isalnum` but not `isalpha`. Inside an identifier they are accepted; at the start they do not produce an identifier at all, because the scanner dispatches on the digit class and begins a number. A leading `²` therefore fails with `error: number literals must use ASCII digits`.

There is no diagnostic saying an identifier cannot start with a digit, because no such rule exists at the token level. `2abc := 1;` lexes as the integer `2` followed by the identifier `abc`. The parser reads `2` as the start of an expression statement, then requires its `;` and reports `error: unexpected token 'abc'` immediately.

error: unexpected token 'abc'
  --> digit-name.glo:4:6
  |
4 |     2abc := 1;
  |      ^^^
The keywords
Nineteen words are reserved. The scanner reads a whole word first and then looks it up, so a word is a keyword only when it is the entire identifier.

Every one of them is rejected as a binding name, though the wording depends on where the parser gives up: `if := 1;` is `error: unexpected token ':='`, `struct := 1;` is `error: unexpected token 'struct'`, and `cast := 1;` is `error: cast requires a type in parentheses; use acast for contextual casts`.
Whole-word matching means a longer word that merely begins or ends with a keyword is an ordinary identifier.
Words that only look reserved

`typeclass`, `instance`, `distinct`, `type`, `ssize` and `string` are plain identifier tokens. Their meaning comes from the position they appear in, which is why each of them can also be bound as a local.
`distinct` is the clearest case: it is recognised only directly after `::` in type position, so one file can declare a nominal type and also bind a local of that name.

`true`, `false` and `null` are not keyword tokens either, but the parser resolves those spellings to literals wherever an expression is expected. A local named `true` can be declared and then never read: the program below binds `false` to `2` and still prints the boolean, which shows as `0`.
`_` on its own is a legal identifier and binds like any other name. Its separate role in patterns is described in The Pattern Vocabulary.
Identifier comparison is exact: neither case folding nor Unicode normalisation is applied to a name before it is looked up.
A decimal integer literal is a run of ASCII digits with optional `_` separators. The separators carry no meaning; they are removed before the value is parsed.

A run of digits may not be empty, may not begin or end with `_`, and may not contain two adjacent separators. That rule is applied independently to four different parts of a number, each with its own message, so the diagnostic names the part that is malformed.

Because the parts are checked separately, a separator next to a `.` or an `e` is legal on both sides: `1_0.2_5` and `1_000e1_0` are accepted. A leading `_` is not a number error at all, since `_1` starts an identifier; that spelling fails later with `error: unbound '_1'`.
Explicit base

A non-decimal integer is written as a base, a `#`, and digits. The base is a decimal number between 2 and 36, and the digits are `0` to `9` and `a` to `z` read case-insensitively. Both the base and the digits may carry `_` separators.

One spelling covers every radix, which is why there is no separate hexadecimal or binary prefix to remember and why base 36 costs nothing extra. The base is scanned as a number in its own right, so `1_6#ff` is the same literal as `16#ff`.

rows: `integer literal base must be between 2 and 36, got 1`
`integer literal base must be between 2 and 36, got 37`
`base-16 integer literal needs at least one digit`

blocks.text: The last row is the one that surprises. The `#` is absorbed by the number scanner only when it immediately follows the digits. With a space in between, `16` is a complete integer literal and `#ff` is an ordinary directive token, which the parser then rejects by name.
A based literal is a bit pattern

A based literal is recorded as a bit pattern rather than as a magnitude, and the checker measures it against the width of the target type instead of against that type's signed range. A mask is written for its bits, so `16#ff` is a legal `s8` and denotes `-1` there.

The relaxation is about width, not about range: a pattern wider than the target is still rejected. `a : s8 = 16#1ff;` gives `error: 511 does not fit s8, whose range is -128..=127` with the note `a based literal is a bit pattern, so it may use every bit of s8 - this one is wider than that`. A decimal `255` at `s8` is rejected as well, since it never had the exemption.

A leading `-` withdraws the exemption, because writing a sign says the literal is meant as a magnitude again. `a : s8 = -16#ff;` gives `error: -255 does not fit s8, whose range is -128..=127`, while `a : s8 = -16#7f;` is the ordinary `-127`.
Decimal integers have arbitrary precision

A decimal integer token has no 128-bit ceiling. While its type is still undecided it is a `comptime_int`; if its magnitude is too large for the token's 128-bit payload, the lexer keeps the separator-free digits and the checker materialises the exact value as a `BigInt`. A destination such as `u129` can therefore receive a decimal value above `u128` with no truncation.

Context still performs the ordinary exact fitting check. A decimal value that is outside its destination reports `does not fit T, whose range is ...`; it is not a lexical error. For example, changing `direct` above to `u128` reports that its exact value does not fit the `u128` range. Based literals are different: they are stored as bit patterns, and that representation remains limited to 128 bits. For example, `16#1_0000_0000_0000_0000_0000_0000_0000_0000` reports `error: base-16 integer literal does not fit in 128 bits`, even with a `u129` destination. Write the value in decimal when more than 128 bits are required.

The remaining 128-bit limit belongs to compile-time VM execution, not to decimal literals, constant folding, or native code. A top-level `#comptime { ... }` step that tries to execute arithmetic on `u129` reports `compile-time execution does not support u129, an integer wider than 128 bits`. Foldable `#comptime` constants such as `FOLD` above and compiled `u129` arithmetic remain exact.
Rejected spellings

The C prefixes are not merely unsupported; they are detected and named, so a constant copied out of a C header fails with an instruction rather than with a confusing split into a zero and an identifier.

rows: `legacy '0x' integer literals are not supported; use '16#digits'`
`legacy '0b' integer literals are not supported; use '2#digits'`

blocks.text: Both letter cases are caught, for both prefixes. There is no `0o` case, so an octal constant in the C spelling does split: `0o7` lexes as the integer `0` followed by the identifier `o7`, and fails with `error: unbound 'o7'`.
A number token becomes a float when either of two shapes appears, and one literal may use both at once.
A `.` followed by at least one digit, which opens the fraction: `1.25`, `1_234.333_333`.
An `e` or `E`, optionally followed by `+` or `-`, followed by at least one digit: `1e3`, `1E10`, `1e+2`, `1.2e-3`.

The exponent is looked for whether or not a fraction was seen, so an integer-looking literal with an exponent is still a float. `_` separators are allowed in the integer part, the fraction and the exponent digits, under the same rules and with the same per-part diagnostics given in Integer Literals.
Anything outside those two shapes is not a float literal. The four spellings below all look like numbers and none of them is one.

rows: `error: float literal '1.' needs a digit after the '.'; write '1.0'`
`1`, then `.`, then the name `e3`: `error: member of non-struct`
An exponent with no digits: `error: scientific number literal needs exponent digits after 'e' or 'E'`

blocks.text: Requiring a digit on each side of the `.` is what keeps a dot next to a number unambiguous. `.` is member access, `..` is a range and `.*` is a dereference, so a fraction allowed to start or end with nothing would collide with all three.
Literal precision and expected types

The scanner strips the separators and parses the remaining text once, at double precision. The token also keeps its source digits, and a literal with no annotation defaults to `f64`: `x := 1.5;` followed by `y : string = x;` reports `error: got f64, expected string`.

For `f16` and `f32`, the checker rounds those original digits directly to the expected format, avoiding a second rounding through `f64`. A literal that overflows that format or rounds a nonzero value to zero is rejected. A wider annotation still changes where the value lands, not how it was read: An `f80` or `f128` literal has already been rounded to double precision by the time the type is known, so digits beyond roughly the seventeenth are gone before the annotation is ever consulted.

f80  literal == 1.0: 1
f128 literal == 1.0: 1
Both comparisons are true. `f80` and `f128` are real storage widths with real arithmetic; only the literal is limited, and a constant more precise than a double cannot be written down as one token.
The lexer's `f64` range check

Every float token is parsed as `f64` before an expected type is applied. The scanner rejects a non-finite result, and it also rejects a nonzero mantissa that underflows to zero. This check is lexical, so an `f80` or `f128` annotation cannot make a token outside the host `f64` range legal.

rows: `error: float literal '1e400' is out of range for f64`
`error: float literal '1e-400' is out of range for f64`
Zero; its mantissa was already zero

blocks.text: That token check is separate from conversion to a narrower destination. A value that is finite as `f64` can still overflow or underflow when the annotation narrows it. For example, `x : f16 = 100000.0;` is accepted and stores positive infinity because `f16` stops at 65504.

The range check concerns the token's `f64` payload, not the eventual storage width. It prevents a literal itself from silently becoming infinity or nonzero-to-zero during lexing; it does not add a general checked float-conversion rule.

A float literal never reaches an integer target. `x : s64 = 1.5;` is `error: cannot implicitly convert comptime_float to s64`, and `x : u8 = 1.0;` is `error: cannot implicitly convert comptime_float to u8` even though the value is whole. That rule and its escape hatches are in Conversions: What Is Implicit.

A string literal is written between double quotes. The scanner walks forward to the closing quote, stepping two characters over any backslash pair so that an escaped quote does not end the literal. It then validates every escape and stores the raw source text found between the quotes.

Decoding is deferred: the stored text still holds the backslashes as written, and escapes become characters later, when the literal turns into a value. Validation is not deferred. An unknown escape, a malformed hexadecimal escape, or an invalid Unicode scalar is a lexical error.
The escape table

rows: U+0000; retained by a counted string, but terminates a C-string view
The code point U+00HH; exactly two hexadecimal digits
One Unicode scalar; one to six hexadecimal digits
Nothing; the backslash and the per-cent sign both survive

blocks.text: The table is closed. `\x` requires exactly two hexadecimal digits. `\u` requires braces, one to six hexadecimal digits, and a value that is a Unicode scalar rather than a surrogate or a value above U+10FFFF. Every other character after a backslash is rejected by name.
`\xHH` and `\u{...}` write code points, not bytes

The hexadecimal digits name a code point, not a storage byte. The character they select is then stored in the string's UTF-8 encoding, so an escape above `\x7f` may occupy several bytes and `.count`, which counts bytes, reports the encoded length.

ascii count 2 bytes 65 127
high  count 2 bytes 195 191

`\xff` is U+00FF encoded as the two bytes 195 and 191, not the single byte 255. An ordinary string literal produces valid UTF-8. To write arbitrary bytes, use a byte-array literal such as `b"\xff"`, whose hexadecimal escape contributes the single byte 255.
`\%` and the runtime formatter
`%` is the placeholder in a format string, so a literal per-cent sign written in a format is counted as a placeholder and the call fails.
error: print: format has 1 '%' placeholder(s) but 0 argument(s) given

`\%` is the answer, and it is the one escape the decoder deliberately leaves alone: both characters survive into the stored value. What turns them into a single `%` is the runtime formatter, which recognises `\%` while scanning the format and emits a per-cent sign without consuming an argument.

100% done
[pct=\%]
The second line shows the division of labour. That `\%` sits in an argument rather than in the format, nothing scans it as a format, and both characters print.
Line breaks and termination

A literal may span physical lines. The newline is part of the text, and the line counter is corrected afterwards so that later diagnostics still report the right line. A backslash immediately before a physical newline is an explicitly accepted escape: decoding drops the backslash and keeps the newline, so it is not a line continuation.

Both strings are three bytes long and both carry a line feed, byte 10, in the middle. A literal with no closing quote is an error rather than a run to end of file: `s := "abc;` alone on its line gives `error: unterminated string literal`, underlining from the opening quote to the end of the line.
The four string types

One literal syntax serves all four built-in string types; the annotation decides which is built, and whether a terminating NUL and a UTF-16 re-encoding are added. `.count` is the element count in every case and never includes a terminator.

All four string types support the default `%` rendering through `Show`. The C forms stop at their first zero unit; counted strings keep an explicit length, including any embedded zeros. Their view layouts and storage lifetimes are covered in Built-in Strings.
C-string and byte-array literals

The adjacent lowercase prefix `c` makes a UTF-8 C-string literal: `c"hello"` has type `cstring` without an annotation. Its static storage has a trailing zero and is borrowed; never free it. An embedded zero ends its visible length. The prefix fixes the type: it does not adapt to `cstring16`. Use `cast(string)` to make a counted view of its visible bytes, or use an ordinary literal for contextual UTF-16 conversion.

The prefix `b` instead makes a fixed `[N]u8` array, with no added terminator. Text and Unicode escapes are encoded as UTF-8, while each `\xNN` contributes exactly one byte. A local array can be modified; copying it copies its bytes. `b""` has type `[0]u8`. The element type stays `u8`, and an explicit length must match. `[_]u8` infers the length from the initializer; `[*]u8` remains a many-pointer type.

C: cstring count=1 terminator=0
bytes: [4]u8 count=4 values=65 169 255 0
copy first=195 empty count=0

The prefix must be one lowercase letter immediately before the quote. `c "text"`, `B"text"`, and `name"text"` are an identifier followed by an ordinary string, not prefixed literals. Both prefixed forms use the same escape validation as ordinary strings.

`#string` builds a string literal out of a run of marked lines. Each line of the block begins with the marker `\\`, and everything after those two backslashes, to the end of that line, is captured. The directive collects every consecutive marked line and joins them into one literal.

[alpha
beta] count=10

The marker is a token in its own right, produced by the scanner wherever two backslashes appear. A single backslash is not a token at all: it is the stray-character error `error: '\'`. A marked line is consumed only by `#string` and by the structured form of `#asm`, described in the assembly chapter; anywhere else the parser reports the captured text as the offending token, so a stray `bare := \\line one` gives `error: unexpected token 'line one'`.
What the marker captures

Capture starts immediately after the second backslash and stops at the newline, which is not part of the text. Whitespace before the marker is ordinary whitespace and is discarded, so a block can be indented to match its surroundings without changing its value. Whitespace after the marker is text. Nothing inside the captured span is interpreted: quotation marks, backslashes, `//` and `/* */` are all ordinary characters.
Indentation written before the marker positions the block in the source and never reaches the string; indentation written after the marker does reach it.
A marked line with no text after the marker contributes an empty line.

Comments are removed before the directive sees the token stream, so a `//` or `/* */` comment written between two marked lines does not interrupt the run: the lines on either side still join into one literal.
No escape decoding runs unless `,escape` is given, so a `\t` written after a marker is a backslash followed by the letter `t`, two characters.

INDENTED   [    four spaces survive
next] count=28
VERBATIM   [he said "hi" // not a comment /* nor this */ \n \t \\] count=53
WITH_BLANK [a

b] count=4
COMMENTED  [alpha
beta] count=10

Because capture runs to the end of the line, the semicolon that ends the declaration must sit on a line of its own. `SAME :: #string \\text ;` is a legal declaration whose value is the six characters `text ;`, not a two-word string.
The joining rule

The consecutive marked lines are collected in source order and joined with a single separator: a newline by default, a single space under `,oneline`. The separator goes between lines only, so a block never ends with one. At least one marked line is required; `V :: #string;` reports the error below.
error: #string expects one or more '\\' lines
`#string` is an expression, not only a declaration form, so a block may appear anywhere a string is expected: a local initialiser, an argument, a struct field.
The two modifiers

Two modifiers exist and no others. They are written as comma-separated identifiers directly after the directive, may be given in either order, and may each be given at most once. `,oneline` changes the separator from a newline to a single space. `,escape` changes how the joined text is stored: without it the text is already final and backslashes stay literal, with it the escape decoder described in the chapter on string literals is applied to the joined text.

Marked `#string` lines are tokenized separately and do not pass through the quoted-literal escape validator. Use the documented escape forms with `,escape`; malformed and unknown sequences are not guaranteed the same clean lexical diagnostics as an ordinary quoted string.

The four forms differ on exactly two axes, so the same two marked lines produce four different strings. This program reports each result by length and by the byte codes at offsets three, four and five, which is where the two axes show up.

RAW                   count=9 bytes 3..5 = 92 116 10
ONELINE               count=9 bytes 3..5 = 92 116 32
ESCAPED               count=8 bytes 3..5 = 9 10 102
ESCAPE + ONELINE      count=8 bytes 3..5 = 9 32 102

Byte 3 is `92` and byte 4 is `116` in the two undecoded forms: a backslash and a `t`, nine characters in all. Under `,escape` the pair has become the single tab `9` and the string is one character shorter. Byte 5 shows the separator: `10` is the newline of the default join, `32` the space of `,oneline`.
Under `,oneline` a blank marked line still contributes a segment, so the three lines `a`, empty, `b` join as `a  b`, four characters with two spaces.
`,escape` decodes escapes written inside the captured text; it has no effect on the marker, which is consumed by the scanner before any of the text exists.

`\%` survives escape decoding as the two characters `\` and `%`, in a marked block exactly as in a quoted literal, because it is the runtime formatter and not the lexer that turns it into a per-cent sign.
That last rule is why an undecoded block still works as a `print` format. The block below carries a literal `\%` and a `%` placeholder, and both behave as they would in a quoted format string.

raw format: 100% and a value 7
[an expression, not only a declaration, joined across two marked lines]
Modifier errors
An identifier after the comma that is neither `oneline` nor `escape` is rejected by name, and so is a repeat of either one. Both diagnostics quote the modifier back.

V :: #string,wrapped
error: unknown #string modifier 'wrapped'; expected 'oneline' or 'escape'

V :: #string,oneline,oneline
error: duplicate #string modifier 'oneline'

V :: #string,escape,escape
error: duplicate #string modifier 'escape'
Capture excludes the line ending. When the scanner finds LF it also removes a CR immediately before it, so a two-line `alpha` / `beta` block has `count == 10` in both LF and CRLF source files.

`#char` writes one character value. The scanner handles the form inside directive scanning and emits a marked integer token; the parser keeps that marker, and the checker defaults ASCII literals to `u8` and other literals to `rune`. The old `char` type has been removed; `#char` remains the spelling of the literal directive.

A      = 65 (u8)
lambda = 955 (rune)
contextual A = 65 (rune)

The form is the directive, then optional spaces and tabs, then a quoted string holding exactly one direct code point, one fixed two-character escape, one exact `\xHH` escape, or one `\u{...}` scalar escape. The separator may be empty, so `#char"A"` is the same literal as `#char "A"`. It may not contain a newline: a string on the following line is `error: #char expects a string literal`.
Bytes and Unicode scalars

`u8` is an ordinary integer byte; `rune` is a four-byte Unicode scalar. Only `rune` is outside `Is_Integer` and `Is_Numeric`: it has equality and ordering but no arithmetic, bitwise, shift, integer-range, or SIMD-lane operations. Direct string indexing yields `u8` or `u16` code units. An ASCII `#char` literal compares directly with a byte; a UTF-8 character above ASCII may occupy several bytes.

first is h: 1
second is a digit: 1
char_to_rune(A): 65
The accepted escapes

The scanner decodes the escape itself rather than deferring to the string machinery, so `#char` has its own closed table. It uses the fixed C escapes, an exact two-digit hexadecimal form, and a Unicode scalar form with one to six hexadecimal digits inside braces.

rows: one to six hexadecimal digits; no surrogates or values above U+10FFFF

blocks.text:
a=7 b=8 f=12 n=10 r=13 t=9 v=11
0=0 backslash=92 quote=34 apostrophe=39 question=63 hex=65
unicode=128512

An escape outside the table is rejected instead of dropping its backslash. Thus `#char "\q"` reports `error: unknown #char escape '\q'`. Escaping a direct non-ASCII character is rejected too rather than truncating the code point.

`\xHH` requires exactly two hexadecimal digits. `\u{...}` accepts one to six hexadecimal digits and must name a Unicode scalar, excluding surrogates and values above U+10FFFF. A non-ASCII result has type `rune`, just as if that code point had been written directly.
A code point above ASCII is written directly instead: `#char "λ"` has scalar value `955`, because the source is decoded to code points before the scan and the literal takes one of them.
The synthesised type

Left alone, an ASCII `#char` synthesises as `u8`; every other code point synthesises as `rune`. Context can select `s8` or `rune` for an ASCII literal. Untyped constants preserve that literal choice, but a stored byte does not: use `u8.char_to_rune` or an explicit cast to widen a byte variable. Where several overloads match an ASCII literal, `u8` is preferred to `s8`, and `s8` to `rune`.

The contextual list is closed: other integer targets are refused even when their representation is wide enough. Low-level conversion remains explicit: `cast(u8)(#char "A")` is `65`, and `cast(u32)(#char "λ")` is `955`. Conversely, an integer cast can forge a `rune` outside its scalar domain, so validate external data before casting. `%c` renders bytes or runes as UTF-8; bare `%` renders their decimal value.

The scanner produces tokens of a fixed set of kinds. Punctuation and operators are drawn from the same eighteen characters, and which one a run of those characters becomes is decided by a table of special cases first and a maximal-munch rule afterwards. Every spelling in the punctuation table below is a token kind of its own, which is why none of them can be redeclared as an operator.
The punctuation table

The middle column names the token kind the scanner emits. Some of these spellings, including `.*`, `.&`, `?`, and `@`, are operator tokens rather than dedicated kinds, but they are punctuation in practice and are listed here with the rest.

rows: statement and declaration terminator; grammar delimiter
pointer dereference, written after the pointer
variadic parameter and the rest pattern
optional type former and the propagation suffix

blocks.text: Two absences are worth naming. `.(`, which opens a tuple literal, is not one token: it is `Dot` followed by `LParen`. And `x : := e` is not a third form; the scanner emits `Colon` and then `ColonEqual`, and the parser reads that pair as `::=`. The remaining token kinds carry text rather than punctuation: `Ident`, `Int`, `Float`, `Str`, `CStr`, `BStr`, `MlStr`, `Directive`, `Op`, `OpName`, `Backtick`, `DoubleBacktick` and `Label`, each covered by the chapter that owns its construct.

K=10 n=3 m=42 q=6 p=1 a=30 t=1
full=5 tail=3 head=2 mid=3
varargs=6
deref x=1
The operator character set
Exactly eighteen ASCII characters may appear in an operator token. Any run of them that is not caught by one of the special cases below is scanned as a single operator token.

What is absent matters as much as what is present. `$`, `#`, `\`, `'`, backtick, `"`, `;` and the six bracket characters are not operator characters, so they always end an operator run. That is why `x: []ssize` and `Err![]T` lex the way they read, and why an operator whose name contains a bracket can only be written in the quoted form described in the chapter on reserved operators.
Maximal munch and its exceptions

The scanner takes the longest run of operator characters it can, which it must: a library may introduce any spelling, so the scanner cannot know that `+|` is one operator and `+` `|` two without preferring the longer read. Five characters carry extra rules on top of that. `?` never continues an operator, so `*?T` is three tokens and a propagation suffix composes with whatever follows it. A lone `@` is taken by itself, but only when no operator character follows, which keeps `@=` and `@>` available as user spellings. After `:` the scanner checks the fixed forms `:::`, `::=`, `::` and `:=` first, then falls into the general scan unless the next character is `*`. The order is load-bearing: `T ::: instance C` is one `TripleColon` token, not a constant-binding token followed by a colon. After `=` it falls into the general scan whenever another operator character follows. A trailing `.` is handed back when the character after it could start a non-operator token. The pointer suffixes `.*` and `.&` are recognized as separate tokens, so `p.*.field.&` chains without spaces. If a token still ends in `.` it is `error: operator token cannot end with '.'`.

Whitespace between two operator characters is load-bearing. The two pairs a program is most likely to write by accident are `x:?T`, which loses the `?` and reports a reserved `:`, and `E!*T`, which glues `!` and `*` into one unknown operator. Both read perfectly well and both fail; a space fixes each.

The punctuation spellings below are reserved. The check lives in the scanner and fires on the token, not on the declaration, so it catches a reserved spelling written as a quoted operator name and a reserved spelling that reaches operator position by accident with the same message. The message always names the operator twice, once for the token and once for the rule.
error: reserved operator token '=' (operator '=' cannot be overloaded)
The reserved spellings
Each of these carries syntax the parser must be able to recognise without consulting any operator table, which is what makes it unavailable for overloading.

Because the check is on the token, a mistyped expression can produce it. Writing `. {` with a space reaches the operator scanner and reports `error: reserved operator token '.' (operator '.' cannot be overloaded)`. Write `.{` without a space to begin a struct literal. A trailing decimal point such as `1.` instead receives a float-literal diagnostic.

The instance separator is reserved all the way down in the lexer. Writing `':::'` as an operator name reports `reserved operator token ':::' (operator ':::' cannot be overloaded)`, and the former `T :: instance C` form no longer parses. Write `T ::: instance C`.
Why `..`, `..=` and `?` are not on the list

All three have dedicated token kinds and dedicated parser handling, so they look like candidates for the list. They are absent on purpose. A range and a propagation are both defined by typeclasses in the library rather than built into the compiler, and a user type joins in by writing an instance. Reserving the spellings would make that impossible.

The proof is in the diagnostic a competing declaration gets. Declaring `'..'` in a new typeclass is not rejected as reserved; it is rejected because the spelling already belongs to a class, which is the ordinary rule for every operator.
The quoted operator-name form

An operator is named by writing its characters between single quotes. After a quote the scanner looks ahead: if what follows is a letter or `_` and the run is not closed by a second quote, the token is a label such as `'again`; otherwise it scans to the next quote and produces an operator name. So `'+'` names an operator and `'done` declares a label, with no ambiguity between them.

The text between the quotes is taken as written. The scanner applies only the reserved-spelling check and the trailing-dot check, so a name may contain characters that could never be lexed as an operator run, including letters and brackets. The declaration then succeeds even when the name can never be written at a use site.
A letters-only name such as `'plus'` declares cleanly, but at a use site the letters lex as an identifier: `2 plus 3` is `error: unexpected token 'plus'`.
`''` is a legal empty name, and using it produces `error: unbound ''`.

`'[]'` and `'[]='` are the indexing and index-assignment operators. They are the only names allowed to contain a bracket; any other gives `error: operator '<[>' cannot contain '[' or ']'` with the offending name quoted back.
Beyond the spelling, the checker constrains what an operator declaration may say. These rules are enforced when the declaration is checked, not when it is scanned.

rows: `operator functions need one, two, or three parameters`
`operator '<~>' must be declared by a typeclass and implemented by its instances`
an all-stars or all-ampersands name is never prefix
`operator '**' cannot be overloaded as a prefix operator`

blocks.text: Prefix `*`, `**`, and longer all-stars spellings are built-in dereferences, or pointer constructors when their operand is a type. Prefix `&`, `&&`, and longer all-ampersands spellings are built-in address operations. They cannot be overloaded as prefix operators, including through macros; binary uses remain available. The suffixes `.*` and `.&` are reserved and cannot be overloaded in any fixity.

Before a file is parsed, its whole token vector is walked once by the prescan, which looks for operator declarations and records their fixity, precedence and associativity. Only then does parsing begin.

The prescan exists because Glosso lets a library introduce operator spellings and precedences. Parsing cannot decide how `2 * 3 %% 4` groups, or even whether `%%` is an operator at all, until every `#operator` declaration available to the file's prescan has been read. A single-pass parser would have to see the declaration first; the prescan removes that ordering requirement by reading the declarations out of the token stream before any of them is parsed.
What the prescan recognises

The pattern is narrow and purely lexical: an operator name, then `::`, then an opening parenthesis. From the matching close parenthesis the scan runs forward to the first `{` or `;`, which is to say across the signature and its directives and no further, looking for `#operator`.

`#operator(prefix)` and `#operator(suffix)` register unary fixity. `#operator(left, prec)`, `#operator(right, prec)` and `#operator(assign, prec)` register precedence and associativity. Use these same forms on the owning typeclass's method signature; there is no separate signature-only precedence directive.

A prefix or suffix mode carries no precedence. Supplying a level, as in `#operator(prefix, 19)`, is `error: unexpected token ','`. A name made only of asterisks is never registered as prefix, because those spellings are the pointer sigils.
An operator may be used before it is declared
That is the whole visible consequence. The declaration below sits after `main`, and `main` uses the operator anyway, at the precedence the later declaration asks for.

Precedence 19 binds tighter than `*` at 18, so the second line is `2 * (3 %% 4)`, which is `2 * 34`. Changing the one number in the declaration changes how the expression above it groups: at 17 the operator binds looser than `*` and the same source reads `(2 * 3) %% 4`.

A new binary operator with no `#operator(left|right|assign, n)` anywhere in the prescanned declarations has no registered precedence, so its use site fails as an unknown token. The declaration is reported too, with the directive it is missing. An instance can omit the directive when its owning class already supplies the level.

error: unexpected token '%%'
error: binary operator '%%' needs #operator(left|right|assign, n)

The precedence must be a written integer literal. The prescan reads it straight out of the token stream, before any name means anything, so a named constant cannot be used: `#operator(left, P)` with `P :: 19;` is `error: unexpected token 'P'`, reported at the constant in the directive, and the declaration is rejected.
Operator syntax across relative modules

The resolver seeds the operator table from the Prelude and prescans relative `#load` and `#export` dependencies before parsing the caller. An operator declared in a loaded file can therefore be written in the loading file. The source files still have separate name visibility: learning an operator's syntax does not grant access to hidden methods or to an unrelated module's instances.

combine(3, 4) = 34
operator = 34
Both calls compile. The dependency prescan supplies `%%`'s precedence before the caller is parsed, and the explicit load supplies the public class and instance needed when the expression is checked.

The early dependency walk follows relative `#load` and `#export` paths recursively. Directory imports have their own entrypoint and dependency traversal; use an explicit relative dependency when an operator's syntax must be available while parsing the caller.
The Prelude is prescanned before anything else and its table seeds every file, which is why the arithmetic, comparison, bitwise and range spellings are available with no import and no declaration.
A directory import reads `module.glo`; it does not discover all other files in the directory automatically. The entrypoint must load, export, or embed every required component explicitly.
A declaration may follow its use within a file because the prescan runs first. Across files, make the module dependency explicit and export the declarations that callers need.

Glosso has no `let`, `var`, or `const` keyword. A declaration is a name, an optional type annotation, and an initialiser, and the punctuation between them carries the whole meaning: whether the name is immutable, whether its value is required at compile time, and whether the type is written or inferred.

A colon introduces the type annotation. When the right side is an ordinary value expression, a single `:` or a `::` before it binds a constant; an `=`, `:=`, or `::=` binds something that can be written to. A declaration with a type and no initialiser is zero-filled. A definition-shaped right side—such as `struct`, `#import`, or a procedure—is the named-definition exception described below.
total=32 scale=1.5 seen=0
The declaration forms

The same eight value-binding spellings are accepted at file scope and inside a procedure body, and two of them mean different things in the two places. The difference is that only a declaration inside a body is entered into the checker's compile-time environment, so only a local value binding can be a compile-time binding. In the first eight rows, `v` means an ordinary value expression.

rows: Named definition in the enclosing lexical scope.
`x := definition`, `x ::= definition`, `x : D : definition`, or `x : D :: definition`
Named definition; its declaration type is inferred, or checked against `D`.
Not the named-definition grammar; `:=` and `::=` take the ordinary local-binding path.

blocks.text: Both `:` and `::` are accepted after a type annotation, so `MAX: ssize : 100` and `MAX: ssize :: 100` declare the same typed constant. Every ordinary value-binding form in the first eight rows ends with `;`, both at file scope and in an ordinary procedure body. A named definition instead follows its own grammar: a braced definition ends at `}`, while a definition such as `distinct` or `#import` carries its own `;`. Inside a `#code` quotation, the parser also lets a binding immediately before any closing `}` end there, including at the end of a nested block. Statements and Semicolons gives the complete rule.

For an ordinary value expression, `::=` is the one spelling whose meaning flips between the two scopes. A file-scope `G ::= 7;` is an ordinary mutable global, not a compile-time constant, and a `#if G == 7` that follows it fails with `error: unknown const G`. A definition-shaped right side takes the named-definition path instead. Use `::` for a file-scope value constant.
Constants

`::` means an immutable binding. It comes in two flavours, and the compiler chooses between them without any help from the source: if the initialiser can be evaluated during checking the name becomes a compile-time constant, and if it cannot the name becomes a runtime-frozen constant instead. A `::` whose initialiser is not compile-time evaluable is not an error.

A runtime-frozen constant is lowered like an ordinary local: the initialiser is evaluated once, at the declaration, and the name is bound to that result for the rest of the scope. Later changes to whatever the initialiser read do not reach it.

FROZEN=14
FROZEN=14

The two flavours differ in exactly one visible way: a frozen constant is not a compile-time value, so it cannot drive a construct that demands one. Adding `#if FROZEN == 14` to the program above gives `error: unknown const FROZEN`, `#assert #comptime FROZEN == 14` gives `error: #assert #comptime condition is not compile-time evaluable`, and passing it to a `#comptime` parameter gives `error: argument for #comptime parameter 'v' must be known at compile time`. Each of those carries `note: unknown const FROZEN`.
Neither flavour has storage. `p := *FROZEN` is `error: cannot take a pointer to a non-addressable expression: 'FROZEN'`, and the same holds for a file-scope constant.
Compile-time bindings

Inside a body, `x ::= v` and `x: T := v` declare a compile-time binding. The initialiser must be compile-time evaluable, the name is registered in the compile-time environment, and the binding may be updated by ordinary assignment during checking. This is what drives `#inline while` counters and static branching.
the static branch saw 8

An initialiser the checker cannot fold is rejected rather than frozen: `K ::= n * 2` over a runtime `n` is `error: comptime variable initializer must be compile-time evaluable`. A compile-time binding also has no runtime storage, so its address cannot be taken: `p := &width` is `error: cannot take pointer to width`. Values with no runtime representation must be bound this way or with `::`. That includes values of type `type`, `Namespace`, `Library`, `Code`, and `Pattern`, as well as typeclass and macro declarations.
Variables

`x := v` and `x: T = v` declare a mutable binding with storage. `:=` infers the type from the initialiser; the annotated form fixes it and checks the initialiser against it. `x: T;` declares a mutable binding with no initialiser, and the storage is zero-filled rather than left holding whatever was on the stack. A declaration with neither a type nor an initialiser has nothing to work from and is rejected.
Assigning to a constant

Assignment to a constant is always rejected, but the diagnostic depends on where the constant was declared and how it was spelled. A file-scope constant is not in the assignable namespace at all, so name resolution fails before the assignment rule is ever consulted; a local constant is found and then refused, with a help line naming the spelling that would have made it mutable.

rows: `error: constant cannot be modified`, with `help: change '::' to ':=' to make the binding mutable`
the same error, with `help: change ':' to '=' to make the binding mutable`
the same error, with `help: change '::' to '=' to make the binding mutable`
Accepted; a global is an ordinary mutable binding.

blocks.text: The refusal reaches through members and indexes, not just through the bare name. For `p :: Point.{ .x = 1, .y = 2 };` the statement `p.x = 5;` is the same `error: constant cannot be modified`, reported at the field, and for `a: [3]s64 :: .[1, 2, 3];` so is `a[0] = 9;`.
`#undefined` initialisers

`x: T = #undefined;` declares a binding whose initial contents are not defined. It exists to skip the zero fill for a buffer that is about to be overwritten in full, which is why the standard library's binary readers open with `bytes: [16]u8 = #undefined;` before reading into the slice. The spelling is the directive; a bare `undefined` is `error: unbound 'undefined'`.

define i8 @glo_zeroed() {
entry:
  %r0 = alloca i64, align 8
  %r1 = alloca [64 x i8], align 1
  %r2 = alloca i64, align 8
  %r3 = alloca i8, align 1
  %temp.mark = load i64, ptr @glo_temp_used, align 8
  store i64 %temp.mark, ptr %r0, align 8
  store [64 x i8] zeroinitializer, ptr %r1, align 1
  store i64 3, ptr %r2, align 8

define i8 @glo_scratch() {
entry:
  %r0 = alloca i64, align 8
  %r1 = alloca [64 x i8], align 1
  %r2 = alloca i64, align 8
  %r3 = alloca i8, align 1
  %temp.mark = load i64, ptr @glo_temp_used, align 8
  store i64 %temp.mark, ptr %r0, align 8
  store i64 3, ptr %r2, align 8

Under `--backend llvm-ir -O0` the two bodies differ by exactly one instruction: `zeroed` emits `store [64 x i8] zeroinitializer, ptr %r1` and `scratch` does not. `#undefined` has no standalone type of its own. It takes the type of the declaration, parameter, or field that receives it; bound alone with `x := #undefined` it falls back to the `label` type used for an absent jump target.

`#undefined` changes nothing at file scope. A global lives in the program image and has to be given some pattern of bytes, so `buffer: [8]u8 = #undefined;` still emits `@glo_global_buffer = internal global [8 x i8] zeroinitializer`. The directive only pays for itself on a local.

A Glosso source file is a flat sequence of top-level declarations. There is no package statement, no header, and no forward-declaration form, because there is nothing to declare forward: the whole file is read before anything in it is checked.

Order is therefore free. `main` may be the first declaration in the file and call a procedure written below it, a global may be typed by a struct declared later, and `#import` and `#load` may sit at the very bottom.

later() = 32
LIMIT = 64 origin.x = 3
What may appear at file scope

rows: A mutable global, type inferred, when the right side is an ordinary expression.
A mutable global with a written type.
An instance; `:::` is its dedicated separator.
A named type, procedure, namespace, library, or macro with its declaration type inferred.
The same named definitions with declaration-value type `D` checked explicitly.
An isolated relative module; use `#load,embed` for a shared source fragment.
A compile-time step; the expression form requires `;`.
A feature gate, sticky to the end of the file.

blocks.text: `#if`, `else #if`, and `else` also select declarations at module scope. The condition must be a compile-time boolean. Only the chosen branch adds declarations or loads dependencies, so an inactive platform branch need not have its files or foreign libraries installed. Custom operator declarations and dependencies that provide operator syntax must stay unconditional, because parsing precedes branch selection. `#assert` remains a statement; use a `#comptime` block for a file-level assertion.
Named definitions are values too

At file scope, a definition may use the traditional `name :: definition` spelling, an inferred `name := definition` or `name ::= definition`, or an explicit declaration-value annotation written `name : D : definition` (with `::` also accepted for the second separator). The parser recognises a definition-shaped right side before deciding that `:=` means a mutable global. Structs, unions, enums, flag enums, distinct types, typeclasses, procedures, imports, loads, libraries, and function-pointer definitions all take this route. Inside a procedure body, only the canonical `name :: definition` form enters the nested definition path; the alternate punctuation above is file-scope syntax.

The annotation describes the value introduced by the declaration, not the values stored inside it. An aggregate, distinct type, or function-pointer definition has type `type`; `#import` and `#load` produce `Namespace`; `#library` produces `Library`; a typeclass uses the parameterized declaration annotation `Typeclass(parameter-kinds...)`; a macro uses `Macro((parameter-types...) -> result)`; and an ordinary procedure has its procedure type. `Typeclass(...)` and `Macro(...)` are recognized in this declaration-annotation position; they are not generally callable type constructors in ordinary expressions. These names are case-sensitive. The former lowercase `namespace`, `library`, and `pattern` spellings are ordinary identifiers, not builtin types.

The checker verifies an explicit declaration-value annotation. For example, `Wrong : Library : struct {}` reports `declaration 'Wrong' has type type, not declared type Library`. In an explicit declaration annotation, `Typeclass` requires at least one parameter kind and `Macro` requires exactly one procedure signature, such as `Macro((ssize) -> void)`.

Procedures and types may also be declared inside a procedure body. Their names belong to the containing lexical block; other top-level declarations cannot reach them. Separate blocks may use the same local name. Function Declarations covers local procedures and their capture rules.
Globals and their initialisers

A global is a mutable binding with static storage. Its name is private by default; use `#public` or `#public(unit)` when another source file needs it. Its initializer is evaluated during compilation and emitted as the symbol's static initial value. Visibility and Ownership Units covers which callers can reach the binding.

That is a hard requirement, not an optimisation. An initialiser the checker cannot fold is an error, and the most common way to hit it is to read another global. A global variable is not a compile-time value, so `second: s64 = first + 1;` gives `error: unknown const first`. Anything that needs the running program is rejected the same way: `buffer: ?*void = alloc(64);` is `error: #magic intrinsic 'ctx_alloc' is not available during compile-time evaluation`.
Anything the compile-time evaluator can run is allowed, including calls to procedures declared later in the file and constants declared later in the file.
Initialisation order

Because every global initial value is a folded constant, there is no runtime global-initialisation pass at all. Nothing runs before `main` to fill globals in, so there is no initialisation order to specify and no order-of-initialisation hazard between files. The guarantee the compiler makes is that every global holds its declared initial value, or zero, from the first instruction of the program.
The visible consequence is that a side effect in a global initialiser happens during the build, not during the run.

glosso: compile program.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
initializer ran
glosso: link program.exe (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
glosso: done program.exe  (backend=llvm, target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
value=1

`initializer ran` is printed by the compiler, on the compiler's stdout, between the `compile` and `link` progress lines. Work that has to happen once at program start belongs at the top of `main` or behind an explicit initialisation procedure, not in a global initialiser.
Thread-local storage

`#thread_local` prefixes a global variable declaration and gives each thread its own copy of the storage. Everything else about the declaration is unchanged: the initialiser is still folded at compile time, and an omitted initialiser still means zero.
depth=1 scratch[0]=7

The directive prefixes a variable and nothing else. `#thread_local K :: 5;` and `#thread_local f :: () { }` are both `error: #thread_local can only prefix a global variable declaration`, and inside a body it is not a statement at all: `error: unexpected directive 'thread_local'`.

Whether `#thread_local` reaches the object file depends on the target. On a hosted target the global is emitted as `@glo_global_depth = internal thread_local global i64 0`; on Windows, on freestanding Linux x86-64, and on bare metal the backend drops the `thread_local` qualifier and emits an ordinary internal global, because those targets do not use the ELF thread-local model the runtime is built around. Targets and Cross-Compilation covers the target list.

rows: An inherent method or associated-function block.
A declaration visibility prefix or transparent group.

blocks.text: `place = value;` is a statement, not an expression. It has no result and it cannot be nested: `y := (x = 2);` is `error: unexpected token '='`, and so is `if x = 1 { }`. An assignment written where a comparison was meant is a parse error rather than a silent truth test. The update-assignment operators described below are a separate mechanism and do produce values.

The type rule is the ordinary conversion rule, with no relaxation for assignment. The right side must already be, or implicitly convert to, the type of the left side. Widening between integer types is implicit; narrowing is not, so `small: s32 = 1; big: s64 = 2; small = big;` is `error: assign s64 to s32`. An unrelated type is the same shape of message: assigning a `string` to an `s32` is `error: assign string to s32`. Conversions: What Is Implicit gives the full rule, and Relaxing Strictness with `lossy_numerics` gives the gate that turns the narrowing case back on.
What can be assigned to

The left side must denote storage. Four forms do: a mutable name, a field of one, an element of one, and the target of a pointer dereference. They compose, and an element reached through a view writes through to the array the view was taken from.

Anything else is `error: left side of assignment is not assignable`. That covers a literal (`5 = 3;`), the result of a call (`f() = 3;`), and any computed expression (`(a + b) = 3;`). Constants get their own diagnostics, listed in Values, Constants, and Variables. Parameters, by contrast, are ordinary mutable bindings and may be assigned to; the caller's value is unaffected because arguments are passed by value.
Assignment copies

Assignment of an aggregate copies it. A struct or fixed array bound from another one is an independent value, and writing through the copy does not disturb the original. Views and pointers are the exception, and only because the thing being copied is the reference, not what it refers to.
Update assignment

Every `op=` spelling is a genuine operator, declared in the Prelude as a typeclass method carrying `#operator(assign, 0)`. Level 0 is the loosest tier on the precedence scale, so everything on the right of it groups first, and the result is stored back into the left operand. Because it is an operator rather than statement syntax, `y := (x += 1);` compiles and binds `y` to the updated value.
total=52 saturated=255 wrapped=4 ready=1

There are nineteen of them, and each has its own two-parameter typeclass with an `Output` associated type. None of those classes has to be implemented directly: the Prelude ships a blanket instance for every one, conditioned on the corresponding binary operator class, so a type that implements `Add` gets `+=` for free.

A type with no instance reports the missing operator rather than a type mismatch: `a: Point; b: Point; a += b;` is `error: no operator '+=' for Point, Point`. The Operator System and Assignment Operators cover declaring new ones and what `#operator(assign, 0)` means for parsing.

The wrapping, saturating, and shifting families exist because the plain arithmetic operators trap on overflow at `-O0` and `-O1`. `+%=` wraps and `+|=` clamps, which is why `250 +%= 10` is `4` and `250 +|= 10` is `255` on a `u8`. Overflow, Traps, and the `-O` Level explains when the trap is emitted.
Binding several names at once

A declaration may take a comma-separated list of names on the left, which destructures a multiple-result call or a tuple. `_` in that list discards a component. This is a declaration form, not an assignment form: `::`, `:=` and `::=` all accept a name list.

q=3 r=1
remainder=1
n=1 s=two

There is no multiple-assignment statement. Once the names exist, `a, b = divmod(9, 4);` is `error: unexpected token '='`, and so is the swap idiom `x, y = y, x;`. The right side of a destructuring declaration is one expression, not a list: `a, b := 1, 2;` is `error: unexpected token ','`, and the tuple literal `a, b := .(1, 2);` is the spelling that works.

The name count must match what the right side produces: `a, b, c := divmod(7, 2);` is `error: destructuring binds 3 names from a 2-value result`. Function Declarations covers multiple and named results, and Tuples covers the values themselves.

A block is a brace-delimited statement list used as a statement in its own right. It introduces a scope: a name declared inside it is unreachable after the closing brace. Scoping is lexical and sequential, so a name is visible from its declaration to the end of the scope that holds it, and not before.

inner sees outer a=1
inner a=99
outer a=1

The first `print` resolves `a` to the outer binding because the inner declaration has not been reached yet, and the inner `a := 99;` declares a second variable rather than assigning to the first, so the outer one is unchanged once the block ends. Naming a binding after its scope has closed is `error: unbound 'hidden'`; in call position the same failure reads `error: unknown function hidden`, because the checker resolves callees through a lookup separate from the one it uses for values.
What introduces a scope

Every construct with a body carries its own scope, and the checker clones the environment when it enters one. A body written without braces is still a body: `if true  a := 5;` followed by a use of `a` on the next line is `error: unbound 'a'`.

rows: A fresh scope, closed by the `}`.
A fresh scope; the parameters are declared in it.
A fresh scope, whether or not it is braced.
A fresh scope, re-entered on every iteration.
A switch or pattern arm body
A fresh scope per arm, holding that arm's captures.
A fresh scope that cannot reach enclosing locals.

blocks.text: Local declarations and lexical scope

A named function or type declared inside a body belongs to its containing lexical block. Other procedures cannot reach that local name. Type aliases can also be used in local annotations. Constants and variables follow the ordinary block scope rules.

collect 3
report 9

collect and report each declare their own Sample type. Their names are independent and their fields may differ. A function declared in one block cannot be called from a separate top-level procedure; pass a callback explicitly when that behavior is needed.

A local function or type inside a braced #if branch stays in that lexical block. At module scope, #if selects complete declaration blocks; only the active branch contributes declarations and dependencies.
Captures and pattern bindings
A pattern capture is a binding whose scope is exactly the branch that proved the pattern. It does not exist before the arm and it does not survive it.

ok 5
tested v=5

Naming `v` after the switch is `error: unbound 'v'`, with `help: did you mean 'r'?`. The `else` of an `if #pattern` test cannot see the captures either: on that path the pattern did not match, so there is nothing for them to name.

The one form that binds outward is `#pattern P := subject else { ... }`, which places the captures in the enclosing scope so a procedure is not indented one level deeper per optional. That is sound only because the `else` block is checked without the bindings and must not fall through; the form is covered in Bind or Diverge.

`using p;` inserts a struct's field names into the current scope for the remainder of it, and they disappear with the scope: reading `x` after the block that said `using p;` is `error: unbound x`. The statement is covered in `using`, `#empty`, and `#as`.

A lambda body is a scope that deliberately cannot reach outward. Reading an enclosing local gives `error: lambda captures local 'base', but captured closures are not supported`, with `help: pass the value as an explicit callback or context argument`. Globals and constants remain readable; see Lambdas.
Shadowing

Inside a procedure, shadowing is unrestricted. A local may hide a parameter, a global variable, a top-level constant, a type name or a procedure name, and a nested block may hide anything the enclosing block declared.
scale=11 LIMIT=100 counter=10

Redeclaring a name in the same block is accepted as well: `a := 1; a := 2;` is two declarations rather than a declaration and an assignment, and the second binding wins from that point on. Call position and value position are resolved separately, so shadowing a procedure name does not make the procedure uncallable: after `print := 3;` the call `print("%\n", print);` still resolves and prints `3`.

Shadowing is refused within one file's top-level namespace. A second declaration there is an error, including declarations brought into the same unit by #load,embed. Local functions and types stay in their lexical blocks, so their names do not collide across procedure bodies. Ordinary #load preserves the loaded module's identity. Qualified loads distinguish equally named declarations in separate modules.

The standard library's public names occupy that same namespace. A top-level `PI :: 3.14;` in a user file is `error: constant 'PI' is already declared`, because the Prelude already owns the name. Local bindings are free to shadow it.

Labels are function-scoped rather than block-scoped: they are collected in a pre-pass over the whole body, so a jump may go forward, and may enter a nested block from outside it. See Labels and `goto`.
A `defer` belongs to the scope it is written in and runs when that scope is left. See `defer` and `#try defer`.
Visibility groups are transparent and restore the enclosing audience when their braces close. See Visibility and Ownership Units.

Functions, types, constants, globals, methods, and named module bindings are private by default. A private declaration is accessible only in its defining physical source file and logical module. Struct fields and enum or union variants start public, subject to the visibility of their enclosing type.

Use `#public` to expose an API, `#public(unit)` to share declarations within one ownership unit, and `#private` to make file privacy explicit. Each directive prefixes one named declaration or a transparent group. Groups introduce no namespace and restore the enclosing default when they end.

The visibility after `:::` sets an inherent block's default member audience. The header accepts `#public`, `#public(unit)`, or `#private`. `Counter ::: #public { ... }` is equivalent to `Counter ::: { #public { ... } }`. A method without an explicit audience in a plain `Counter ::: { ... }` block remains private, even if the type or surrounding declaration group is public. Put a block visibility before its optional `where` clause, as in `Box($T) ::: #public where true { ... }`.

Visibility on locals or parameters is rejected. An inherent block takes its visibility after `:::`, not before the owner type name. Typeclass requirements and instance slots follow the class contract. A public name beginning with `_` is still public; its spelling does not hide it from imports.

The former `#enable(private_section)`, `#disable(private_section)`, `private_sections`, and `siblings` forms have been removed and produce a migration diagnostic. Replace them with declaration prefixes or visibility groups. Other feature gates keep their file-scoped behavior.

Imports, loads, and reexports never widen an item's audience. Each module still declares its own dependencies. `#load,embed` shares a logical module but preserves each physical file's private identity: declarations used by another embedded file need `#public(unit)` or `#public`.

In this example both files are in the entry file's project directory and therefore share an ownership unit by default. The caller can use `STORE_SHARED` through its explicit load, while `key` remains accessible only inside `store.glo`. Loading a file alone never makes its private declarations callable.

Ownership controls who may add inherent methods and use unit-visible names. It is separate from module scope. Without explicit mappings, the entry file and other files under its source directory form a project unit. A configured `--module-path` directory creates dependency boundaries by its first relative path component. Other external files get separate file units.

Repeated `--unit-source UNIT=FILE` options configure ownership explicitly. Once any mapping is given, every loaded non-standard source, including the entry file, requires an exact mapping. Canonical paths keep their unit across aliases, reexports, and embedded loads. Standard sources belong to the reserved `builtin:std` unit, and names starting with `builtin:` are reserved.

// app and its implementation share a unit; the dependency has its own.
// glosso --unit-source app=app.glo --unit-source app=parts/store.glo app.glo

Private fields cannot be read by a method in another file, even in the same unit. An inaccessible field also blocks external aggregate literals, spread construction, and recursive default initialization. Expose a factory such as `Counter.make()` to construct the value. Copying an existing value and updating its accessible fields remain permitted.

Public signatures cannot expose less-visible types. Generic bodies and default expressions retain the access rights of their defining file; specialization does not grant access to the caller's private members. Reflection omits inaccessible fields and variants without changing layout or discriminants. Matching a type with hidden variants requires a catch-all.

Language visibility is independent of native symbol export. A defined `#c_call` function can retain its external linker name while remaining private to Glosso callers. An ordinary private `main` is a valid entry point; it does not need a public annotation.

`defer` schedules a statement to run when the enclosing scope is left. Two forms are accepted: `defer <statement>;` and `defer { ... }`. The statement is not executed where it is written; it is pushed onto the scope's pending list and run on the way out.

block body
C1
C2
B
A
after block
end of main

Pending statements run last-in, first-out, so cleanup unwinds in the reverse of the order it was set up, which is the order that matches acquisition. The block form is a single entry: `C1` and `C2` run together, and together they run before `B`.
Each entry belongs to the scope it was written in, not to the procedure. The inner block's three entries run at its closing brace; the entry in `main` waits until `main` returns.
Which exits run the pending statements

body i=1
  defer sees i=1
  defer sees i=2
  body i=3
  defer sees i=3
  defer sees i=4
done i=4

The loop body is a scope, so the entry is registered and discharged once per iteration: four times, including the iteration cut short by `continue` and the one cut short by `break`. The printed value is equally informative. `i` is incremented after the `defer` line, and the trace shows the incremented value, because a deferred statement is evaluated when it runs and not when it is written.

rows: Run, for every scope between the `return` and the procedure body.
Run, for every scope up to and including the loop body.
The end of a loop iteration
Not run; the process ends inside the call.

blocks.text: `goto` transfers to a label rather than unwinding scopes, so it steps over the pending list entirely. That is why `defer` cannot carry cleanup in a procedure that uses the jump library for control transfer; see Explicit Control Transfer with the Jump Library.

before goto
after goto

Pending statements run before the caller observes the result, and a result named by a bare local is read after they have run. In `by_name` below the caller sees `99`; writing `return x + 0;` materializes a temporary first and yields `1`. Do not assign in a deferred statement to a local that the same scope returns by name.
by_name=99 by_value=1
`#try defer`

`#try defer <statement>` registers an entry that runs only when the scope is left along an error path. It is the rollback half of a two-part cleanup: `defer` releases what was acquired either way, and `#try defer` undoes work that only a successful completion should keep.

An error path means propagation through postfix `?`, so the form requires a boundary that `?` can return through. Without one it is `error: #try defer requires a Try-returning function or an enclosing #try block`. Propagation itself is covered in `Try`, `?`, and `#try`.

success path:
  acquire
  commit
  release
  -> ok 11
failure path:
  acquire
  release
  rollback
  -> err step failed

On the success path `run` reaches `commit`, the plain entry runs, and the rollback is discarded unexecuted. On the failure path `step` returns `.Err`, the `?` carries it out of `run` without reaching `commit`, and both entries run. The order is worth reading: the rollback was registered first, so it runs last.

Both kinds share one last-in, first-out list. An error-only entry is skipped on the success path but keeps its position, so the interleaved order of the two kinds is the reverse of the order they were written in.

ok:
  always 2
  always 1
err:
  always 2
  undo 2
  always 1
  undo 1

Only propagation through `?` counts as an error path. A hand-written `return .Err(...);` is an ordinary return: the plain entries run and the `#try defer` entries do not. A procedure that mixes explicit error returns with `#try defer` rollback silently skips the rollback on exactly the paths it was written for.

explicit .Err:
  release
The boundary may be any `Try`-returning result, including the option type: in a procedure returning `?ssize`, a `?` applied to a `.None` runs the error-only entries exactly as an `.Err` does.

The warning is accurate here. `return .Err(.Bad);` is not a `?` propagation, so `#try defer p.free()` never runs on that path and the allocation really does leak. Replacing it with a plain `defer p.free();` and dropping the later `p.free();` makes the procedure correct and the warning disappear. Release obligations are covered in Ownership and Release Obligations.
`defer` accepts any statement, including a call, an assignment or a block; the block form counts as one entry and its statements run in written order.
A deferred statement reads its operands at the moment it runs, so it observes every mutation made after it was written.
A `#try defer` written inside a nested block belongs to that block. It is discarded when the block is left normally, so a failure that happens after the block does not run it.

A primitive type is one the compiler knows without a declaration. The spellings below are recognised directly, and the checker also accepts the fixed C integer names, the arbitrary-width families `sN` and `uN`, and the primitive type constructors `Simd` and `Matrix`. In the integer families `N` is an unpadded decimal width from 1 through 65535. Everything else in the language is assembled out of these primitives.

A primitive spelling is not a keyword. The lexer produces an ordinary identifier and the name is resolved during checking, after locals and globals have been consulted. A binding therefore shadows a primitive: `ssize := 5;` declares a local named `ssize`, and `Pattern := 5;` declares one named `Pattern`. The lowercase name `pattern` is just an ordinary identifier; the compile-time pattern type is spelled with a capital `P`.
Sizes and alignments

Both numbers come from `type_info(T)`, whose result carries `.size` and `.alignment`. There is no separate alignment intrinsic: `align_of(s64)` is `error: unknown function align_of`. The figures below are for `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`. Pointer-derived sizes change with the target, and scalar alignment can change too: never infer a portable record layout from this host table.

s16   size 2   align 2
s32   size 4   align 4
s64   size 8   align 8
s128   size 16   align 16
ssize   size 8   align 8
u8   size 1   align 1
u16   size 2   align 2
u32   size 4   align 4
u64   size 8   align 8
u128   size 16   align 16
usize   size 8   align 8
rune   size 4   align 4
f16   size 2   align 2
f32   size 4   align 4

f80   size 16   align 16
f128   size 16   align 16

cstring   size 8   align 8
