Size equals alignment for the listed integers and floats on this target. That is not a language-wide identity: on `x86-linux-musl`, `f64` is size 8 / alignment 4; on Linux x86, `f80` is 12 / 4; wide integers on 32-bit Arm, MIPS, and PowerPC have alignment 8 rather than 16.
`s128`, `u128`, `f80` and `f128` all occupy sixteen bytes. `f80` is the x87 80-bit extended format, with a 64-bit significand; its in-memory representation is padded to sixteen bytes.
A complex type is aligned to its component, not to the pair, so `c32` is four bytes with alignment two and `c128` is sixteen bytes with alignment eight.

`void`, `type`, `Code`, `Pattern`, `Namespace`, and `Library` are zero-sized. The annotation-only `Typeclass(...)` and `Macro(...)` declaration types have no runtime representation. `any` is two pointers wide and `label` is one.
Native-size integers and character types

`ssize` and `usize` are target-sized signed and unsigned integers. They are 64 bits on x86-64 and wasm64, and 32 bits on 32-bit targets. They remain distinct type values from fixed-width `s32`, `s64`, `u32`, and `u64`, even when their layouts agree. An unconstrained integer literal defaults to `ssize`; counts, indices, tuple counts, string counts, capacities, and `it_index` use it as well. The old source spellings `isize`, `int`, `uint`, and `char` are not accepted type names.

type_name(ssize)  ssize
type_name(s64)  s64
type_name(usize) usize
type_name(u64)   u64
ssize == s64      0
usize == u64     0
s64 == int64_t    1
ASCII literal == u8 1
rune == u32       0

The fixed C spellings are normalized to their corresponding fixed Glosso types, so `int64_t` and `s64` are one type value. Native-size spellings are different: diagnostics preserve `ssize`, `usize`, `s64`, and `u64`. `rune` likewise retains its identity instead of becoming its `u32` storage type. ASCII character literals default to ordinary `u8`.
Bytes and `rune`

`u8` stores bytes and is the default type of an ASCII `#char` literal. It has the ordinary integer operations. `rune` stores a Unicode scalar in four unsigned bytes and has equality, total-equality, ordering, and `Show` instances. A rune is not an integer: `Is_Integer` and `Is_Numeric` return false, and arithmetic, bitwise operations, shifts, integer ranges, and `Simd(rune, N)` are rejected.

An ASCII `#char` literal may adopt `u8`, `s8`, or `rune`; a non-ASCII literal may adopt only `rune`. A stored byte does not convert implicitly to a rune. Use `c.char_to_rune()` for the safe widening, while `cast` is the explicit low-level bridge to integer storage. The literal rules and exact diagnostics are in `#char` Character Literals.
The accepted C spellings

These names exist because Bindgen emits them. They are resolved by the checker rather than listed as builtin names in the parser, which is why they can appear in a type annotation without being reserved words. Each is a named integer type of the stated width and converts to its Glosso counterpart implicitly, both being the same width and signedness.
The last row has no source spelling: the name contains a space, so it is reachable only from inside the compiler. Write `u128`.
`void`, `type`, `any`, `label`, `Code`, `Pattern`, and definition types

`void` is the no-value type. It has exactly one value, written `.()`, and zero bytes. A procedure with no return annotation returns it, and a union variant with no payload carries it. `(void, void)` has `PartialEq` and `PartialOrd` instances that always answer equal.

void == void  1
size of void  0
show of void  .()

rows: a type, as a first-class value
any value, boxed with its type
a jump target within a procedure
an unexpanded fragment of program text
a match pattern as a compile-time value
annotation-only type of a typeclass declaration
annotation-only type of a macro declaration

blocks.text: `any` is the boxing target: the coercion rule accepts every type into it, which is how variadic arguments are collected. A compile-time number takes its default type on the way in. `type` values should be bound as compile-time constants for reflection and formatting; a mutable local is not a compile-time constant; `Types as Values` covers that boundary. `Code`, `Pattern`, `Namespace`, `Library`, `Typeclass(...)` and `Macro(...)` exist only during compilation. `type_kind` reports `0` for the four ordinary type expressions in that list because `Type_Info_Tag` has no dedicated tags for them; the two parameterised annotation-only forms have the same internal fallback.

These annotations describe the compile-time value produced by each definition. Aggregate definitions have type `type`; an ordinary procedure definition has its function type; imported and loaded modules produce `Namespace`; `#library` produces `Library`; and typeclass and macro definitions carry parameterised declaration types. In this role, `Typeclass` requires at least one parameter-kind argument and `Macro` takes exactly one function-signature argument. These two forms are accepted in declaration type annotations; they are not callable type constructors or general type-value expressions. The checker validates the annotation against the definition it introduces.
A `void` value can be passed directly to `print` and renders as `.()`. It is also supported as a zero-sized struct, tuple, or array member; the members after it keep their declaration-order indexes.

`#Never` is the uninhabited type: no expression can produce a value of that type and complete normally. Declare a nonreturning function with `-> #Never`; the old `#noreturn` directive is rejected. `#Never!T` is an infallible result, whose `?` needs no fallible enclosing boundary. It is also the `Drop.Error` type for cleanup that cannot fail.

Glosso has signed and unsigned integer types for every width from one through 65535 bits. Write `sN` for a signed N-bit type and `uN` for an unsigned one. The fixed spellings below are the conventional widths. `ssize` and `usize` instead follow the target's pointer width and retain identities distinct from the fixed-width spellings. Integer arithmetic is homogeneous, so two operands must already share a type before an operator will accept them.
Arbitrary-width integers

In `sN` and `uN`, `N` must be an unpadded decimal integer from 1 through 65535. Thus `s7` is a signed seven-bit integer and `u3` an unsigned three-bit integer. `s0`, `u65536`, and `s08` are not type spellings. The fixed-width entries above are the convenient names with established machine and C-ABI representations.

The ranges above are the compiler's own: a written literal that leaves them is rejected with the range quoted back, as in `error: 300 does not fit u8, whose range is 0..=255`. The rule and its exceptions belong to `Compile-Time Numbers and Literal Defaulting`.
Two's complement

Every integer is a two's-complement bit pattern, at compile time and at run time alike. The compile-time evaluator carries values in a 128-bit signed payload and re-widens at each operation, so every width up to 128 bits computes exactly. A cast between a signed and an unsigned type of the same width therefore reinterprets rather than converts, and `~0` is all ones at every width.

Plain `+`, `-`, `*` and unary `-` do not wrap silently: they are checked at `-O0` and `-O1` and abort on overflow. `+%` and `-%`, used above, are the operators that ask for the wrap explicitly; `*%` completes that family and `+|`, `-|`, `*|` saturate instead. See `Overflow, Traps, and the -O Level` for the checks and `The Operator System` for the full family.
Division and remainder

Both truncate toward zero. The quotient of a negative dividend is rounded up toward zero rather than down, and the remainder takes the sign of the dividend, so `(a / b) * b + (a % b)` reproduces `a` for every pair that does not overflow.

7 / 2 = 3   7 rem 2 = 1
-7 / 2 = -3  -7 rem 2 = -1
 7 / -2 = -3   7 rem -2 = 1
-7 / -2 = 3  -7 rem -2 = -1
quotient times divisor plus remainder: -7
`%` is integer-only. There is no float instance of `Rem`, so `a % b` on two `f64` values is `error: no operator '%' for f64, f64`.

At `-O0` and `-O1`, `/`, `//`, and `%` check for a zero divisor and abort before reaching the hardware. Signed division also checks the one unrepresentable quotient, `T.MIN / -1`. Signed remainder is different: `T.MIN % -1` is well-defined as zero and produces zero at every optimisation level. At `-O2` and above the division guards are omitted.
The three shifts

There are three shift operators, each owned by its own typeclass. `>>` is arithmetic on a signed operand and logical on an unsigned one; the operand type decides, because the instance is selected on it. There is no saturating right shift, since a right shift cannot leave the range it started in.

rows: shift left, discarding the bits that leave the width
shift right, sign-filling when signed and zero-filling when unsigned
shift left, clamping to the extreme value instead of discarding

blocks.text: The shift count has the same type as the shifted value, and a written literal count is checked against the width rather than against the value range. A literal count at least as large as the width is rejected. A count known only at run time is defined instead: over-shifting left or logically right yields zero, while an arithmetic right shift yields the sign (`0` or `-1`). A negative signed count has a large unsigned bit pattern and follows the same over-shift rule. LLVM lowering clamps or selects the count so none of these cases produces poison.

error: shift count 8 is not less than the 8 bits of u8
  --> shift.glo:3:18
  |
3 |     b: u8 = a << 8;
  |                  ^
note: a shift by the width or more has no defined result
128-bit and wider integers

`s128` and `u128` are ordinary integer types, not a library emulation. Decimal literals are kept at arbitrary precision while the checker finds their context, so a magnitude beyond 128 bits is accepted when its target is a wider `sN` or `uN`. Native arithmetic and `print` use that declared width exactly, up to the 65535-bit type limit.

A 128-bit value needs an annotation. An unannotated literal defaults to `ssize`, so `big := 170141183460469231731687303715884105727;` is `error: 170141183460469231731687303715884105727 does not fit ssize, whose range is -9223372036854775808..=9223372036854775807`. Write `: s128` or `: u128`, or cast.

The constant folder and generated native code handle integers wider than 128 bits, but the compile-time register VM does not: its registers hold `i128`. Trying to execute an operation on `u129` in a `#comptime` block reports `compile-time execution does not support u129, an integer wider than 128 bits` instead of producing a truncated answer. A directly foldable constant expression can still be exact at that width.

Five float spellings are recognised. Each names a semantic width, which is how many bits the arithmetic actually uses, and a storage size, which is how many bytes the value occupies. The two differ for `f80`: on x86, the x87 80-bit extended format, with a 64-bit significand, is stored in sixteen bytes. The table shows x86-64 Windows layout; other targets can use different alignments and an alternative carrier for `f80`.

`f64` is the default: an unannotated float literal becomes one, and the unnamed float type prints as `f64`. The backend lowers the five to the LLVM types `half`, `float`, `double`, `x86_fp80` and `fp128`. Literal defaulting itself is covered in `Compile-Time Numbers and Literal Defaulting`.
binary16 is real

`f16` is not a storage-only format that widens for arithmetic. The compile-time evaluator rounds through a binary16 encode and decode with round-to-nearest, ties-to-even, so a compile-time result and a run-time result agree. One third is `0.333252` at `f16` against `0.333333` at `f32`, and the next representable value above `1.0` is `1.000977`, which is one plus two to the minus tenth. The largest finite `f16` is `65504`.
`f80` is x87 only

`f80` is the x87 extended format, and only an x86 target has it in hardware. The backend asks the target: for cpu `x86_64`, `x86` or `i386` it emits LLVM's `x86_fp80`, and on every other target it carries the value in an `fp128` instead. The storage size stays sixteen bytes either way, but alignment is target-dependent. In particular, 32-bit x86 with a non-Microsoft C ABI aligns `f80` to four bytes, so a containing record can change layout in a cross-build.

The two carriers are not the same bit image. On an x86 target the storage holds an x87 extended value; its byte size follows the target ABI. Elsewhere f80 uses an IEEE binary128. An `f80` written to a file by one build is not readable as an `f80` by the other. `f80` is for reaching x87 precision, not for portable storage.

On x86-64 Windows, generated programs widen the x87 precision-control setting at startup. Runtime `f80` arithmetic therefore keeps the format's full 64-bit significand instead of being rounded to the legacy 53-bit control setting.
Float literals and runtime overflow

A finite float literal must fit the target type. For example, over: f16 = 100000.0 reports float literal '100000.0' is out of range for f16. A nonzero literal that rounds to zero is also rejected. Runtime narrowing and arithmetic can still produce infinity; very small values may round to zero. The example below narrows an ordinary f32 variable at runtime rather than an out-of-range literal.

over <= f16 max : 0
over == over    : 1
over + over     : 1
over / over     : 0
under == 0.0    : 1

That output is the signature of a positive infinity. `over` is not below the largest finite `f16`, it equals itself so it is not a NaN, and adding it to itself leaves it unchanged. Dividing it by itself does produce a NaN, which is why the fourth comparison fails. `under` has become an exact zero.

`print` names the infinity directly: a positive one renders as `inf`, a negative one as `-inf`, and a NaN as `nan`. Float rendering is described in `Show, FromString, and print Formatting`; comparisons remain the reliable test of which special value a magnitude became.
f16 100000.0 prints as inf
Conversions and operators

No float converts implicitly to another float, in either direction, and no runtime integer converts implicitly to a float. Widening is rejected as firmly as narrowing: the conversion rule has a lossless-widening branch for integers and none at all for floats. `#enable(lossy_numerics)` does not change this, because the gate is consulted only in the integer-to-integer branch; `f32` to `f64` still fails under it.

error: got f32, expected f64
  --> widen.glo:3:14
  |
3 |     y: f64 = x;
  |              ^
`cast(T)` is the bridge in both directions, and it truncates toward zero going to an integer. `cast` and `acast` covers it.
Operators are homogeneous. `a + b` with `a: f32` and `b: f64` is `error: got f64, expected f32`, not a promotion.
`%` has no float instance: `error: no operator '%' for f64, f64`.
Floats are `PartialEq` but explicitly not `Eq`. The Prelude declares a negative instance, `$T ::: instance !Eq where Is_Float(T)`, because NaN is not equal to itself.

On `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`, the driver builds and links a bundled quad-precision helper archive. `f128` arithmetic, comparison, conversion, boxing, and printing therefore work when that archive is available. If the helper build cannot be produced, the driver warns and the eventual link can still report unresolved compiler-runtime symbols; other targets depend on their target runtime and toolchain. Linux musl and WebAssembly links also include target-specific bundled floating-point helpers; an emitted object alone does not supply them.
Wide conversions and display

A binary128 significand holds every bit of a `u64` or `s64` exactly. Convert the value, not an intermediate `f64`, if those bits matter. The reverse cast succeeds exactly for these in-range integers; more general float-to-integer casts still truncate and saturate as described in `cast` and `acast`.

Default float display narrows to binary64; printing is not a way to recover every significant bit of `f80` or `f128`. On 32-bit Arm, MIPS, and PowerPC musl targets, the binary128-to-binary64 path uses an integer-word helper because the C target has no binary128 calling convention. That conversion rounds to nearest, ties to even, and also handles subnormals, overflow, infinities, and NaNs.

A complex type is a primitive, not a two-field struct. Five widths exist, each a pair of same-width floats laid out as real part then imaginary part. The name gives the total number of semantic bits, so `c128` is a pair of `f64` and `c32` a pair of `f16`. Alignment follows the component, not the pair.

`c160` and `c256` are thirty-two bytes rather than twenty and thirty-two respectively, because each component uses the sixteen byte storage its scalar type uses. The components round to their own widths: one third is `0.333252` in a `c32` and `0.333333` in a `c64`, exactly as it is in `f16` and `f32`. The alignments shown are for x86-64 Windows. Query the corresponding float on another target: `type_info(c160).alignment == type_info(f80).alignment`, including alignment 4 on `x86-linux-musl` and alignment 8 on `s390x-linux-musl`.

`type_kind` reports `15` for a complex type, its own tag. `Is_Complex(T)` answers true; `Is_Numeric(T)` does not, because `Is_Numeric` is defined as integer or float. That definition is the reason for everything in the next section.
Why the arithmetic is not in the Prelude

Every primitive operator instance in the Prelude is keyed on `Is_Integer(T)` or on `Is_Float(T)`. A complex type satisfies neither, so none of those instances reaches it. `Add`, `Sub`, `Mul`, `Div`, `Neg`, `Num` and `PartialEq` for `Is_Complex(T)` are declared in `std/Math/Complex.glo` instead, together with the constructors and accessors, which are `#magic` functions. Nothing about complex arithmetic is in scope until that file is imported.

error: unknown function complex128
  --> nocomplex.glo:4:10
  |
4 |     a := complex128(1.0, 2.0);
  |          ^^^^^^^^^^

Importing `Math/Complex` supplies the operators and inherent methods. Constructors such as `complex128(real, imaginary)` keep their width-specific free-function names; accessors use receiver calls such as `z.real_part()` and infer the matching component width from `z`.

rows: a complex value from a real and an imaginary component
the real component, as the matching float type
the Euclidean magnitude, as the matching float type

blocks.text:
sum  re 4 im -2
prod re 11 im 2
conj re 1 im -2
norm b  5
a == a  1
default re 0 im 0
Complex accessors belong to their owning type. They are not namespace functions such as `Math.real_part128`: call `z.real_part()`, `z.norm()`, or the explicit receiver form `c128.real_part(z)`.
There is no imaginary literal

Construction is explicit. Glosso has no suffix or directive for an imaginary part; `#I` in particular is not a token, and writing it is `error: unexpected directive 'I'`. The only way to make a complex value with a non-zero imaginary component is a constructor call.

error: unexpected directive 'I'
  --> imaginary.glo:4:24
  |
4 |     a: c128 = 2.0 + 3.0#I;
  |                        ^^

A compile-time integer does reach a complex target and lands in the real part, since the compile-time number rules let an integer family widen into the complex family. That is the whole of the implicit path: there is no conversion from a runtime scalar.

from comptime_int re 3 im 0
built re 1.5 im 0
Mixing a complex and a scalar in one operator is rejected: with `a: c128` and `r: f64`, `a + r` is `error: no operator '+' for c128, f64`. Widen the scalar with a constructor first.
A complex type does not implement `Show`, so a bare `%` has no matching `Formatter` instance for `c128`. Print the components or supply a custom `Formatter` instance.

`c256` components are `f128` and use that type's compiler-runtime helpers when printed; the driver supplies target-specific archives for x86-64 Windows, musl, and WebAssembly. `c160` components are `f80` and print directly as well. Neither component display preserves all the precision of a wide float: the display path narrows to `f64`.
`c160` uses x87 arithmetic on x86 targets and an `fp128` carrier elsewhere, for the same reason `f80` does. `Floating Point` has the detail.

`bool` is one byte with two values, `true` and `false`. It is its own type kind, not a narrow integer: `Is_Bool(bool)` is true and `Is_Integer(bool)` is false, so none of the integer arithmetic instances reaches it and `true + false` is `error: no operator '+' for bool, bool`.

Nothing converts to `bool` implicitly and `bool` converts to nothing. `b: bool = 1;` is `error: got ssize, expected bool`, and `x: s64 = true;` is `error: got bool, expected s64`. The strictness is deliberate: an integer used where a truth value was meant is the most common way for a condition to be silently wrong, and Glosso answers that question in the condition position only, where it is visible.
`cast` is the only bridge

show true/false  1 0
cast(ssize) true   1
cast(bool) 0     0
cast(bool) 5     1
cast(bool) -1    1
size / kind      1 3
default          0
and / or / not   0 1 0
`show` renders a `bool` as `1` or `0`, not as `true` or `false`. The Prelude's shower emits the C strings `"1"` and `"0"`.
`cast(bool)` of an integer is a not-equal-to-zero test, so `5` and `-1` both become `true`.
An uninitialised `bool` local is `false`; the default value of every primitive is its zero.

`&&` and `||` have a single instance each, `(bool, bool)`, with a `#lazy` right operand. A non-`bool` operand is rejected rather than tested: `n && b` with `n: s64` is `error: no operator '&&' for s64, bool`.
Truthiness

A condition does not have to be a `bool`. `if` and `while` accept any type for which the backend has a truth rule, and the rule is chosen by the type's kind. The table below is the complete set; anything outside it is rejected, not guessed at.

rows: the value is ordered-unequal to zero, so `-0.0` and NaN are both false
the optional is present, which is the same null test

blocks.text:
0        skipped
-2       taken
-0.0     skipped
nan      skipped
""       skipped
"x"      taken
*s64     taken
?*s64 .None  skipped

A NaN is false. The float test is an ordered comparison against zero, and an ordered comparison involving a NaN is false whatever the other operand is. So `if x` and `if x != 0.0` disagree on a NaN, and neither `if x` nor `if !x` will be entered by one.

A pointer optional is truthy exactly when it is present because it has no tag to consult: `?*T` is laid out as the bare pointer and `.None` is address zero, so the presence test and the null test are the same instruction. An optional over a value type is a real tagged union, and the rule does not extend to it.

error: values of type Option_s64 have no native truthiness rule [opcode Jz]
  while lowering 'main' at IR instruction 4

The same refusal covers structs, tuples, unions and every other aggregate: `if p` on a struct `P` is `error: values of type P have no native truthiness rule`. Every entry in the table above rests on a word the value already carries: a tag-free null, or a count at offset zero. A fixed `[N]T` carries neither, so write `arr[..]` or `arr.count` and test that.
`!` is a typeclass operator

`!` is not built into the language. It is owned by the `LogicalNot` typeclass, whose declaration lives in `std/Prelude/Primitive_Operators.glo`, and it does only what an instance says it does. The Prelude ships three instances, and no instance covers integers or pointers.

rows: the value is `false`; the body is `#magic "bool_not"`
the optional is `.None`, for every `T`, niche or not

blocks.text:
!false     1
!.Some(5)  0
!.None     1
!.Ok(1)    0
!.Err      1

The two mechanisms answer different questions and cover different types. `!o` works on a `?s64` because `LogicalNot` has an instance for every `?T`, while `if o` on the same value does not, because the truth rule stops at the niche layouts. In the other direction, `if n` on an integer works and `!n` does not: `error: no prefix operator '!' for ssize`.

Truthiness belongs to `if` and `while` alone. `#if` requires a `bool` outright: `#if 3` is `error: #if condition must be bool, got comptime_int`. `ifx` requires one too, reporting it as an ordinary conversion failure: `ifx 3 "a" else "b"` is `error: got ssize, expected bool`. See `Static Branching with #if` and `ifx Expressions`.

Glosso has four built-in string view types. They borrow existing storage and differ in code-unit width and how they determine its length. Counted strings store a pointer and count; C strings store a zero-terminated pointer. No import is needed to use any of them.

All four are one kind to the compiler: `type_kind` answers `4` (`Type_Info_Tag.String`) for every one of them. `string` and `string16` have the layout `{ data, count }`: two native words, or 16 bytes on a 64-bit target and 8 on a 32-bit target. `cstring` and `cstring16` are one pointer wide. Passing any of them by value copies the view, never the character data, and does not transfer ownership of the storage.

rows: stored count, or a scan to the first zero for C strings
a string view does not track an allocation's capacity

blocks.text: `.count` is measured in code units, not in bytes and not in Unicode scalars: a `string16` containing four BMP scalars has `.count` four, but a non-BMP scalar needs two surrogate units. `.data` is a many-pointer to the unit type; `type_name` prints `[*]u8` for the UTF-8 types and `[*]u16` for the UTF-16 ones. The descriptor fields are read-only: assigning `.count` or `.data`, taking their addresses, and assigning `text[index]` are rejected.

count 5
s[0] 104  s[1..3] el
concat hello world
equal 1  differ 0

Indexing yields one code unit as an integer, so `s[0]` on a `string` is a `u8` and prints as the byte value `104`, not as the character `h`. Indexing `string16` or `cstring16` yields a `u16` UTF-16 code unit, including during constant folding; a non-BMP character therefore occupies the lead and trail surrogate at two indexes. Slicing with a range yields a borrowed counted string: `string` for either UTF-8 input and `string16` for either UTF-16 input. It does not preserve C termination. `+` concatenates constant strings only. Build runtime text with `String_Builder`, or use `format` for an owned allocation and `tprint` for temporary text. Repetition uses a loop that writes to a builder. The former string `cat` and `repeat` helpers have been removed.

Iteration is scalar-oriented even though indexing is code-unit-oriented. A `for` over any of the four string types decodes and yields `rune`; malformed input yields U+FFFD, and `it_index` is a scalar ordinal. Iteration and `for <` are detailed in `for` Loops and Iterable.

Use `string.bytes` when the algorithm operates on encoded bytes, and iterate the string itself when it operates on Unicode scalars. The explicit rune-to-`u32` cast above asks the formatter for numeric code points instead of displaying the characters. A reverse string walk also counts iterations from zero; its index is not a byte offset or the original forward scalar index.

`.count` counts code units, so it is not a character count for anything outside ASCII. The four-character string `café` has `.count` five as a `string` and `.count` four as a `string16`, because the `é` occupies two UTF-8 bytes and one UTF-16 unit.

bytes 5 first 99 last 169
utf-16 units 4
cstring count 5 terminator 0
The trailing zero

A non-null `cstring` or `cstring16` points at zero-terminated storage. Its `.count` scans up to the first zero and excludes that terminator; there is no stored length or capacity. Thus `c: cstring = "A\0BC"` has count 1. A default-initialised C string is null and has count zero. Do not dereference its `.data` or assume an empty view is non-null.

`c"text"` directly infers `cstring`, with borrowed static storage and a terminating zero. In contrast, `b"text"` is a fixed `u8` array without an added terminator. Its bytes can be copied or modified like any other fixed array; String Literals covers the prefixes and their escape rules.

`string` and `string16` make no such promise. A string literal happens to carry one, because a literal is emitted as a static constant that is one unit longer than its count. A borrowed slice or an allocating library result need not have a readable zero at `data[count]`. The counted view permits embedded zeros without shortening its count.

Never assume a `string` is terminated. Convert with `string.cstring_from_string` or `string.c_string` from `Strings/Utf8` when a terminator is required; the first takes an allocator and must be released with `cstring.free`, the second allocates from the temporary allocator.
Reaching C

C strings and string literals can supply a read-only pointer of the matching code-unit type. A runtime counted string cannot: its view does not promise termination. For a C API that scans to zero, first construct a C string. For an API that accepts a separate length, pass `.data` and `.count` explicitly.

.data is [*]u8 for string, [*]u16 for string16
104 104 104

The reverse direction is refused by name, because a pointer has no length to recover: `back: string = p;` reports `cannot implicitly convert [*]u8 to string, which carries a count the pointer does not; make a slice of known length and use byte_slice_to_string`. Scanning for a terminator would be a hidden traversal of a buffer that never promised to have one, so the compiler asks for the length instead of inventing it.

Explicit view casts preserve matching code units: `cast(string)bytes` accepts `[]u8`, and `cast([]u8)text` exposes a counted UTF-8 view. The corresponding UTF-16 pair is `string16` and `[]u16`. `cast(string)c_text` and `c_text.to_string()` scan a C string and borrow its storage. None of these operations copies or validates the contents. A runtime counted view still cannot cast to a C string: use an explicit terminating conversion. `cast(cstring)pointer` trusts the caller's termination guarantee; transcoding between UTF-8 and UTF-16 allocates.

cstring count 2 terminator 0
back to string hi
view count 2 first 104
round trip hi
Comparison

`==` and `!=` compare contents, not descriptors: the Prelude declares `($T, T) ::: instance PartialEq where Is_String(T)` with the `str_eq` and `str_ne` intrinsics, and `$T ::: instance Eq where Is_String(T)` makes the relation a full equality. Counted strings compare equal when their counts and code units agree. C strings additionally distinguish a null pointer from a non-null pointer to an empty string, although both have count zero. Two null C strings compare equal.

All four types have lexicographic `PartialOrd` instances. `<=>` uses the `str_cmp` intrinsic; `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=` are the class defaults written over that result. UTF-8 byte order agrees with code-point order for valid UTF-8, and length breaks a shared-prefix tie. `string16` and `cstring16` compare unsigned UTF-16 code units rather than raw bytes, so their order is independent of the target's endianness.
Both operands must still be the same string type. Ordering is declared for pairs of the same type, so comparing a `string` against a `cstring` requires an explicit conversion to a common view type.

All four types implement `Show` and support the default `%` selector. `string` renders its view unchanged; `cstring` first scans for the terminator and borrows the resulting bytes. Both UTF-16 forms decode into temporary UTF-8 text for display. Rendering does not transfer ownership of the input or make its backing storage live longer.
Backing storage and ownership

Slicing, `substring`, trimming, byte views, and split pieces borrow the input. `split` allocates an array of views, so free that array without freeing its pieces. A view cannot outlive its backing storage or survive an operation that invalidates it. A literal's storage is static.

`String_Builder` owns a growable buffer and remembers its allocator. Scope exit releases it through `Drop`; `to_string()` borrows the buffer until the next mutation or release. `clone()` creates an independent allocation, while consuming `into_string()` transfers the buffer. Those returned string views do not remember an allocator or free themselves: release an allocated result once with its producing allocator. Import `Strings/Memory` to use `text.free(allocator)` on owned UTF-8 buffers. `Strings/Utf8` and the `Strings` umbrella also export it; `String_Builder` imports it for its own implementation. UTF-16 and C-string cleanup comes from the matching `Strings/Utf16` or `Strings/Utf8` component. A freed descriptor and all its aliases become invalid. Never free a literal, a borrowed substring, or a temporary-arena result with the ordinary heap allocator. For an owned arena allocation, text.into_temporary() transfers its release obligation to that arena. It preserves the bytes only until the next arena reset or restore.

`Simd(T, N)` is a first-class primitive type constructor holding exactly `N` inline lanes of type `T`; it needs no import to spell. `std/Simd.glo` supplies its helpers and operator instances. The compile-time evaluator executes each lane scalarly; the LLVM backend receives a fixed-width vector and selects native instructions where the target has them.

sum 11 22 33 44
lanes 4 element f32 size 16 kind 16
count 4 name Simd(f32, 4)
after lane store 99

A `Simd` is not an array. Internally it is an array type carrying a vector flag, so `Is_Simd(V4)` is `1` while `Is_Array(V4)` is `0`, and `type_kind` answers `16` rather than `6`. `Type::repr` renders it `Simd(f32, 4)`, which is what every diagnostic naming one prints.
Lane counts and lane types

The lane count must be a literal in `1..64`, and the lane type must be an integer of at most 64 bits, `f32`, or `f64`. Both limits are checked where the type is written, so a bad shape is a type error and never a backend surprise.

`Simd lane count must be a literal in 1..64`

A vector literal is `#simd` followed by a dot-bracket literal. The prefix is required and the context must already be a `Simd(T, N)`: an unprefixed `.[...]` builds an ordinary fixed array and is never reinterpreted, which is what keeps the two shapes from silently swapping places. The element count must equal the lane count exactly.

blocks.text: Lane access, and the missing `.data`

`value[i]` and `value[i] = lane` go through the ordinary `[]` and `[]=` operators and lower to LLVM `extractelement` and `insertelement`; the store replaces a lane in the value, it does not write through a pointer. `.count` reports the lane count. There is deliberately no `.data` (`Simd has no stable .data pointer`) and no slicing (`slice constructor does not support SIMD arrays`), because the register layout of a vector is a target decision and exposing an address would make it a promise.

The internal vector ABI is not a C ABI. Cross a foreign boundary with ordinary scalar memory and move lanes with `simd_load` and `simd_store`, which accept unaligned addresses and lower with alignment 1.

A `Simd(T, N)` and a fixed `[N]T` of the same element type convert in both directions, but only through `cast` or `acast`, and only at exactly matching shape. There is no implicit conversion: `v: V4 = src;` reports `cannot implicitly convert [4]f32 to Simd(f32, 4); use cast(Simd(f32, 4))value or acast`. A mismatched shape is not castable either, so `cast(Simd(f32, 4)) src` on a `[8]f32` is `cannot cast [8]f32 to Simd(f32, 4)`.
Helpers and operators

`std/Simd.glo` declares `($V, V)` instances of `Add`, `Sub`, `Mul`, `Div`, `BitAnd`, `BitOr`, `BitXor`, `ShiftLeft` and `ShiftRight`, plus `Neg` and `BitNot` over `Is_Simd(V)`, so vectors use the ordinary operator spellings lane-wise. Both operands must be the same vector type; there is no scalar-against-vector instance, which is what `simd_splat` exists for.

`Matrix(T, Rows, Cols)` is the other primitive flagged array type: fixed inline row-major storage, dimensions part of the type, no allocator and no view state. `std/Math/Matrix.glo` supplies its helpers. The flat index of `(row, column)` is `row * Cols + column`, and that flat index is what `[]` takes. A matrix value copies like any other value, so pass a pointer when a caller should mutate one or when the value is large.

`value.get` returns a `(value, ok)` tuple rather than trapping, and `value.set` is functional: it returns a new matrix and leaves its argument alone, which is what keeps matrix values ordinary values in both the compile-time evaluator and native code. The shape intrinsics `matrix_transpose_type`, `matrix_product_type` and `matrix_matvec_result_type` compute result types at compile time and reject mismatched shapes there; the vector argument of the last one is a fixed `[Cols]T`, not a `Simd`.

`type` is a type whose values are types. A type value is obtained by naming a type, and it can be bound to a constant, compared, passed as a parameter and switched on. It is a compile-time value: `size_of(type)` is `0`, because a type carries no runtime representation of its own.

The introspection intrinsics live in `std/Meta/Utilities.glo` and the classifying predicates in `std/Meta/Types.glo`; both come in with `#import "Meta";`. Every one of them is folded to a constant during checking, so they belong in `#comptime`, `#if`, `where`, constant initialisers and `#insert`.

`type_of(value)` is the static type of an expression, `type_name(T)` its printed spelling, `size_of(T)` its size in bytes under natural C layout, `type_kind(T)` its `Type_Info_Tag`, and `type_info(T)` a record holding all of that at once. There is no `align_of`: writing one is `unknown function align_of`, and alignment is read from `type_info(T).alignment`. Field, variant and enum reflection is a larger surface and is covered in Reflection.

`type_kind` returns an enum, and `show` prints an enum's numeric value rather than its name, so `print("%", type_kind(s8))` prints `1`. The tag set is closed and is declared as `Type_Info_Tag` in `std/Meta/Types.glo`.

The tag values are `0` through `17` and `19`; `18` remains reserved for ABI compatibility. `Code`, `Pattern`, `Namespace`, and `Library` currently fall back to `Void`/`0` in `type_kind`; the annotation-only `Typeclass(...)` and `Macro(...)` forms have the same internal fallback. That classification does not make any of them the `void` type.
Types of named definitions

A declaration can state the type of the compile-time definition value between its name and initializer. Aggregate and distinct-type definitions produce `type`; imports and loads produce `Namespace`; a `#library` definition produces `Library`; typeclasses produce `Typeclass(parameter kinds...)`; and macros produce `Macro(function signature)`. An ordinary procedure definition instead has its function type.

`Typeclass` needs at least one type argument, each describing a parameter kind. `Macro` needs exactly one function-signature argument. Both parameterised forms are valid only in this declaration-annotation position: they are not callable constructors or ordinary first-class type expressions. They describe compile-time definitions, not runtime payloads, and the checker rejects a mismatched annotation.
The `Is_*` predicates

`std/Meta/Types.glo` wraps the tag comparison in a family of named predicates: `Is_Integer`, `Is_Rune`, `Is_Character`, `Is_Float`, `Is_Complex`, `Is_Numeric`, `Is_Bool`, `Is_String`, `Is_Pointer`, `Is_Procedure`, `Is_Addressable`, `Is_Enum`, `Is_Struct`, `Is_Union`, `Is_Array`, `Is_Simd`, `Is_Matrix` and `Is_Label`. They are what `where` clauses and instance heads are written against, so they are the working vocabulary rather than `type_kind` comparisons.

`Is_Numeric` is `Is_Integer(T) || Is_Float(T)` and therefore excludes complex numbers and runes: `Is_Numeric(c128)` and `Is_Numeric(rune)` are both `0`. Bytes remain integers, so `Is_Numeric(u8)` is `1`.

`Is_Character(T)` is `Is_Rune(T)`. The former `Is_Char` predicate has been removed with the `char` type. A rune has integer-width storage internally, but its dedicated tag keeps it out of generic integer and numeric instances.
`Is_Addressable` is `Is_Pointer(T) || Is_Procedure(T)`, which is the predicate the pointer-equality instance is keyed on.
The checker answers these for the compile-time number kinds too: `Is_Integer(comptime_int)` is true, which is what lets `1 + 2` resolve against instances declared over `Is_Integer(T)`.
The predicates are capitalised. `is_integer(s32)` is `unknown function is_integer` with `help: did you mean 'Is_Integer'?`.

A parameter declared `Q: type` receives a type as its argument. For a `where` clause to see it, the parameter has to be a binder the signature already depends on or be marked `#comptime`, as above; a bare `Q: type` that appears nowhere else in the signature leaves the constraint unevaluated and every call fails with `constraint failed`. Equality and switching

`(type, type)` has a `PartialEq` instance, so `T == s32` is an ordinary comparison folded at compile time, and a `case` list of types is the natural way to branch on one. Equality is over the type value, so native and fixed widths remain distinguishable: `ssize != s64` and `usize != u64`, even on a 64-bit target. C spellings normalize to the fixed-width type instead, so `int64_t == s64`.

Type queries fold during checking. Bind a query to a constant, such as `X :: type_of(x);`, when its answer is needed by another intrinsic. A mutable local holding a type value is not a compile-time constant: `type_kind(t)` on such a local reports `unknown const t`.
Unevaluated type queries

`type_of(value)` is a free function imported from Meta. Its argument is typechecked but never evaluated, so a call inside it has no side effects and a managed argument does not move. It reports the expression's static type: an any value reports any, rather than its boxed payload type.
type=s64 calls=0

A written numeric literal does not have `ssize` or `f64`. It has one of three compile-time kinds whose exact value the checker knows and whose runtime type a context chooses: `comptime_int`, `comptime_float` and `comptime_complex`. Keeping the value exact until something concrete decides it is what makes `x: u8 = 200` and `x: s128 = 200` both mean the number two hundred rather than a widening of a 64-bit payload.

Annotating a declaration with a numeric constant rather than a type produces one: with `M :: 4;`, writing `m: M = .[1, 2, 3];` reports `got [3]comptime_int, expected comptime_int`. `comptime_complex` is currently unreachable, because there is no imaginary literal; `#I` is `unexpected directive 'I'`. A `#char` literal is a separate case rather than a `comptime_int`: ASCII defaults to `u8`, and non-ASCII defaults to `rune`. `#char` Character Literals covers its contextual rule.
Defaulting

When nothing decides a compile-time number, it takes its default. That happens at a `:=` binding, which has no annotation to consult, and at a generic parameter that binds the literal directly, so `describe(5)` on `describe :: (value: $T)` instantiates `T` as `ssize`. The defaults are the target's native signed width for integers and `f64` for floats.

5 -> ssize / 5.0 -> f64 / 1 + 2 -> ssize (3)
f64 from an integer literal 5 ; c128 from one is c128

Arithmetic over two compile-time numbers stays compile-time and meets at the wider family: integer is narrower than float, which is narrower than complex. `+`, `-`, `*` and `/` keep the joined kind; `%`, `&`, `|`, `^`, `<<` and `>>` are integer-only, and `1.5 % 2.0` falls out of the compile-time rule and then fails as `no operator '%' for f64, f64`; comparisons produce `bool`. When one operand is concrete the concrete side decides outright, which is why `x + 1` on a `u8` is `u8` arithmetic and `f * 2.0` on an `f32` is `f32` arithmetic, with no promotion to the default width.
Which types a compile-time number reaches
A compile-time number may become any type in its own family or a wider one. The relation is one-directional and stops at `distinct` types, which convert in neither direction without a `cast`.

rows: any integer, any float, any complex

blocks.text: This is a rule about literals, not about values. `f: f64 = 5;` compiles and a named `K :: 5; b: f64 = K;` compiles, because both are still compile-time integers. Once a value has a runtime type the families are sealed: `x: s64 = 5; y: f64 = x;` is `got s64, expected f64`, and the reverse is `got f64, expected s64`.

Going the other way across the families is refused with the kind named: `x: s64 = 1.5;` is `cannot implicitly convert comptime_float to s64` and `x: u8 = 1.0;` is `cannot implicitly convert comptime_float to u8`. A `distinct` target refuses a cross-family literal for the same reason: with `Meters :: distinct f64;`, `m: Meters = 3;` is `cannot implicitly convert comptime_int to Meters`. `cast` and `acast` covers the explicit spelling, and `distinct` Nominal Types covers the nominal rule.
Joint defaulting across a call

When several instances could take the same call because every argument is still undecided, the tie is broken by defaulting: the candidate whose parameter types are exactly what those arguments would default to wins. The rule fires only when a tie exists and only when some argument was undecided, so an already unambiguous call is untouched.

(1, 2)     chose ssize, ssize
(1.5, 2.5) chose f64, f64

All three instances accept `(1, 2)`, since a `comptime_int` reaches `ssize`, `f64` and `f32` alike; the joint default `(ssize, ssize)` picks one. The narrowing is joint and exact: adding `pair_name(1, 2.5)` to the program above is `ambiguous typeclass operation 'pair_name' for these argument types`, because the joint default is `(ssize, f64)` and no instance has that shape. Delete the `(f32, f32)` instance and the same call resolves to `(f64, f64)`, as the only remaining candidate every argument can reach.
The value-fitting rule

Reaching a type is a question about families; fitting it is a question about the value. At an integer context the checker asks whether the magnitude and sign the programmer wrote fit the target's range, and answers from the written syntax rather than from a wrapped payload. That is why a value at the exact edge of a type is accepted and one past it is a compile error rather than a runtime abort.

rows: accepted; the sign folds into the literal, so no negation runs
`-129 does not fit s8, whose range is -128..=127`
`300 does not fit u8, whose range is 0..=255`
`-1 does not fit u8, whose range is 0..=255`
accepted; a based literal is a bit pattern
`511 does not fit s8, whose range is -128..=127`

blocks.text: A based literal is read as a bit pattern, so it may use every bit of the target width and `16#ffff_ffff_ffff_ffff` is `18446744073709551615` at `u64` and `-1` at `s64`. Over-wide ones say so: the `s8` row above carries `note: a based literal is a bit pattern, so it may use every bit of s8 - this one is wider than that`. A leading `-` drops the relaxation, because it means a magnitude again. `~` is re-evaluated at the target width, so `~127` is `-128` at `s8` and `128` at `u8`, and negating it at `s8` asks for `+128`, which does not fit.

The check recurses into the operands of integer arithmetic but does not fold the result: each written operand must fit, so `x: u8 = 255 + 0;` compiles and prints `255`, while `x: u8 = 300 + 0;` is rejected on the `300`. An expression whose operands each fit but whose result does not is a runtime question, and `x: u8 = 200 + 100;` compiles and aborts under the checked arithmetic of `-O0` and `-O1`. A shift count is exempted from this rule and judged against the shifted type's width instead.

Named compile-time integers and explicit `#comptime` results must fit the type they receive too. With `K :: 300;`, `x: u8 = K;` is rejected just as `x: u8 = 300;` is. A provably fitting typed constant can narrow without a cast; that exception does not permit an out-of-range value.

Coercion is the conversion the compiler performs without being asked: at a declaration's initialiser, at an assignment, at a call argument, at a `return`, and at every aggregate-literal field. Glosso's default is strict. C's rule that any arithmetic type converts to any other is gone, because it silently truncates and silently reinterprets signs; what remains implicit is the set of conversions that cannot lose information. `cast` and `acast` is the explicit way to do the rest.
The order the checker asks in

`Checker::coercible` tries the rules below in order and stops at the first that accepts. The order matters at one point in particular: the `distinct` guard runs before every structural rule, so a nominal type never slips through the integer or pointer cases.

rows: every source; the value is boxed
nothing across a nominal boundary, in either direction
only a lossless widening, or anything under `lossy_numerics`
matching calling convention, varargs and `noalias`, with every parameter and the return coercing
a target its family reaches, if the value fits
only a niche optional pointer, never a bare one
the same element type with compatible mutability and `volatile`
`&.[...]` to `[]T` when its element type and qualifiers are compatible
the same pointer kind, compatible pointees, never read-only to mutable
C string or string literal to pointer
read-only pointer of the matching code-unit type

blocks.text: Everything else is rejected, and there are two shapes of message. A rejected assignment or return reports `got <actual>, expected <expected>`; a rejected argument reports `arg type <actual> != <expected> in call <name>`. A handful of cases have their own wording where the generic form would not say what to do instead.
Lossless integer widening

Integer to integer is accepted when no value of the source is unrepresentable in the target. Same signedness needs only a target at least as wide. An unsigned source reaching a signed target needs a strictly wider target, because the sign bit costs a bit. A signed source never reaches an unsigned target at any width, because negatives have nowhere to go.

The rule is asked of a width-and-signedness profile. Native integers use the target width, while fixed and normalized C spellings keep their written widths. On x86-64, `s64` and `ssize` therefore have the same profile but remain different type values and print under their own names. They may widen to the same destinations without becoming interchangeable. Relaxing Strictness with `lossy_numerics` covers the section-scoped gate that turns the whole integer rule off.
Floats never convert

No float type converts implicitly to any other, in either direction: `y: f64 = x;` on an `f32` is `got f32, expected f64`, and the narrowing is `got f64, expected f32`. Widening is arguably lossless, but making it implicit would make the narrowing look symmetrical, and a mixed-precision expression would silently pick a width. Cross-family conversion is likewise closed once a value has a runtime type: `y: f64 = x;` on an `s64` is `got s64, expected f64`, and `y: s64 = x;` on an `f64` is `got f64, expected s64`. `bool` participates in neither direction: `b: bool = 1;` is `got ssize, expected bool` because the literal defaults, while `x: s64 = true;` is `got bool, expected s64`.
`#enable(lossy_numerics)` does not change any of this. The gate is consulted only in the integer-to-integer branch, so both directions between float types stay errors under it.
Pointers, slices, and optionals

A pointer reaches a pointer of the same kind with a compatible pointee, and writable reaches read-only but never the reverse. `*void` is the deliberate any-pointer spelling and matches every pointee. A pointer-like value reaches the matching niche optional for free, because the representations are identical; `null` reaches only such an optional, and a bare pointer excludes zero precisely so that the niche can put `.None` there.

mutable pointer at a read-only parameter 7
pointer at an optional pointer 7
null at an optional pointer -1
mutable slice at a read-only slice 3
temporary fixed-array pointer at a slice 3

`&.[...]` materialises anonymous fixed-array storage and points at it; an expected borrowed-slice type recovers the element pointer and count. The storage lasts only for the surrounding expression, which makes an immediate call safe. Do not retain or return that slice; give the array a name before slicing it when the borrow must live longer.

The rejections are as narrow as the acceptances. Passing a read-only pointer where writable access is required is `arg type *s64 != *mut s64`; `*T` and `[*]T` describe different things, one element against a run of them, and do not interconvert, so passing a `*s64` where `[*]s64` is wanted is `arg type *s64 != [*]s64`; a differing pointee is `arg type *s64 != *s32`. `p: *s64 = null;` is `'null' is not a value of *s64`, with `note: a plain pointer excludes zero - write ?*s64 for a pointer that may be absent` and `note: its absent value is spelled '.None'`. `#enable(pointer_punning)`, described in Feature Gates, relaxes the pointer rules.
Strings

A `cstring` reaches a `*u8` or `*s8` pointer, and a `cstring16` reaches a `*u16` or `*s16` pointer. Literals also support these conversions. Counted `string` and `string16` variables do not promise C termination, so pass their data and count explicitly or construct a C string. Explicit matching-code-unit view casts are covered in Built-in Strings.
Compile-time native integers and collection elements

A compile-time scalar of the native/default `ssize` type may narrow where an ordinary fixed-width value cannot, provided its value is provably in range; an explicit `: ssize :` annotation still uses that native route. Elements read from immutable compile-time collections receive the same value-based exception even when the collection element type is fixed, which keeps byte tables such as `[N]s64` convenient. A scalar declared as `A : s64 : 100` retains `s64` and does not take either route.

A value that is not foldable gets nothing: `runtime: s64 = 100; narrow: u8 = runtime;` is `got s64, expected u8`, because a local is not a constant the checker may evaluate. The fit check still applies to an annotated native constant: `Limit : ssize : 300;` makes the same declaration `got ssize, expected u8`. Collection lookup never bypasses it either: `VALUES : [1]s64 : .[300]; byte: u8 = VALUES[0];` is `got s64, expected u8`. The earlier literal-fitting chapter records the current scalar-name exception for an out-of-range `::` constant.

A cast is the explicit conversion. Everything Glosso converts on its own is described in the chapter on conversions; a cast is what the program writes when the conversion loses information, changes the interpretation of a bit pattern, or crosses a nominal boundary the checker will not cross silently.

There are two spellings and they differ in exactly one respect: where the target type comes from. `cast(T)` writes the target down; `acast` takes the type the surrounding context expects. Both produce the same node in the checker, so every rule below applies to both.

headers: Where the target type comes from

blocks.text: The parentheses on `cast` are mandatory and the diagnostic points at the other form: `cast ssize 5` is `error: cast requires a type in parentheses; use acast for contextual casts`. `acast` is the mirror image and never takes a parenthesised type at all; `acast(f64) 3` is not a form, and the compiler reads it as an `acast` with no context followed by a parenthesised expression.
Where `acast` finds a type
`acast` resolves in any position that already carries an expected type. That is the same set of positions a literal is checked against, and it is a closed set.
The initialiser of a declaration with a type annotation.
The right side of a plain assignment to a typed place.
An argument at a parameter with a declared type.
A field of an aggregate literal at a known field type.
A `return` in a procedure with a declared return type.

Everywhere else there is nothing to read the target from, and the compiler says so rather than guessing: `a := acast 5`, an operand of a binary operator, and a variadic argument all produce `error: acast needs a target type from context or an explicit cast type`. In those positions `cast(T)` is the only spelling.
What a cast accepts

A cast is legal when the source and target are semantically the same type, or when they fall into one of the pairs below. The list is small on purpose: a cast reinterprets or converts a value, it does not restructure one, so there is no cast between aggregates and no cast that builds a `string`.

rows: numeric conversion: truncate, extend, or round toward zero
the number as an address, asserted non-zero
exact shape only; the lane type and count must match

blocks.text: Everything else is `cannot cast <source> to <target>`, with both types printed under their own names. `cast(ssize) s` on a `string` is `error: cannot cast string to ssize`; `cast(ssize) p` on a struct `P` is `error: cannot cast P to ssize`; `cast(any) 5` is `error: cannot cast ssize to any`, because boxing into `any` is an implicit conversion and not a cast. A fixed array casts only to a `Simd` of its exact shape, so `cast([2]f32) a` on a `[4]f32` is `error: cannot cast [4]f32 to [2]f32`.

Narrowing truncates instead of erroring, and signedness is reinterpreted rather than rejected. `b: s8 = wide` on a `u64` is `error: got u64, expected s8`; `cast(s8) wide` keeps the low bits, and `cast(u8) -1` is `255`.

Float to integer truncates toward zero while the value is in range and saturates to the target's nearest bound when it is not. This applies to a float literal directly under `cast` as well as a runtime value, so `cast(u8)(300.0)` is `255` and `cast(s8)(300.0)` is `127`. Integer to float and `f64` to `f32` also convert. Negative values cast to an unsigned integer clamp to zero, and NaN converts to zero. These are the conversion's semantics, not optional `-O1` safety checks. None of these runtime numeric conversions is implicit.

A compile-time integer reaches any integer target without the fitting check: `cast(u8) 300` keeps the low bits and is `44`, where `x: u8 = 300` is `error: 300 does not fit u8, whose range is 0..=255`. A compile-time float follows the saturating float-to-integer rule instead.

An `enum` crosses to and from its base integer in both directions, and a `distinct` type crosses to and from its representation in both directions. Nothing else in the language crosses both ways; the `distinct` case is covered in the chapter on `distinct` nominal types.

A cast supplies the target context while preserving the exact compile-time magnitude, which matters for literals wider than 64 bits. Thus `cast(u128) 340282366920938463463374607431768211455` prints the number that was written, while the same literal bound with `:=` is `error: 340282366920938463463374607431768211455 does not fit ssize, whose range is -9223372036854775808..=9223372036854775807`.
`cast(*T)` asserts, `cast(?*T)` is total

Every pointer flavour in Glosso excludes zero. That is what gives `?*T` a free niche, where `.None` is address 0: a zero `*T` would be indistinguishable from `.None`, and `.Some(p)` would match `.None`. A cast from an address integer to a bare pointer therefore asserts the address is not zero. When the compiler can already fold the address to zero, `cast(*T)` is a compile error rather than a value, and the diagnostic points at the spelling that is total.

error: cast to *ssize of an address that is zero at compile time
note: a plain pointer excludes zero - that is what gives ?T its niche, where .None IS address 0
note: cast to ?*ssize instead, which is total and yields .None here

An address that is not known until run time carries the assertion as a safety check instead. That check covers `*T`, `[*]T`, and `#fn_ptr` alike, because all three take the same niche; it reports the target type and aborts, and it is emitted at `-O0` and `-O1` only, like every other runtime check.

start
cast to [*]ssize of an address that is zero
glosso: program exited with status exit code: 134
`cast(?*T) addr` is the same reinterpretation with the assertion dropped. It is total: zero becomes `.None`, anything else becomes `.Some`, and no check is emitted because no case is excluded.

none
some 7

The reverse direction is deliberately absent. `cast(*T) opt` on a `?*T` is `error: cannot cast Option__ssize to *ssize`, even though the niche layout would make it free. An optional already has a total spelling that the compiler verifies rather than asserts, so a cast that unwrapped one would be a second escape hatch with no gate and no check above `-O1`.

`distinct T` declares a type with the representation of `T` and an identity of its own. Nothing about the layout changes: the size, the alignment, and the machine operations are those of `T`. What changes is that the checker treats the two as unrelated, so a length cannot be assigned to a duration and a file handle cannot be added to a socket handle.
`distinct` is a contextual keyword. It is recognised only in type position directly after `::`, so it remains available as an ordinary identifier everywhere else.
identifier still works: 5
Representation and identity

A distinct type carries the representation's kind and name untouched and adds a nominal tag. `size_of(Handle)` is `4` because `u32` is 4 bytes, and `type_name(Handle)` is `Handle` because the tag is what names the type. The same tag is what diagnostics print, so a mismatch reads `got Meters, expected f64` rather than the useless `got f64, expected f64`.

The representation may be any scalar, pointer, `bool`, or `enum`. It may not be a struct: `distinct P` over a struct `P` declares fine but has no way to construct a value, because `cast(Q) p` is `error: cannot cast P to Q`. The same is true of `distinct string`, which is therefore unusable in practice.
Crossing the boundary

There is no implicit conversion in either direction. This rule is checked before every other coercion rule, which is why it applies even where the representations are identical: `x: f64 = m` on a `Meters` is `error: got Meters, expected f64`, `f: Feet = m` is `error: got Meters, expected Feet`, and `c: Count = x` on an `s64` is `error: got s64, expected Count`.
A cast crosses in both directions, and a distinct type is the only thing in the language a cast will cross both ways.
a+b = 7 a<b = 1

A literal of the representation's own family is stamped with the distinct type directly, so `a: Meters = 3.0` compiles without a cast. A literal of a different family is not: `m: Meters = 3` is `error: cannot implicitly convert comptime_int to Meters`. The rule that refuses a compile-time number at a distinct target runs after the one that stamps a matching literal kind, and the asymmetry is visible in nothing else.
`#derive` and the operations a distinct type has

A distinct type gets only the classes it names. Without a `#derive` it has no operators at all, and the diagnostic names the fix: `error: no operator '+' for Meters and Meters: a distinct type gets only the classes it derives; add '#derive(...)' or '#derive,all' on the declaration of 'Meters'`.

This is the point of the feature rather than an inconvenience. A type that inherited everything from its representation would be a type alias with a different spelling; naming the classes is how a distinct type says which of the representation's operations are meaningful for it. Adding two lengths is meaningful, multiplying two lengths is not, and scaling a length by a plain number is.

rows: the same-type instance: every operand and the result are the nominal type
spells the operand types out where they differ
a comma-separated list; the two forms mix freely

blocks.text: No code is generated. The operator is resolved on the representation and the nominal tag is put back when the representation's result is the representation, so `Meters + Meters` is `Meters` and `Meters * f64` is `Meters`, while `Meters == Meters` stays `bool` and `Meters <=> Meters` stays `Ordering`.

scaled = 6
s/t = 3.5 s<t = 0

Each entry grants exactly what it names and nothing adjacent. `#derive(Mul(Meters, f64))` does not give `Meters * Meters`, and `#derive(Add)` does not give `Meters + f64`; both are the same `no operator` error. `#derive,all` waves every operator through, but the operation still has to exist on the representation: `s % t` on a `distinct f64` with `#derive,all` falls through to `error: no operator '%' for f64, f64`.

Two spellings are rejected outright. `#derive` with neither a list nor a mode is `error: '#derive' on a distinct type needs a class list or ',all'`, and any other mode is `error: unknown '#derive' mode 'every'; the only one is 'all'`.

The derive list gates operators only. A named typeclass method still resolves through the ordinary generic instances, because the representation's predicate is still true of the distinct type: `Is_Float(Meters)` holds, so `show(a)` on a `Meters :: distinct f64` with no `#derive` at all prints `3.5`.

Glosso converts between numeric types implicitly only when the conversion cannot lose anything: an integer widens to a type that can hold every one of its values, and nothing else. Floats never convert implicitly in either direction, and neither does `bool`. `#enable(lossy_numerics)` relaxes exactly one clause of that rule.

Under the gate, any integer type coerces to any other integer type. Narrowing truncates and a signedness change reinterprets the bits, both silently, at every position where a coercion happens: assignment, argument passing, and `return`.
Section scoping

`#enable` and `#disable` are parser directives, not statements. They may appear only between top-level declarations, and the gate is stamped on every declaration parsed while it is on. Writing `#enable(lossy_numerics)` inside a procedure body is `error: unexpected directive 'enable'`.

The stamp is per declaration and covers the whole of it, body included. A declaration after the matching `#disable` is unaffected: in the fragment below `inside` compiles and `outside` is `error: got u64, expected s8`.

Because the gate belongs to the declaration that performs the coercion, it does not travel with a procedure to its call sites. A `takes :: (v: s8)` declared under the gate does not accept a `u64` argument from an ungated caller: the call is `error: arg type u64 != s8 in call takes`. The parser state also ends with the file, so the gate never reaches a `#load`ed or `#import`ed source.
What the gate does not restore
The gate is consulted in one branch of one function: the integer to integer case of the coercion rule. Every other rejection stands, and each of the following still fails with the gate on.

rows: `error: 300 does not fit u8, whose range is 0..=255`

blocks.text: Two of those are worth spelling out. The distinct-type rule runs before the numeric rules and is not a numeric rule at all, so no gate reaches it; `cast` remains the only bridge. And the fitting check on a written literal is a question about the literal, not about a conversion, so it survives too: the gate makes a `u64` variable narrow to `u8`, it does not make `300` fit in one.

The gate also does not touch operator resolution. Every primitive operator instance is homogeneous, keyed on `($T, T)`, and mixed operand widths are an instance-selection failure rather than a coercion failure. With the gate on, `a + b` for `a: u8` and `b: u16` is still `error: no operator '+' for u8, u16`.

Feature names are checked: `#enable(lossy_stuff)` is `error: unknown feature 'lossy_stuff'`. The siblings of this gate are `pointer_punning` and `allow_union_unwrap`, described in the chapter on feature gates.
Why the default is strict

C's conversion rules are the reason integer bugs are hard to see: the truncation and the sign flip look exactly like the code that does not convert at all. Making them explicit costs a `cast` at each site and buys three things.
Every place a value can change is written down, so a narrowing is found by reading rather than by running.
A diagnostic can name both types, which is only useful when the program did not ask for the conversion. `got usize, expected ssize` is a question about intent; a silent truncation is not.

Overflow checking has something to check. The runtime checks described in the chapter on overflow assume a value's type is the type the program chose for it, which is false as soon as widths convert on their own.

`lossy_numerics` exists for the code where that trade is wrong: hand-translated C, a hash or checksum written in terms of deliberate truncation, or a block of bit manipulation where every line would otherwise carry a cast. Bracketing such a block with `#enable` and `#disable` keeps the relaxation visible and bounded, which a command-line flag would not.

Signed and unsigned integer overflow is a checked failure in Glosso, not wraparound and not undefined behaviour. The check is emitted by the backend, so whether it is present is a property of the build, and the property is exactly the optimisation level.
Runtime checks are on when the optimisation level is 0 or 1. `-O1` is the default, so a plain `glosso --run bump.glo` is a checked build; the line the driver prints names the level it used.
glosso: link bump.exe (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)

The size modes -Os, -Oz, and -Ozz produce runnable artifacts. They combine LLVM optimization with optsize/minsize attributes and target-specific linker size policies. Runtime checks are disabled in these modes; use -O0 or -O1 for checked builds. -Ozz also strips symbols and metadata.
What is checked

The arithmetic check covers `+`, `-`, and `*` on integers, and unary `-`, which is lowered as a checked `0 - x`. Each is emitted as an LLVM overflow intrinsic in the operand's own signedness, and the overflow bit branches to an abort.

$ glosso --run bump.glo
glosso: compile bump.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
glosso: link bump.exe (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
glosso: done bump.exe  (backend=llvm, target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
before
runtime check failed: arithmetic.overflow
glosso: program exited with status 134

$ glosso --run -O2 bump.glo
glosso: compile bump.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
glosso: link bump.exe (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O2)
glosso: done bump.exe  (backend=llvm, target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O2)
before
after: -128
The same flag gates the complete backend check family, so an unchecked build drops all of them together.

rows: integer `/`, `//`, `%` by zero, and signed division `T.MIN / -1`
`runtime check failed: divide.by.zero` or `divide.overflow`, then abort
when available, a source position followed by `runtime check failed: array.bounds`, then abort
`cast` of a runtime-zero address to a pointer
`cast to *ssize of an address that is zero`, then abort
`union access: expected .Square, but the value holds one of .Circle | .Square`, then abort
integer formatting with a base outside 2..=16
`integer formatting base is outside 2..=16`, then abort

blocks.text: Every check prints a category before terminating. Array bounds and a union mismatch carry a source position when available; arithmetic, division, and slice bounds name the failed operation without a source position or stack trace.
What is not checked

At `-O2` and above, division checks are omitted. Division by zero and signed `T.MIN / -1` then reach LLVM and the target hardware with no language-level result. Remainder by zero is likewise invalid in an unchecked build. Signed `T.MIN % -1` is not an overflow case: the backend substitutes a divisor of `1`, so the result is reliably `0` at every optimisation level.
The wrapping operators `+%`, `-%`, `*%`, and prefix `-%` are never checked; wrapping is what they mean.
The saturating operators `+|`, `-|`, `*|`, and `<<|` are never checked; clamping is what they mean.

Shifts do not trap at run time. A written literal count at least as large as the operand width is rejected, but a dynamic over-shift has a defined result: left and logical-right shifts yield zero, and arithmetic-right shift yields the sign. A negative signed count is treated as out of range by the same rule. The backend avoids LLVM poison for every case.
Float arithmetic is never checked. IEEE 754 produces an infinity or a NaN and the program continues.
A many-pointer index carries no length, so it cannot be bounds checked at any level.
Compile-time integer arithmetic is checked

Ordinary constant integer arithmetic must fit its target type. Overflow in a compile-time expression is rejected with the operands, result, and allowed range. Use explicit wrapping operators such as +% when wrapping is intended. Runtime optimization levels do not permit overflowing constant expressions. Invalid constant division is also rejected.
error: constant arithmetic overflow: 200 + 100 = 300 does not fit u8, whose range is 0..=255

At runtime, -O0 and -O1 check ordinary integer arithmetic and counted array access. Optimized builds may omit those runtime checks. Explicit wrapping and saturating operators retain their specified behavior.

Binary operator precedence in Glosso is an integer from 0 to 20. Higher binds tighter. The scale is deliberately sparse: odd and unused tiers are left free so a library can introduce an operator that lands between two existing families without renumbering anything.

A level is not a property of a spelling the compiler knows in advance. It comes from the `#operator` directive on the typeclass method that declares the operator, and the prescan reads every visible declaration before parsing begins. That mechanism is described in the chapter on the operator prescan; this chapter is the table it produces for the prelude, and the rules a new entry must follow.

Tiers 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, and 15 are unoccupied as well. The prelude uses twelve of the twenty-one levels, and a user-declared operator may claim any level from 0 to 1000; the top of that range binds tighter than everything in the table.

Unary operators have no tier. A prefix operator binds tighter than every infix operator, and a suffix operator binds to the primary expression it follows, so `-a + b` is `(-a) + b` and `~a & b` is `(~a) & b`.
Bitwise binds tighter than comparison

This is the one place the table departs from C. In C, and in Glosso before the rescale, `&` `^` `|` sit below the comparisons, so `flags & MASK == 0` parses as `flags & (MASK == 0)`. That grouping has been a standing source of bugs since it was chosen; Rust and Go both corrected it and the 0-20 table does the same. Relative order is preserved everywhere else.

Because exactly one family moved, the expressions whose meaning changed are exactly those that mix the two families without parentheses, and the source does not say which reading its author meant. The compiler lints them.

warning: this expression changes meaning under the 0-20 precedence
  table: bitwise operators now bind tighter than comparisons
note: add parentheses to say which reading you mean

The lint fires when an unparenthesised bitwise expression is an operand of a comparison, or an unparenthesised comparison is an operand of a bitwise operator, and in no other case. `flags & mask == 4` and `a < b & c` both warn; `(a & b) == 4` does not, and neither does `a & b | c`, where both operators belong to the same family. Adding the parentheses is what silences it, and the parenthesised form reads the same under either table.
Associativity

Every binary operator declares its associativity alongside its level. Every entry in the table above is declared `left` except the assignment tier, which uses the `assign` mode and groups to the right. Two operators that share a level but disagree on associativity cannot be mixed without parentheses, and the parse fails rather than picking one: `error: operators '**' and '~>' both have precedence 19 but different associativity, so '** ~>' is ambiguous; add parentheses`.
How a user-declared operator takes a level

The level is written on the class method, in the `#operator` directive, as `#operator(mode, level)`. The instance that implements the operator does not repeat the level; the class has already registered it, and an instance may omit the directive entirely for a binary operator.

`#operator` is the only directive for declaring operator syntax. Older code using `#precedence(left, n)`, `#precedence(right, n)` or `#precedence(assign, n)` must use `#operator` with the same arguments; the old spelling is no longer accepted or registered by the prescan. Unary operators use `#operator(prefix)` or `#operator(suffix)` without a level.
