blocks.text: The remaining rules about operator declaration, including which spellings are reserved and how ownership is keyed by name, arity, and fixity, belong to the chapter on the operator system.

A struct is a nominal record type: a fixed set of named fields, with an identity that comes from its name rather than from its shape. It is introduced by an ordinary constant declaration whose value is a `struct` body, so the declaration form is `Name :: struct { ... }`.

Every member ends with a semicolon, and the diagnostic names the offending member: a comma gives `error: struct member 'x' must end with ';'`. A member is a terminated declaration rather than an element of a list because it may carry a default expression, and that expression can itself contain commas. `union` and `enum` members are terminated the same way, with the same wording.

The closing brace ends the declaration and nothing may follow it. A trailing semicolon at file scope is `error: expected a declaration, found ';'`, with help to remove it because a declaration whose body is braced ends at `}`. A struct may be declared at file scope or inside a procedure body, and a procedure-local declaration keeps its plain name, so `type_name` on a local `Local` reports `Local`.
Field defaults

A field may carry `= expr` after its annotation. The expression is an ordinary runtime expression, not a compile-time constant, and it is evaluated afresh on every default initialization of the struct. A field with no default is zeroed.

fresh defaults: 1 2
string default: anon
declared: 7 0
undefined then set: 1 2
array element: 0 0

`a` and `b` receive different identifiers because `next_id()` runs twice. `u: Slot = #undefined;` skips initialization entirely, so neither the default nor the zeroing happens. A default cannot name a sibling field: `b: s64 = a + 1;` is `error: unbound 'a'`, because the defaults are checked in the enclosing scope and a field name is not a binding there.

Field defaults are not applied to the elements of an array. `row: [2]Slot;` gives `row[0].x == 0`, not `7`. An array of structs is zeroed as a block. Where the defaults matter, initialize the elements from a literal.
Generic fields

A field annotation containing `$T` introduces an inferred type parameter for the whole struct. Later fields spell it as plain `T`. The struct is then instantiated by applying it to type arguments, and each instantiation is a separate type with its own mangled name.

1 2 pair
1.5 2.5
Pair_s64
Pair_f64

`Pair_s64` and `Pair_f64` are unrelated types: `q: Pair(f64) = p;` is `error: got Pair_s64, expected Pair_f64`. An applied generic cannot carry a qualified literal, because the qualified form only accepts a bare identifier: `Pair(f64).{ 1.5, 2.5 }` is `error: struct literal needs a type`. Annotate the binding and use the inferred form instead.
The two literal forms

A struct value is written with a brace literal. The qualified form names the type; the inferred form leaves the type to context. Both accept positional elements, named elements `.field = value`, or a mix, and both accept fewer elements than the struct has fields, in which case the remaining fields take their defaults.

rows: The expected type at that position.

blocks.text:
qualified positional: 10 20
qualified named:      1 7
mixed:                3 4
inferred:             5 6
assigned:  8 9
argument:  7
returned:  6 7
in array:  1 2

The inferred form works wherever the checker already has a concrete expectation: an annotated declaration, the left side of an assignment, an argument position, a `return`, and an element of an array literal whose element type is known. Without an expectation it is `error: struct literal needs a type`, which is what `v := .{ 1, 2 };` produces.

Positional elements follow declaration order, which is not the order the fields are stored in. The layout rule is covered in the chapter on struct memory layout; the point here is that a literal is written against the source, never against the record.

positional: a=1 b=2 c=3
offsets:     a=10 b=0 c=8

Two literal mistakes have their own wording. Supplying more positional elements than the struct has fields is `error: no field '' in struct literal for V` (the empty name is the missing field it tried to fill), and a named element that does not match any field is `error: no field 'z' in struct literal for V`. Reading an absent field off a value is a different diagnostic, `error: no field 'z' in 'V'`, and it carries a `help: did you mean 'x'?` suggestion.
Recursive structs

A struct is a value, so it cannot contain itself by value: the size would not be finite. Recursion goes through an indirection whose size does not depend on the pointee, which means `*T`, `?*T`, `[*]T`, a view, or a dynamic array.

1 2
size_of(Node)=16

Direct or indirect by-value recursion has no finite layout and is rejected. For `Node :: struct { next: Node; }`, the diagnostic identifies the self-containing struct and its field path. A pointer breaks the layout cycle, which is why the linked-node example is valid.
Field restrictions and zero-sized values

A nested named type declaration. `Inner :: struct { ... }` written inside a struct body is `error: unexpected token '::'`. An anonymous aggregate written directly as a field type is the supported spelling; see the chapter on inline aggregate field types.
A `void` field is allowed and occupies zero bytes. It remains a member for reflection and declaration-order indexing, so a later field keeps its index. The default value of that field is `.()`.
Nothing at all is fine: `Empty :: struct { }` is a legal type of size `0`.

Directives written between `struct` and the opening brace change layout, generate instances, or rewrite type parameters. `#c_call` and `#packed` are covered in the chapter on struct memory layout, `#derive` in the chapter on deriving instances, and `#modify` in the chapter on function and aggregate directives.

An undecorated struct does not store its fields in declaration order. The compiler sorts them before assigning offsets, so that a record needs no internal padding beyond what the field alignments themselves require. Declaration order still governs everything a program writes: positional literals and the field indices reflection reports are both in source order, and a directive can pin the record to source order as well.

The sort is a single stable ordering with three keys, applied to the stored fields only. Placing the strictest alignments first means every following field lands on a boundary it already satisfies, and ordering by decreasing size within one alignment class packs the tail densely.

Bytes size=5 a=3 b=0 c=4
Tie   size=8 a=0 b=4
Mixed size=16 id=0 ratio=8 code=12 flag=14

`Bytes` shows the size key on its own: every field has alignment `1`, so the three-byte array goes first and `a` and `c` follow in declaration order. `Tie` shows the tiebreak: identical alignment and identical size, so the declared order is kept. `Mixed` shows the whole rule: `8`, `4`, `2`, `1`, giving `16` bytes with a single padding byte at the end, against the `24` bytes the declared order would have needed.
Without #align, the record's alignment is the largest field alignment, and its size is the end of the last field rounded up to that alignment. A struct with no fields has size `0`.
Measuring a layout

There is no `offset_of` and no `align_of`. Offsets are obtained by subtracting the address of the value from the address of the field, and alignment is read from the type's `Type_Info` record. A generic helper keeps this to one line per field.

rows: Raises record alignment to at least 16 bytes.

blocks.text: #align(N) requests an explicit record alignment. N must be a literal positive power of two no greater than 268435456. Ordinary structs keep at least their natural field alignment. The record size rounds up to its alignment, including when it has no fields. #packed removes internal field padding; with #align(N), its record alignment is N and its size still rounds up to N. Match any corresponding C declaration exactly.
`#c_call`: declaration order and the C ABI

`struct #c_call { ... }` suppresses the sort. The fields are laid out in declaration order with the padding the target's C compiler would insert, which is what a record shared with C requires: the two sides must agree on offsets, and only the declared order is common to both languages.

The directive also makes the compiler check that every field type has a C ABI at all. `V :: struct #c_call { r: c64; }` is `error: primitive c64 has no declared C ABI; pass its real and imaginary components separately`, and the check recurses into nested aggregates. The rest of the boundary is covered in the chapter on C data across the boundary.
`#packed`: no field padding

`struct #packed { ... }` also suppresses the sort, and additionally removes internal padding: without #align, the size is the sum of the field sizes and the record alignment is `1`. Writing both directives is accepted, and `#packed` wins, because it is the stronger constraint.

Plain  size=16 align=8 a=8 b=0 c=9
C_Aln  size=24 align=8 a=0 b=8 c=16
Packed size=10 align=1 a=0 b=1 c=9

Three layouts of one declaration. `Plain` stores `b` at offset `0` although it is written second, and fits in `16` bytes. `C_Aln` keeps the written order and costs `8` bytes more for it. `Packed` keeps the written order and costs nothing, at the price of a `u64` sitting at offset `1`. Neither directive exists on a union: `union #packed { ... }` is `error: unexpected token 'packed'`, since a union's size is fixed by its tag and its largest payload.

Header size=9 magic=0 version=4 length=5
read back: 1 2 3
Inner=16 Nested=17

`#packed` is not contagious. It removes the padding this record would have inserted between its own fields; a field whose type is another aggregate keeps that aggregate's own size, padding included. `Nested` is `1 + 16`, not `1 + 9`. A wire format made of nested records needs `#packed` on every level.
Reflection reports declaration order

fields: a b c
count=3
types: u8 u64

`field_count`, `field_name`, and `field_type` walk the storage fields in declaration order. The sorted order is used only to compute sizes and to emit code, and is not exposed. The index argument must be a compile-time constant: neither `for i: 0..field_count(T)` nor `#inline for` over the same range works, and both are `error: unknown const i`. A traversal is written as a recursive procedure whose index is a parameter, evaluated by `#comptime`.

blocks.text: `using` on a field promotes nothing

A `using` field is an ordinary field. The parser consumes the keyword and records nothing about it, so the struct has the same fields, the same size, and the same member namespace it would have had without it. There is no member promotion and no inheritance.

through the field: 1 2 3
size=24 field_count=2 names=base z

Reaching a base field by its bare name fails: `d.x` is `error: no field 'x' in 'Derived'` with `help: did you mean 'z'?`, and the suggestion naming a sibling rather than a base member is the clearest sign that the marker had no effect. `d.base.x` is the spelling that works.
`using` as a statement and as a parameter modifier

The two forms that do work are both about a binding rather than about a type. `using b;` opens a struct-typed local so its fields are readable as bare names; `(using b: Base)` on a parameter is rewritten by the parser into exactly that statement at the top of the body.

parameter: 9
promoted:  10 20

The promoted names read the original storage, not a snapshot: writing `local.x` afterwards changes what the bare `x` reports. The promotion is block-scoped and ends with the block that opened it, so a `using` inside a nested block leaves nothing behind: reading the promoted name after that block is `error: unbound x`.

Promoted names are read-only. `x = 5;` after `using local;` is `error: unbound 'x'`, because the promotion lives in expression resolution and never installs an assignable binding. Write through the original name.

The operand must be a struct value. A pointer is `error: using expects a struct, got *Base`, and there is no automatic dereference. It must also be a plain name, not a path: `using d.base;` stops at the identifier and the remaining `.base` is read as a variant shorthand, giving `error: enum shorthand needs an enum context`.

A promoted name is the last thing an identifier lookup consults. A local, a global, or a constant of the same name wins, so opening a struct that happens to have an `x` cannot capture an existing `x`. Among several open `using` statements the earliest one wins, not the most recent, because the open list is searched in the order the statements were executed.
`#empty`: fields with no storage

`#empty: T;` declares a marker field. It occupies no bytes, has no name a program can write, and is filtered out of the storage fields, so it is invisible to `size_of`, `field_count`, and every literal form. Several markers may share one directive, separated by commas and terminated by a semicolon; omitting the terminator is `error: missing ';' after #empty field marker`.

phantom size=8 fields=1 raw=5 name=Phantom_f64
other instance name=Phantom_s8
marker size=8 fields=1 first=v v=9

The generic form is the one that earns its keep. Type-parameter collection still walks the annotation of an `#empty` field, so `#empty: $T;` makes the struct generic over a type it does not store. `Phantom(f64)` and `Phantom(s8)` are then distinct types of eight bytes each, and assigning one to the other is `error: got Phantom_f64, expected Phantom_s8`. The standard library uses this for containers that keep their elements behind an indirection, such as `LinkedList` in `std/Container/LinkedList.glo` and `RangeFull` in the prelude.

`#empty:` in a parameter list is a different feature with the same spelling. `f :: (#empty: $T, ...)` declares a type-witness parameter that carries a type and no value; it is described in the chapter on compile-time and type-only parameters. Nothing about the field form applies to it.
`#as`: the conversion field

`#as` marks one stored field as the struct's implicit conversion target. A value of the struct is then accepted anywhere that field's type is expected, and the compiler substitutes the field. This is how a wrapper stays a distinct type while remaining usable as the thing it wraps.

declaration: 77
assignment:  77
argument:    154
return:      77

The conversion is outward only. There is no route from the field's type back into the struct: with `f :: (i: Id)`, the call `f(5)` is `error: arg type ssize != Id in call f`. The struct is still a distinct type; `#as` only widens where it may be spent.

It fires only where a concrete expected type already exists, which is the same set of positions the inferred literal `.{ ... }` works in. Operator resolution is not one of them: with the `Id` above, `i + 1` is `error: no operator '+' for Id, ssize`. Operators are chosen by the operand types, before any coercion is attempted.

The conversion is one step deep. If `Outer` has `#as i: Inner` and `Inner` has `#as v: s64`, then `n: s64 = o;` is `error: got Outer, expected s64`; the compiler tests the marked field's type against the expectation and does not recur.

A struct can mark only one field with `#as`; a second marker is rejected and the diagnostic names the existing conversion field. `#as` and `using` combine on one field in either order, `#as using inner: Base;` or `using #as inner: Base;`, though the `using` half still does nothing. `#as` is a struct-only directive: on a union variant it is `error: unexpected token 'as'`.

`Path` in `std/File_System/Path.glo` is deliberately not an example of `#as` any more. It owns a root anchor and separator-free components, has no `.value` text field, and does not convert implicitly to `string`. Path-taking APIs instead accept a generic `P` constrained by `AsView(P, Path_View)`. The standard library supplies that zero-copy view for `string`, pointers to `Path`, and `Path_View`. An owning path's `as_view()` method borrows its components without moving it.

A `struct`, `union`, `enum`, or `enum_flags` body may be written directly where a field's type annotation goes. The aggregate is not anonymous: the compiler gives it a nominal name built from the field it was written on, hoists the declaration out to the enclosing scope, and puts that name in the annotation. This is the only nesting a struct body supports; a named `Inner :: struct { ... }` inside a struct body is `error: unexpected token '::'`.

The name hint follows the field being parsed, so an inline aggregate may appear anywhere inside that field's type: under a pointer, under an array or view, under an option, and inside a further inline aggregate. Where an inline aggregate is refused
Everywhere else. A type body written outside an aggregate field is `error: inline aggregate types are only allowed in aggregate fields`, with the span on the `struct`, `union`, or `enum` keyword.

The rule is a naming rule rather than a policy. The parser can only mint a nominal name when it already knows an owner and a field, and it knows both only while it is parsing a struct field or a union variant. Elsewhere there is nothing to call the type, so it is rejected rather than made anonymous. A type that is needed in a signature is declared at the top level and named once.

A tuple is an anonymous product type written `(A, B, C)`. It has no declaration and no name of its own: its identity is its element list, so two procedures that independently write `(s64, string)` agree on the type. The elements are positional and unnamed, which is the whole difference between a tuple and a `struct`.

The literal is `.(a, b, c)` and element access is `.0`, `.1`, and so on. The index is a decimal literal that the parser reads as part of the access, not an expression, so a named constant does not work there: `t.i` is `error: tuple member must be a numeric field like .0`.

An annotation supplies the element types and the element count. With no annotation the element types are inferred from the values, and an integer literal stays a compile-time number: `.(5)` has the element type `comptime_int`. A literal whose length disagrees with the annotation is `error: tuple literal has 2 value(s), expected 3`.

Tuples are not field-reordered

An undecorated `struct` is laid out by sorting its fields by descending alignment, so a record can be smaller than the sum of its declared members. A tuple keeps declaration order, because the program names element positions directly with `.0` and `.1` and a reordering would silently renumber them.

`void` is the empty tuple

An enum is a named set of integer constants that share a type of their own. Each member is written on its own line and, like every other aggregate member, ends with a semicolon; a comma is `error: enum member 'Red' must end with ';'`.

An explicit value is attached with `::`, never with `=`. `=` is the assignment and field-default spelling everywhere else in the language, while `::` is how a constant is bound, and an enum member is a constant. Writing `=` is rejected outright with `error: enum variant integer values use '::', not '='` rather than being quietly accepted as a second spelling.

0 5 6
size 8 count 3

Numbering starts at zero and each member takes one more than the member before it. An explicit value resets that counter, so `Blue` above is 6 and not 2. The value after `::` is a single integer literal token, optionally preceded by `-`, not an expression: naming a constant, `Red :: K;`, is rejected. Negative values such as `Low :: -1;` require a signed backing type. Hexadecimal literals such as `16#1` are accepted, and two members may carry the same value.
Backing type and size

The backing type is written between `enum` and the brace. It fixes the size and the alignment of the type and must resolve to an integer type. With no backing type an enum uses `ssize`, so its size follows the target's native word rather than always being eight bytes.

A `union` holds exactly one of several named variants at a time, together with a tag that records which one. Each variant is written `Name: Type;` and, like a struct member, ends with a semicolon; a comma is `error: union member 'A' must end with ';'`. A variant that carries nothing is declared with the payload type `void`.

Variant names are capitalised by convention and nothing enforces it. A payload is never read by writing `s.Circle`; the only way in is a pattern capture, which the chapter on reading a union payload covers in full. Like an enum, a union subject makes a plain `if x == { ... }` switch exhaustiveness-checked, so a missing arm is `error: non-exhaustive switch` with one `note: missing case:` line per uncovered variant; the chapter on exhaustiveness, guards, and reachability has the details.
The tag, the size, and the alignment

A tagged union is laid out as a target-width `ssize` tag followed by the largest payload, and the record takes the larger of the tag's alignment and the largest payload alignment. `void` variants contribute nothing to either figure. The tag is independent of the variant count: it is eight bytes on a 64-bit target and four on a 32-bit target. The two-variant `union { A: u8; B: u8; }` is therefore 16 bytes on x86-64 Windows, but 8 bytes on `x86-linux-musl` or `wasm32`.

Tiny 16 / 8
Big  32 / 8
Wide 32 / 16

That output is for x86-64 Windows. On `x86-linux-musl` and `wasm32-freestanding`, `Tiny` is 8 / 4 and `Big` is 28 / 4. The payload offset is the tag size rounded up to the payload alignment, not an unconditional eight-byte prefix. A union holding `string` or `s64` has offset 4 on `x86-linux-musl` but offset 8 on `wasm32`, whose `s64` alignment is 8. Compile-time execution uses the output target's layout too.
`Wide` shows the alignment rule: a 16-byte SIMD payload raises the record's alignment to 16, so the payload starts at offset 16 and the whole union is 32 bytes rather than 24.

A union declared in a program never gets a niche. `union { A: void; B: *u8; }` is 16 bytes on x86-64 even though the pointer has a spare null representation. Only the compiler's own `?T` and `E!T` are laid out that way; see the chapters on the option and result types.

There is no layout control. `union #packed { ... }` is `error: unexpected token 'packed'` and `union #c_call { ... }` is `error: unexpected token 'c_call'`. A union that must match a C layout is a raw union, covered in its own chapter.

A tagged union's payload is only readable through a pattern match. Writing `s.Circle` as an expression is a compile error even when the preceding line stored that very variant.

The tag is the only evidence that a payload is the one being read, and a member access has nowhere to put the test that consults it. A pattern does: the capture exists inside a branch that the match has already proved is the right one. Requiring the pattern makes every payload read dominated by a tag test by construction, instead of by the programmer's discipline.
The three legal readers
A switch arm, a pattern test, and a bind-or-diverge binding are the three shapes that produce a capture. All three bind the payload to a fresh name that is in scope only where the tag is known.

An arm that only needs the tag omits the capture: `case .Circle;` is legal and binds nothing. In a pattern test, `_` serves as the capture name when the shape must be written but the payload is unwanted: `if #pattern .Circle(_) = s`.

The `else` of a `:=` binding must not fall through. Ending it without a jump is `error: the 'else' of a '#pattern ... :=' binding must not return normally` The failure path must end with `return`, `break`, `continue`, or a call that returns `#Never`.

`#enable(allow_union_unwrap)`

The gate suspends the requirement to prove the tag statically. It is a section gate written at the top level of a file: `#enable` applies to every declaration that starts after it, and `#disable` restores the rule for everything that follows. Because it is stamped on whole declarations rather than on statements, it also reaches constant initializers and top-level `#comptime` blocks, which have no other escape hatch.

What the gate suspends is the compile-time proof, not the check. At `-O0` and `-O1` the read lowers to a tag test; the program above prints `5`, then prints the source position of the read followed by `union access: expected .Circle, but the value holds one of .Circle | .Box | .Empty`, and aborts. Hosted Windows and Linux x86-64 use exit status 134; WASI uses 125.
At `-O2` and above the check and its message are omitted. The same binary reads the payload bits of whatever variant is actually stored and exits normally.

This is the sharpest edge in the area: a program that aborts loudly during development returns a wrong answer silently in a release build. The gate is for interoperability and for generated code, not for convenience; a pattern match is checked at every optimization level.
`#enable` is a top-level directive. Inside a procedure body it is `error: unexpected directive 'enable'`.
`#disable(allow_union_unwrap)` genuinely restores the rule: a declaration written after it that reads a payload is rejected again with the ordinary message.
When the tag is already known

If the compiler can see which variant the subject holds, the gate escalates to a compile error rather than emitting a check that could never pass. A check whose outcome is already decided is not a check; it is a fault that would fire on every execution.

note: the tag is known at compile time, so the gate's runtime check would fail on every execution
The escalation only applies when the tag is a compile-time fact. A value that arrives at runtime keeps the runtime check, which is what the `peek` example above demonstrates.

`#from` is a per-variant directive on a tagged union. It marks one variant as the landing place for its own payload type, and the compiler generates a `Propagate` instance from that payload type into the union. A `Disk_Error` can then be widened into the union that carries it without a hand-written conversion.

The instance exists for `?`. When `?` breaks out of a function whose carrier residual differs from the operand's, the inherited operator makes a `propagate` call between the two residual types, and the Prelude lifts a `Propagate` between two error types to a `Propagate` between the matching `Result_Residual` types. `#from` is therefore what lets a function returning `App_Error!s64` call one returning `Disk_Error!s64` and write `?` after it. The propagation machinery itself is described in `Try`, `?`, and `#try` and in `Propagate` and Multi-Error Programs.

The directive is written before the variant name and does not change the variant itself: `parse` and `disk` are ordinary variants with ordinary payloads, matched as `.parse(inner)` and `.disk(inner)`, and a union may mix `#from` variants with plain ones as `Refused` shows. What changes is that one extra declaration is injected per marked variant. The union above generates the equivalent of this, twice:

The generated body writes the variant rather than reading it. `out.disk = value;` is variant selection, which the payload rule exempts because an assignment chooses the tag instead of trusting it; see Reading a Union Payload. Writing this instance by hand instead of marking the variant works and is what `#from` saves.

The generated instance is an ordinary one, so `propagate` may also be called directly. The witness parameter carries the target type, so the call is written `propagate(App_Error, value)`, as the last two lines of `main` show.
Without the directive
Dropping `#from` leaves the variants intact and removes the conversion. The `?` in `load` then fails its residual-conversion constraint, so no inherited operator overload accepts the call:
error: no overload '?' accepts these arguments
What a source type may be

The payload may be any type with a non-zero size: a struct, a scalar, a `string`. Nothing requires it to implement `Error`; that requirement belongs to `#derive(Error)`, which is a separate directive.
Calling `wrap(false)` produces `Small.n(7)` inside the `.Err` arm; calling `wrap(true)` produces `.Ok(true)`.
Rejections
Four shapes are refused outright, each with its own message. They are reported at the union declaration, not at the `?` that would have used the instance.

rows: `error: #from variant 'b' duplicates the source type E1`
`error: #from does not yet support generic unions`

blocks.text: A raw union has no tag, so there is no variant for the generated body to select; see Raw Unions. A `void` payload has nothing to convert from. Two variants with the same source type would produce two instances with identical heads, and instance selection keys on the type pair alone, so the pair would be ambiguous at every use.
`#from` is a union directive. On a struct field it does not reach the checker at all: `S :: struct { #from a: s64; }` is `error: unexpected token 'from'`.
Propagation is one hop

`Propagate` is not transitive. A union whose `#from` variant carries another `#from` union gets an instance for that one step only. A `?` that would need both conversions fails its operator constraint: the two generated instances cannot substitute for a direct one.
error: no overload '?' accepts these arguments

Chaining requires a hand-written `Propagate` instance for the pair that is actually needed, or a `#from` variant on the outer union that names the innermost payload type directly. Adding intermediate unions does not compose.
With a derived `Error`

`#from` and `#derive(Error)` are the pair a multi-error program usually wants: the first makes `?` widen into the union, the second gives the union the `Error` instance that a `main` returning `App_Error!void` needs. `#derive(Error)` requires every variant to carry a payload that itself implements `Error`, which is why the union below has no payload-less variant.

n = 17
bad number: nope
glosso: program exited with status exit code: 1

The second `?` breaks with a `Bad_Number`, the generated instance widens it to `App_Error`, and the `Termination` instance on `E!void` reports it through `Error` before turning it into status 1. That chain is covered in `Error`, `Termination`, and `main`.

`union #raw { ... }` is the untagged union: the C `union`, with C's rules. It carries no tag word, every variant begins at offset zero, and any variant may be read at any time regardless of which one was written last. It exists so that reinterpretation of a value's bits and foreign declarations that use a C union can be expressed.
`#raw` is written after the `union` keyword and before the brace, in any order with the other union directives. Members follow the same rule as a tagged union's: each ends with `;`.

`w.i` after `w.f = 1.0` is the IEEE-754 bit pattern of `1.0` read as an integer, and `w.bytes` is the same eight bytes in memory order, little end first. Nothing about the read is a conversion: the three members name three ways of spelling the same eight bytes.
Size and alignment

The size of a raw union is the size of its largest member, rounded up to the union's alignment; the alignment is the largest member alignment. A `void` member contributes nothing. The tagged union with the same members costs an extra target-width tag and takes that tag's alignment.

raw    size=8 align=4
tagged size=16 align=8

The largest member is `[3]u16`, six bytes with alignment 2, but `c` raises the alignment to 4, so the record rounds to 8. Struct layout, including the field reordering that raw unions have no equivalent of, is covered in Struct Memory Layout.
Construction and reading
The construction forms are the tagged union's, minus the ones that only set a tag. A qualified call needs its parentheses; an assignment to a member stores through it.

rows: Qualified call; stores 258 through the `i` member.
Member assignment; stores through `i` in place.
Member read; reinterprets the stored bytes as an `f64`.

blocks.text: The read is the important difference. On a tagged union, naming a payload member is a compile error that redirects the program to a pattern match, and the value comes out only through a capture or the `#enable(allow_union_unwrap)` gate; see Reading a Union Payload. A raw union is exempt from that rule entirely, because the rule exists to stop a program from trusting a tag, and a raw union has no tag to trust.

Nothing checks a raw-union read, at any optimization level. The tagged-union gate emits a runtime tag check at `-O0` and `-O1` and drops it at `-O2`; a raw union has no check to drop, so `-O0` and `-O2` produce identical results. Keeping the discriminant correct is entirely the program's job.
What a raw union gives up
Every feature that reads the tag is unavailable, and each is rejected by name rather than silently misbehaving.

rows: `error: cannot switch on a raw union (it has no tag)`
`error: Show derive is not defined for #raw union`
`error: PartialEq derive is not defined for #raw union`
`error: Error derive is not defined for #raw union`

blocks.text: Exhaustiveness has no meaning without a tag, so the checks described in Exhaustiveness, Guards, and Reachability never apply.

`#pattern` against a raw union is not refused at check time. It reaches lowering, where the missing tag surfaces as an `error: internal error:` naming the `GetTag` opcode. Read the member directly instead.

`#raw`, `#derive`, and `#magic` are the only union directives. `union #packed` is `error: unexpected token 'packed'` and `union #c_call` is `error: unexpected token 'c_call'`; a union has no field order to pack or to fix.
Reflection still works, because it reads the declaration rather than a value: `variant_count(Word)` is 3 and `variant_name(Word, 0)` is `i`.
Carrying the tag by hand

The C idiom a raw union usually appears in is a struct that pairs an explicit discriminant with the raw payload. The discriminant is an ordinary enum, so it can be switched on with the exhaustiveness the raw union cannot offer, and the payload member read in each arm is the one that arm's tag value promises.

int 7 / float 2.5
size=16

`Cell` is sixteen bytes: a one-byte tag padded out beside the eight-byte payload. The tagged union `union { As_Int: s64; As_Float: f64; }` is also sixteen, and it carries its own discriminant, is exhaustiveness-checked, and refuses a mismatched read. The hand-rolled pair buys nothing here, which is the general case: reach for `#raw` when a C declaration or a deliberate reinterpretation requires it, not to save space.

`?T` is the option type: a value of type `T`, or nothing. It is a compiler-built-in, injected the way `#Context` is rather than declared in any `.glo` file, so it is available in every program with no import. Its definition is exactly this two-variant union:
That block is shown for reference and is not writable source. The name is the compiler's; `?T` is the only spelling a program has, and writing the identifier produces a parse error that says so:
error: the built-in option type is written '?T'; its variants are '.Some(x)' and '.None'

The compiler owns the declaration for two reasons. The `#magic "option"` marker is what buys the niche layout described below, which is the guarantee that non-null `*T` rests on. And the parser rewrites `?T` into this name, so a program able to redeclare or shadow the union would leave the syntax pointing at nothing.
`?` is a prefix type modifier

`?` has no precedence tier of its own. It is annotation syntax that rewrites to the built-in union, it applies to whatever type follows it, and it nests. It binds tighter than `!`, so in `?E1!s64` the `?` takes the error type and the result is a fallible `s64` whose error is optional.

?s64   = Option_s64
??s64  = Option_Option_s64
?*s64  = Option__s64
?E1!s64 = Result_s64_Option_E1
size_of(?s64) = 16

The mangled names show the tree directly. `Option_Option_s64` is `?(?s64)`, and `Result_s64_Option_E1` is a result whose payload is `s64` and whose error is `?E1`. Operator precedence generally is covered in Operator Precedence and the 0-20 Scale. One further property of `?` is that it parses where a type-valued expression is expected, so both `size_of(?s64)` and `size_of(?[*]s64)` work. Bracket types such as `[]u8`, `[4]s64`, `[*]u8`, and `[..]u8` are accepted directly as type values too.
`.Some` and `.None`

The variants are dotted. `.Some(x)`, `.None`, and a pattern's `.Some(binding)` all resolve in the subject's namespace, so no qualifier is needed wherever an expected type is present. Where one is needed, the sugar supplies it in parentheses.

rows: Dotted, no parentheses, for the empty variant.
Qualified call where no expected type exists.
Qualified empty variant; the parentheses are required.

blocks.text: The asymmetry in the last two rows is the general union rule, not an option quirk: a qualified variant is a call and always needs its parentheses, so `(?s64).None` is `error: member of non-struct`. In the other direction a bare `.None` with no expected type at all is `error: enum shorthand needs an enum context`.
Reading the payload

`?T` is an ordinary tagged union as far as the payload rule is concerned, so `o.Some` is `error: tagged-union payload '.Some' may only be bound by a pattern match`. A switch arm, an `if #pattern` test, or a `#pattern ... :=` binding is how the value comes out; Reading a Union Payload covers all three and the gate that suspends the rule.

switch captured 3
pattern captured 7
not: 0 1
propagated: 20 -1
bind or diverge: 10 -1

`!o` is the `LogicalNot` instance and means "is none". `?` on an option is the `Try` instance, whose `Output` is `T` and whose `Residual` is the one-variant enum `Option_Residual`, so `lookup(key)?` either yields the `s64` or returns `.None` from the enclosing function.
The null niche

When a built-in option or result has exactly two variants, one of them zero-sized and the other carrying a pointer-like payload, the tag word is dropped and the empty variant is represented by the null bit pattern. A valid pointer is never zero, so zero is a spare pattern the payload can never occupy, and dropping the tag stays sound. `?*T` is therefore exactly a `*T` in memory and crosses a C ABI boundary as an ordinary pointer.

None bits = 0
Some bits = zero? 0
sizes: ?*s64=8 *s64=8 ?s64=16 s64=8
null test: 0 1
Reading the same eight bytes through a raw union shows that `.None` is literally address zero. Which types get the niche and which pay for a tag follows entirely from the pointer-like rule:

rows: Tag plus a 16-byte counted string view.
The inner takes the niche; the outer's payload is a union.

blocks.text: A user-written union never gets a niche, however its variants are shaped: only the compiler's `#magic "option"` and `#magic "result"` unions qualify. `union { A: void; B: *u8; }` is sixteen bytes.
Widening, and `null`

`*T` widens to `?*T` implicitly, in an assignment and at a call site, because the niche makes the conversion a no-op. Nothing else widens: `o: ?s64 = 5;` is `error: got ssize, expected Option_s64`, and the payload must be written `.Some(5)`. In the other direction `null` no longer reaches a plain pointer at all, and the diagnostic names `?*T` as the replacement. Pointers themselves are covered in Pointers and in Many-Pointers and Null.

error: 'null' is not a value of *ssize
note: a plain pointer excludes zero - write ?*ssize for a pointer that may be absent
note: its absent value is spelled '.None'
`p == null` and `p != null` compile on a `?*T` and test for absence. On an option with a non-pointer payload there is no such operator: `error: no operator '==' for Option_s64, null`.
Testing does not refine the type. After `if p != null`, `p.*` is `error: operator '.*' expects a typed pointer, got Option__s64`. A capture is the only route to the pointer.
A declaration cannot use `null` as an option initializer even where the niche applies: `op: ?[*]s64 = null;` is `error: null is not a valid Option____s64`. Write `.None`.
The library surface
Everything except the union itself is ordinary Glosso in `std/Prelude/Option.glo`, and needs no import.

rows: The empty value for an explicit type.
Inspect the current variant through a borrowed receiver.

blocks.text: The instances are `LogicalNot`, `Try`, a hand-written `PartialEq` (`?T` is `#magic`, so it cannot carry `#derive`), and `Show` for any `T` that is itself `Show`. Two options compare equal when both are `.None` or both hold equal payloads.

The default `Formatter` instantiates `Show` for `?T` directly. `print("%\n", o)` therefore prints `Some(3)` for an option holding `3`, or `None` for an empty option. An earlier direct `show` call is unnecessary. See `Show`, `FromString`, and `print` Formatting.

Options also support `map`, `map_or`, `and_then`, `or_else`, `filter`, `ok_or`, and `ok_or_else`. `unwrap_or_else` and the other `_else` forms call their fallback only when needed. `unwrap_or`, `map_or`, and `ok_or` evaluate the supplied fallback argument eagerly.

`E!T` is the result type: a `T`, or an error of type `E`. It is the binary counterpart to `?T` and, like it, a compiler-built-in that no `.glo` file declares and every program has without an import. Its definition is this two-variant union:

The sugar is error-first: the LEFT operand of `!` is what `.Err` carries and the right is what `.Ok` carries, so `Disk_Error!s64` is a fallible `s64`. The union's own parameters stay payload-first, as written above; the sugar is what swaps, not the declaration, which is why `type_name(Disk_Error!s64)` is `Result_s64_Disk_Error`.

Error-first is the order that reads. A signature ends on the type its success path hands back, which is the type the caller is looking for, and the error type sits next to the `!` that introduces it. It is also the order Zig's `E!T` and Haskell's `Either e a` use, and it is what makes right associativity the natural rule for a repeated `!`.
As with `?T`, the compiler's name for the union is not writable. `E!T` is the only spelling and the identifier is a parse error:
error: the built-in result type is written 'E!T'; its variants are '.Ok(x)' and '.Err(e)'
Precedence and associativity

`!` binds looser than every prefix type modifier, so `?`, `*`, `[]`, `[..]`, and `[*]` all stay glued to whichever operand they were written next to. It is right-associative, which is what error-first order asks for: `E1!E2!T` is `E1!(E2!T)`, each `!` wrapping the one payload in another result.

E1!?*User  = Result_Option__User_E1
?E1!User   = Result_User_Option_E1
E1!E2!User = Result_Result_User_E2_E1
E1![]u8    = Result___u8_E1
[]u8!E1    = Result_E1___u8
The mangled name is `Result_<payload>_<error>`, so each line can be read straight off:

rows: A fallible optional pointer: error `E1`, payload `?*User`.
A result whose ERROR is optional, not an optional result.
Error `[]u8`, payload `E1`; the slice modifier stayed on the left.

blocks.text: `!*` lexes as a single operator token, so `E1!*User` is `error: unexpected token '!*'` and `E1!**User` is `error: unexpected token '!**'`. Separate them with a space, as `E1! *User`, or write the pointer through a named alias. `!?` and `![` do not have this problem, because `?` is emitted alone and `[` is not an operator character.
`.Ok` and `.Err`
The variants are dotted and resolve in the subject's namespace, and the qualified form parenthesises the type exactly as an option's does. `.Ok()` with no argument is how an `E!void` reports success.

switch ok 3
pattern err nope
is_ok: 1 0 1 0
not: 0 1
unwrap_or: 3 -1

`!r` is the `LogicalNot` instance and means "is err", the mirror of `!o` on an option. Payload reads obey the same rule as any tagged union: `r.Ok` is `error: tagged-union payload '.Ok' may only be bound by a pattern match`, and the legal readers are the ones in Reading a Union Payload.
`Try` and `?`

`E!T` carries a `Try` instance whose `Output` is `T` and whose `Residual` is `Result_Residual(E)`, a one-field struct holding the error. `x?` on a result therefore yields the payload or returns early with the error already wrapped in the enclosing function's carrier. Returning a bare `Output` from a result-returning function is also legal: `from_output` wraps it, so `return x + y;` means `return .Ok(x + y);`.

ok 42
bad 3x
try block: ok 9

`?` needs an enclosing Try boundary. Outside one it is `error: postfix '?' requires a Try-returning function or an enclosing #try block`; `#try { ... }` supplies a boundary for a single expression, as the last two lines show. The operator itself is documented in `Try`, `?`, and `#try`.

When the propagated error type differs from the enclosing function's, the inherited `?` body calls `propagate` between the two residuals. The Prelude lifts any `Propagate(From, To)` between error types to the corresponding `Result_Residual` pair, and `#from` variants on a union generate those instances; see `#from` Variants and `Propagate` and Multi-Error Programs.
A result-returning `main`

`$E!void ::: instance Termination where Error(E)` is what lets `main` return a result: `.Ok` becomes status 0, and `.Err` reports the error through its `Error` instance and becomes status 1. The constraint is real, so an `E` with no `Error` instance gives `error: main return type Result_void_E does not implement Termination`. Only `E!void` qualifies; a general `E!T` and `?T` do not.
