missing: config
glosso: program exited with status exit code: 1
Size and niche

A result is a tag word plus the larger of its two payloads. With `Small :: struct { c: s64; }`, `size_of(Small!s64)` is 16; with `Bad :: struct { text: string; }`, whose `string` view is 16 bytes, `size_of(Bad!s64)` is 24. A result takes the niche under the same rule as an option, and either side may be the zero-sized one.

8 24
Result_Nil__s64 Result_Nil___u8

`*s64!Nil` has a zero-sized `.Ok` payload and a pointer `.Err` payload, so the tag goes and the whole result is one pointer word. `[]u8!Nil` does not qualify because a view is not pointer-like, and pays the tag.
`E!T` has no `Show` instance, so a default `%` has no matching `Formatter` for the result. Match on the result and format the arms, or implement a selector for that result type.

`E!T` has no `PartialEq` either, and unlike `Show` the omission is not caught in the checker: `a == b` on two results passes checking and fails during code generation with `error: Invalid operand types for ICmp instruction`.
The library surface

The Prelude provides result constructors and inherent methods without an import. `map` transforms a success payload; `map_error`, `bind_error`, and `ap_error` operate on the error side. `and_then` chains a fallible success callback. `ok()` and `err()` select one side as an option.

rows: Success with an explicit result or error type.
Failure with an explicit result or payload type.
Inspect the current variant through a borrowed receiver.
Rewrites the error type while preserving a success.

blocks.text: `unwrap_or_else` and `map_or_else` defer fallback work until it is needed. `unwrap_or` and `map_or` evaluate their fallback eagerly. `Result_Residual :: struct { error: $E; }` remains an ordinary type, so a hand-written `Propagate` instance can convert between residuals.

*T points to one non-null T and is read-only by default. *mut T permits writes through the pointer. Both are one machine word and carry no count. Use [*]T for an unbounded run of elements and []T for a counted view.
Address-of and dereference

&value and value.& take an address. *pointer and pointer.* dereference it. Address-of requires addressable storage, such as a local, field, or array element. Dereferencing a read-only pointer permits reads; only a writable pointer permits assignment. The old address-of use of prefix * has been removed.

Member access does not implicitly dereference. Use p.*.field or (*p).field. Pointer receiver methods can use an existing compatible pointer or take the address of an addressable value; mutable receivers require writable storage.
Qualifiers and nested pointers

A writable pointer converts implicitly to a read-only pointer, preserving the pointee type. The reverse conversion is rejected. The const qualifier has been removed: omit it for read-only access and write mut for writable access.
**T is a read-only pointer to a read-only pointer. Write *mut *mut T when both levels must be writable. In **mut T, mut applies to the innermost pointee; the outer pointer remains read-only.
Nullability

*T excludes address zero. Use ?*T for an optional pointer: .None occupies the zero niche, so the optional has the same size as a pointer. Match the optional before dereferencing. cast(*T) of a known zero is rejected, and a runtime zero is checked at -O0 and -O1.
An unassigned non-null pointer uses an invalid nonzero sentinel, not useful storage. Initialize it before dereferencing. Pointers do not own their pointee and do not keep its storage alive.
Single-element pointer operations

A single pointer has dereference and address comparison, but no arithmetic or indexing. Many-pointers provide those operations. Use an explicit cast when crossing pointer shapes; pointer_punning relaxes shape checks without granting writable access to read-only storage.

[*]T is a read-only many-pointer: one address with no element count. [*]mut T permits writes. These shapes support element indexing and arithmetic scaled by size_of(T). The caller must know that every accessed element exists; the compiler cannot bounds-check an unbounded pointer.

A fixed array, view, dynamic array, or string exposes its data pointer through .data. Read-only storage yields a read-only pointer. A many-pointer carries no .count and cannot itself be sliced; slice the original counted array or view.
Non-null pointers and absence

Single pointers, many-pointers, and function pointers all exclude zero. The literal null cannot initialize a bare [*]T or #fn_ptr. Use ?[*]T or an optional function-pointer type for absence; their .None variant occupies address zero without adding storage.

Match an optional pointer before using its payload. A cast from a runtime integer to a bare pointer checks zero at -O0 and -O1; a known zero is rejected at compile time. An uninitialized non-null pointer is an invalid sentinel, not valid storage.
Converting pointer shapes

Single pointers and many-pointers do not convert implicitly. Use cast([*]T) or cast(*T) when the backing storage justifies the new shape. Writable forms can be used through their matching read-only form; adding writable access implicitly is rejected.

The pointer_punning feature gate relaxes pointee and pointer-shape checks but does not permit read-only storage to acquire writable access. Keep casts and gates adjacent to the code that needs them. Neither a pointer nor its optional form owns the pointee or extends its lifetime.

sections.title: Fixed Arrays, Views, and Dynamic Arrays

blocks.text: [N]T stores N elements inline. []T borrows a counted read-only run; []mut T permits writes. [..]T is a move-only owner of a growable allocation. [_]T infers the fixed length from the initializer, including b"..." byte-array literals.

rows: count followed by data, two native words
count, data, capacity, three native words

blocks.text: An unallocated dynamic array has zero count and capacity. Declare one without an initializer, then call push(), append(), or reserve(). reserve() requests total capacity and does not change count. push() appends one or more values and grows geometrically.

A dynamic array owns its live elements. Passing it by value moves it; pointers and views borrow it. Iterate through managed elements with for *item: values. take() transfers storage and leaves an empty reusable source; replace(new_array) installs a moved array and returns the previous allocation.

free() and deinit() destroy live elements and release storage, leaving an empty array. They require infallible element destruction. reset() retains allocation and is available only when elements do not need destruction. release_storage() frees only storage and is for code that has already managed every element's lifetime.
Dynamic arrays allocate and release through context.allocator. Keep that allocator installed through destruction. Standard container constructors instead capture their supplied allocator.
Views and invalidation

A view copies a pointer and count; it does not copy elements or update its count after mutation. Growth may relocate storage. Freeing, replacing, or destroying an array can leave existing views dangling. Memory analysis diagnoses tracked invalidation and dangling views; use --borrow-check=error to reject findings. Keep backing storage valid for every access.

Writable views convert to read-only views. Read-only views cannot be used as writable ones. Indexing fixed arrays, slices, dynamic arrays, and counted strings is checked at -O0 and -O1; [*]T carries no count and is never bounds-checked.

`..` builds a range that excludes its upper bound and `..=` builds one that includes it. Both are ordinary operators declared in the prelude at precedence 2, left-associative, so they bind looser than arithmetic: `0..n - 1` is `0..(n - 1)`. There is no `..<`; writing it is `error: unexpected token '<'`.

Either bound may be omitted, and the omitted bound changes the type rather than filling in a default. That is what lets `a[2..]` and `a[..3]` mean different things to the same container without any special syntax in the index: five ranges are five distinct struct types, and slicing is an `Indexable` instance for each.

2..5   Range_ssize start=2 end=5 size=16
2..=5  RangeInclusive_ssize start=2 end=5 size=16
2..    RangeFrom_ssize start=2 size=8
..5    RangeTo_ssize end=5 size=8
..=5   RangeToInclusive_ssize end=5 size=8

The bound type is carried through: `lo..hi` over two `u8` values is a `Range(u8)`, not the `Range(ssize)` inferred from untyped integer bounds. The operators are provided by instances constrained on `Step`, which the integer types satisfy and the float types do not: `0.0..1.0` is `error: no operator '..' for f64, f64`.
Ranges are values

A range is an ordinary struct value. It can be stored in a variable, passed to a procedure, returned, and used as an index later; `a[r]` for a stored `r` means exactly what `a[2..5]` would have meant. `RangeFull(T)` has no fields and `size_of` is 0, so an all-elements index costs nothing to carry.

stored Range: count=3 first=20
stored RangeFull: count=6 size=0
Range_u8 count=3
Ranges have no `Show` instance, so `print("%\n", r)` has no matching default `Formatter` for `Range_ssize`. The fields print individually.
The slice spellings

Indexing a container with a range slices it. Each spelling is a separate `Indexable` instance keyed on the container type and the range type, which is why all six work uniformly on fixed arrays, views, dynamic arrays, and strings. Indexing and Slicing Operators describes the typeclass; the table below is what the six mean.
What a slice produces

Slicing a fixed array, a view, or a dynamic array all give `[]T`, and none of the three copies an element: the result is a count and a pointer into the original storage. Slicing `string` or `cstring` gives a borrowed `string`; slicing either UTF-16 form gives `string16`. A many-pointer cannot be sliced at all, because it has no length to bound the result: `mp[1..3]` is `error: no operator '[]' for [*]s64, Range_ssize`.

view sliced:   count=2 type=[]s64
dyn sliced:    count=3 type=[]s64
string sliced: 'hello' type=string

`type_name` and diagnostics preserve `[]s64`; a slice whose element is the native integer instead prints `[]ssize`. A slice of a dynamic array is a borrow, so a later `array.push` invalidates it: see Aliasing, Invalidation, and Storage Generations.
Slicing is bounds-checked

A slice is checked like an index. The range's bounds are compared against the container's own count at `-O0` and `-O1`, and the slice prints `runtime check failed: slice.bounds` and aborts when the start is negative, when the end runs past the count, or when the end precedes the start. An empty slice whose bounds are equal and within the count is legal, and so is one that ends exactly at the count. At `-O2` and above the check is not emitted and the descriptor is built from the bounds as written. In compile-time evaluation the same failure is `error: slice 0..5 is out of bounds`.

a[2..2] count=0
a[0..3] count=3
a[1..]  count=2
runtime check failed: slice.bounds
glosso: program exited with status exit code: 134

The guard is a runtime check like the others, so it disappears at `-O2` and above. A slice bound that comes from input, arithmetic, or a search result should still be clamped against `.count` before it reaches the brackets; an optimized build will not do it.
Ranges as iterables

A `for` loop accepts a range directly, and the open-ended shapes iterate too: `RangeTo` and `RangeToInclusive` start from the type's origin, which is 0 for the integers, and `RangeFrom` never terminates on its own. `for` Loops and Iteration and Range Typeclasses cover the loop forms and the `Step` and `RangeOrigin` contracts behind them.

`#soa` and `#aos` are prefixes written in front of an array type. They select how the elements are stored without changing the element type or anything written at a use site. `#aos` stores whole elements one after another; `#soa` stores each field of the element in its own contiguous run.

`#aos` is the layout every array already has, so the prefix exists only to state the choice in the source. `#soa` is the one that changes the representation: the descriptor stops carrying a single `data` pointer and carries one pointer per storage field of the element type instead.

aos: count=2 [1].y=40
soa: count=2 x[1]=30
descriptors: aos=24 soa=40

The descriptor sizes follow from that. `Particle` has three storage fields, so its `#soa` descriptor holds three data pointers where the `#aos` descriptor holds one. The pointer count comes from the laid-out field list, so an `#empty` marker field contributes none; the plain array shapes are described in the chapter on fixed arrays, views, and dynamic arrays.
Where the prefixes may be written

Both prefixes apply to an array type and to nothing else. `#soa` is further restricted to the two descriptor-carrying forms, `[..]T` and `[]T`, since those are the only shapes with a header that can hold more than one pointer. Everything else is rejected by name.

rows: Accepted; per-field runs, plus a count and a capacity.
Accepted; per-field pointers, plus a count.

blocks.text: The element type must be a struct, since a scalar has no fields to split: `#soa [..]s64` is `error: #soa arrays require a struct element type, got s64`. `#aos` carries no restriction at all; it is accepted on `[N]T`, `[]T`, and `[..]T` alike and changes nothing about any of them.
Element syntax is unchanged

Nothing at a use site distinguishes the two layouts. Elements are appended with `array.push` and a whole element value, read back with `array[i]`, and iterated with `for`, which yields reassembled elements and an optional index. A `#soa [..]T` is also an ordinary struct field type.
Per-field views

On a `#soa` array a field name of the element type reads as a view of that field's run: `soa.x` has type `[]s64` and length `soa.count`. The view aliases the array rather than copying it, so a store through the view is a store into the array. Indexing the array itself gathers a whole element on a read and scatters on a write, whether the write names one field or replaces the element.

field view: type=[]s64 count=2 size=16
gathered: id=2 x=30 y=99
scattered: id=7 x=70 y=7000
raw run: 30

`soa.data` is `error: #soa array has per-field data`: there is no single run for it to name. A raw pointer comes from one field view instead, as `soa.x.data`, which is an ordinary `[*]s64` over that field's run.
The split is one level deep. A field whose own type is a struct becomes a view of that struct; it is not decomposed further.

pos view: []V2 / mass view: []f64
bodies.pos[1].x=3

The descriptor's own members win over element fields of the same name. On a `#soa [..]P` whose `P` declares `count: s64`, `d.count` is the element count and not a view; that field is reachable only through a gathered element, as `d[0].count`. The same shadowing applies to `capacity` and to `data`.
`#soa []T` as a parameter

`array.view` on a `#soa [..]T` yields a `#soa []T`, and a parameter declared `#soa []T` receives it. The prefix is part of the parameter type, so a routine written against per-field views states that in its signature, and a plain `[]T` parameter will not accept the value.

view type=[]Particle size=32
total_x=40
y=200 400

The element type may be inferred, so `f :: (v: #soa []$T)` is a generic routine over any struct-element SoA view. Diagnostics render both view kinds as `[]P`, which makes a mismatch read as `error: arg type []P != []P in call take_plain`; the prefix is the difference the message is not showing.

A structure-of-arrays descriptor cannot be sliced as an ordinary array of structs. Use array.view() for its #soa view, or slice one field's column, such as array.x[lo..hi]. Ordinary array slicing is rejected because each element field lives in its own buffer.

A literal that names no type is written with a leading dot and brackets chosen by what it builds: `.{ }` for an aggregate, `.[ ]` for an array, and `.( )` for a tuple. The tuple form belongs to the chapter on tuples. `.{ }` also has a qualified spelling, `T.{ }`, which carries its own type and therefore needs no context.

Inside `.{ }`, elements are either positional or named. Positional elements follow declaration order, which is not the same as storage order; named elements are written `.field = value`. A literal may stop early, may mix the two so long as no field is written twice, and may be empty, in which case every field takes its declared default. Separate elements with commas; a trailing comma is allowed. Array literals likewise require a comma between elements.
More positional elements than fields is `error: no field '' in struct literal for Vec2`; the empty name is the field that was not found.
A name that is not a field is `error: no field 'z' in struct literal for Vec2`.
Writing one field twice, whether by two names or by a positional element that a named one repeats, is `error: field 'x' is initialized more than once`.
Fields a literal omits take their declared defaults, and fields with no default are zeroed, exactly as a bare `v: Vec2;` initializes them.
Where the expected type comes from
The inferred form is legal wherever checking already knows the type the expression must produce. That is a fixed list of positions, and each one serves `.{ }` and `.[ ]` alike.

rows: Return with a declared result type
An element of an enclosing literal

blocks.text: An `ifx` arm may need its own type: qualify its literal as `Vec2.{ ... }` rather than relying on the surrounding target annotation.

rows: A variadic argument of known element type

blocks.text:
argument: 10
return endpoints: 1 4
constant x: 0 global x: 8
nested: 2 9 g 4
union payload: Option_Vec2
assignment: 50 60

Nesting works because each inner literal is checked against the field or element type the outer one already fixed. `.{ .a = .{ 1, 2 } }` needs no inner type name, and `.[ .[ 1, 2, 3 ], .[ 4, 5, 6 ] ]` builds a `[2][3]s64` from the annotation alone.

variadic x: 1 3
soa: 7
default parameter: 0 42
ifx arm: 1 0
Where the qualified form is required

Outside that list there is no expected type, and a bare `.{ }` is `error: struct literal needs a type`. `a := .{ 1, 2 };` is the everyday case: `:=` takes its type from the initializer, so the initializer cannot take its type from `:=`. A literal handed to an inferred generic parameter has no expected type either, and the call reports `error: no overload 'generic' accepts these arguments`.

A qualified literal accepts a struct type value, including a generic application such as `Box(f64).{ .value = 1.5 }` or an alias such as `Alias.{ 1, 2 }`. The qualifier fixes the type without an annotation on the variable. An annotation with the inferred `.{ ... }` form remains useful when the surrounding declaration already names the type.
Collection literals

`.[ ]` builds a fixed array. Against an annotation the element count must equal the declared count exactly, and that count may be spelled by a constant. With no annotation the literal synthesizes `[N]T` from what it holds, which for bare integer elements means an element type of `comptime_int`; compile-time numbers and their defaulting have their own chapter. The expected fixed-array type is also preserved through `#comptime`, so `a: [3]ssize = #comptime .[1, 2, 3];` has exactly the type named by the annotation.

fixed=3 named=4 lane0=1
inferred: count=3 type=[3]comptime_int
trailing=3 field default=4
A wrong count is `error: fixed array literal has 2 element(s), expected 3`, with the same wording when there are too many.
`.[]` with nothing to fix its type is `error: empty array literal needs an array context`.

A view or a dynamic array cannot be initialized from a collection literal. `a: []s64 = .[ 1, 2, 3 ];` is `error: runtime array literals require a fixed array, Simd, or Matrix context`. Build a fixed array and take `a[..]`, or grow a `[..]T` with `array.push`. For an immediate borrowed view, `&.[1, 2, 3]` instead creates a pointer to temporary fixed-array storage that can coerce to an expected `[]s64`; that storage lasts only for the surrounding expression.

A SIMD value takes the `#simd .[ ... ]` spelling and needs its own context: a bare `#simd .[ ... ]` is `error: #simd literal requires a Simd(T, N) context`, and a plain `.[ ... ]` against a SIMD annotation is `error: ordinary array literal .[...] cannot initialize Simd(f32, 4); use #simd .[...]`. SIMD vectors and matrices have their own chapter.
Both bracket forms accept a trailing comma before the closing bracket.

There is no `T.[ ... ]`. The qualified spelling exists for `.{ }` only, and `s64.[10, 20, 30]` does not fail to parse: it reads as the type `s64` followed by an unrelated statement, so the binding ends up with type `type` and the next use reports something remote such as `error: no operator '[]' for type, ssize`. Annotate the target instead.

The two bracket forms are not interchangeable. `.[ 1, 2 ]` against a struct annotation is `error: got [2]comptime_int, expected Vec2`, and `.{ ... }` against an array or a tuple annotation is `error: struct literal needs a type`, because neither an array type nor a tuple type names a struct the literal could be checked against. A tagged union takes neither form; it is built by variant, as the chapter on tagged unions describes.

sections.title: Member Access, Calls, and Argument Expansion

blocks.text: A dot followed by a name selects a member. Fields resolve against the object's type. Calls can also resolve inherent methods and named typeclass operations, with an implicit receiver argument. An ordinary free function does not become a method merely because its first parameter has this type.

rows: `.count`, one view per element field; dynamic arrays also have `.capacity`
Variant names, bound by a pattern.

blocks.text: Member access composes with indexing, slicing, and calls, so a field of an element of a slice of a call result is one expression. The array and string members are described in the chapter on fixed arrays, views, and dynamic arrays; union variants in the chapter on reading a union payload; `any` in the chapter on reflection.

chained: 2
call result: 3
index then field: 3
slice then field: 2
many-pointer: 4
tuple: .count=3 .1=a
any: name=ssize size=8

An unknown field on a struct is `error: no field 'z' in 'Vec2'`, and the compiler offers the nearest declared name as `help: did you mean 'x'?`. A bad tuple member is `error: tuple member must be a numeric field like .0` for a name and `error: tuple index .5 is out of range for 2-value tuple` for a number. `any` reports its whole member set: `error: any has fields type and value, not 'size'`.
Field access follows pointers explicitly

A pointer is not one of the objects in that table, so `p.x` where `p` is a `*Vec2` is `error: member of non-struct`. The dereference is written: the suffix `.*` produces the pointee, and `p.*.x` reads its field. This follows from `*T` and `T` being different types with no coercion between them, and it holds on the left of an assignment as well.

read: 3
after: 4 40
double: 4

The symmetric conversion does not happen either. The prefix `&` takes an address and is written at the call site, as in `bump(&v)`. Passing the value where a pointer is declared is `error: arg type Vec2 != *Vec2 in call bump`, and passing the pointer where the value is declared is `error: arg type *Vec2 != Vec2 in call byval`. Pointer syntax is covered in the chapter on pointers.

`member of non-struct` is the message for every pointer-shaped object, not only struct pointers. `p.count` where `p` is a `*[..]s64` reports it, and so does `.count` on a `[*]T`, which carries no length at all. The first is written `p.*.count`; for the second there is nothing to write.
Inherent methods and associated functions

Attach methods to an owned type with `Vec2 ::: { ... }`. The first parameter `#self` receives a value, `*mut #self` a mutable pointer, and `*#self` a read-only pointer. `#Self_Type` names the complete owner type. A function without a receiver is an associated function, called through the type. The block below makes its members public explicitly.

`v.length2()` inserts the receiver; `Vec2.length2(v)` spells it explicitly. A pointer receiver can use an existing pointer or borrow an addressable value automatically. Mutable receivers cannot borrow a temporary or accept a read-only pointer. Field access inside a pointer receiver still writes `#self.*.x`. A parameter default cannot refer to `#self`: defaults are evaluated at the call site, where the receiver binding is not in scope.

length2=25
shifted=32

Methods live in the owner's namespace and do not create unqualified functions. `v.make(...)` is invalid for an associated function, and `v.length2` or `Vec2.length2` cannot be stored as a first-class method reference. A function-pointer field remains a normal field whose value can be called; function pointers have their own chapter.
Calls

A call is a callee expression followed by a parenthesized argument list. Arguments are separated by commas, and a trailing comma before the closing parenthesis is accepted. Named arguments and defaults are covered in the chapter on default and named parameters; matching against a generic signature in the chapter on generic functions.
Variadic packs

Inside the callee a variadic parameter is an ordinary value with `.count` and indexing. Its shape depends on how the parameter was declared and how the call supplied it: a typed pack such as `...s64` is a `[]s64`, an `...any` pack written out at the call site is a tuple of the argument types, and the same `...any` pack filled by expansion is a `[]any` with every element boxed.

[]ssize count=3
(ssize, string) count=2
[]any count=3
Argument expansion

A suffix `...` on a call argument spreads an existing array into the pack instead of passing it as a single element. The source may be a fixed array, a view, or a dynamic array. Fixed parameters ahead of the variadic one are unaffected and are still written normally.

written out: 6
fixed array: 10
view:        10
dynamic:     11
empty pack:  0

An expanded argument replaces the whole pack rather than contributing to it, and the next two rules follow from that: there is no operation that concatenates a run-time array onto written-out arguments, so the compiler refuses the mixture instead of inventing one.

rows: At most one expanded argument per call.
call `sum_all` has more than one expanded argument
The expansion must be the only argument in the variadic slot.
expanded argument must be the final variadic argument in call `sum_all`
The source must be an array type.
expanded variadic argument to `sum_all` must be an array
Its element type must match the pack's.
expanded variadic arg type `[2]f64` != `[]ssize` in call `sum_all`
Its element type must satisfy the pack's constraints.
a `...Show` wrapper rejects elements without `Show`; `print` checks each selected `Formatter`

blocks.text: `sum_all(100, xs...)` and `sum_all(xs..., 100)` both fail the second rule, even though the expansion is written last in the first of them: the test is that the variadic slot holds exactly one argument, not that the expansion comes last.
A `string` is not an array for this purpose, so `take(s...)` reports the third rule's message rather than spreading the bytes.
`...` is call-argument syntax and nothing else. `y := xs...;` is `error: unexpected token '...'`.

`array.push` does not accept an expanded argument. Its variadic parameter is served by a `#magic` implementation that expansion does not reach, so `d.push(xs...)` is `error: got [4]s64, expected s64`; append in a loop, or route through an ordinary variadic. `print` does accept expansion but counts the pack as one argument when it checks placeholders, so `print("% %\n", ss...)` is `error: print: format has 2 '%' placeholder(s) but 1 argument(s) given`.

A generic owner head such as `Box($T) ::: { ... }` binds `T` from the receiver or concrete type. Methods may add their own generic parameters. An inherent block must be defined in the ownership unit that owns its type; importing a type or aliasing it does not transfer ownership. User code cannot add inherent blocks to primitives, arrays, pointers, options, or results. Wrap a dependency's type in a locally owned type to add behavior.

Named typeclass operations also support receiver syntax. `reader.read(buffer)` uses the first non-erased argument of `Reader.read(reader, buffer)` as its receiver. Fields and applicable inherent methods take precedence. If more than one class applies, qualify the class explicitly. Core standard-library behavior uses methods, including `array.push(...)` and `text.substring(...)`. Type queries use the free function `type_of(value)`. Domain operations with independent inputs use free functions, such as `alloc(size)`, `exists(path)`, and `simd_store(destination, value)`.

Factories belong to the type they construct. For example, `Path.path_from_string(text)` creates a path and `f64.from_bits(bits)` creates a float; neither operation is a method on its input string or integer. Once constructed, a resource's own operations remain methods, such as `file.read()` and `file.close()`. Import the component that declares each factory, function, or method.

A procedure is declared the way every other compile-time constant is declared: a name, `::`, and an initializer. What makes it a procedure is that the initializer begins with a parenthesized parameter list. Nothing about the declaration is a separate "function" statement, which is why a procedure may appear anywhere a declaration may appear, including inside another procedure's body.

procedure := name "::" "(" [ parameters ] ")"
             [ "->" result-type ]
             { function-directive }
             { "where" comptime-bool-expression }
             ( block | ";" )

result-type := type
             | "(" type { "," type } ")"
             | "(" name ":" type { "," name ":" type } ")"

The order of those five slots is fixed. The parser reads all function directives in one loop and stops at the first `where`, so a directive written after a constraint is no longer in the directive position and the declaration is rejected: `f :: (a: ssize) where true #inline { }` gives `error: function directives must appear before where clauses`. The corrected spelling puts every directive first and every constraint after them, as in `plain :: (a: ssize) -> ssize #inline where true { return a + 1; }`.

rows: any number, after the last directive
required, except on `#magic`, `#foreign`, and signature-only typeclass requirements

blocks.text: The directive vocabulary is given in the chapter Function and Aggregate Directives, and the constraint language in Constraints with `where`. This chapter covers only the shape the two of them sit in.
Result types

A procedure with no `->` returns `void`. Writing `-> void` explicitly is accepted and means the same thing. A result type that is not `void` constrains every `return` expression in the body: returning a value from a `void` procedure is `error: got ssize, expected void`, and returning the wrong type is the ordinary conversion diagnostic, `error: got ssize, expected string`.
`add3` uses a shared type annotation: one type applies to every name in the group. Shared annotations, defaults, and named arguments are the subject of Default and Named Parameters.

A procedure whose result type is neither `void` nor a union, and whose body can reach its closing brace without executing a `return`, is rejected at the declaration: `error: function 'no_return_stmt' can reach the end of its body without returning a value`, framed on the name. The check is on the control flow, not on the presence of the keyword, so a body whose only exit is a forgotten branch is caught too. Three shapes are exempt: a `void` procedure needs no `return`; a union result, `E!T` and `?T` included, still yields its zero value, because reaching the end of an `E!void` body is that type's success path; and the named-result form below has its `return` appended by the parser.

error: function 'no_return_stmt' can reach the end of its body without returning a value
  --> ret.glo:3:1
  |
3 | no_return_stmt :: (a: ssize) -> ssize { }
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
Multiple and named results

A parenthesized list after the arrow declares more than one result. There are two spellings. A list of bare types produces a tuple result; a list in which every element is written `name: type` produces named results.

q=3 r=1
t.0=3 t.1=1
lo=4 hi=9
only_r=1

A named result list is rewritten by the parser before checking: each name becomes a zero-initialized local at the top of the body, and an implicit `return <names>;` is appended at the end. A bare `return;` inside such a body is rewritten to return the names too. This is why `minmax` can assign `lo` and `hi` and then leave, and why a named-result procedure with an empty body returns zeroes rather than being rejected.
`q, r := divmod(7, 2);` destructures the result into two bindings.
`t := divmod(7, 2);` binds the whole tuple; the elements are then `t.0` and `t.1`.
`_` in a destructuring position discards that result.
`return e1, e2;` is a statement form only. A comma in value position belongs to an argument list, so there is no comma expression that builds a multiple-result value.
A tuple result has no `Show` instance, so the default `%` has no matching `Formatter` for it. Destructure the result and print its elements, or supply a custom rendering.
Bodyless declarations

A body is required except in three cases: the declaration carries `#magic`, it carries `#foreign`, or it is a requirement inside a typeclass. In those cases the declaration ends at a semicolon and the implementation comes from the compiler, the linker, or an instance.
c_abs=5 raw_add=5

The rule runs in both directions. An ordinary signature ended with a semicolon instead of a body is `error: unexpected token ';'`. At file scope, a `#foreign` or `#magic` declaration must itself end with `;`: putting a body directly after the directive first gives `error: declaration must end with ';'`, while putting the required semicolon before that body leaves `{` to be read as the next declaration. It gives `error: bad decl name '{'`. Conversely, a procedure that has a body already ended at its `}`. At file scope, following it with `;` is `error: expected a declaration, found ';'`; inside another body the stray token is the ordinary `error: unexpected token ';'`. The nested-declaration parser currently accepts an omitted terminator on a bodyless `#foreign` or `#magic` signature; that narrow exception does not apply at file scope.
Nested procedures

A procedure declared inside a body is visible within its containing lexical block, including to sibling local procedures. It can be called before its declaration. Structs, enums, unions, distinct types, typeclasses, and function-pointer aliases declared in a body also stay local. Their names do not escape into other top-level procedures.
nested=42 other=3
A top-level procedure cannot call either local nested function. Pass a function pointer explicitly when a helper must escape its scope.
An ordinary local procedure cannot capture enclosing runtime locals. Pass them as parameters. A macro expands into its caller and follows the macro hygiene rules described in Macros with #expand.
Local functions with the same name in different blocks are independent. Duplicate function declarations within one block are rejected.
A name :: expression binding remains a local constant. Type aliases such as Byte :: u8 may be used in annotations within that same scope.

A parameter may carry a default expression, and a call may select parameters by name instead of by position. The two features are designed together: a default is what makes a parameter skippable, and a named argument is what makes a skipped parameter reachable again.

rows: one shared type and one shared default, applied to both names
a default whose type is inferred from it; exactly one name
a named argument at the call site

blocks.text: The default expression is written in the declaration and is evaluated at the call, not stored with the procedure. Its type must convert to the parameter's type under the ordinary rules.

hello world!
hello world?
hi world?
Shared types and shared defaults

A group of names separated by commas and ended with one `: type` gives every name in the group that type. If the group also carries `= value`, the default is shared as well; it is not attached only to the last name. This follows from the grammar: the annotation and the default belong to the parameter group, and the group is what the names were collected into.
shared()=33 shared(1)=13 shared(1,2)=12
Inferred-type defaults

`name := value` in a parameter list declares a defaulted parameter whose type is taken from the default expression, with no annotation written. The `:=` form takes exactly one name, because there is no type annotation for a group to share; `(a, b := 2)` is `error: unexpected token ','`.
scaled=10 scaled3=15
Defaults need not come last

A defaulted parameter may precede a non-defaulted one. Nothing in the declaration is rejected; the consequence lands at the call site, where the later parameter can no longer be reached positionally and must be named. Named arguments are what make this coherent, so the language does not need the usual "defaults last" restriction.

early=102
named-first=902
Named arguments

A named argument is written `.name = value`. The leading dot is part of the syntax and is not optional: `f(1, b = 3)` is `error: unexpected token '='`, because without the dot the parser is reading an assignment expression in an argument list. The dot spelling matches the one used for enum variants and aggregate literal fields.
box=24 box2=24
Named and positional arguments may be mixed in one call, as `box(3, .d = 2, .h = 4)` does.
A named argument may precede a positional one. In `early(.b = 2, 9)` the `9` fills the first parameter that no name claimed, which is `a`, giving `902`.
A trailing comma is allowed after the last parameter in the declaration, so a long defaulted parameter list can be written one parameter per line without a ragged last entry.

A name that matches no parameter is not a separate diagnostic; it is reported as a failed call, together with the signatures that were considered. This is the same message a wrong argument count or a wrong argument type produces.

error: no overload 'f' accepts these arguments
note: possible candidates for 'f':
candidate: f :: (a: ssize, b: ssize = ...) -> ssize
When a default is evaluated

The default is an expression, evaluated at each call that omits the argument. It is not folded once at the declaration, so a default that calls a procedure calls it again on every such call, and a default that reads a mutable global reads its current value.
call1=1 call2=2 counter=2

Evaluation at the call does not relocate source syntax. `location: Source_Location = #source_location` captures the position where that default was written, not the caller. The parser already materialized the directive's filename, line, and column as constants. Pass `.location = #source_location` explicitly to capture a call site.
default=2 caller=6
Defaults and overloading

Glosso has no ad-hoc overloading: two ordinary procedures may not share a name, and the second one is `error: function 'render' is already declared`. The only overloading is typeclass method dispatch, described in Typeclasses: Declaring a Contract and How an Instance Is Chosen. Defaults therefore never participate in choosing between candidates by arity; the instance is chosen by the argument types first, and the chosen method's defaults fill the rest.

ssize  = 12 / 30
bool = 9 / 2

`render(true)` prints `9`, not `4`. The default that applies is the one written on the instance method that was selected, not the one written on the class requirement. A named argument works the same way at a typeclass method call as anywhere else: `render(3, .width = 5)` gives `15`.

An instance method must repeat the requirement's defaults. Declaring `render :: (value: s64, width: ssize)` against a requirement that reads `width: ssize = 4` no longer matches, and the instance is rejected with `error: instance 's64 :: Render' does not satisfy the implicit minimal definition; missing render`. The value of the default may differ; its presence may not.

A variadic parameter accepts any number of trailing arguments and presents them to the body as one collection. It is spelled with `...` as a prefix on the parameter's type, and what follows the `...` decides how much the body knows about the elements.

rows: a heterogeneous tuple; constant indices retain concrete types
a pack whose elements keep their own types

blocks.text: The `...` is a type prefix, not a suffix on the name, and it is three dots. Two dots is the range operator, and the compiler says so: `xs: ..ssize` is `error: variadic parameter uses '...T'; '..' is the range operator`. A variadic parameter takes exactly one name (`variadic parameter must have one name`) and cannot carry a default (`variadic parameter cannot have a default value`), since the empty pack already is the default.
The pack interface

Every form supports the same three operations: `.count` gives the number of arguments as an `ssize`, `for` walks the elements with `it` and `it_index`, and a constant index selects one element. A call that passes no variadic arguments is legal and gives a pack of count zero.

count=3
  0: 7
  1: hi
  2: 1
  first=7
count=0

For the untyped, homogeneous, and generic forms the parameter really is an array view and can be bound as one: `view: []any = xs;` inside `describe`, `view: []ssize = xs;` inside a `...ssize` procedure, and `view: []T = xs;` inside a `...$T` procedure all compile.

An untyped pack boxes each argument into `any`, and a bare integer literal has no type to box. `count_all(1, 2)` against `count_all :: (xs: ...)` reaches the backend undecided and fails late with `error: comptime_int reached code generation without a decided type [opcode BoxAny] while lowering 'main'`. Give the argument a type, or use a typed pack.

Explicit `...any` is different from bare `...`: it preserves the argument types in a heterogeneous tuple and accepts ordinary numeric literals. A constant index or inline iteration retains each element's type, which lets a forwarding wrapper select a `Formatter` instance. The whole pack cannot be assigned to `[]any`; that assignment reports `got tuple, expected []any`. Expand it with `args...` when forwarding.

Variadic packs do not destroy their elements. Passing a managed owner through a variadic parameter is rejected, including through `print`'s pack. Supply a borrowed pointer or non-owning view supported by the callee, or render an owner to a string without moving it into the pack.
Homogeneous and generic packs

`...T` fixes the element type in the declaration; every argument must convert to `T`. `...$T` leaves the element type open and captures it from the call, so each call site is a separate instantiation but a single call is still homogeneous.

sum=10 sum0=0
firstof=10 firstofs=a

A wrong element type is reported per argument: `sum(1, "two")` is `error: arg type string != ssize in call sum`. For a generic pack the first argument decides, and the message names the type it decided on: `firstof(1, "two")` is `error: arg type string != comptime_int in call firstof`.
Typeclass-constrained packs

`...C`, where `C` is a typeclass, accepts arguments of different types so long as each one has an instance of `C`. Several classes are combined with `&&` inside parentheses. `&&` is the only connective; `...(Show || PartialEq)` is `error: unexpected token '||'`, and an empty list is `error: constrained variadic parameter needs at least one typeclass`. `print` instead uses `args: ...any`: its compile-time format parser checks `Formatter` for each argument's selected rendering. A wrapper that specifically requires default `Show` values can use `...Show`.

A constrained pack is not an array of `any`. Each element keeps its own static type, and the `for` over it is unrolled at compile time so that `it` has a different type on each iteration. That is what allows the per-element instance to be selected. It also means a body that is valid for one argument list can be invalid for another.
error: arg type string != ssize in call only_int

The same body compiles and runs when both arguments are `ssize`. Indexing follows the same rule in reverse: a constant index selects an element with its own type, but an index the compiler cannot fold degrades the element to `any`, giving `error: arg type any != ssize in call only_int`.
Parameters after a variadic

A variadic parameter does not have to be last, but every parameter after it must have a default: otherwise there is no way to tell where the pack ends. Writing one without a default is `error: parameters after a variadic parameter must have default values`. The trailing parameters are then supplied by name.

sum = 6

Call-site expansion

An existing array can be passed as the whole pack by suffixing the argument with `...`. Use a fixed array or a view whose element type matches the pack. A dynamic array owns its storage and cannot move into a variadic pack; expand its borrowed view instead, as in sum(dyn[..]...). Managed elements cannot be passed by value through a pack, which does not destroy them.

fixed=6 view=6
dyn=30
forward=106

`sum_plus` shows the other use of the suffix: a procedure forwards its own pack to another variadic procedure by expanding it. An expansion must be the only variadic argument in the call, so it can neither be preceded nor followed by loose elements. Fixed parameters before the variadic are unaffected, which is why `sum_plus(100, 1, 2, 3)` and `sum(xs...)` are both fine.
`sum(5, a...)` and `sum(a..., 5)` both report error: expanded argument must be the final variadic argument in call `sum`.
`sum(a..., b...)` reports error: call `sum` has more than one expanded argument.

Expanding something that is not an array reports error: expanded variadic argument to `sum` must be an array. Expanding the wrong element type reports error: expanded variadic arg type `[2]string` != `[]ssize` in call `sum`.

A bare `...` as the last parameter, with no name and no type, is a different feature: it is the C varargs marker, legal only on `#foreign` declarations and `#c_call` definitions. It is covered in Calling C from Glosso.

noalias is a pointer parameter modifier and a promise made by the caller. During the call, access through that pointer must obey the non-aliasing contract. It is independent of pointer mutability and ownership.

A receiver can also carry noalias, as in noalias *mut #self. A writable destination and a read-only source still need distinct storage when the noalias contract requires it. Memory analysis checks overlapping arguments and conflicting live borrows; findings are warnings by default and errors under --borrow-check=error.
Keep noalias only where callers can satisfy it. Backend optimization may rely on the declaration; runtime bounds and null checks do not check aliasing.

A parameter marked `#lazy` is not evaluated at the call. The argument expression travels to the callee unevaluated, is evaluated the first time the body reads the parameter, and the value produced by that evaluation is reused for every later read. A `#lazy` parameter the body never reads is never evaluated at all, so a call can discard an expensive or failing computation without paying for it.

ignore_it:
  result=0 evals=0
use_once:
  evaluated b
  result=1 evals=1
use_twice:
  evaluated c
  result=3 evals=1

Three calls pass the same side-effecting expression. `ignore_it` never names `v`, and `probe` does not run. `use_once` and `use_twice` both run it exactly once, whether the body reads the parameter one time or two. The counter is the whole story: zero reads means zero evaluations, and any positive number of reads means one.
Evaluated at first use, not at the call

The delay is observable, not merely an optimization. Because the argument expression is evaluated inside the callee, it sees the state the callee has already produced, not the state that existed at the call.
delayed=100 eager=1

`eager` receives the value `1` that `counter` held at the call. `delayed` receives the expression `counter`, reads it after the assignment, and gets `100`. A `#lazy` parameter is therefore a deferred expression rather than a deferred value, and an argument with a side effect changes when that side effect happens.
Forwarding, and reads inside a loop

Memoisation is per call, and it survives forwarding: passing a `#lazy` parameter on to another `#lazy` parameter does not force it, and the inner function's first read is the one evaluation the whole chain gets.
outer=1 n=1
A read inside a loop is still one evaluation. A body that writes `while i < n` over a `#lazy` parameter `n` evaluates the bound once and compares against the memoised value on every iteration.

`#lazy` is not textual substitution. A macro would re-run the expression at every occurrence; a `#lazy` parameter runs it at most once and caches the result. If the intent is to re-evaluate, pass a procedure or a lambda and call it, or use `#expand`, which is covered in Macros with `#expand`.
How `&&` and `||` are built on it

`&&` and `||` are not built-in control flow. They are ordinary operators owned by the Prelude typeclasses `LogicalAnd` and `LogicalOr`, and short-circuiting is spelled out in the class declaration as `#lazy` on the right operand.

The checker marks a binary expression as short-circuiting exactly when the second parameter of the instance it selected carries `#lazy`. Short-circuiting is therefore a property of the chosen instance, not of the spelling `&&`: the same source text is a short-circuit for one operand type and a plain two-argument call for another.

false && side:
  eval L
  = 0
true && side:
  eval L
  eval R
  = 0
true || side:
  eval L
  = 1
false || side:
  eval L
  eval R
  = 1

`%` prints a `bool` as `1` or `0`. The right operand runs only when the left one fails to decide the result, which is what makes the ordinary guard idiom safe: the bounds test below never indexes out of range, because `view[i]` is the unevaluated right operand of a `&&` whose left operand is already false.
guard held
A user type that short-circuits
Writing an instance of `LogicalAnd` or `LogicalOr` gives a user type the same behaviour, and unlike the Prelude's `bool` instance the body is ordinary Glosso rather than a `#magic` intrinsic.
r=0 hits=0

The laziness of an instance method has to agree with the class it implements, parameter for parameter. Dropping the `#lazy` from the instance above is `error: operator '&&' must match the #lazy parameter contract of typeclass 'LogicalAnd'`; the same check on a non-operator method reads `error: function 'pick' must match the #lazy parameter contract of typeclass 'Pick'`. Without it a caller could not tell from the class whether its argument will run.
The inlining requirement

Deferring an expression into a callee means splicing the expression into the callee's body, so a call that passes a `#lazy` argument is always inlined and the callee gets no independent definition: a program whose only lazy procedure is `pick` compiles to LLVM IR containing no `glo_pick` symbol at all. Everything that would defeat that splice is rejected.

Combining with `#comptime`

`#lazy` and `#comptime` may qualify the same parameter, in either order. The argument then has to be compile-time known, and it is still only evaluated if the body reads it, which is how a compile-time call can pass an expression that would fail to fold.
UNUSED=7 USED=42

`1 / 0` is never evaluated because `comptime_ignore` never names `value`. `#comptime` parameters in general are covered in Compile-Time and Type-Only Parameters, and the operator machinery behind `&&` in The Operator System.

Two parameter qualifiers move a parameter out of the runtime calling convention entirely. `#comptime` keeps the parameter's value but demands that the caller supply it as a compile-time constant; `#empty:` keeps only a type and no value at all. Both occupy an argument position at the call site, and neither appears in the generated function's parameter list.
`#comptime` parameters

`#comptime` prefixes the parameter name. Inside the body the parameter is a compile-time constant, so it may drive `#inline for`, `#if`, `#assert`, an array length, or any other construct that needs a value before the program runs.

One `#comptime` covers every name in a shared-type group, so `(#comptime a, b: ssize)` makes both `a` and `b` compile-time. The argument must be a constant the compile-time evaluator can reduce: a literal, a `::` constant, or a compile-time call. A mutable local is not one, and `k := 3; pow(k, 2)` is `error: argument for #comptime parameter 'n' must be known at compile time` with `note: unknown const k`.
A `#comptime` parameter is otherwise an ordinary parameter. It may carry a default, and it may be supplied by name with the usual `.name = value` spelling.
Erasure and specialization identity

A `#comptime` argument is part of the identity of the specialization, not part of its signature. Two calls with different constants compile to two functions; each of them takes only the runtime parameters. The program below has one `scale` in source and two in the object code.
Compiled with `--backend llvm-ir`, the three definitions the file produces are these.

Each `scale` specialization takes one `i64`, the runtime `x`; the constant `k` survives only in the mangled name and in the folded body. `zero_of` takes nothing at all, because its only parameter is a `#empty:` slot. A `#comptime` parameter is consequently a code-size decision as much as a typing one: every distinct constant is another copy of the body.
`#empty:` type-only parameters

`#empty:` replaces the parameter name with the marker itself and declares a slot that carries a type and no value. The caller writes a type where the argument goes. This is how a procedure whose result type cannot be inferred from any argument gets told which type to produce.

zero_of(ssize)=0
zero_of(f64)=0
zero_of(bool)=0
name_of=two types
parse_as=0

One `#empty:` marker may list several types separated by commas, as `name_of` does, and a signature may contain several markers. All anonymous witnesses must appear before runtime parameters: `pair :: (#empty: $A, #empty: $B, x: s64)` is called as `pair(s16, s32, 1)`. A witness after `x` is rejected with `#empty parameters must appear before runtime parameters`. Named `#comptime` parameters retain their own placement rules.

What the slot takes is the type of the expression written there, and the expression itself is discarded rather than evaluated. Passing a call in a `#empty:` position selects that call's return type and does not run it.
z=0 hits=0

A type name such as `f64` is the normal spelling and the one to prefer, because it says what is meant. A generic type application is not an expression, so `zero_of(Box(s64))` fails with `error: unknown function Box`; a `#empty:` slot cannot select a partially applied generic carrier.

`#empty:` parameters are anonymous. The compiler names them `__empty0`, `__empty1`, and so on, which is what surfaces in an overload note: calling `pair :: (#empty: $A, $B)` with one type gives `error: no overload 'pair' accepts these arguments` and `candidate: pair :: (__empty0: A, __empty1: B) -> s64`. They cannot be passed by name, cannot take a default, and cannot be qualified with `using`, `noalias`, or `#lazy`.
Choosing an instance by its output type

The standard library uses `#empty:` wherever a typeclass has to dispatch on a type that appears only in the result. `FromString` declares `from_string :: (#empty: T, text: string) -> ?T`, so the destination type is an argument and instance selection has something to match on.

Without the witness the class parameter `To` would appear nowhere in the argument list and no call could ever decide it. The same pattern appears in `Try` (`from_output`, `from_residual`, and `?`) and in `Propagate`; see `Try`, `?`, and `#try`.

A procedure is generic when its signature introduces a type variable. There are two spellings. A `$` prefix on a name inside a parameter annotation captures that name as a type parameter and infers it from the argument; a parameter declared `T: type` names the type parameter explicitly and is supplied by the caller. Both produce the same thing: a template that is instantiated once per distinct set of type arguments.

idf=3 idf=hi
wider=9
first=10
deref=7
unbox=41
tag=201

The captured name is an ordinary type name inside the signature and the body: `size_of(A)`, a local `d: T`, a `cast(T)`, and a `where` clause all see it. Distinct captures in one signature are independent type parameters, so `tag` is generic in two.
Where a `$` capture may appear

The capture does not have to be the whole annotation. It may sit at any depth inside it, and the compiler matches the annotation's shape against the argument's type to solve for it. That is what makes `(xs: []$T)` mean "a view of anything" rather than "a view of a type literally named T".

The element type of a dynamic array

The parameter and result of a function type

opt=9
res=4
many=1

Only types are captured. There is no capture for the length of a fixed array: `xs: [$N]$T` is `error: bracket type expects [], [*], [..], [N], or [_]`. A procedure that has to work over fixed arrays of several lengths takes a view instead, and reads `xs.count`.
The rebinding rule

A `$` prefix declares the parameter. Every later mention of the same name, in the same signature, is written plain. Repeating the `$` is `error: polymorph $T is already bound; use plain T after the first $T`, and the rule applies at any depth: `(a: []$T, b: []$T)` is rejected for the same reason `(a: $T, b: $T)` is.

The reason is that a `$` name is a binder, not a wildcard. Two independent element types are two names, `$A` and `$B`; one shared element type is `$T` then `T`. Nothing about the annotation would otherwise distinguish the two intentions.
Passing a captured parameter explicitly

Captured type parameters may also be supplied at the call, positionally and before the runtime arguments. This matters when inference has nothing to work from, which is the case for a type variable that appears only in the return type: such a variable becomes a synthetic type parameter appended after the ones bound by the parameter list.

explicit=3
zero=0
convert=3

The order is the declaration order: parameter captures first, then return-only captures. Supplying too few produces a diagnostic that spells the order out, so `convert(f64, 3)` is `error: call convert supplies 1 compact generic type(s), but unresolved order is (T, R)`.
Explicit `type` parameters

A parameter annotated `type` is a type-valued parameter. It is promoted to a real type parameter when its name is used elsewhere in the signature; if it is used only in the body it stays an ordinary compile-time value of type `type`, which behaves the same at the call site.

make=9
idt=3
conv default=3
conv f32=3
defaulted=11
defaulted s8=11

Accepted; the name must start with an uppercase letter

blocks.text: The trailing-position rule accepts only the inferred spelling. Writing `f :: (x: ssize, T: type = f64)` still fails with `error: type parameter 'T' must appear before runtime parameters unless it has a default`, even though the parameter has one; the accepted form is `T := f64`, with no `: type` annotation and an uppercase initial letter.
One specialization per distinct argument tuple

Generics are monomorphised. The compiler instantiates the body once for each distinct tuple of type arguments and reuses that instantiation for every call that resolves to it. Four calls to one generic procedure over three distinct types give three functions.

The mangled name is the procedure name followed by the argument types, which is exactly the specialization key; the two `s64` calls share one definition. Because the key is the whole tuple, a procedure generic in two parameters distinguishes the orders: `tag :: (a: $A, b: $B)` yields `glo_tag__s64_s16` and `glo_tag__s16_s64` as separate functions.

Instantiation is also where a generic body is really checked. Two procedures may not share a name, so a generic procedure cannot be split into per-type overloads: `f :: (x: $T) -> string where Is_Integer(T)` next to `f :: (x: $T) -> string where Is_Float(T)` is `error: function 'f' is already declared`. Selecting behaviour by type is done with `#if` inside one body, or with typeclass instances; see Static Branching with `#if` and How an Instance Is Chosen.
The guards that restrict which types may instantiate a generic procedure are `where` clauses, covered in Constraints with `where`.

A `where` clause is a compile-time boolean guard attached to a declaration. It is evaluated at each call, after the call's type arguments have been solved and before the candidate is accepted. A clause that evaluates to false removes the declaration from consideration; if nothing is left, the call fails.

scaled=42
scaled=3
rep=ababab
Placement and repetition

The clauses come after the parameter list, after the return type, and after every function directive, immediately before the body. The order is fixed: `f :: (a: ssize) where true #inline { }` is `error: function directives must appear before where clauses`.

A declaration may carry any number of `where` clauses. They are conjoined, so repeating the keyword means "and". Writing `where A where B` and `where A && B` are the same constraint; the repeated form is usually easier to read when the predicates are long.

both :: (x: $T) -> T where is_int_like(T) where T != s32 { return x; }
conj :: (x: $T) -> T where Show(T) && PartialEq(T, T) { return x; }
Compile-time predicates over type parameters

Any expression the compile-time evaluator can reduce to a `bool` is a legal clause, and a type parameter is an ordinary compile-time value inside it. Type equality, `size_of`, and the `Is_*` reflection helpers from `Meta` are all available; so is a user procedure taking a `type`.

double=42
show_it=1.5
both=3
conj=7

A clause may also constrain a `#comptime` value parameter rather than a type. `rep :: (#comptime n: ssize, s: string) -> string where n > 0` accepts `rep(3, "ab")` and rejects `rep(0, "ab")`, because the guard sees the constant the caller supplied.
Typeclass predicates

A class name applied to a type is an evidence query: `Show(T)` is a compile-time `bool` meaning "does `T` have a `Show` instance?". This is the form to reach for whenever the body calls a class method, because it states the requirement the body actually has. Multi-parameter classes are written with all their arguments, as in `PartialEq(T, T)`.
Evidence queries are not general expressions. The evaluator handles a bare query and a conjunction of queries; anything else is `error: non-constant function call` at the declaration.

What a failed constraint looks like

A call whose only candidate fails its guard reports the guard, not the body: `double("hi")` for the `double` above is `error: constraint failed for double`. The diagnostic names the declaration and points at the call, and it does not say which clause failed, so a declaration with several clauses is easier to diagnose when they are split across repeated `where` keywords.

A `where` clause naming something that does not exist is not reported at the declaration. `f :: (x: $T) -> ssize where Show(U)`, with no `U` anywhere, compiles; every call to `f` then fails with `error: constraint failed for f`. A constraint that rejects every argument is usually a misspelled type-parameter name.
The definition-site pre-check

A generic body is normally checked once per instantiation, which means a mistake in it surfaces at a call site rather than at the declaration. To narrow that gap the checker also runs the body once at its definition with every type parameter bound to a skolem: an opaque type that supports exactly the classes the declaration's `where` clauses name, and nothing else. An operator or method used on a skolem is resolved against that evidence set instead of against the global instance table.

The pre-check is deliberately one-sided. It reports only what the declared evidence provably cannot support, and it stays silent everywhere a decision would need the concrete type. Literals do not default against a skolem, class methods resolve abstractly with no dictionary, and `#meaningful` probes are not run at all, because a structural probe asks a question about a concrete type by construction. What it finds it reports as a warning as a warning, never as an error, so a program the pre-check complains about still compiles and runs.

An operator the declared evidence cannot supply is exactly what the pre-check reports. A body that adds two values of a type parameter whose `where` clause names only `Show` draws `warning: no '+' for <T>: the where-clause only provides Show` at the declaration, with `note: reported at the definition; add the class to the 'where' clause`. The error itself is raised by the first instantiation that lacks the instance, and it is anchored inside the body rather than at the call; that error aborts the compilation, so the program below reports it alone and the warning is not printed beside it.

error: no operator '+' for Point, Point
  --> sum.glo:3:56
  |
3 | sum_two :: (a: $T, b: T) -> T where Show(T) { return a + b; }
  |                                                        ^

The same file with the call removed compiles clean, which is the other half of the picture: a generic procedure that is never instantiated is not checked in any other way, and its body can name things that do not exist.
x

That program compiles and runs. Adding one call to `never_called` is what turns `totally_unbound_name` into an error. The practical rule is that a generic procedure is only as checked as its call sites make it, so a library generic wants a test that instantiates it.
Where else `where` appears

The same clause syntax attaches to a typeclass declaration, where it states a superclass requirement, and to an instance, where its clauses are copied onto every method and associated type of that instance. Those are covered in Typeclasses: Declaring a Contract and in Instances: Heads, Bodies, and `where`.

A constraint that asks whether an operation typechecks at all, rather than whether a named class is implemented, is written with `#meaningful`; a predicate such as `Addable :: (T: type) -> bool { return #meaningful { p, q: T; p + q; }; }` is a legal `where` predicate and is the subject of Structural Constraints with `#meaningful`.

`#meaningful` asks the checker a question: would this code type-check? It takes a block, checks every statement in it against the current type environment, and folds to `true` if all of them passed and `false` if any of them failed. The verdict is an ordinary compile-time `bool`, so it can initialize a constant, guard a `#if`, stand in a `where` clause, or be the condition of an `#assert`.

This is a structural constraint: it is satisfied by the shape of the type rather than by a registered instance. A typeclass predicate asks whether evidence was declared; `#meaningful` asks whether the expression the generic body actually writes would resolve. Field access, indexing, calls to ordinary generic procedures and operator resolution all fall inside its reach, and none of them is a typeclass query.

Statements inside the probe are type-checked and then discarded. They are not lowered, not run at compile time, and not run at runtime, so a call written inside a probe has no effect on the program. The declarations a probe introduces are local to it and are gone when it finishes.
ok=1 no=0 calls=0
The two spellings

A brace after `#meaningful` starts a block, which runs to its closing brace and may hold any number of statements. Without a brace the directive takes exactly one unary expression and wraps it in a single-statement block. The block form is the one to reach for by default, because it can declare the values the probe needs.

Write `#meaningful { v.left == 3; }` when the probe should cover the comparison.
How it differs from a typeclass predicate

`Class(T)` and `#meaningful` answer different questions, and they disagree. The evidence query consults the instance table for the class named; the probe re-runs the checker over the code written. A type can satisfy one and fail the other in either direction.

rows: is there an instance of this class for `T`?
does this code type-check for these types?

The evidence query says yes and the structural probe says no, and both are correct about the question they were asked.
Show=1 adds=0 show=3.5
Only the probe can constrain an operation no typeclass owns: a field by name, a member call, a call to an ordinary generic procedure.
Only the evidence query can name a class that no single expression exercises, and it is the form that participates in instance selection. How an Instance Is Chosen covers that side.
In a `where` clause

A `where` clause accepts a `#meaningful` block directly; the clause evaluator recognises the node before it tries constant folding. The clause's environment is the candidate's binding environment, so the parameter names of the signature are in scope inside the probe.

Wrapping the probe in a `(T: type) -> bool` procedure gives it a name and, more usefully, makes it an ordinary compile-time boolean. Such a predicate composes with `!`, `&&` and `||` in a `where` clause, because the clause is then just a constant-foldable call.

error: constraint failed for read_left
   --> probe.glo:12:18

12 |     print("%\n", read_left(r));

A raw evidence query does not compose the same way. `where Class(T)` and `where A(T) && B(T)` are the only shapes the clause evaluator understands; `where Show(T) || PartialOrd(T, T)` is `error: non-constant function call`. Routing the same question through a `#meaningful` predicate is the way to get negation and disjunction.
In `#assert`

When a probe fails, the checker keeps the diagnostic that made it fail. `#assert` prints that reason underneath the assertion message, which turns an opaque "does not work" into the specific resolution failure. This is the most useful place to spend a probe.

error: assertion failed: Vec does not support +
  --> probe.glo:4:5
  |
4 |     #assert #meaningful { p, q: Vec; p + q; }, "Vec does not support +";
  |     ^^^^^^^

Probe hygiene and rollback

A probe is a transaction. Nothing it caused survives it unless some non-probe context asks for the same work: constants it forced are restored to their previous state, source it generated is dropped, its `#insert` expansions are unwound, and every generic instance it triggered is marked speculative. A speculative instance is skipped during lowering, so asking whether `sort_items(x)` would compile does not put `sort_items` in the binary. A later real call clears the mark and the instance is emitted normally.

Errors do not escape either, and that includes deliberate ones. A `#compile_error` reached while checking a probe becomes the probe's `false` answer rather than a compile failure, so a generic guarded by `#compile_error` can still be asked about.
probe=0 call=4

Probes nest, and each answers only for itself. The checker stashes the enclosing failure reason before running an inner probe and puts it back when that probe succeeds, so the reason cited against a constraint is the one that constraint produced rather than whichever probe happened to run last. An outer probe over a call whose own `where` clause failed reports `constraint failed for take_left`, not the inner probe's missing-field message.

The verdict is computed once per probe and cached on the expression together with its reason. Consumers that run later, such as an `#assert` diagnostic or overload resolution, read the cached answer instead of re-running the block, which is why a failing probe can still explain itself.

A `where #meaningful` clause is part of a typeclass method's signature key. An instance method must repeat an equivalent probe or the instance fails its minimal check: probing `value.right` against a class that probed `value.left` gives `error: instance 'Carrier :: Witness' does not satisfy the implicit minimal definition; missing inspect`. `#minimal` and Required Methods covers the comparison.

A lambda is an anonymous procedure written inline. The parameter list is delimited by `|` rather than parentheses, which is what keeps it distinguishable from a parenthesised expression; `||` is the empty parameter list, and `||->` is the empty list followed by a return arrow. The lexer produces `||` and `||->` as single tokens and the parser splits them.

A lambda's value is a function pointer. It can initialize a local, be passed as an argument, sit in an array, and convert to any `#fn_ptr` type with a matching signature. It cannot capture; that restriction is what lets the value be a bare code pointer.

inc=5 zero=0 dbl=42 z2=5
add=3
apply=42
The spellings

An explicit return type requires a block. Without one the body is a single expression that is wrapped in an implicit `return`, and there is nowhere for the arrow to attach: `|x: ssize| -> ssize x * 2` is `error: a lambda with an explicit return type requires a block`. A block body without a return type is fine; the type comes from the body.
Named results work in a lambda return type exactly as in a procedure: `|v: s64| -> (lo: s64, hi: s64) { lo = v % 10; hi = v / 10; }` declares both names and returns them.
Repeating a parameter name is `error: duplicate lambda parameter 'x'`, and omitting the separator is `error: expected ',' or '|' after lambda parameter`.
Where the parameter types come from

An unannotated parameter has no type of its own. The checker gives the lambda a signature of inference variables and defers it. Two things can fill those variables in: an expected type at the point the lambda is written, or the arguments of the first call made through it.

The first call decides the parameters permanently, and a compile-time number reaching a parameter takes its default type rather than staying a literal, because a parameter is a runtime binding and needs a representation. So `add := |a, b| a + b; add(1, 2); add(1.0, 2.0);` fixes the parameters at `ssize` and then rejects the second call with `error: callback argument comptime_float != ssize`.

A lambda with nothing at all to fix its parameters is rejected at the binding rather than at some later use: a lone `f := |a| a + 1;` is `error: cannot infer a type here; annotate it or give it a use that fixes one`.
The return type comes from the body

Only the parameters have to be decided from outside. Once they are concrete the body is checked and whatever it produces is the return type, which is why an unannotated lambda can return a `string` built from an `s64` parameter. When both an annotation and a target type are present they must agree: `f: Op = |x: ssize| -> string { … };` against `Op :: #fn_ptr(a: ssize) -> ssize;` is `error: lambda return type is string, but the expected type is ssize`.

Captures

There are no closures. A lambda body may read anything with static storage, which means globals, top-level constants and other procedures, but reaching an enclosing local is rejected. A captured local would have to be copied into an environment record and carried alongside the code pointer, and a lambda is a bare code pointer.

error: lambda captures local 'outer_total', but captured closures are not supported
  --> capture.glo:3:39
  |
3 |     f := |x: ssize| -> ssize { return x + outer_total; };
  |                                       ^^^^^^^^^^^
help: pass the value as an explicit callback or context argument

The expression-body form reports the weaker `error: unbound 'outer_total'`, because the name never resolves far enough to be recognised as a capture. Either way the fix is the same: pass the value as an extra parameter, or put it in the implicit context.

Lambdas as values

A lambda and a named procedure produce the same kind of value, so they mix freely in a table of function pointers, and a block-bodied lambda assigned to a `#fn_ptr` variable takes its parameter from the target type and its result from the body.

f=12
table[0]=7
table[1]=18
table[2]=-6

A lambda cannot appear in a top-level initializer. Both `bump: Op = |v: s64| -> s64 { return v + 1; };` and the constant form `BUMP : Op : |v: s64| -> s64 { … };` fail with `error: unknown const __glo_lambda_0`. Declare a named procedure at file scope and assign that instead; the lambda forms are for use inside a body.

`#fn_ptr` declares a named function-pointer type. It is a top-level declaration form, written after `::` like any other type declaration, and it may not be spelled inline in a type position: writing `f: #fn_ptr(v: s64) -> s64` as a parameter type is `error: unexpected token 'fn_ptr'`. For an unnamed function type there is a separate syntax, described below.

Parameter names are mandatory here, even though they contribute nothing to the type. The parser reads each parameter as `name: type` and a bare type is a parse error: `#fn_ptr(s64, s64) -> s64` reports `error: unexpected token ','` at the comma that follows the name it thought it was reading. The arrow and return type are optional and default to `void`.
The suffixes

rows: C calling convention, no implicit context

blocks.text: A convention mismatch in either direction is `error: got fnptr, expected fnptr`. The message repeats itself because both sides print as `fnptr`; the difference is in the convention, not in the parameters. A `#foreign` declaration does not carry `#c_call` implicitly, so a foreign function assigns to a plain `#fn_ptr` type and not to a `#c_call` one.
