Parameter names are not part of the identity: a value of `#fn_ptr(a: s64) -> s64` assigns to `#fn_ptr(different: s64) -> s64`.

`noalias` is. `Copy :: #fn_ptr(noalias dst: *mut s64, noalias src: *s64);` rejects a procedure without both markers with `error: cannot implicitly convert fnptr to fnptr because their noalias parameter contracts differ`. `noalias` Pointer Parameters covers the marker itself.
Inside a `#no_context` or `#c_call` body, `context` is unreachable: `error: cannot access 'context' in a #c_call / #no_context procedure`.
C varargs in a function-pointer type

A bare `...` may be the last parameter, with no name and no type. It requires the C convention: without `#c_call` the declaration is `error: C vararg function pointer 'Varargs' requires #c_call`. The type then accepts a `#c_call` vararg function, including a `#foreign` one.

A call made through a vararg function pointer accepts only the fixed parameters. `s: Summer = sum_s64;` is fine, but `s(3, 10, 20, 12)` against `Summer :: #fn_ptr(count: ssize, ...) -> s64 #c_call;` reports `error: callback expects 1 argument(s), got 4`. Call the vararg function by name when the extra arguments matter.
The anonymous function type

Any parenthesised type list followed by `->` is a function type. This is the form to use in a parameter, a field, or anywhere else a type is expected. Names and `noalias` are optional; the names are documentation only.

Without the arrow the same parentheses are a tuple type, and a single unnamed element in parentheses is just that type. `(s64, string)` is a two-element tuple; `(s64, string) -> bool` is a function type. `noalias` outside a function type is `error: noalias is only valid on function parameters`.
Null and function pointers

A `#fn_ptr` type excludes the zero address, in the same way `*T` and `[*]T` do, because the optional form takes the null representation as its niche. `?Op` is therefore the same size as `Op` on a 64-bit target and costs nothing to carry. An absent callback is `.None`, and reading it back goes through a pattern match like any other option payload.

none=-1
some=10
Op=8 ?Op=8

This is the shape the standard library uses for every vtable slot. `Allocator :: struct { procedure: ?Allocator_Proc; data: ?*void; }` relies on `.None` being address zero, so a zero-initialized `Allocator` is the "none installed" value without any extra tag.

Producing a function pointer from an address is a checked cast. At `-O0` and `-O1` a zero address aborts with `cast to fnptr of an address that is zero`. Hosted Windows and Linux x86-64 use exit status 134; WASI uses 125. The check fires for a written literal too: `cast(Op) 0` builds and then aborts rather than being rejected during checking. At `-O2` and above the check is not emitted. Runtime Safety Checks and Panics covers the family.

`f: Op = null;` currently compiles and produces a value the program must not call: at `-O0` the resulting binary traps, and at higher levels the call is undefined. `null` denotes `.None` and belongs to an optional type; write `?Op` when a slot may be empty.
There is no unknown-directive diagnostic. A name the parser does not accept in that position simply fails to parse, and the error names the token rather than the concept.

Function directives

Ordinary function directives are written after the return type and before the `where` clauses. The order is fixed, and reversing it is diagnosed rather than accepted, because the clause parser stops looking for directives once a `where` has been seen.

Three directives may prefix a parameter, after the `using` and `noalias` keywords and before the name. `#comptime` and `#lazy` may appear together in either order; each may appear once.

Aggregate and field directives
Aggregate directives sit between the `struct`, `union`, `typeclass` or `distinct` keyword and the body. Each kind accepts a different set, and `enum` and `enum_flags` accept none at all.

It is not an extension point: a name the compiler does not recognise is `error: unknown aggregate #magic "nope_struct"`.

`#c_call` and `#packed` both switch a struct off the default layout, which sorts fields by alignment and then size. `#c_call` keeps declaration order with normal padding, so a C header's layout is reproduced; `#packed` keeps declaration order and removes the padding. reordered=16 c_call=24 packed=10
Statement, expression, and type positions

The remaining directives are not attached to a declaration at all. Several spellings appear in more than one of these positions and mean something different in each; `#comptime` and `#inline` are the two that catch readers out, and What Runs When and `#inline for` respectively cover them.

blocks.text: `#inline` outside a loop is rejected by name: `error: #inline can only prefix while or for`. `#Context` is the only spelling of the built-in context type, and writing `Context` without the `#` reports `error: the built-in Context type is written #Context`.

`#char` is not a parser directive. The lexer consumes the whole `#char "A"` form and emits a numeric token carrying scalar value `65` plus a character-literal marker. The checker preserves that marker: ASCII defaults to `u8` and may adopt `s8` or `rune` context, while a non-ASCII value defaults to and accepts only `rune`. Because validation happens while lexing, malformed forms report `#char expects a string literal` or `unterminated #char string literal`. `#char` Character Literals covers the complete contextual-typing and escape rules.

first parameter of an inherent method

blocks.text: A typeclass is a named contract over one or more type parameters. It is introduced by an ordinary constant declaration whose value is a `typeclass` body, so the form is `Name :: typeclass (P: kind, ...) { ... }`. The body lists requirements: methods that an instance must supply and associated types that an instance must choose. A class declares no representation and produces no runtime value of its own; it fixes a set of names and signatures that instances then fill in.
port 80

Class names live in a single global namespace, and so do method names. Re-declaring a name the standard library already uses is `error: typeclass 'Show' is already declared`, and declaring a method whose name another class owns is `error: function 'show' is already owned by typeclass 'Show'`. The second rule applies between two user classes as well, so a class body may not reuse `show`, `fmap`, `bind`, or any other name already claimed. The reason is dispatch: a method call is resolved by name across every instance in the program, so one name can belong to only one contract.
The declaration header

The header between `typeclass` and the opening brace has a fixed clause order. Everything after the parameter list is optional, but a `where` clause may not follow a directive: `#minimal(f) where Base(T)` is `error: unexpected token 'where'`.

A trailing comma is allowed in the parameter list. `#derive` may appear more than once; the macro it names is what generates an instance when a type asks for one, which is the subject of Deriving Instances with `#derive`. A second `#minimal` is `error: duplicate #minimal directive on typeclass 'K'`.
Parameter kinds

A parameter is written as an ordinary annotated binding, and the annotation is its kind. `type` binds a type and an arrow binds a type constructor. A `#comptime` string parameter binds a value, as in `Formatter`. The number of parameters decides the shape of every instance head for the class.

s64
7x
inside

The three heads differ because the classes do. A one-parameter class takes a single type; a two-parameter class takes a parenthesised argument tuple; a constructor parameter takes the bare constructor name, with evidence asked at the applied type. Arrows of higher arity are accepted, so `(type, type) -> type` binds a two-argument constructor. Value parameters must be marked `#comptime` and currently require `string`; another type reports `compile-time typeclass value parameters currently require string`. A mixed head such as `(Token, "token", $W)` therefore fixes both a type and a selector while leaving the writer generic. Instance heads are the subject of Instances: Heads, Bodies, and `where`, and constructor parameters of Higher-Kinded Typeclasses.

A class declared with an empty parameter list parses, but it can never acquire evidence, because an evidence query is a question about a type argument and there is nowhere to put one. Its instance methods fail that check at every call, so `ping(n)` is `error: no overload 'ping' accepts these arguments` even when an instance declares exactly that signature. Give every class at least one parameter.
Methods and associated types

A class body holds two kinds of member. A member whose value starts with a parenthesis is a method; any other member is an associated type. The distinction is made at parse time, which is why there are no associated constants: a non-parenthesised member is read with the type parser.

rows: an associated type an instance must choose
a method requirement with no default
a method requirement with a default body

blocks.text:
port 80 / port 80
host pair

`Port` inherits the default `describe_twice`; `Host` replaces it. An instance method always beats a class default, because selection drops every default candidate as soon as one instance candidate has matched. A default body is therefore a fallback, never a preference. The class parameters are in scope through the whole body as plain names, and writing one of them again as a generic is `error: typeclass parameter 'T' is already declared; use plain T inside the typeclass method`.
Superclass constraints

A `where` clause on the class declaration is a superclass constraint: it is a condition on the class parameters that must hold before any instance of the class counts. The clauses are evaluated on every evidence query, ahead of the instance list.

Ranked(Crate)=1 Ranked(Balloon)=0
rank 1

The `Balloon` instance is accepted at its declaration: a superclass clause is not checked when an instance is written, only when the class is consulted. The declaration is simply inert. Every query answers `0` and every call is rejected, so calling `rank_of` on a `Balloon` in the program above is `error: no overload 'rank_of' accepts these arguments`. Supplying the missing `Weighted` instance revives the `Ranked` one with no other edit.

The standard library uses this to layer contracts: `Eq :: typeclass (T: type) where PartialEq(T, T) {}` is a marker over structural equality, `Applicative` requires `Functor`, `Monad` requires `Applicative`, and `Fractional` requires `Num(T) && Div(T, T)`. A single clause may join conditions with `&&`, and several clauses may be chained; all of them are conjoined.
What a class declaration emits
A compile-time predicate under the class's own name. `Describable(Port)` is a constant boolean, described in Evidence, Constraints, and Negative Instances.
One globally owned overload set per method name. Instance methods and class defaults are candidates in that set; nothing else may declare the name.
One projectable name per associated type, written `Class(args).Name` in type position and covered in Associated Types.

For an operator member, the spelling, arity, fixity and precedence, all registered globally. The class alone makes `a <*> b` parse; only the instance is missing, and the call is `error: no operator '<*>' for ssize, ssize` until one exists. The Operator System covers the rules.

`#minimal` states the smallest set of members an instance must supply for the class to consider it complete. Members outside that set are expected to have default bodies that are written in terms of the members inside it, so the directive is what makes a class with several mutually defined methods usable: an instance picks whichever member it can implement directly and the rest follow.

Floor low=5 high=-5
Ceil  low=-9 high=9

Both members carry default bodies, so without the directive neither would be required, an empty instance would be accepted, and `low` and `high` would call each other forever. `#minimal(low | high)` states the real obligation: implement one of the two, and the other is derived.
The formula grammar

The formula is a small propositional language over method names. It is parsed by a dedicated parser, not by the expression parser, so the operator table plays no part and the spellings below are the whole vocabulary.

rows: grouping; empty parentheses are an error

blocks.text: Conjunction binds tighter than disjunction, so `a, b | c` means `(a, b) | c`. Parentheses are needed only for the other reading. An empty group is `error: #minimal parentheses cannot be empty`, and a dangling separator is `error: expected a method name after ',' in #minimal` or the matching message for `|`. A name that is not a method of the class is `error: #minimal references unknown typeclass method nope`.

Joined head=4 tail=7 whole=47
Parted head=1 tail=2 whole=12
Operator atoms

An operator member is named in a formula with its quoted spelling, the same form used to declare it. Quoting is required: the formula parser reads an unquoted operator token as punctuation, and `#minimal(+)` is `error: operators in #minimal must use quoted operator names`.

x ~= y  1
x !~ z  1

This is exactly the shape of the Prelude's `PartialEq`, which is declared `#minimal('==' | '!=')` with each operator defaulting to the negation of the other. An unsatisfied operator formula reports the quoted names back: `error: instance '(Z, Z) :: Nearby' does not satisfy #minimal('~=' | '!~')`.
The empty formula and the implicit minimal
`#minimal()` requires nothing. It marks a class whose purpose is the evidence itself rather than any method, and it is what lets an instance body be empty even when the class declares members.
audit=0 evidence=1

Omitting the directive is not the same as writing `#minimal()`. With no directive the class gets an implicit minimal: every method requirement that has no default body must be implemented. That is the common case and the reason most classes need no directive at all. Its failure has its own wording, and it names the members that are missing.

error: instance 'Empty :: Pairish' does not satisfy the implicit minimal definition; missing first, second
  --> minimal.glo:8:1
  |
8 | Empty ::: instance Pairish {}
  | ^^^^^
How satisfaction is decided

The check runs at declaration time, once per instance group, before any call is resolved. For each member the class requires, the compiler builds a signature key from the name, the arity, the fixity, and the parameter and return annotations with the head arguments and the instance's associated types substituted in; a supplied method satisfies a requirement when the two keys agree. The formula is then evaluated over the requirements that were matched.

error: instance 'Span :: Bounded' does not satisfy #minimal(least, greatest)
  --> formula.glo:7:1
  |
7 | Span ::: instance Bounded {
  | ^^^^
note: minimal complete definition declared here
  --> formula.glo:1:32
  |
1 | Bounded :: typeclass (T: type) #minimal(least, greatest) {
  |                                ^^^^^^^^

Because the comparison is on whole signature keys, a method that is present but wrong reports as absent. Declaring `size_of_it :: (value: Z) -> s32` against a requirement returning `s64`, or adding a parameter the requirement does not have, both produce `error: instance 'Z :: K' does not satisfy #minimal(size_of_it)` rather than a separate mismatch message. When a formula fails, comparing the supplied signature against the class declaration character by character is the way to read it. The message re-renders the formula from its parse, so grouping parentheses are dropped: `#minimal((head_of, tail_of) | whole_of)` reports as `#minimal(head_of, tail_of | whole_of)`.

A supplied method that matches no requirement at all is reported separately, once the minimal formula is satisfied: `error: instance method hint does not match any declaration in typeclass 'K'`. An instance may therefore not carry a helper of its own; helpers belong outside the instance body.

A `#modify` block on an instance method changes the signature key the compiler computes, so the instance fails its `#minimal` check even when the body is correct. Express the condition as a `where` clause on the instance instead; that path is checked by evaluating the clause, not by comparing keys.

rows: the formula is unsatisfied, or a member's signature differs
`does not satisfy the implicit minimal definition; missing ...`
no directive, and a defaultless requirement was not supplied
`instance method X does not match any declaration in typeclass 'C'`
a supplied member matches no requirement
an atom names something the class does not declare

blocks.text: An instance supplies a class's members for particular type arguments. It is written `<head> ::: instance Class { ... }`, where the head names the type or types the instance is for and the body holds the methods and associated type values. An instance has no name of its own and is never referred to directly; it is found by the head, through the ordinary overload machinery described in How an Instance Is Chosen.

The head is every token before the `:::`. The parser collects those tokens raw, then re-lexes and re-parses them as a type annotation, which is why a head may be any type expression and why a malformed one reports the text it collected: `Z + ::: instance K` is `error: invalid instance head 'Z+'`. The `:::` is what ends the scan, so omitting it does not give a bad head; it gives no instance at all, and the declaration fails as `error: unexpected token 'instance'`.

The head supplies exactly one argument per class parameter. For a one-parameter class the whole head is that argument; for a class with more than one, the head is a parenthesised tuple read left to right. A head with the wrong number of arguments cannot be substituted into the requirement signatures, so it surfaces as a `#minimal` failure rather than as an arity message.
Head shapes

rows: every instantiation of the generic struct `Box`
the bare constructor, for a class with a `(type) -> type` parameter
a view over any element type
the built-in result type, error first
one argument per parameter of a multi-parameter class

blocks.text: s64 Box float view pointer read-only many-pointer option result Pair(s64, B)

A `$X` anywhere in the head declares a section generic that is bound when the head is matched. Inside the body it is spelled without the `$`, as `Box(A)` and `[]T` above, because the binder is already introduced. The body may use it in parameter annotations, in return types, and in associated type values.

Structural heads match on the exact form, not on what converts to it. The `[]mut $T` instance does not accept a `[..]s64` or a `[*]s64`, and the `[*]$T` instance does not accept a writable `[*]mut s64`; each is `error: no overload 'label_of' accepts these arguments`. Where two forms should behave alike, declare both heads, as the program above declares `[]mut $T` and `[*]$T` separately.
Tuple heads

A class with several parameters is keyed on the whole argument tuple, so `(s64, string)` and `(string, s64)` are different instances. This is what makes asymmetric operations expressible: a program may give `Mul` a `(Vector, f64)` instance and an `(f64, Vector)` instance with different bodies. A tuple head may mix concrete types, section generics, and a repeated binder.

`($T, T)` is a single binder used twice: it matches only when both arguments are the same type. The `#empty:` parameter carries the second class parameter into the signature so that a call can decide it; witness parameters are covered in Compile-Time and Type-Only Parameters. Giving a two-parameter class a bare head such as `s64 ::: instance Convert` is `error: instance 's64 :: Convert' does not satisfy #minimal(convert)`, because nothing binds `To`.
Instance-level `where`
A `where` clause after the class name guards the whole instance. It is what turns a blanket head into a targeted one, and it is evaluated at compile time against the bound head arguments.
small integer / wide integer / float

Several `where` clauses may be chained and are conjoined, and a single clause may join conditions with `&&`; the two spellings above are equivalent. A clause is an ordinary compile-time expression, so a type predicate, `size_of`, an equality on types, and an evidence query all work. The clauses are copied onto every member of the instance, so an associated type value is guarded exactly as the methods are: three blanket instances can supply three different associated types for three disjoint families of type.

A `#modify` block is not accepted on an instance head: `$T ::: instance C #modify { ... }` is `error: unexpected token 'modify'`. On an instance method it parses but breaks the `#minimal` check. Instance conditions belong in `where`.
Instance bodies

A body holds two kinds of member, matching the class: a method, written like any procedure but with the head's type arguments substituted in, and an associated type value, written `Name :: <type>;`. A body may be empty, which is what a marker class and a negative instance use. A method may end at a `#magic` intrinsic instead of a body; the Prelude's arithmetic instances are written that way, as `'+' :: (left: T, right: T) -> Output #magic "int_add";`.

Every member must correspond to a declaration in the class. A member the class does not declare is `error: function 'g' has no owning typeclass`, which is also what naming an unknown class reports when the body holds a method; with an empty body the same mistake is `error: unknown typeclass 'Nonexistent'`. Associated type names are checked too: `error: typeclass 'Registry' has no associated type 'Wrong'`.

There is no orphan rule. An instance may pair anyone's type with anyone's class, including a standard-library type with a standard-library class. Which instance wins is decided by specificity, not by locality; see Evidence, Constraints, and Negative Instances.
`<head> ::: instance !Class { }` declares that the head explicitly does not implement the class. Negative instances are covered in Evidence, Constraints, and Negative Instances.

An associated type is a type that the instance chooses rather than the caller. The class declares the name and the instance supplies a value for it, so a single class parameter can carry a whole family of dependent types: `Indexable` names the element an index produces, `Try` names the output and the residual of a fallible carrier, `Add` names the type a sum has.

alpha 4
2 2

On the class side the member is `Elem :: type;`: a name followed by a type expression and a semicolon, with no parentheses, which is what tells the parser it is not a method. On the instance side the same name is bound to a concrete type, `Elem :: string;`. Inside the class, the name is used as an ordinary type in the requirement signatures, and the minimal check substitutes the instance's value before comparing signatures, which is why `first_of :: (container: Words) -> string` satisfies `first_of :: (container: C) -> Elem`.

There is no default value. The type expression the class writes is a requirement, not a fallback: writing a concrete type such as `Key :: s64;` on the class side and omitting `Key` from the instance still fails the minimal check, because the requirement signatures keep an unresolved `Key` in them and nothing the instance supplies can match. The class side is not a constraint on the choice either: an instance that answers `Key :: string;` to a class that wrote `Key :: s64;` is accepted. The conventional spelling is therefore `Name :: type;`.
Projection

An associated type is read back with `Class(args).Name`. This is a type annotation form: it names a type and may appear anywhere a type may. The arguments are the class's parameters, so the projection is resolved by finding the instance for those arguments and reading its value.

`Widen(s16).Wide` is `s64` and `Widen(f32).Wide` is `f64`, decided by the same `where` guards that decide which `widen` runs. The instance-level clauses are copied onto the associated type value as well as onto the methods, so a projection can never resolve through an instance whose guard is false.
Projection in generic code
The arguments of a projection may be generic binders, which is the form that matters: a generic procedure states its return type in terms of the caller's type without knowing it.
alpha 9

A projection works in a return annotation but not in a parameter annotation. Adding `fallback: Collection(C).Elem` as a second parameter to `head_of` above and calling it makes the call `error: generic argument does not match call head_of`, even when the argument's type is exactly what the projection resolves to. Take such a value through a second generic binder and constrain it separately.
The argument-free projection

`Class.Name` with no arguments is accepted when exactly one instance in the program supplies that associated type. It is a convenience for a class with a single implementation, and it stops being legal the moment a second instance appears.
Adding a second instance turns the same annotation into an error, and the fix is to write the arguments.

error: associated type 'Registry.Key' is ambiguous; provide type arguments
   --> assoc.glo:13:8
   |
13 |     k: Registry.Key = 1;
   |        ^^^^^^^^^^^^
Why the projection is not an expression

`Class(args).name` is also the spelling for a scoped typeclass method reference, and that is the reading the expression parser takes. The two forms are told apart by position, not by the name: in a type annotation the member is looked up among the class's associated types, and in an expression it is looked up among the class's methods.

The annotation projects the associated type and the initializer calls the method, from the same spelling of the same class at the same argument. Using an associated type in expression position therefore reports a missing method: `t := Registry(Session).Key;` is `error: typeclass 'Registry' has no method 'Key'`. Where the projected type is wanted as a value, declare a binding with the projection as its annotation and take `type_of(value)` of the binding.
Projecting another class

A projection may appear inside an instance, including in the value of that instance's own associated type. This is how a derived type is threaded through: the instance defers to whatever `Add` decided rather than committing to a concrete type.

rows: the matching instance does not supply it
`associated type 'Registry.Key' is ambiguous; provide type arguments`
the argument-free form with more than one instance
`associated type arguments must follow the typeclass name`
an instance supplies a name the class does not declare

blocks.text: Applying a class to a type produces a compile-time boolean: `Marker(s64)` asks whether `s64` has a `Marker` instance and folds to `1` or `0` during checking. This is the same query the compiler runs when it selects an instance, exposed to the program so that generic code can branch on it or demand it.

constants = 1 0
static if = marked unmarked
where     = both
comptime  = 1

The query folds only in the contexts the constraint evaluator understands. A `where` clause accepts a bare query or several joined with `&&`; every other shape of `where` expression containing a query is rejected, because the evaluator recognises the call form itself rather than evaluating an arbitrary expression that contains it.

rows: no: `error: internal error: 'Marker' is called but was never lowered`

blocks.text: A negated or disjoint constraint is therefore written with `#if` inside the body rather than with `where` on the signature, or split into two procedures. Wrapping a query in a helper predicate does not work either: the evaluator needs to see the class name at the call site, so `where P(T)` where `P` returns `Class(T)` is `error: constraint failed for use_it`.

An evidence query supplies the class's full compile-time argument list. `PartialEq(s64, s64)` asks about both operand types, just as it does in a `where` clause. Omitting an argument is diagnosed as `PartialEq expects 2 compile-time argument(s)`; it does not silently produce false evidence.
Eq(s64)=1 Eq(f64)=0 PartialEq(s64,s64)=1
Negative instances

`<head> ::: instance !Class { }` declares that the head does not implement the class. It is not the absence of an instance but a statement of absence, and it overrides any positive instance that would otherwise match: evidence is positive and not negative.

Tagged(s64)=1 Tagged(u8)=0
integer

The exclusion reaches dispatch as well as queries. With the declaration above, calling `tag_of` on a `u8` value is `error: no overload 'tag_of' accepts these arguments`: the blanket instance matches the argument, then loses its evidence and is dropped. A generic procedure guarded by `where Tagged(T)` reports the constraint instead, as `error: constraint failed for guarded`.

A negative instance's body is not checked and is never used, so it may be empty even for a class with required methods, and a body written into one is dead. Its purpose is to carve an exception out of a blanket instance that is otherwise right. The Prelude uses it for floating point: `$T ::: instance !Eq where Is_Float(T) {}` keeps floats comparable with `==` while denying them the total-equality marker, because NaN is not equal to itself.
Coherence and overlap

Glosso has no orphan rule and no coherence check at declaration time. Two instances may cover the same type, and the program compiles until a call needs one of them. Overlap is reported at the use site, with a note on each of the two instances that tied.

error: ambiguous typeclass operation 'label_of' for these argument types
   --> overlap.glo:12:18
   |
12 |     print("%\n", label_of(n));
   |                  ^^^^^^^^
note: first matching instance is declared here
  --> overlap.glo:8:47
  |
8 | $T ::: instance Label_Of where Is_Integer(T) { label_of :: (value: T) -> string { return "two"; } }
  |                                               ^^^^^^^^
note: another matching instance is declared here
  --> overlap.glo:7:47
  |
7 | $T ::: instance Label_Of where Is_Integer(T) { label_of :: (value: T) -> string { return "one"; } }
  |                                               ^^^^^^^^

Most overlap is not ambiguous, because selection scores candidates and a concrete parameter outranks a generic one. A specific instance placed beside a blanket instance wins for the type it names and leaves the rest to the blanket, with no annotation and no ordering rule.
specifically s64 / an integer

The same freedom applies across module boundaries. A program may add an instance for a standard-library type and a standard-library class, and it outranks the Prelude's blanket instance for the same type by being concrete.
byte(7) 7

Evidence and dispatch are different questions. A method call is ordinary overload resolution, so it goes through implicit coercions and a concrete instance can capture an argument of a different but convertible type, even though the evidence query for that type is false. Where an instance must key on one type exactly, use a blanket head with `where T == s64` rather than a concrete head.

call    = the s64 instance
evidence = 0
Associated-type definitions are checked eagerly

The lazy overlap rule applies to methods, not to two definitions of the same associated type. Those definitions are registered as a compile-time mapping, so a duplicate semantic instance head is rejected immediately with `associated type 'Class.Name' for <head> is already defined`. The checker normalises generic names and the order of `where` terms while it compares definitions. Two instances with genuinely different predicates, such as `where Is_Integer(T)` and `where Is_Float(T)`, remain separate.

Concrete native and fixed-width heads use their target representation for this duplicate check. On a 64-bit target, associated-type definitions for `ssize` and `s64` are the same head when their `where` clauses are the same; on a 32-bit target the corresponding pair is `ssize` and `s32`. This is protocol-head compatibility, not ordinary type equality.

Glosso has no separate constraint-solving pass for typeclasses. A call to a class method is resolved by the ordinary overload machinery, over the set of every instance method and every class default that carries that name. Instance selection is overload resolution, and every rule that governs overloads governs it.

That single design decision produces most of the behaviour worth memorising. A more specific instance outranks a more general one. An implicit conversion applied to an argument can change which instance is selected. Two equally good instances are a diagnostic at the call site, not at the declaration.
The resolution steps

The checker performs these steps in order for every call whose name is owned by a typeclass. Steps 5 and 6 exist only to break ties, and a program that never writes overlapping instances never reaches them.

rows: Collect every declaration with that name. A call written `Class(T).m(...)` drops candidates that do not belong to `Class`.
Unify and coerce every argument against each candidate's parameter annotations, accumulating a specificity score.
Run the candidate's `#modify` block, then its `where` clauses, then check that the instance head itself has evidence.
If any surviving match is a real instance method, discard every class-default match.
Sort by implicit `#empty` witness first, then by score, highest first.
If the top two still tie, narrow by the expected return type, then by compile-time-number defaulting.
A remaining tie is `error: ambiguous typeclass operation '<name>' for these argument types`.

blocks.text: The specificity score

The score is a small integer accumulated while the arguments are matched. It measures how much of the candidate's signature was pinned down by the call rather than left generic, so a signature that names a concrete type outscores one that names a type variable.

rows: A parameter with a concrete annotation that the argument coerced to.
A generic parameter, when the candidate is an instance method or a class default.
An argument that is a typeclass method reference resolved against a concrete function parameter.
Every argument's own type equalled its parameter type, with no coercion anywhere.

blocks.text: The exactness bonus dominates everything else, which is why an instance that matches the argument type on the nose beats one that would need a widening conversion, however concrete the second one is. The primary sort key is not the score at all: a candidate that consumed an implicit `#empty:` type witness sorts behind one that did not, and only then does the score decide.
Specific instances beat general ones
A blanket instance guarded by a `where` predicate and a concrete instance for one type may both apply. When both match exactly, the concrete one scores `+2` against the blanket's `+1` and wins.

s64
integer
exactly s64
exactly s64

`label_of(a)` scores `10002` for the `s64` instance against `10001` for the blanket, so the concrete instance is chosen. `label_of(b)` reverses it: `u16` matches the blanket's `T` exactly and earns the exactness bonus, while the `s64` instance needs a widening conversion and scores only `2`.

The last line is the one that surprises. `describe(b)` has two candidates: the class default, which matches `u16` exactly for `10001`, and the `s64` instance method, which scores `2`. Step 4 runs before the sort, so the default is discarded the moment any instance matched, and the low-scoring instance method is what remains. An instance method always beats a class default, regardless of score, because the default exists to be overridden.

Because selection runs through the ordinary implicit conversions, an instance written for one concrete type can capture arguments of every type that converts to it. With no blanket instance in the program, there is nothing to score higher and the conversion goes unremarked.
u16 -> s64 instance

An instance keyed on exactly one type is written as a blanket instance whose predicate is a type equality, because a `where` clause is checked after the argument has been bound and admits no conversion. `$T ::: instance Tag_Of where T == s64` matches `s64` and nothing else, and `where Is_Integer(T) && T != s64` is the complementary instance.
Dispatch by the expected return type

A method whose class parameter appears only in return position gives the arguments nothing to decide. Every instance then matches equally well, the scores tie, and step 6 consults the type the call site expects.

annotated = 7
returned  = 1.5
assigned  = 1.5

An annotated binding, a `return` in a function with a declared return type, and an assignment to an already-typed variable all supply an expected type. Nothing else does. `x := unit_of();` and `cast(f64)unit_of()` both leave the call undirected and are `error: ambiguous typeclass operation 'unit_of' for these argument types`, with a note pointing at each of the two instances.

The narrowing prefers a candidate whose return type equals the expected type exactly; if exactly one candidate's return type merely converts to it, that one is taken instead, and two exact matches leave the tie standing. An undecided numeric literal can match several numeric instances and leave a call ambiguous. Give the argument an explicit type when the overload set accepts both integers and floats; this fixes the instance before the call is checked.

twice(3)   = 6
twice(2.5) = 5
Coherence, orphans, and evidence

Two identical instances are legal to declare. Coherence is checked lazily, at the call that cannot choose between them, and the diagnostic names both declarations: `error: ambiguous typeclass operation 'tag_of' for these argument types`, then `note: first matching instance is declared here` and `note: another matching instance is declared here`. The instance declared last is reported first, because candidates are matched in reverse declaration order.

There is no orphan rule. A program may declare an instance of a standard class for a standard type, and it wins wherever it is more specific: `u8 ::: instance Show` outranks the Prelude's `$T ::: instance Show where Is_Integer(T)` for `u8` values and leaves every other integer alone. Specificity, not locality, decides.

Step 3 is where a class-level `where` takes effect. The clause is a superclass constraint evaluated when evidence is asked for, not when the instance is declared, so an instance of `Refined :: typeclass (T: type) where Base(T)` for a type with no `Base` instance compiles and is then dropped from every candidate list. The call reports `error: no overload 'sub_of' accepts these arguments` and lists the candidates it rejected.

Selection never consults a dictionary, so an instance method that is selected is called directly and instance dispatch costs nothing at run time. A class default and an instance method are distinguished only by which body was written where; both are ordinary declarations in the same candidate set.

A class default whose signature omits one of the class parameters can never be dispatched. For `Convert :: typeclass (From: type, To: type)`, a default `describe :: (value: From) -> string` leaves `To` undetermined and calling it is `error: no overload 'describe' accepts these arguments`. Give every class parameter a position in the signature; an anonymous `#empty:` witness parameter is the usual way to place one that carries no value.
Native and fixed-width protocol heads

Protocol dispatch has one narrow target-dependent compatibility rule. A concrete fixed-width instance can service the native integer type with the same signedness and target representation: `s64` covers `ssize` on a 64-bit target, and `s32` covers it on a 32-bit target. The unsigned pairs are `u64`/`usize` and `u32`/`usize`. Matching recurses through pointers, arrays, tuples, and function-shaped protocol heads.

The selected declaration still has its written formal type: in the example, the operator body receives `s64`. The same fallback works for multi-parameter protocols such as `IndexSet`, including assignment lowering. It does not merge the language types: `ssize == s64` remains false, ordinary generic unification keeps them separate, and a matrix or other value whose element type is `s64` is not a matrix of `ssize`.
This relation never crosses width or signedness, never removes a nominal `distinct` boundary, and never treats `rune` as its `u32` storage type. It exists only for protocol instance heads.
Receiver calls and explicit class selection

A named typeclass operation may be called through its first non-erased parameter: `value.show()` uses the same evidence as `Show.show(value)`, and `reader.read(buffer)` dispatches through `Reader`. A storage field or applicable inherent method takes precedence over this lookup. When the intended class is ambiguous, write `Reader.read(reader, buffer)` or `Reader(T).read(reader, buffer)` explicitly.

Receiver syntax does not change defaults, associated types, or instance selection. In instance signatures, associated type definitions, and bodies, `#Self_Type` denotes the complete matched type. For `?$T ::: instance Try` it denotes `?T`, including the option wrapper. Typeclass requirements and instance slots follow the class contract's visibility.

A typeclass parameter carries a kind, written as an ordinary type annotation. `T: type` declares a parameter that stands for a type; `F: (type) -> type` declares one that stands for a type constructor, a generic type that has not yet been applied to its argument. A class over such a parameter is higher-kinded.

Inside the class body the parameter is applied like a generic type: `F($A)` is the constructor at some inferred element type, and `F(B)` is the same constructor at another. This is what lets one method signature describe a transformation that changes the element type but keeps the container.

box  = 42
pair = 6
retype = n
Bare-constructor instance heads

The instance head for a higher-kinded class is the bare constructor name. `Box ::: instance Container` supplies `Box` itself, not `Box` at some element type, so a single instance covers every application of the constructor at once. Writing `Box($A) ::: instance Container` would supply a type where a constructor is wanted.

In both forms the method's own generics are introduced with `$` at their first occurrence and referred to without it afterwards. In the higher-kinded form the `$A` belongs to the method, not to the head, which is exactly why the head has no hole to fill.
Evidence is asked at the applied type

Although the instance is registered against the bare constructor, an evidence query is answered for the applied type. `Box(s64)` and `Box(string)` both implement `Functor` on the strength of one `Box ::: instance Functor`, and a type with no such instance is rejected with the element type in the message.
functors = 2

Passing a `Plain` to the same procedure is ``error: variadic arg type `Plain` does not implement `Functor` in call `count_functors` ``. Typeclass-constrained variadics are covered in Typeclass-Constrained Variadics.

There is no source-level spelling for a higher-kinded evidence query. The constructor form `Container(Box)` is `error: generic struct Box needs type arguments`, and the applied form `Container(Box(s64))` is `error: non-constant function call`. Ask for the evidence through a constrained variadic or a `where` clause on a method that takes the applied type as an argument.
Functor, Applicative, and Monad

The standard library declares three higher-kinded classes in `std/Typeclass`. They form a chain: each names the previous one as a superclass in its class-level `where`, so evidence for `Monad` requires evidence for `Applicative`, which requires `Functor`.

All three carry a derive hook, so a one-field struct or a tagged union can request the instances instead of writing them. The derived `Applicative` and `Monad` for a struct handle one-field structs only; for a union they pick the single variant whose payload is the focused type parameter.

fmap = 5
ap   = 5
bind = 50

`fmap`, `ap` and `bind` all dispatch on an argument whose type mentions the class parameter, so ordinary selection resolves them. Deriving Instances with `#derive` covers what the three macros generate, and Writing a Derive Macro covers how they generate it.
`pure` cannot be called

`pure :: (x: $A) -> F(A)` mentions the class parameter only in return position. The expected-type narrowing described in How an Instance Is Chosen does not rescue it, because the candidate's return type is itself generic and never equals the expected type.

error: no overload 'pure' accepts these arguments
note: call pure cannot produce expected type Ident_s64
note: possible candidates for 'pure':
candidate: pure :: (x: A) -> Ident(A)
candidate: pure :: (x: A) -> F(A)

A hand-written instance does not help; the limitation is in the dispatcher, not in the derive macro. Construct the carrier directly instead: `p: Ident(s64) = .{ .value = 3 };` says the same thing and resolves without a class method.
A worked example

`examples/typeclasses.glo` in the compiler repository derives `Functor` for a generic tagged union and writes `Applicative` and `Monad` by hand on top of it. Both hand-written instance heads are the bare `Foo`.
typeclass totals 43 53
A union payload is read through a pattern capture, never through `ma.Some`. Every derived instance emits `case Variant(payload);` arms for the same reason.

A class-level `where` on a higher-kinded class behaves exactly as it does on a first-order one: it is evaluated when evidence is asked for, and an instance that fails it is silently unusable rather than rejected at its declaration.

A parameter of kind `(type) -> type` accepts a generic struct or a generic union. The built-in `?T` and `E!T` have no bare constructor spelling: the head `?$T ::: instance C` supplies a type, and a lone `?` is `error: invalid instance head '?'`.

The standard `Show` derive macro generates formatting code for structs and tagged unions. Its compile-time formatting path supports managed builders in the current compiler; the examples below run as written.

A `struct` or `union` declaration may carry `#derive(Class, ...)` between the keyword and the body. Each named class must itself declare a derive macro; the compiler runs that macro at declaration time and splices the instance it produces into the program.

show   = {1, left}
a == b = 1
a == c = 0
union  = Line(7)
dot    = Dot
s == t = 1
s == u = 0

The generated instance is an ordinary instance in every respect. It takes part in selection on the same terms as a hand-written one, under the rules in How an Instance Is Chosen, and a second instance declared for the same type is the ordinary ambiguity rather than an override.

A class with no derive macro cannot be derived. Naming one is `error: typeclass 'Plain' does not declare a derive macro`, reported at the type declaration, and every later call to the class method fails as well because no instance was ever created.
What the standard classes generate

rows: `{f1, f2}` for a struct, `Variant` or `Variant(payload)` for a union.
Field-by-field `&&` for a struct; same-variant payload comparison for a union.
`fmap` over the final type parameter, mapping every field or variant that uses it.
`pure` and `ap`; one-field structs only, or the single focused union variant.
`bind`, under the same shape restrictions as `Applicative`.
`report_error` for a non-generic tagged union whose every variant payload is itself `Error`.
Field-wise and variant-wise encoders and decoders, in `Serialization`.

blocks.text: `FromString` deliberately ships no derive macro. A parser for a user type has to decide what its accepted spellings are, and no field-wise rule produces a useful answer. The `Error` derive and the `#from` union variants that pair with it are covered in the chapter on `Error`, `Termination`, and `main`.

The `#derive(...)` list on a struct or union is a comma-separated list of plain identifiers. There is no syntax for passing options to a macro, so the `Derive_Options` a macro receives is always empty and every macro uses its default focus.
`#derive` is accepted on `struct`, `union`, and `distinct` declarations. On an `enum` it does not parse: `Color :: enum #derive(Show) { ... }` is `error: unexpected token 'derive'`.

A derive macro that rejects the shape it was handed reports its own `#compile_error` text, such as `Show derive is not defined for #raw union` or `Functor derive needs exactly one focused type parameter`.

The default `Formatter` instance calls the selected `Show` method directly. `print("%", value)` therefore instantiates a generic derived `Show` on demand, just as `show(value)` does. No preliminary direct `show` call is needed for a generic struct, union, or option.
through print = Some(9)
Deriving on a `distinct` type

`#derive` on a `distinct` declaration is a different feature that shares the spelling. It generates no code at all. A `distinct` type inherits none of its representation's operators by default, and the derive list is the list of operator classes it is permitted to borrow.

The operator is resolved on the representation and the nominal tag is put back only when the representation's result is the representation itself. `Meters + Meters` is `Meters`, and so is `Meters / Meters`, but `Meters == Meters` stays `bool`.
Naming operand types

A bare class name in the list derives the same-type instance: every operand and the result are the nominal type. An entry with type arguments names the operand types where they differ, which is what makes scaling a dimensioned quantity expressible.

rows: `Meters * f64`, yielding `Meters`. The mirrored form needs its own `Mul(f64, Meters)`.
Every operator the representation supports, written instead of a list.

blocks.text:
a * scale = 6
scale * a = 6
a / b     = 0.75
ratio type= Meters
cmp  type = bool

An operator that was not derived names the fix in its diagnostic: `no operator '*' for Meters and Meters: a distinct type gets only the classes it derives; add '#derive(...)' or '#derive,all' on the declaration of 'Meters'`. `#derive` on a `distinct` with neither a list nor `,all` is `error: '#derive' on a distinct type needs a class list or ',all'`.

The derive list on a `distinct` type gates operators only. A named typeclass method still resolves through the ordinary generic instances, because the predicates those instances test are true of the representation. `Meters :: distinct f64;` with no derive at all still answers `show(a)` with `3.5`.

A derive macro is an ordinary `#expand` macro, named by the `#derive(...)` directive on a typeclass declaration. The compiler calls it once per type that requests the class, and the macro's job is to `#insert` an `instance` declaration.
The call is always made with the same three parameters: the type itself, a reflection summary of it, and the options the request carried. The macro returns nothing; its effect is whatever it inserts.

Point  {1, 2} arity=2
Triple arity=3
Pair   arity=2

Everything the macro computes is spliced into the `#code` block with the double-backtick escape. `section` and `input_type` are `Code` values built by the reflection intrinsics, and `count` is an ordinary compile-time integer; splicing all three is what makes one macro serve `Point`, `Triple`, and the generic `Pair`. A body whose shape depends on a loop over the members is usually built as a source string and `#insert`ed instead, which is what the standard derives do.
The reflection types

`std/Typeclass/Derive.glo` declares the structures the compiler fills in. The Prelude imports `Typeclass`, so `Derive_Type_Info`, `Derive_Options`, `Code`, and the intrinsics below resolve in a program with no import line at all; the `#import "Typeclass";` commonly written beside a derive macro is not what makes them visible.

Generic parameters in declaration order, as `Type_Param_Info`.
Struct fields, as `Derive_Field_Info`. Empty for a union.
Tagged-union variants, as `Derive_Variant_Info`. Empty for a struct.
True for a `#raw union`, where tagged-union logic does not apply.
Source name and zero-based position; `index` is what the query helpers take.
Field name and its type resolved in the type's generic scope.
Variant name and payload type; a payload-less variant reports `void`.

blocks.text: Because there is no syntax for passing options in `#derive(...)`, a macro that calls `info.focus_params(opts, n)` always gets the default: the final `n` type parameters. A macro with no use for `opts` may leave the parameter untouched; `derive_error` writes `_ := opts;` to record the intent, and the other standard derives that ignore it write nothing.
The code-building intrinsics

The instance head, with focused parameters left as holes: `Pair($K, _)`.
A concrete type expression, substituting `reps` for the focused parameters.
True when `T` is exactly parameter `i`: true for `A`, false for `[]A`.
True when every occurrence of parameter `i` in `T` is covariant.
The `n` focused parameter indexes, defaulting to the final `n`.

blocks.text: The head shape a macro must emit depends on the arity of the class. A one-parameter class takes the section alone; a two-parameter class such as `PartialEq(L, R)` takes a tuple head, which for a same-type instance pairs the section with the applied type.

Reading fields and variants

`Formatter` selects a rendering by value type, compile-time selector, and writer type. The default selector in `%` and `%{}` delegates to `Show`; selectors such as `%x` and `%{token}` use their own instances. A type can therefore support a named rendering without implementing `Show`. `FromString` is the parsing counterpart to `Show`: `Show` ships a derive macro, while `FromString` does not.
The Prelude instances

The Prelude keys most of its `Show` instances on a predicate rather than on a type, so a whole family is covered by one instance. A program may still add a concrete instance for any of these types; a concrete head outranks a blanket one, and there is no orphan rule.

`FromString` has four Prelude instances: `string`, and blanket instances guarded by `Is_Bool(T)`, `Is_Integer(T)` and `Is_Float(T)`. The integer parser is overflow checked at every width including 128 bits, and the float parser accepts `inf`, `-inf`, `nan`, exponents and subnormals. All of them consume the whole string and answer `.None` on any leftover byte.

A bare `%` or `%{}` selects the empty key. `%c` selects the one-letter key `"c"`, and `%{name}` selects `"name"`. A short selector consumes exactly one ASCII letter whether an instance exists or not, so `%xray` means hexadecimal followed by `ray`. The declaration lives in `std/Prelude/Try.glo` and is available without an import. Matching residuals need no `Propagate` instance, even when the source and destination success types differ.

On `.Break(carrier)`, the compiler exits the nearest boundary with that already completed carrier. The operator's conversion and construction finish before the exiting scopes run their `defer` and `#try defer` entries in reverse registration order.

`#try { expr }` introduces a boundary without introducing a function. It is an expression whose value is the carrier, so a `?` inside it stops at the closing brace instead of leaving the enclosing function. `Propagate` is the conversion `?` performs when the value being propagated fails with one residual and the enclosing boundary requires another. It is deliberately narrower than a general implicit conversion protocol: nothing else in the language consults it, and it is never applied to a successful value.

The class has two parameters and one method, and the head is written as a tuple: `(From_Type, To_Type) ::: instance Propagate`. The leading `#empty:` witness names the target so instance selection can match its destination. The inherited `?` body calls `propagate` only when the two residual types differ; matching residuals need no conversion instance, even for carriers with different success types.

A residual is not the error; for `E!T` it is `Result_Residual(E)`, a struct wrapping one `E`. Writing conversions at the residual level would mean writing wrapper structs by hand for every pair of error types. The Prelude removes that step with one blanket instance in `std/Prelude/Result.glo`.

The consequence is the rule to remember: a `Propagate` instance between two error types is enough to make `?` widen between the corresponding results. `Error` and `Termination` are the two classes at the edge of a program. `Error` says how a value explains itself to the operator; `Termination` says how a value becomes a process exit status. `main` may return any type that implements `Termination`, and the standard pairing of the two is what makes `main :: () -> App_Error!void` a complete error-reporting program.

Reporting is the last thing a failing program does, and it must work when the allocator is exhausted and when the higher-level output modules are themselves the thing that failed, since their own error types implement `Error`. `std/Typeclass/Error.glo` therefore provides two helpers that write straight to file descriptor 2 through the `file_write_result` intrinsic, touching neither the allocator nor `Io`.

Both ignore the write result. A report that cannot be written has nowhere left to report that fact, so the failure is dropped rather than escalated. An instance that wants formatted output can still call `tprint`, at the cost of depending on the temporary allocator on the failure path.
