A plain `for` over the pack is unrolled, so `it` has the element's own static type in each iteration and `name_of(it)` dispatches to the right instance. `it_index` is the position.
A runtime index is allowed and reads through the boxed view, so a `while i < values.count` loop over `values[i]` renders each element correctly even though the index is not a constant.

The view is read-only. Assigning to a pack element is not supported and currently fails during lowering with `error: internal error: 'op_lbrrbreq_tuple_ssize_ssize' is called but was never lowered`; copy the element into a local instead.
`#inline for` and per-element evidence

`#inline for` over a pack is the tool for code that must differ per element. The body is expanded once per argument with the element's type known, so `type_of(it)` can be bound to a compile-time constant and that constant used in an evidence query. `#if Class(T)` answers whether `T` has an instance, and only the taken branch is checked.

Meters (m) shows as meters
  Seconds (s) has no Show

`Show(elem).show` in that body is a scoped typeclass method reference: it names the `show` of the instance for exactly `elem`, which is what lets the call be written in a branch that only some elements reach. The unqualified `unit_of(it)` needs no scope because the constraint on the pack already guarantees an instance.

Structural conditions rather than class membership are written with `#if !#meaningful { it.field; } continue;`, which skips an element whose shape the body cannot use. That form belongs to Structural Constraints with `#meaningful`.

An evidence query is compile-time only. `Class(T)` in a runtime expression is `error: internal error: 'Marker' is called but was never lowered`; bind it to a constant or use it directly in `#if`. Supply every declared compile-time argument: a two-parameter class is queried as `Convert(s64, string)`. The same full argument list works in constant expressions and `where` clauses; a missing argument produces an arity diagnostic.

Every operator in Glosso is a typeclass method. There is no separate operator-overloading feature and no free operator function: a spelling is declared by exactly one typeclass, and the bodies that give it meaning live in that class's instances. Writing an operator at top level is rejected outright with `error: operator '<+>' must be declared by a typeclass and implemented by its instances`.

The class declares the operator's signature, its fixity and, for a binary operator, its precedence; each instance supplies a body for one operand-type combination. Because instance heads are keyed on the complete operand tuple, `(Vec2, f64)` and `(f64, Vec2)` are separate instances and an asymmetric operator is expressible.

The `Output` associated type is the house pattern for an operator class: it lets `<*>` return `f64` from two `Vec2` operands without the class fixing a result type for everybody. Associated types are covered in Associated Types; instance heads in Instances: Heads, Bodies, and `where`.
One owner per name

Ownership is recorded when the class is declared, and a second claim on the same operator is an error wherever it comes from. The check also runs on instances, so an instance may only implement an operator its own class declares.

error: operator '+' is already owned by typeclass 'Add'
error: operator '[]' is already owned by typeclass 'Indexable'
error: operator '<+>' has no owning typeclass
error: operator '<+>' declares conflicting precedence

The first two come from a class trying to redeclare a Prelude spelling. The third comes from an instance whose class never declared that operator. The fourth comes from an instance repeating `#operator` with a level or associativity that disagrees with the class.

'<+>' :: (a: s64, b: s64) -> s64 #operator(left, 17) { return a + b; }
main :: () {}
error: operator '<+>' must be declared by a typeclass and implemented by its instances
Arity and fixity are part of the name

The ownership key is the spelling together with its arity and its fixity: `prefix` or `suffix` for a unary operator, `infix` for everything else. Two classes may therefore share a spelling as long as they differ in fixity, which is exactly how the Prelude gives `-` and `..` more than one meaning.
A program can do the same with its own spellings. Two classes below claim `~~` as a prefix operator and `~~~` as a suffix operator, and one type implements both.

A suffix instance method must repeat `#operator(suffix)`. Fixity is part of the ownership key and defaults to `prefix`, so an instance that omits the directive is looking for a prefix owner and reports `error: operator '~~~' has no owning typeclass`. Prefix and infix instances may omit the directive, because the class already settled the fixity that its key matches.
The `#operator` directive

#operator( left | right | assign , level )
#operator( prefix | suffix )
#operator( suffix, try(Target) )

`#operator` registers all five modes, on both typeclass method signatures and instance implementations. Levels are integer literals from 0 to 1000; the standard operators use the 0-20 scale described in Operator Precedence and the 0-20 Scale. An instance method may repeat the mode alone, as `#operator(left)`, and inherit the level from its class.
A binary or assignment operator with no level anywhere is `error: binary operator '<+>' needs #operator(left|right|assign, n)`. Bare `#operator(left)` on the class declaration counts as no level.

A level on a unary mode does not parse. Write `#operator(prefix)` or `#operator(suffix)` with no numeric argument. A suffix can also carry `try(Target)`, which requests a Try boundary rather than a precedence level.
An unknown mode is `error: #operator expects left, right, prefix, suffix, or assign`, and a level outside the range is `error: operator precedence level must be between 0 and 1000`.

An operator function takes one, two or three parameters; anything else is `error: operator functions need one, two, or three parameters`. `assign` additionally requires arity 2, and `[]` and `[]=` are fixed at 2 and 3 and may not declare precedence at all.
Claiming a spelling

An operator name is written between single quotes, which is the only way to get characters like `[` past the lexer, and its characters must come from the eighteen-character operator set `+ - * / < > ! @ % ^ & | ~ ? . , : =`. Built-in spellings are reserved and rejected at the token level; the full rules, including why `?` can never appear inside a longer operator, are in Reserved Operators and Operator Names.
A name made only of letters can be declared but never written: at a use site the letters lex as an identifier, so `2 plus 3` is `error: unexpected token 'plus'`.

`[` and `]` are refused except in the two fixed forms `[]` and `[]=`: `error: operator '<[]>' cannot contain '[' or ']'`. All-stars and all-ampersands names are reserved as prefix operators: `*p` dereferences and `&x` takes an address. For example, an attempted prefix `**` overload reports `operator '**' cannot be overloaded as a prefix operator`. The postfix spellings `.*` and `.&` are also built in. Mixed names such as `&&*&&` remain available for custom operators.

The parser learns fixities and levels from an early prescan. It scans the Prelude and relative `#load`/`#export` dependencies before parsing the caller, so a loaded module can supply new operator syntax there. The owning class and instance must also be visible to resolve the expression. The prescan is described in The Operator Prescan.
Suffix operators with a Try boundary

`#operator(suffix, try(Target))` gives a suffix operator one erased boundary witness followed by its operand. Its signature is `(#empty: $Target, value: Source)` and its result must be `Try_Branch(Try(Source).Output, Target)`. Both carriers implement `Try`. The witness is excluded from the unary ownership key, but is included when specializing the operator for a destination type.

41
failed

Postfix `input!!` passes the nearest boundary's carrier type and interprets `.Continue` as a value and `.Break` as an early exit. The quoted call `'!!'(Target, input)` returns the ordinary token; it works outside a boundary. Scoped calls such as `Forward_Try.'!!'(Target, input)` do the same. `?` uses this same annotation; its body can be overridden by a `Try` instance.

`try(Target)` is accepted only on a suffix operator. Write the plain identifier `Target` inside the annotation, matching `$Target` in the leading witness. The operand cannot be lazy, variadic, or defaulted. The declaration must have a Glosso body or be a typeclass signature; `#expand`, `#magic`, and foreign bodies are rejected. An instance override must retain the class's Try boundary contract.

An update assignment such as `x += y` is resolved through a typeclass of its own, one per operator, named after the operation it updates. Plain `=` is not one of them: it is a reserved token, it cannot be overloaded, and the statement form is covered in Assignment and Update Assignment.

Each class follows the same shape as any other binary operator class, with `#operator(assign, 0)` in place of a normal precedence, and each is paired in the Prelude with a blanket instance that defines the compound form in terms of the plain one.

The consequence is that `+=` starts working the moment `+` does. A type that implements `Add` needs no further declaration, and a type that wants a different compound behaviour writes its own instance, which outranks the blanket one by ordinary overload scoring.
The assignment classes
Nineteen classes, nineteen blanket instances, and no others. There is no compound form of a unary operator, and no class for `=`.
Declaring a new assignment operator

A new one is an ordinary operator class whose member carries `#operator(assign, level)`. The level is mandatory; a non-zero level compiles, but `0` is the tier the Prelude uses for the whole family and is what an assignment operator should take. `#operator(assign)` without a level is `error: binary operator '<<<=' needs #operator(left|right|assign, n)`, and arity 1 or 3 is `error: assignment operator '<<<=' must have arity 2`.

`+=` here came from the blanket `AddAssign` instance over the program's own `Add`; nothing in the program mentions `AddAssign`. `<<<=` came from `Merge`, and it would work just as well written above the `Merge` declaration, because the prescan registers the spelling for the whole file before parsing begins.
The right-hand side is coerced first

A compound assignment is checked by coercing the right operand to the type of the left one and only then resolving `op=`. Every compound assignment is therefore homogeneous, whatever instances exist. A heterogeneous `Add` gives a working `+` and an unreachable `+=`.
error: no operator '+=' for Counter, Counter

The diagnostic is the proof: the program wrote `c += 5`, and the compiler reports `Counter, Counter`, because the literal `5` was already coerced to the left type before any instance was consulted. Adding the matching `(Counter, s64)` instance of `AddAssign` changes nothing, since the resolution never asks for that pair.
The fix is to write the expression form: `c = c + 5;` resolves `(Counter, s64) ::: instance Add` and compiles.
The standard library hits this too. Pointer offsetting is `([*]$T, ssize) ::: instance Add`, so `p += 1` on a `[*]s64` is `error: no operator '+=' for [*]ssize, [*]ssize`. Write `p = p + 1;`.

This is the limitation to remember about the operator system: `+` and `+=` are not interchangeable for mixed operand types. An API that wants both scaled multiplication and `*=` must offer a same-type `Mul` as well as the mixed one.
The result type

A compound assignment stores the operator's result back into the left operand, so `Output` must be assignable to the left type. When it is not, the failure is reported as a missing operator with a note naming the real problem.

error: no operator '<<<=' for Counter, Counter
note: assign ssize to Counter
When the left operand is a subscript, both halves of the indexing protocol run: `a[i] += 1` reads through `'[]'` and stores through `'[]='`. Indexing and Slicing Operators shows the expansion.

A subscript expression is an operator call like any other. Reading `c[k]` dispatches on `Indexable`, storing `c[k] = v` dispatches on `IndexSet`, and both classes are declared in the Prelude and available without an import.

`[]` and `[]=` are the only operator names allowed to contain brackets, and they are special in two further ways: their arities are fixed at 2 and 3, and they may not declare precedence, because the subscript is parsed as syntax rather than as an infix operator. A `#operator(left, level)` directive on either is `error: operator '[]' is special syntax and cannot declare operator precedence`.
Declaring them for a container

`Key` is an arbitrary type. A grid indexed by a coordinate struct needs one `Indexable` instance for reading and one `IndexSet` instance for storing; a third `Indexable` instance keyed on a range type adds slicing.

g[{1, 2}] = 42
after += : 50
view.count = 3, view[2] = 50

`IndexSet` has no `Output`: a store is a statement, and the requirement returns nothing. A read with no matching instance names the exact tuple that failed to resolve, as in `error: no operator '[]' for Bag, ssize`; a store with no matching instance is the case the compiler still handles badly, described at the end of this chapter.
What a subscript lowers to

`c[k]` becomes the call `'[]'(c, k)`, `c[k] = v` becomes `'[]='(c, k, v)`, and a compound assignment to a subscript becomes both: `c[k] += n` is `'[]='(c, k, '[]'(c, k) + n)`. Printing from the two operator bodies makes the order visible.

b[1] = 7:
  set 1 = 7
read b[1]:
  get 1
b[1] += 2:
  get 1
  set 1 = 9
final 7

The quoted names are also callable directly. `'[]'(b, 1)` and `'[]='(b, 1, 9)` are legal expressions that are rewritten into the same subscript nodes, which is occasionally useful inside a macro that is building an index expression by hand.

`'[]='` receives the container by value. A container that owns its elements inline, such as a struct holding a `[4]s64`, will appear to accept a store and then read back the old element, because the instance mutated a copy. Mutation has to travel through an interior pointer or a view: hold a `[]s64` rather than a `[4]s64`.
Index types

The built-in containers coerce their index to `ssize` before resolving. That covers strings, arrays, views and many-pointers, so `a[i]` on a `[]s64` accepts a `u8` or an `s32` index. This conversion must not narrow: a fixed-width `s64` index needs a checked conversion on a 32-bit target. The examples use `ssize` coordinates and range keys to work at either pointer width, while the stored values stay `s64`. A user container does not get that conversion: its key is synthesised as written, given the default type if it is a compile-time number, and matched against the instance heads. With only `(Bag, ssize) ::: instance Indexable` in scope, `b[3]` resolves and `b[i]` with `i: u8` is `error: no operator '[]' for Bag, u8`.

The remedy is either a blanket instance, `(Bag, $K) ::: instance Indexable where Is_Integer(K)`, or a second concrete instance for the key type in question. Instance selection itself is described in How an Instance Is Chosen.
Slicing

Slicing is not a separate feature. A slice expression is a subscript whose key is one of the six range values, so a container supports the shapes it declares `Indexable` instances for and no others. The Prelude supplies all six for `string`, `cstring`, `string16`, `cstring16`, views in every mutability and volatile combination, and dynamic arrays; a fixed array reaches them by coercing to a view.

The last row is the odd one. A bare `..` inside brackets is its own syntax node, typed as `RangeFull(ssize)` by the checker; there is no class that produces a `RangeFull` value, and it cannot be written anywhere else. Declaring `Indexable` on `RangeFull(ssize)` is what makes `c[..]` legal for a user container.

b[..].count  = 4
b[2..].count = 2 first = 20

Reading and writing are resolved independently. A container that is `Indexable` but has no matching `IndexSet` instance is rejected during checking: assigning an `s64` through `(Bag, ssize) ::: Indexable` reports `error: no operator '[]=' for Bag, ssize, s64`. Likewise `s[0] = 65` on a read-only `string` reports no `[]=` for `string, ssize, u8` rather than reaching lowering. Declare `IndexSet`, or do not write the store.
Range values, their fields, and the classes that build them are covered in Iteration and Range Typeclasses; the slicing semantics of the built-in collections are in Ranges and Slicing.

An ordinary `for` over an array, string, `Simd`, matrix, or custom container goes through `Iterable`. Direct and stored ranges keep their native lowering, and tuples are expanded statically. The class has one requirement, a macro: the loop body arrives as a `Code` value and the instance decides what to do with it.

`for x: container { ... }` becomes a call to `for_expansion` with the container, the body wrapped as `Code`, and the direction as a literal `true` or `false`. The instance declares the loop variables with the backtick escape so that they land in the caller's scope rather than being renamed by macro hygiene, and inserts the body wherever an iteration belongs.

4 (index 0)
3 (index 1)
2 (index 2)
1 (index 3)
named 4
named 3
named 2
named 1
reversed 1
reversed 2
reversed 3
reversed 4

The names the body sees are `it` and `it_index`; the named form `for x: c` is an alias the compiler inserts ahead of the body, so an instance never has to know which spelling the caller used. Keep the expansion's own cursor hygienic, snapshot the public names immediately before insertion, and advance private state first. That prevents a `continue` in the inserted body from repeating an element and prevents a nested expansion's public loop names from corrupting the outer walk.

rows: the container by value; `reverse` is `false`, then `true`
the container by pointer, plus the same `reverse`

blocks.text: An instance is free to ignore `reverse`, in which case `for <` and `for` iterate identically. The argument arrives as a literal, so `#if reverse` folds at expansion time and an expansion pays nothing for the direction it was not called with. Binding by pointer is a separate class rather than a flag: `for *x: c` on a type with only an `Iterable` instance is `error: 'for *x:' needs a PointerIterable instance for Countdown`. The loop statement itself, including `break`, `continue` and the explicit `for :macro_name` form, is described in `for` Loops and Custom Iteration with `for_expansion`.
The range operators

`..` and `..=` are ordinary user-visible operators with ordinary classes. Five classes cover the five writable shapes, split by fixity: two infix, two prefix, one suffix. The two infix ones sit at precedence level 2, which binds looser than everything except assignment, so `1 .. 1 + 3` is the range `1 .. 4`.

Each produces a plain struct. All six range types are ordinary generic structs in the Prelude and their fields are readable like any other; `RangeFull($T)` is the one with no operator behind it, produced only by a bare `..` inside a subscript.

2 .. 5  -> Range_ssize  start=2 end=5
2 ..= 5 -> RangeInclusive_ssize
2 ..    -> RangeFrom_ssize  start=2
..5     -> RangeTo_ssize  end=5
..=5    -> RangeToInclusive_ssize
`Step` and `RangeOrigin`

Nothing above is specific to integers. The Prelude's range-operator instances are blanket instances guarded by two small classes, so a type becomes rangeable by implementing them rather than by implementing `..`.

`Step` alone unlocks `a .. b`, `a ..= b` and `a ..`. The two open-at-the-start forms `.. b` and `..= b` additionally need `RangeOrigin`, which supplies the value the iteration begins at. To iterate the resulting range the type also needs `PartialOrd`, because the Prelude's `Iterable` instances for the range structs compare `it` against the endpoint.

Without `Step` the operator does not resolve at all: `error: no operator '..' for Tick, Tick`. Without `RangeOrigin` the prefix form fails on its own with `error: no prefix operator '..' for Tick`, while `a .. b` keeps working. Trying to iterate a bare value with no `Iterable` instance is `error: 'Tick' is not iterable; it needs an Iterable instance`.
`ToPattern`

`ToPattern` is what lets a range appear in a `case` arm. It is compile-time only by construction: `to_pattern` takes a `#comptime` value and returns a `Pattern`, and `Pattern` values cannot reach lowering, so an instance is resolved during checking and erased afterwards. The Prelude implements it for all six range shapes over integers, each with an intrinsic body that normalises the shape to a closed interval before the coverage analysis sees it.

-5 -> non-positive
0 -> non-positive
3 -> small
42 -> medium
1000 -> large

The ranges are exclusive where written exclusive: `10..100` does not cover `100`, which is why the last arm starts there. Because the class is keyed on `Is_Integer`, a user `Step` type does not get range patterns for free. Ranges in Patterns and `ToPattern` covers the matching side, and Exhaustiveness, Guards, and Reachability covers what the normalised intervals are used for.

A statement is the unit a procedure body is built from. The ordinary simple forms are terminated statements: local declarations, assignments and update assignments, expression statements such as a call, `return`, and legacy inline assembly all require `;`. A newline never substitutes for it. Control-flow and other body-ended statements instead finish when their own body finishes.
Newlines are not terminators

A line break is ordinary whitespace. Glosso is C-like on this point and not Go-like: nothing is inserted at the end of a line, so a statement continues across as many lines as its grammar needs. The consequence is that a token which could continue the previous expression will continue it, however the source is laid out.

`double` on one line and `(3)` on the next is one call expression, `double(3)`, not a reference to `double` followed by a parenthesised `3`; the required terminator comes after the closing parenthesis. A leading `(`, `[`, `.`, or binary operator on a continuation line joins the line above it, however the source is laid out.
Where a semicolon is mandatory
Required semicolons fall into the simple-statement forms and the delimiter positions below. File scope adds its own declaration rule.

rows: After an expression statement or legacy `#asm`

blocks.text: A `#code` quote provides the main contextual exception. A local declaration, assignment, expression statement, value-bearing `return`, or legacy `#asm` immediately before any `}` while inside the quote may end there. The quote mode includes nested blocks, not just the outer quote; at the outer brace this is what makes `#code { value }` an expression. In an expression-position `#inline while` or `#inline for`, an ordinary expression statement in the generated body may instead end with `,`. Outside a `#code` quotation, ordinary runtime and compile-time blocks receive neither shortcut.
A case label is an ordinary expression, so without the semicolon the parser has no way to know that the label has ended and the arm body has begun. Omitting it reports the first token of the body.

error: unexpected token 'print'
  --> switch.glo:6:12
  |
6 |     case 1 print("one\n");
  |            ^^^^^
`else` without its semicolon reports the same way: `else print("other");` is `error: unexpected token 'print'`. The switch shape is set out in Switching on a Value.

A `'name` token is read as a label statement only when the next token is `;` or `:`. Without either punctuation it begins an ordinary expression statement, whose required terminator is missing; the parser immediately blames the first token of the following statement.

error: unexpected token 'i'
  --> label.glo:7:5
  |
7 |     i += 1;
  |     ^

There is no empty statement. A semicolon is consumed only by the statement in front of it, so a stray one has nothing to attach to. Inside a body, both `;` on its own and the second `;` of `a := 1;;` are `error: unexpected token ';'`. At file scope a stray semicolon is `error: expected a declaration, found ';'`; after a braced definition its help says that the declaration already ended at `}`.
The statement inventory

The parser tests the statement forms in a fixed order and the first match wins. The order matters only where two forms can begin with the same token: a nested declaration is recognised before an expression statement because `name ::` would otherwise start an expression, and a label is recognised before an expression for the same reason.

A bare block, which introduces a scope.
Leaves or restarts the innermost loop.
Runs a statement at block exit.
Opens an aggregate's fields into the scope.
The conditional, the switch, and the pattern switch.
The static conditional and the static switch.
Overrides the implicit context or its allocator.

A case fragment. Legal only inside a `#code` quote.

blocks.text: A nested `X :: (...)`, `struct`, `enum`, `union` or `distinct` inside a procedure body is not a local: it is lifted onto the file's declaration list at parse time and is visible from every procedure in the file. Blocks, Scope, and Shadowing covers what this does and does not scope.
`return`, `break` and `continue` are also expressions, of the bottom type `#Never`, so they may appear where a value is expected. `ifx` Expressions shows the arms this makes possible.
`#pattern P := subject else { ... };` is parsed as an expression and reaches statement position inside an expression statement. It is described in Bind or Diverge.
One program that exercises the less common entries follows. Every required terminator is shown, and body-ended forms close with `}`:

using 1 2
block 3
N 10
generated 5
push_allocator
push_context
static if
deferred

`if` takes a condition and a body. The condition is not parenthesised, and the body is either a braced block or one statement. Parentheses are accepted around a condition, but only as grouping; they are not part of the form. `else` follows the body, and `else if` chains without a separate keyword.

gt3
le100
eq5
parens are grouping

An unbraced body is a single statement, which includes a nested `if`. Either spelling gets its own scope, so a declaration made in an unbraced body is no more visible afterwards than one made in a braced one: `if n > 0 x := 5;` followed by a use of `x` is `error: unbound 'x'`.
The dangling else

When an `else` could attach to either of two nested `if` statements, it attaches to the nearest one. The parser reads the inner `if` as the outer one's body, and the `else` it then meets belongs to the statement it is still parsing.
dangling else went to the inner if
Indentation has no effect on this. An `else` that is meant for the outer `if` has to be forced there by bracing the inner one.
Truthiness

A condition does not have to be `bool`. Branching on a value applies a truthiness rule chosen by the value's representation, and the same rule serves `if` and `while`. The rule is per representation rather than per type, which is why it is total over the scalar kinds and undefined for anything with no distinguished zero.

rows: The value is not zero. An enum is tested by discriminant, so its first constant is falsy.
The value compares ordered-unequal to zero, so `0.0`, `-0.0` and NaN are all falsy.

blocks.text:
0 falsy
-2 truthy
0.0 falsy
"" falsy
"x" truthy
Level.Info falsy
null ?*ssize falsy
empty view falsy

`?*T` is truthy exactly when it is present because the optional pointer is stored in the pointer's null niche: `.None` is the null bit pattern, so the presence test and the null test are the same instruction. An optional over a payload with no niche has no such coincidence, and it has no rule at all.

A value whose kind is not in the table is rejected when the branch is lowered. A struct condition is `error: values of type P have no native truthiness rule`, and `o: ?s64` is `error: values of type Option_s64 have no native truthiness rule`. Test a struct against something explicit, and match an optional with `if #pattern .Some(v) = o` or `if o == { case .Some(v); ... }`.
The three conditionals compared

`if` is the only one of the three that accepts a non-`bool` condition. `ifx` coerces its condition to `bool` because it is an expression whose arms have to agree on a type, and `#if` demands a `bool` that is also known at compile time because it selects which branch is checked at all.

rows: Any kind with a truthiness rule

blocks.text: `ifx 3 "a" else "b"` is `error: got ssize, expected bool`, and `#if 1` is `error: #if condition must be bool, got comptime_int`. The expression form is covered in `ifx` Expressions and the static form in Static Branching with `#if`.

An `if` whose condition is a subject followed by `== {` is not a conditional at all but a switch, and an `if` whose condition begins with `#pattern` is a pattern test. Both are separate forms of the same keyword; see Switching on a Value and Pattern Matching with `#pattern`.

Glosso has no `switch` keyword. A switch is an `if` whose condition is a subject expression followed immediately by `==` and `{`. The braces hold case arms rather than statements, each arm opening with a `case` label that ends in a semicolon, and the default arm is spelled `else;`.
non-positive non-positive small single digit large
Why `== {` is a switch

The rule lives in the binary-operator loop of the expression parser: `==` stops binding as an operator when the token after it is `{`. It is a lexical rule rather than an `if`-specific one, and it costs nothing, because `{` can never begin an expression in Glosso. An aggregate literal is written `.{ ... }`, so a brace where a right operand was expected is always a mistake.

error: unexpected token '{'
  --> brace.glo:6:12
  |
6 |     p: P = { .a = 1 };
  |            ^

Only the `==` directly in front of the brace is affected, so an ordinary comparison followed by a block is unambiguous: `if a == b { ... }` is a conditional, because the token after `==` is `b`. To switch on the result of a comparison, parenthesise it and let the outer `==` be the switch marker: `if (a == b) == { case true; ... }`. Any expression may be the subject, including a call or an arithmetic expression.
The shape

The semicolon after a label and after `else` is mandatory, and it is mandatory because a label is an ordinary expression: nothing else marks where the label ends and the arm body begins. Omitting it reports the first token of the body, `error: unexpected token 'print'` for `case 1 print("one\n");`. Arm bodies are statement lists, not blocks, and they are not braced.

An arm runs to the next `case`, the `else`, or the closing brace. There is no implicit fall-through and no `break` is needed to prevent it; entering the next arm's body has to be asked for with `#falling`, which is described together with multi-label arms in `case A, B;` Groups and `#falling`.
Case labels by subject type
A label is a literal, a range, an enum constant, or a union variant, depending on what the subject is. Several labels may share one arm by separating them with commas.

Range labels go through the `ToPattern` conversion rather than through dedicated grammar, so `4..=9` in a label is the same range expression it would be anywhere else. Its bounds must be known at compile time. A bare `..` is not accepted as a label: `case ..;` is `error: bare '..' needs an index context`. Ranges in Patterns and `ToPattern` covers the conversion.

An enum constant may be written qualified or with a leading dot, but a union variant may not be qualified here: `case Token.Name(s);` is `error: '' is not a variant of union Token`. Use `Name(s)` or `.Name(s)`. The qualified spelling is accepted in a `#pattern` switch, which is a different form.
Nothing matched

A #partial statement switch can leave values unhandled. If no arm matches and there is no else, execution continues after that switch. Without #partial, the compiler requires exhaustive coverage or an else arm. An ifx expression must always produce a value.

Scalar and enum statement switches are coverage-checked by default. A gap reports non-exhaustive switch with a missing-case witness. Cover every value, add else, or use #partial for intentional fall-through. Tagged-union switches likewise require all variants, else, or #partial. Covered arms can receive an unreachable-pattern warning.

`#partial` waives that requirement and is written immediately after `if`, before the subject and before a `#pattern` marker. Elsewhere it is rejected: `if #partial true { }` is `error: #partial can only modify an if-switch`, and `if #pattern #partial s == { ... }` is `error: unexpected directive 'partial'`.

A union payload is reachable only through a capture in the arm that proved the tag. Reading `t.Code` directly is `error: tagged-union payload '.Code' may only be bound by a pattern match`. Reading a Union Payload gives the rule and the escape hatch, and a raw union has no tag to switch on at all: `error: cannot switch on a raw union (it has no tag)`.

One arm may not capture from several tags whose payloads differ: `case .Name(x), .Code(x);` is `error: a case with several tags cannot capture a payload - the tags have different payload types`. Grouping tags that share a body is covered in `case A, B;` Groups and `#falling`, and the coverage analysis itself in Exhaustiveness, Guards, and Reachability.

`ifx` is the expression conditional. It exists because `if` is a statement and produces nothing, and because a value that depends on a test should not have to be built by declaring a variable and assigning to it from two branches. Every `ifx` must produce a value on every path, which is the single rule the rest of its behaviour follows from.

The switch forms share the subject and label grammar of the statement switch, including the mandatory semicolon after each label and after `else`. The subject-less pattern form takes arbitrary boolean predicates as its labels. `ifx` does not accept `#partial`: `ifx #partial c == { ... }` is `error: unexpected directive 'partial'`, since waiving coverage would leave the expression with no value to produce.
The `else` is mandatory on the conditional form
A two-armed test with one arm missing has nothing to yield when the condition is false, so the omission is an error rather than a `void` result.

Arms end in an expression
An arm of a switch form is a statement list, so it may compute before it answers, but its last statement has to be an expression. That expression is the arm's value.

computing

An arm ending in something that is not an expression is `error: an ifx arm must end in an expression`, reported at the offending statement. An arm that ends in a `void` call is subtler: the arm's type becomes `void`, and the mismatch surfaces on the next arm instead, as `error: got ssize, expected void`.
The arms are expressions, not blocks. `ifx b { 1 } else { 2 }` does not parse: a brace never begins an expression, so this is `error: unexpected token '{'`.
The join across arms

The arms meet at a numeric join rather than at the first arm's type. An integer literal beside a float arm becomes the float type, and a sized integer or a narrower float on one side pulls a literal on the other side to it. This is the same defaulting the rest of the language uses, applied to the set of arms.
Arms with no join are an error reported against the arm that does not fit: `ifx b 1 else "two"` is `error: got ssize, expected string`.
Totality

A switch form must be provably total or carry `else;`. Totality is computed, not demanded: an enum or union subject whose arms name every constructor needs no `else`, which is why the `Color` example above ends at `case .Blue;`. When the proof fails the compiler names the witnesses it found.

note: cover every case, or add an 'else' arm

Subjects whose domain cannot be enumerated are never total on literals alone. An `f64` or `string` subject with only literal labels reports `note: missing case: _`, and the subject-less predicate form reports the same witness under `error: non-exhaustive #pattern switch`, because an arbitrary boolean predicate proves nothing about coverage. The analysis behind the witnesses is described in Exhaustiveness, Guards, and Reachability.
When the subject is known at compile time and no arm matches it, the failure is escalated rather than left to run time, because the panic would be unconditional.

The lowerer still emits a backstop on the no-arm path, reporting `ifx matched no arm and has no else` through the assertion machinery. A correct totality proof makes it unreachable; it exists so that a gap in the analysis fails loudly rather than yielding an undefined value.
Diverging arms

`return`, `break` and `continue` are expressions of type `#Never`, the bottom type, which coerces to every type because the coercion can never run. An `ifx` arm may therefore leave instead of producing a value, which is how a loop body filters and binds in one step.

The join takes the other arm's type first, so a bare numeric literal beside a diverging arm is checked against `#Never` and fails: `x := ifx b 1 else return -1;` is `error: got ssize, expected #Never`. Naming the value first (`ifx b y else return -1`) or writing the `ifx` directly in a `return` both work, because the expected type is then known from context.

`#pattern` introduces the pattern language. A pattern is one construct that does two things at once: it tests a value's shape and it binds names to the parts it found. That pairing is why patterns are the only way to read a tagged union's payload, since the binding cannot happen without the test having succeeded.

This chapter covers where a pattern may appear and the two rules that govern all of the positions. The patterns themselves are catalogued in The Pattern Vocabulary, ranges in Ranges in Patterns and `ToPattern`, and coverage in Exhaustiveness, Guards, and Reachability.

blocks.text: The parser tells these apart by scanning ahead from the pattern for a depth-zero `=` or `:=`. A depth-zero `=` makes it a test, a `:=` makes it the bind-or-diverge form, and neither makes it a quote. `==` is a different token, so a `== CONST` element inside a pattern is never mistaken for the test marker, and a `{` found at depth zero ends the scan because that brace is the enclosing `if`'s body.

The multi-arm block form tests several subjects at once and succeeds only when every arm matches; the captures of all arms are then in scope together, and a later arm may read an earlier arm's capture.
both start at 4

A pattern test is an expression of type `bool`, and the subject side is parsed at a precedence above `&&` and `||`, so `if #pattern P = subject && g` reads as `(#pattern P = subject) && g` rather than testing `P` against `subject && g`. The extra condition then sees the captures.

wide rect 3
not huge

Do not put `||` between two pattern tests. It compiles, but `||` short circuits, so the untaken alternative's captures are in scope and never written; the arm reads uninitialised storage. `|` inside a single pattern is the supported spelling for alternatives, and it forces every alternative to bind the same names at the same types.

A test cannot be negated. `!(#pattern P = subject)` is `error: a '#pattern' test cannot be negated`, with `note: its captures would have no scope to bind into - '!' inverts the value, not the branch they belong to` and a pointer to the `:=` form. Bind or Diverge covers that form.
The quote

`#pattern P` with no subject is not a test but a quote: a value of the built-in type `Pattern`. The type is compile-time only and has no storage, so a quote is bound with `::` and spliced back into pattern position with `#insert`. Binding one with `:=` is `error: a 'Pattern' value is compile-time only; bind it with '::' rather than ':='`. Patterns as Compile-Time Values covers the introspection intrinsics built on this.
Tag-first lowering

A variant pattern lowers to a tag comparison and a branch to the failure label. The payload is only extracted after that branch, so a pattern that does not match never forms the payload it was going to bind. The reason is that a union's storage read as the wrong variant is not a value of that variant's type at all; forming it first and testing afterwards would mean building an ill-typed value on every miss.

The consequence a program can observe is that a subpattern under a variant is only ever applied to that variant's payload. An interval test nested inside `Value.Number(...)` never runs against a `Value.Text` payload, even though the two share storage.

small number
big number
hello
nothing

The same ordering discipline runs through the other composite patterns. A slice pattern emits its length test before any index is formed, so an element is never read out of a slice too short to hold it, and a struct pattern's fields are tested left to right with each failure jumping straight to the pattern's failure label.

This is also the mechanism behind the rule that a tagged-union payload may only be reached through a capture. A direct `value.Variant` read has no tag test in front of it, so there is nothing to make it well typed: `error: tagged-union payload '.Code' may only be bound by a pattern match`. Reading a Union Payload has the full rule.
Captures bind in the block that proved the match

A capture is written where the whole pattern succeeded, not at the textual point of the binder. A binder that appears early in a pattern therefore has no effect if a later part of the same pattern rejects, and an outer name of the same spelling survives untouched.

after, d = 7
both fields are 4

The second half of that program shows the compensating rule: within one pattern, a later element may refer to an earlier capture, because the register holding the matched part is computed on the straight-line path before any sibling test runs. What is deferred is the binding the surrounding block sees, not the value the pattern is working with.
Captures do not escape the construct that proved them. Using a capture after the `if` that bound it is `error: unbound 'r'`.
Alternatives inside one pattern funnel their captures into a shared set of registers, so an arm body reads the alternative that actually matched rather than the last one written.
A `void` payload still binds a name; the name has a type and no storage, and it compares equal to the empty tuple `.()`.

`#pattern P := subject else { ... };` is the exception that binds into the enclosing scope. It is sound only because the `else` is required to diverge, so the binding is unreachable on the failing path.

A pattern is a shape a value is tested against, together with the names the test introduces when it succeeds. Every shape below composes with every other to any depth: a variant capture may hold a struct pattern whose field pattern is a range, and an or-pattern may join two of those. The positions in which a pattern may be written are described in the chapter on pattern matching with `#pattern`; this chapter is the vocabulary those positions accept.

Two rules govern how a pattern is read. A bare identifier always binds, so `LIMIT` in pattern position names the matched value rather than comparing against the constant `LIMIT`; the `==` form exists for the comparison. And an element that is not pattern syntax is an ordinary expression, evaluated at compile time and converted to a pattern, which is how ranges and spliced quotes enter without new grammar.

blocks.text: Literals, bindings, and the wildcard

An integer, float, string, `#char` or boolean literal matches a value equal to it. A bare identifier matches anything and binds it. `_` matches anything and binds nothing, which is what it is for: a position that must be present but is not read. `*name` also matches anything, but binds a pointer to the place the value occupies rather than a copy of it, so an assignment through it writes back into the subject.

Variants and enum constants

A tagged-union variant is written qualified (`Token.Name`) or with a leading dot (`.Name`); both spellings are accepted everywhere a pattern is. Parentheses after the tag hold the payload pattern, which is usually a binding. An enum constant takes the same two spellings and never carries a payload. A variant written without parentheses proves the tag and discards the payload.

A `void` payload still admits a capture: `Token.Eof(nothing)` binds the empty tuple, so `nothing == .()` is true. `?T` and `E!T` are ordinary tagged unions to the checker, so `.Some`, `.None`, `.Ok` and `.Err` are variant patterns like any other; the two types have their own chapters.
Struct and slice patterns

A struct pattern is written with the aggregate-literal punctuation: `Pair.{ ... }` names the type, `.{ ... }` infers it. Fields may be given by name (`.first = a`), by shorthand (`.second`, which binds a name equal to the field name), or positionally in declaration order. `...` as the last element states that the fields not mentioned are ignored; it is documentation rather than a requirement, because an unmentioned field is treated as a wildcard in any case, both when matching and in the coverage analysis. A positional pattern may likewise stop short and bind a prefix of the fields. A slice pattern uses `.[ ... ]` and matches a fixed array, a view or a dynamic array; `...` inside it stands for any number of skipped elements and may appear at most once, so the compiler can fix each named element's offset from one end or the other.

A second `...` is rejected: `.[a, ..., b, ..., c]` is `error: a slice pattern may use '...' at most once`, because two gaps of unknown width leave the elements between them at no fixed offset. A slice pattern applied to a non-array is `error: slice pattern needs an array or slice value, got ssize`, and a struct pattern applied to a non-struct is `error: struct pattern needs a struct value, got ssize`.
Or-patterns, `@`, and constant patterns

`P | Q` matches when either alternative matches, and the alternatives must bind the same names at the same types, because the block that runs afterwards cannot know which alternative proved the match. `whole @ P` matches `P` and additionally binds `whole` to the value as a whole, which is how a pattern can destructure and still keep the original. `== expr` compares the matched value against `expr` instead of binding; `expr` is an ordinary expression, so it may be a named constant or an earlier capture from the same pattern.

The three ways an or-pattern's alternatives can disagree each have their own diagnostic: `error: or-pattern binds 'r' as f64 here but as ssize in another alternative`, `error: or-pattern alternative binds 'q', which the other alternatives do not`, and `error: or-pattern alternative does not bind 'r', which another alternative does`.
Guards and compound conditions

A case in a `#pattern` switch may carry a guard: `case P if <cond>;` matches when `P` matches and `cond` is then true, and a failing guard tries the next case rather than leaving the switch. That is the behaviour an `if` nested inside the arm body cannot express. The guard is checked with the full condition grammar, so it sees the arm's captures and may itself contain a `#pattern` test that binds more names. Outside a switch, `&&` composes a test with an ordinary condition in the same way.

A non-bool guard is `error: case guard must be bool, got f64`. A guarded arm contributes nothing to the coverage analysis, since the guard can fail at run time; the chapter on exhaustiveness, guards, and reachability has the consequences.

`||` between two pattern tests compiles but is unsound. `||` short-circuits, so the captures of the alternative that was not evaluated are in scope and were never written: `if #pattern .X(p) = u || #pattern .Y(q) = w print("% %\n", p, q);` prints `1 0`, where the `0` is an uninitialised capture. Use a switch or nested tests instead.

A pattern test cannot be negated. `if !(#pattern .Some(v) = o)` is `error: a '#pattern' test cannot be negated`, with `note: its captures would have no scope to bind into - '!' inverts the value, not the branch they belong to` and a second note pointing at the bind-or-diverge form, which is the construct for leaving on failure.

`..` and `..=` are operators, not pattern syntax. A case or pattern element that uses one is therefore parsed as an ordinary expression and converted into a pattern afterwards, through the `ToPattern` typeclass. That is why `0..=9`, `100..` and `..` work in pattern position without a single new production, and why the same conversion admits user types.

The consequence to keep in mind is that a bound is an expression, so a bare name in a bound is a constant to look up, not a capture to introduce. This is the one place inside a pattern where an identifier does not bind. The range types themselves are described in the chapter on ranges and slicing.

Every shape normalises to a closed interval, and the interval is then clamped to the subject's own domain. Both steps exist for the coverage analysis: it never has to reason about a half-open interval, and an open end needs no separate intrinsic for the type's extreme value, because the widest interval plus a clamp says exactly what `100..=max` would say. Clamping is also why a witness over a `u8` subject reads `10..=99` rather than a signed 64-bit span.
In a switch the same spellings are case labels. Because each one is a closed interval over an enumerable domain, a set of ranges that tiles the subject's type is proved total and needs no `else`.

Subjects and bounds

A bound must be known at compile time, because the interval is baked into the pattern the analysis reasons over. A runtime local as a bound is `error: a range bound must be known at compile time: unknown const hi`, naming the offending identifier. A non-integer bound is `error: a range bound must be an integer`, which is what a float range such as `0.0..=9.0` produces: the Prelude instances are all constrained `where Is_Integer(T)`.

The subject must be an integer or an enum. Anything else is `error: a range pattern needs an integer subject, got string`. Enum subjects work because a discriminant is an integer underneath. ASCII `#char` literals default to `u8`, so byte ranges work directly. `rune` is not an integer: a rune subject reports `error: a range pattern needs an integer subject, got rune`. Cast to an integer explicitly when the intended domain is scalar numbers.

The `ToPattern` typeclass

`ToPattern` is a one-method class declared in the Prelude. Its method takes its argument `#comptime`, since the whole point is to produce a pattern during checking, and returns the compile-time-only type `Pattern`.

`RangeFrom`, `RangeTo`, `RangeToInclusive` and `RangeFull` follow the same shape, each with its own intrinsic and each constrained `where Is_Integer(T)`. Those six instances are the specification of what a range means as a pattern. In practice the checker recognises the six built-in shapes from their syntax and builds the interval directly, because only the two bounds matter and they are plain integers; a user type is not special-cased away, and reaches its instance through an actual synthesized call to `to_pattern`.
Writing an instance

A user type joins the pattern language by declaring a `ToPattern` instance whose method returns a pattern quote. `#insert` in pattern position is the splice, both for a value that is already a `Pattern` and for a value whose type has an instance, which is what makes `case #insert Ascii_Class.Digit;` legal against a `u8` subject.

`#insert` is required. Written bare, `Ascii_Class.Digit` is an ordinary enum-constant pattern and is checked against the subject's type, giving `error: got Ascii_Class, expected u8`. Splicing a value whose type has no instance is `error: this case is not a pattern, and its type has no 'ToPattern' instance`, followed by the candidate list for `to_pattern`.

Because the conversion happens before the coverage analysis runs, an instance joins that analysis on the same footing as the built-in ranges. Dropping the `else` from `describe` above produces witnesses drawn from the intervals the instance returned, clamped to `u8`.

A `Pattern` value is compile-time only. `p := #pattern .Some(v);` is `error: a 'Pattern' value is compile-time only; bind it with '::' rather than ':='`. The type and its introspection intrinsics belong to the chapter on patterns as compile-time values.

Exhaustiveness in Glosso is computed, not demanded. The compiler runs a usefulness analysis over a matrix of deconstructed patterns: one row per arm, one column per position being matched. A row is useful if some value matches it that no earlier row already matches. The same routine answers both questions the language needs: a switch is exhaustive when the all-wildcard row is no longer useful against its arms, and arm `N` is reachable exactly when row `N` is useful against rows `0` through `N - 1`.

When a switch is not exhaustive the analysis reconstructs a concrete value that no arm matches, by unspecializing on the way back out of the recursion, and prints it as a witness. A witness is a pattern, not a value, so it may contain `_` where any value would do.

The coverage analysis governs #pattern switches, scalar and enum statement switches, and the switch forms of ifx. An incomplete statement switch reports non-exhaustive switch and lists missing cases; add else or #partial when coverage is intentionally incomplete. An ifx reports cannot decide a value for this ifx and requires an else arm or complete coverage. Tagged-union statement switches also check that every variant is handled.
Enumerable and opaque domains

Whether coverage can be proved depends on whether the subject's constructors can be enumerated. Three answers are possible: a finite set of constructors that can be listed, an infinite domain that only a wildcard covers, and a pattern the analysis cannot interpret as a constructor at all.

The same holds for `==` constant patterns and for slice patterns: they are matched at run time, and absent from the coverage matrix.

How a guard affects coverage

A guarded arm contributes nothing. The pattern may match and the guard may still decline at run time, so the arm proves no coverage and is absent from the matrix altogether. Covering a variant only under a guard therefore leaves it missing.

`#falling` is the opposite case and is easy to confuse with a guard: a `#falling` arm does not decline its match, it adds the next arm's body to its own, so it covers its case exactly like an ordinary arm. The chapter on `case A, B;` groups and `#falling` has the rest.
Reachability

The same usefulness call, run against the arms that precede each arm, reports arms that can never be entered. This is a warning, not an error, and it runs whether or not the switch has an `else`. It applies only to `#pattern` switches with a subject; duplicate labels in a plain switch are not diagnosed, and the first matching arm wins.

warning: unreachable pattern - already covered by an earlier case
low

A guarded arm is neither reported by this lint nor counted against later arms, for the same reason it contributes no coverage: it can decline. So `case any if false;` written first leaves every following arm reachable, while an unguarded `case any;` makes them all dead.

`#partial`, written immediately after `if` and before `#pattern`, waives the coverage requirement; control then falls out of the switch when nothing matches. It is the right answer when the uncovered cases are genuinely uninteresting, and the wrong answer when a later edit adds a variant, because `#partial` is exactly the annotation that stops the compiler from pointing at the new one.

A case label may name several values at once: `case A, B;` runs its body when the subject matches any of the listed labels. The labels are values of the subject's type, so the form works for integers, strings, `#char` literals, floats, booleans, enum constants and union tags. It is one arm with several labels, not several arms.

The no-binding restriction

A multi-label case may not capture. The arm body would have to be checked against every listed tag at once, and the captured name would have a different type in each, so the compiler rejects the combination outright rather than picking one.
error: a case with several tags cannot capture a payload - the tags have different payload types

The diagnostic fires on the presence of a capture in a multi-tag case, not on a comparison of the payload types, so it appears even when the tags agree, as `Name` and `Text` do above. Grouping tags whose payloads are irrelevant is fine: `case .Eof, .Nil;` on two `void` variants compiles and covers both.

The construct for one body over several shapes with a capture is the or-pattern in a `#pattern` switch, which requires the alternatives to bind the same names at the same types and so has no such problem.

The comma spelling is not available in a `#pattern` switch: `case Shape.Circle(r), Shape.Rect(r);` there is `error: unexpected token ','`. A pattern case takes exactly one pattern, and `|` is how alternatives are written inside it.
`#falling`

`#falling;` gives C-style fall-through, with one meaning: it appends the next case's body to this one, unconditionally and without running that case's test. The arm does its own work and then the following arm's. It must be the last statement of the case body.

Four placements are rejected, each with its own message. Anything written after `#falling` in the same body is unreachable by construction, so the parser refuses it; an `else` arm and the final case have no following body to enter. The fourth is the restriction on binding switches, developed below.
