blocks.text: The last-case error carries `note: it would leave the switch on every subject that reaches it; delete it`. A `#falling` with nowhere to fall is not a subtle mistake: it turns the arm into a no-op exit on every subject that reaches it, and the compiler can see that at check time.
Where `#falling` is allowed

Entering a body whose test never ran is harmless when that body binds nothing, and unsound the moment it binds something: the body would read a payload from a variant it was not dispatched on. The rule follows the hazard rather than trying to re-test. Two switch forms can bind and are excluded outright: the tagged-union switch and every `#pattern` switch. What remains is the plain value switch over integers, strings, characters, floats and booleans, and the enum switch, which is what the feature is for.

error: '#falling' enters the next case's body without running its test, so it is not allowed in a switch whose cases can bind
note: S8 requires a tagged union's payload to be reached through a capture in the arm that proved the tag, so every case here binds
note: group the tags with 'case A, B;' if they share a body, or lift the shared work into a function

In a `#pattern` switch the first note reads `note: a #pattern switch exists to destructure, so its cases bind` instead. The second note is the same in both, and is the whole remedy: group the labels, or move the shared work into a procedure both arms call.

A `#falling` arm still covers its own case. It always runs its own body, so it is an ordinary row in the coverage matrix, unlike a guarded arm; the chapter on exhaustiveness, guards, and reachability draws that distinction. `#falling` also composes with a grouped label.
info
`#falling` means something different in a `#if` switch: a static `#falling` arm re-tests from the next case rather than entering its body. The chapter on static branching with `#if` covers that form.

sections.title: Bind or Diverge: `#pattern P := subject else`

blocks.text: `#pattern P := subject else { ... }` binds `P`'s captures into the enclosing scope and requires the `else` block to leave. It exists because the ordinary test nests: every optional unwrapped with `if #pattern .Some(v) = e { ... }` pushes the rest of the procedure one block deeper, and a procedure that unwraps four things ends up written four levels in, with the failure handling scattered down the right margin.

The bind form inverts that. The failure path is stated once, immediately, and the success path continues at the same indentation with the captures live from that statement to the end of the enclosing block.

serving svc on 8080
ok = 8080
missing = -1
total = 4

`cfg` is an ordinary local from the statement onwards, not a name that lives only inside a nested block. Inside a loop the `else` may `continue`, which turns the form into "skip the elements that are not there", as the `total = 4` line shows: the `.None` element is skipped and `1 + 3` remains.
Why the `else` must diverge

Binding into the enclosing scope is only sound if the code after the statement is unreachable when the match failed. That is exactly what requiring the `else` to leave buys: there is no path on which `cfg` is read without having been written. The requirement is not a style rule, it is the premise the scoping decision rests on.

error: the 'else' of a '#pattern ... :=' binding must not return normally
note: it has to be #Never - end it with 'return', 'break', 'continue', or a call to a #Never function

For the same reason the `else` block is checked without the bindings. They do not exist on the failure path, so naming one there is `error: unbound 'v'`, with the usual `help: did you mean 'o'?` suggestion pointing at the subject.
What counts as diverging
The check is a syntactic walk over the block's statements, asking whether control can reach the end. Any of the following forms as the last thing the block does satisfies it.

rows: the declaration says it does not return
an exhaustive switch, all arms diverging
every arm leaves and one always runs
the walk does not evaluate the condition

blocks.text: The last row is the trap. An infinite loop plainly never returns, but the check does not reason about loop conditions, so `#pattern .Some(v) := o else { while true { } }` is rejected with the same "must not return normally" error. Write an explicit `return` or a call to a `#Never` procedure instead.
Shape and restrictions

The `else` is mandatory and must be a block. Omitting it is `error: unexpected token ';'` at the end of the statement, and writing a single statement instead of a block, as in `else return -1;`, is `error: unexpected token 'return'`. This form explicitly accepts an optional trailing `;` after the block.

The parser decides between the bind form, the test form and the quote by scanning ahead for a `:=` at nesting depth zero. That scan counts `(`, `[` and `{` as openers but does not count `.{` or `.[`, so a top-level struct or slice pattern makes the scan stop early and the statement is read as a test. Both of the following are `error: unexpected token ':='`.

#pattern Pair.{ .first = a, .second = b } := p else { return -1; }
#pattern .[a, b] := xs else { return -1; }

A variant pattern is unaffected, because its payload sits inside `(` and `)`, so the practical form is to bind the payload and destructure it afterwards: `#pattern .Some(p) := o else { return -1; }` accepts a `?Pair` and leaves `p` a plain `Pair`. `whole @ .Some(v) := o` also parses, for the same reason.

Every pattern shape is otherwise available, and the subject may be any expression. `?T` and `E!T` are the common subjects: `#pattern .Ok(v) := parse(text) else { return -1; }` is the error-handling spelling for a procedure that does not want to propagate, which the chapter on `Try`, `?`, and `#try` contrasts with propagation.

The bind form is the answer the compiler points at when a pattern test is negated. `if !(#pattern .Some(v) = o)` is rejected with `note: to bind and leave on failure, write '#pattern P := subject else { ... }'`, because inverting a test would leave its captures with no branch to bind into.

A `#pattern P` written without `= subject` is a quote rather than a test: it produces a value of the built-in type `Pattern` that carries the pattern's syntax. The parser decides between the two by scanning ahead for a depth-zero `=`. `==` is a different token, so a constant pattern such as `#pattern == LIMIT` is never mistaken for a test.

A pattern was the one piece of Glosso syntax that could not be named. A predicate can be a procedure, a type can be a value, a block can be a `Code` value, but a pattern had to be written out in full at every site that matched it. The quote names it; `#insert` in pattern position puts it back.

number 2.5
name hi
eof

A quote carries its binders with it. The arm that spliced `NUMBER` reads `n` and the arm that spliced `NAME` reads `text`, under the names the quote wrote, in the scope the splice landed in. Everything the pattern vocabulary accepts may be quoted; the vocabulary itself is in The Pattern Vocabulary.
A pattern has no storage

`Pattern` is a compile-time-only type. `size_of(Pattern)` is `0`, its values are dropped from every runtime argument list, and reaching lowering with one is an error. The checker rejects them where they are written rather than where they are first used, which is why the diagnostics below point at the declaration.
A pattern must therefore be bound with `::`, the compile-time constant form, and may not be stored in an aggregate or in a runtime variable.
`p := #pattern .Some(v);` is `error: a 'Pattern' value is compile-time only; bind it with '::' rather than ':='`.
`Holder :: struct { p: Pattern; }` is `error: field 'p' has the compile-time-only type 'Pattern', which has no storage`.
A quote written where a test was meant, as in `if #pattern n { ... }`, reaches the lowerer and is `error: cannot lower PatternQuote expression`.

`Code` is the other compile-time-only type and obeys the same rules; the two share their machinery. `Pattern` differs in two ways, both covered below: identity is structural rather than by node, and a splice deep-clones instead of adopting the quoted nodes.
Splicing with `#insert`

`#insert e` where a pattern is expected splices the pattern that `e` evaluates to. `#insert` keeps its single meaning, "splice this compile-time syntax value here", and the position selects which kind of syntax is expected. Every pattern position accepts it: the test form, a case label, the bind-or-diverge form, and the inside of another quote.

A splice binds tighter than `|` and at the same level as the `==` constant marker, and looser than the postfix forms. `#insert A | #insert B` is therefore an or-pattern over two splices rather than one bitwise-or expression.
either r=3

The splice deep-clones the quoted syntax at every site. A `Code` value spliced at two differently typed sites reuses the same nodes, and the types stamped by the first check survive into the second; a pattern is matched against a type by definition, so it cannot afford that. A spliced value that is not already a `Pattern` is converted through its type's `ToPattern` instance, which is how a range enters a pattern; see Ranges in Patterns and `ToPattern`.
Patterns as arguments

A procedure takes a pattern through a `#comptime` parameter. The argument is const-evaluated at the call site and bound into the callee's compile-time environment, which is what lets the callee splice it.

Pattern identity is structural. The monomorphization key is a rendering of node kinds and parser-set attributes only, never node ids and never spans, so two quotes that read the same are one instantiation. The three calls above are two: `--backend llvm-ir` emits two definitions of `matches`, because `EOF_PATTERN` and the quote written at the call site render identically.

define i1 @glo_matches__pattern_Token__comptime_8a4b84710d3e5507
define i1 @glo_matches__pattern_Token__comptime_fc76ffc729883eba
The two binding tiers

A bare identifier in a pattern binds, so a quote needs a way to say "this name is a name". Two markers do it, the pair `Code` already has. A single-backtick name is a name rather than a binder: it is read as an ordinary constant when the pattern is checked. A double-backtick name is evaluated in the environment the quote was written in, and the value it had is baked into the quote.

backtick name vs MAX: 1 0
bare ident binds:     1 1

The eager tier is what lets a quote built inside a generic carry a value that does not exist at the splice site. `exactly` below is evaluated at compile time with `v` bound to `2.5`; the pattern it returns holds `2.5`, not a reference to a parameter named `v`.

A single-backtick name is looked up among the file's compile-time constants, not among the locals of the procedure that splices the pattern. A quote that names a constant declared inside that procedure is `error: unbound 'LIMIT'`, reported at the quote. Where the value is known at quote time, the double-backtick tier avoids the question entirely.
The pattern intrinsics

Six intrinsics in `std/Meta/Utilities.glo` read a pattern. Each is a compile-time `#magic` declaration, shown here without its directives. The subject type comes first in every one of them because a binder's type depends on both the pattern and the type it is matched against: `Token.Number(n)` binds `n` as `f64` only against `Token`.

pattern_binder_count  :: (T: type, #comptime P: Pattern) -> ssize
pattern_binder_name   :: (T: type, #comptime P: Pattern, i: ssize) -> string
pattern_binder_type   :: (T: type, #comptime P: Pattern, i: ssize) -> type
pattern_missing_count :: (T: type, Ps: []mut Pattern) -> ssize
pattern_missing       :: (T: type, Ps: []mut Pattern, i: ssize) -> string
pattern_is_useful     :: (T: type, Ps: []mut Pattern, #comptime Q: Pattern) -> bool

binder count = 1
binder 0 = n : f64
missing count = 1
missing 0 = Token.Eof
useful = 0
useful2 = 1

`pattern_missing_count` and `pattern_is_useful` are the coverage analysis, asked directly. The contract is one-sided: the analysis errs only towards reporting more missing cases than a reader would, so a count of zero is a genuine totality proof and a non-zero count means "not proved" rather than "not total". Scalars, guarded arms and raw unions are the usual reasons for the difference; Exhaustiveness, Guards, and Reachability describes them, and Pattern Reflection covers the wider reflection surface.

`#if` chooses between branches while the program is being checked. The condition is const-evaluated, the selected branch is spliced in, and the branches that were not selected are neither type-checked nor lowered. That last property is the whole point: a branch written for another target may name procedures that do not exist on this one.

There are two spellings, matching the two runtime forms. The conditional form takes a `bool` condition and an optional `else`; the switch form takes a subject and `==` followed immediately by a brace, with `case` labels and an optional `else;` arm. Neither takes parentheses, and both accept a single statement in place of a block.

single statement, no braces
windows
64-bit x86

A static chain continues with `else #if`. Written `else if`, without the directive, the else branch is one ordinary runtime `if` statement: if the chain selects it, its condition is evaluated at run time and may read runtime locals, and both of its arms are checked and lowered.
The condition

The condition must be `bool`. `#if` does not take the truthiness rule that `if` takes, so `#if 1 { ... }` is `error: #if condition must be bool, got comptime_int`. The reason is that a static branch is a decision about the program text, and a silent coercion there would delete code on the strength of a guess.

The condition must also be compile-time evaluable. A runtime local reports `error: unknown const i` against the name it could not read. What qualifies is anything the constant evaluator can reach: `::` constants, `#comptime` parameters, compile-time intrinsics such as `Is_Integer(T)` and `size_of(T)`, and the target constants below.

A file-scope `::=` binding is not entered into the compile-time environment, only local ones are, so `G ::= 7` at top level followed by `#if G == 7` is `error: unknown const G`. Use `::` for a file-scope constant.
Only the selected branch is checked
The branch that was not selected is stored and then ignored. It is parsed, so it must be syntactically well-formed, but no name in it is resolved and no type in it is computed.

selected
windows
The same property makes `#if` the instantiation guard for generic code. A `#compile_error` in the branch that a bad instantiation selects turns a deep type error into one sentence at the call site.

`only_ints(1.5)` selects the other branch and reports `error: only_ints requires an integer` at the `#compile_error`. Constraints that belong to the signature rather than the body are better written with `where`; see Constraints with `where`.
`OUT` and `HOST`

Two constants are installed by the compiler and are the usual subjects of a `#if`. They are ordinary struct values of the types declared in `std/Prelude/Utilities.glo`, so their fields are read with `.`.

The field types are the enums `Target_OS`, `Target_CPU` and `Target_ABI`; their members and the flags that set them are in Targets and Cross-Compilation. The standard library uses exactly this shape, for instance to answer the byte order of the target:

`OUT` and `HOST` differ whenever the build is a cross-compilation. A `#comptime` block runs on the host and a compiled procedure runs on the target, so a gate around a system call in ordinary code reads `OUT`, and a gate around something the compiler itself will do reads `HOST`.
The limits

At module scope, #if selects declarations, imports, and libraries. Only the active branch contributes them to the module. Operator syntax and loads that supply operators must remain unconditional because the operator prescan runs before semantic branch selection.

Inside a procedure, local functions and types belong to their lexical block. A function declared inside a braced #if branch does not become a top-level function. Use module-level conditional declarations when a selected function should be callable elsewhere in the module.
selected=1

Module-level #if can select between complete implementations with the same name. Inactive branches introduce no declarations or dependencies. Source Files, Imports, and Loads covers conditional module loading.

A braced `#if` branch does not open a scope of its own. The selected block's statements are spliced into the enclosing block, so a variable declared in the taken branch is visible after it. This is a consequence of splicing rather than a decision, and it is what lets a `#if` chain define one name three different ways.

`#falling` means something different here. In a runtime switch it enters the next case's body unconditionally; in a `#if` switch it re-tests from the next case, so an arm that falls out of a static switch whose remaining labels do not match lands in `else`.

x86_64
re-tested into else

`while` takes a condition and a body, and re-tests the condition before every iteration. The body may be a block or a single statement, and the condition is not parenthesised; parentheses around it are ordinary grouping.

The condition is mandatory. `while { ... }` is `error: unexpected token '{'`, because the parser reads an expression immediately after the keyword and a block is not one. The infinite loop is spelled `while true`.

i=0
i=1
i=2
j=2
k=4
seen=9
countdown=0

The condition follows the same truthiness rule as `if`, so the integer `countdown` above is a legal condition and stops the loop at zero. The full set of falsy values is in `if`, `else`, and Truthiness.

`break` leaves the innermost loop and `continue` starts its next iteration. Neither takes an argument and neither takes a label; to leave a nested loop, jump with `goto`, described in Labels and `goto`.
A `defer` written in the body runs at the end of every iteration, including the iteration that `break`s or `continue`s out of it.
A loop that never terminates is not diagnosed, and neither is a procedure that ends in one without returning; a function that runs off its end returns the zero value.
Pattern conditions

The condition may be a `#pattern` test. The captures reach the loop body and are re-bound from scratch on every iteration, which makes the form the natural spelling for walking an optional-terminated structure.

v=3
v=2
v=1
steps=2
total=6

The subject side of a test is parsed at a precedence above `&&` and `||`, so `while #pattern .Some(v) = o && v > 2` reads as `(#pattern .Some(v) = o) && v > 2`: the test runs first and the guard sees its capture.

The multi-arm block form takes several tests against several subjects. Every arm must match for the loop to run, and every arm is re-tested on every iteration, so the loop stops as soon as any one of them fails.

l=3 r=10
l=2 r=20
l=1 r=30
stopped

Two pattern tests must not be joined with `||`. The combination compiles, but `||` short-circuits, so the alternative that did not run leaves its captures in scope and never writes them, and a body that reads them sees zeroes. `&&` between tests is sound, and so is the multi-arm block above.
`#inline while`

`#inline while` is a compile-time loop. The condition is re-evaluated in the compile-time environment and the body is unrolled into straight-line statements until the condition is false. Nothing about the loop survives into the program.

The counter must therefore be a compile-time binding. `i ::= 0` declares one; a plain `i := 0` is an ordinary runtime variable and the condition that reads it is `error: #inline while condition must be compile-time evaluable`.

sum=6
field x
field y
field z

The second loop is what `#inline while` is for. `field_name` demands a compile-time index, and `#inline while` records its counter as one; `#inline for` deliberately does not, which is the difference between the two constructs and is covered in `#inline for`.

Each iteration must change some compile-time variable that the condition reads. Without that the unroller cannot terminate, so it refuses rather than looping, and there is a hard cap on the count in case the change never reaches the bound.

rows: `#inline while condition must be compile-time evaluable`
a body that never updates it
`#inline while made no compile-time progress; update a compile-time variable used by the condition`

blocks.text: `break` inside `#inline while` is `error: break outside loop`. The construct unrolls into a run of ordinary statements, so at the point the checker reaches the `break` there is no loop to leave. The same applies to a genuinely unrolled `#inline for`. End the unrolling with the condition instead.
`for` iterates. Its header names an iterable and, optionally, the variables the body reads it through; everything else in the header is a one-token modifier.
for [ "<" ] [ ":" expansion ] [ [ "*" ] value [ "," index ] ":" ] iterable body

The value variable defaults to `it` and the index variable to `it_index`. Renaming them adds names rather than replacing them: the compiler prepends `v := it;` and `i := it_index;` to the body, so both the chosen name and the default are live in the same body. Compiler-native and bundled collection and range paths bind the index as `ssize`; a user expansion may deliberately bind another type. Runtime and macro-expanded loops count steps from zero, including in reverse; a statically expanded tuple or fixed array instead uses the element's actual index, so those indices descend in reverse.

it=0 it_index=0
it=1 it_index=1
it=2 it_index=2
i=0
i=1
i=2
value=10 index=0
value=11 index=1
value=12 index=2
both live: n=0 it=0 it_index=0
both live: n=1 it=1 it_index=1
Ranges

A range in the header is iterated by the compiler directly rather than through a library. Written inline or stored in a variable, all five usable shapes work; `..` alone is not one of them, because a bare `..` is `error: bare '..' needs an index context` and cannot be stored at all.

inclusive 0
inclusive 1
inclusive 2
inclusive 3
reverse 3
reverse 2
reverse 1
reverse 0
stored Range 0
stored Range 1
stored Range 2
RangeTo 0
RangeTo 1
RangeTo 2
RangeTo 3
RangeToInclusive 0
RangeToInclusive 1
RangeToInclusive 2
RangeFrom 10
RangeFrom 11
RangeFrom 12
reverse RangeTo 3
reverse RangeTo 2
reverse RangeTo 1
reverse RangeTo 0

The induction variable takes the low bound's type, and a literal low bound is a compile-time number that takes the default `ssize`. So `for i: 0..count` counts in `ssize`, so `count` must be convertible to that width without narrowing. An `s64` upper bound is rejected on a 32-bit target even when its runtime value is small; write `for i: cast(s64)0..count` to keep a fixed-width induction variable, or check the bound before converting it to `ssize`. `for i: lo..hi` with `lo` declared `u8` counts in `u8`. A stored range does not go through that rule at all: `Range(T)` unified both operands when it was built, so `r := 0..count; for i: r` counts in `count`'s type.

A finite range decides whether another value exists before stepping outside its bounds. Narrow and unsigned endpoints are therefore safe: `for < i: lo..hi` over `u8` bounds `0` and `3` yields `2, 1, 0` and stops, while `0..=255` yields all 256 `u8` values and stops at `255`. An open-ended `RangeFrom` has no such end condition; integer stepping wraps after the maximum, so its body must eventually `break` or return.

Reverse iteration of an open-ended range is `error: reverse for cannot use an open-ended RangeFrom`, since there is no last element to start from. A float range is `error: for range needs prev/next for f64`: the element type must be an integer or supply a `Step` instance. An enum without one receives the same diagnostic; defining `Step` makes a bounded enum range iterable. Prefix ranges such as `..last` additionally require a `RangeOrigin` instance.
Arrays, views, and dynamic arrays

A fixed array, a view and a dynamic array all use the prelude's blanket `Iterable` instance. They iterate by element, with `it_index` counting steps. A view produced by slicing iterates the slice, and its indices start at zero rather than at the slice's offset.

fixed x=10 at 0
fixed x=20 at 1
fixed x=30 at 2
fixed x=40 at 3
view x=20 at 0
view x=30 at 1
dyn x=7 at 0
dyn x=8 at 1

A tuple is also iterable, and is unrolled rather than looped, because its elements need not share a type. Writing `#inline for` over one is the explicit spelling of the same expansion; see `#inline for`. Strings instead decode Unicode and yield `rune` for every encoding. UTF-8 and UTF-16 iteration combines a complete scalar, malformed input produces U+FFFD while consuming at least one code unit, and reverse iteration follows scalar boundaries. `it_index` is an `ssize` scalar ordinal starting at zero in either direction, not a byte or code-unit offset. Direct indexing remains code-unit-oriented. `Simd` vectors and matrices are iterable too; a matrix walks row-major. These non-tuple paths are Prelude instances.

0:rune:65
1:rune:44032
reverse 0:44032
reverse 1:65

A by-value array walk snapshots the container before it starts: its count and element reads come from that snapshot even if the original is changed in the body. The element variable is a copy, so assigning to it does not write back. `for <` is honoured and reads the snapshot from the high end; its `it_index` is still the step count `0, 1, 2, ...`, not the original element position.

reverse v=3 at step 0
reverse v=2 at step 1
reverse v=1 at step 2
array unchanged: 1 2 3
range i=0
range i=3
index k=0
index k=1
index k=2

Assigning to the induction variable of a native range loop changes its counter, so the range above visits `0` and `3`. The array expansion's named value and index are aliases local to the inserted body: changing `v` leaves the array untouched, and changing `k` does not change the expansion's private cursor, so every index is still visited.
Iterating by pointer

`for *v: xs` selects `PointerIterable.for_pointer_expansion` and binds `v` (and the default `it`) to `*T`, the address of the current element. Write through `v.*` to change the container. The prelude supplies this instance for every array shape, and `for < *v: xs` walks it backwards.

The container expression must be addressable. Ranges compute values and have no elements to point into; tuples have no addressable homogeneous element; strings are read-only; and `Simd` lanes and matrix elements have no pointer iteration instance. Mutable local array storage is addressable inside `#comptime` too, so pointer iteration can update it. A pointer array walk is deliberately not snapshotted: a dynamic array's count is reread each step, and growing it far enough to reallocate can leave the current element pointer dangling. Avoid structural mutation while such a loop is active.
after write-through: 11 22 33 44

`break`, `continue` and `defer` behave in a `for` exactly as they do in a `while`: `break` leaves the loop, `continue` starts the next iteration, and a `defer` in the body runs at the end of every iteration. A type without the protocol is `'P' is not iterable; it needs an Iterable instance`; supplying that instance is Custom Iteration with `for_expansion`.

A non-inline `for` over an array, string, `Simd`, matrix, or custom container dispatches to a macro named `for_expansion`, chosen by the target's type. The contract is a one-method typeclass, so a container joins the loop syntax by writing an instance. Direct and stored ranges retain native range lowering, while tuples are expanded statically.

`#expand` makes it a macro: the body is cloned into the loop's place rather than called. The loop body arrives as the `Code` parameter, and the expansion decides how many times and in what order to splice it. When the loop renamed its variables, the compiler has already prepended `v := it;` and `i := it_index;` to that `Code`, which is why an expansion never sees the chosen names. A pointer expansion instead receives `*T`, the address of the container, and must bind `it` to an element address rather than an element copy.
What an expansion owes the loop
It declares `it` with a leading backtick, holding the current element.
It declares `it_index` with a leading backtick, counting iterations from zero.
It writes `#insert body` where one iteration's work belongs.

The backticks are load-bearing. Macro expansion renames every local a macro declares, to keep it from colliding with the caller's names; a leading backtick opts out of that renaming, which is exactly what these two names need, since the spliced body refers to them. An expansion that declares a plain `it` compiles until a loop uses it, and then the body reports `error: unbound 'it'`.

default names: 10 at 0
default names: 20 at 1
default names: 30 at 2
named: 10 at 0
named: 20 at 1
named: 30 at 2
total = 60

A linked list is the case that makes the feature necessary: it has no contiguous storage and no length, so no array or range spelling describes it, and yet the loop that walks it reads like every other loop.
The direction parameter

The third parameter carries what the loop header asked for. The compiler builds it from the header alone, and it is a macro parameter, so `#if reverse` selects a branch at expansion time. Walking by pointer is not a flag on this class: `for *x: c` selects `PointerIterable.for_pointer_expansion`, which receives the container by pointer and binds `it` to each element's address.

An expansion that ignores `reverse` silently iterates forward. Honouring it is a matter of reading the parameter and choosing a direction; the prelude's own instances all do, arrays and ranges included, which is why `for <` over an array walks backwards without the compiler lowering the loop itself.

10 at 0
20 at 1
30 at 2
reverse 30 at 0
reverse 20 at 1
reverse 10 at 2
kept 10
kept 30

The ring's elements wrap around its storage, so the three values start at slot six and continue at slot zero. Nothing about that reaches the loop: the expansion converts a step count into a slot, and the body sees only `it` and `it_index`.
`break` and `continue`

The body is spliced literally into whatever loop the expansion wrote, so `break` leaves that loop and `continue` jumps to its condition test. `break` needs no thought. `continue` does, because it skips everything the expansion placed after `#insert body`.

An expansion must advance its cursor before `#insert body`, not after, or `continue` in a loop body repeats the same element forever. The `Ring` above increments `step` first for this reason. Every prelude instance follows the same rule, including the `Range` instance reached explicitly by `for :for_expansion`; `continue` is therefore safe on both the native and macro-expanded paths.
Naming an expansion

`for :name` selects an expansion by name instead of by type. The named procedure need not be a typeclass method: any `#expand` macro with the value, `Code` and `bool` parameters will do, which is the way to give one type several iteration orders.

stepping 100 at 0
stepping 102 at 1
stepping 104 at 2
explicit builtin 1 at 0
explicit builtin 2 at 1
explicit builtin 3 at 2

A name that does not resolve is `error: unknown for expansion 'nosuch'`. `:for_expansion` names the ordinary path explicitly, and on a range that is not a no-op: it routes the loop through the prelude's `Iterable` instance rather than the compiler's native range lowering.

An explicit expansion selector is consulted only on the non-inline path, so `#inline` cannot select it. A selector also cannot be combined with the pointer binder: because a named expansion decides what `it` means, write `for :for_pointer_expansion x: value` without `*` when that is deliberately the macro you want. A type with no instance and no named expansion is `'P' is not iterable; it needs an Iterable instance`. The related range protocols, `Step` and `RangeOrigin`, are described in Iteration and Range Typeclasses.

`#inline for` is an ordinary `for` prefixed with the `#inline` directive. It asks the checker to replace the loop with one copy of the body per element rather than emit a loop. The request is honoured for exactly two iterables: a tuple and a fixed-size array. Every other iterable either compiles to an ordinary runtime loop or is rejected outright.

Static expansion is a dedicated compiler path. A tuple and a fixed array have a shape the checker can enumerate, while a view or dynamic array has only a run-time count. A user `Iterable` is rejected even if its author knows a fixed length: `#inline` does not invoke iteration macros, so custom compile-time unrolling must be written explicitly.

p=10
tuple elem: 1
tuple elem: two
tuple elem: 3
q=3
v=10 i=0
v=20 i=1
v=30 i=2

Three of those four loops behave differently. The tuple and the two arrays are expanded into straight-line statements; the `0..3` range loop is a plain runtime loop that happens to carry a directive the range path never reads. The array case does not require the array's elements to be constants, only its length: `ys` is an ordinary local and still unrolls.

rows: unrolled; `#inline` is optional, a tuple is always expanded statically
unrolled into N copies; `#inline for *x:` may bind each copy to an element address
an ordinary runtime loop; the directive is ignored
a view `[]T` or a dynamic array `[..]T`

blocks.text: The two rejections have distinct wording. A view or a dynamic array gives `error: #inline for needs a compile-time iterable; a runtime-length array expansion cannot be unrolled`, because the type is an array and only the length is missing. Everything else gives `error: #inline for expects a compile-time array`, which is what a stored range, an `Iterable` struct, and a bare integer all produce. Putting `#inline` in front of any other statement is `error: #inline can only prefix while or for`.
Heterogeneous elements

Unrolling is what makes a tuple iterable at all. Each copy of the body is checked against the type of the element it was made for, so one loop can call a generic procedure at four different instantiations and can branch on the element type with `#if`.

7 : ssize
seven : string
7.5 : f64
1 : bool
  not a string
  a string
  not a string
  not a string

Writing `for row` without the directive produces the same expansion. A tuple has no runtime element type to loop over, so the checker takes the static path whether or not `#inline` is present. The directive matters only for a fixed array, where both lowerings exist and the plain `for` expands through the prelude to a real loop.
The loop variable is not a compile-time constant

Each unrolled copy begins with a synthesised `it := <element>` and an `it_index := <literal>`, declared as ordinary non-constant locals. `it` therefore has a known type in every copy but no known value, and any construct that demands a compile-time value fails.
error: unknown const it

`#inline while` does record its counter. The two constructs unroll through different code paths, and only the `while` path raises the checker's inline-expansion depth, which is the flag that turns an assignment into a recorded compile-time value.

The difference is deliberate and the checker records why at that code path: raising the depth in the `for` path does make `it` a known constant, but it also changes constant folding and const-argument resolution inside the body, which moves conformance cases. It is a change to make on its own rather than a side effect of unrolling.
The most common way to hit the rule is an array of types. `type_name` and `size_of` take their argument as a compile-time `type`, so the loop variable cannot be handed to them.
error: unknown const T
The replacement is an `#inline while` over a compile-time index, which indexes the same constant array. The index is a recorded constant, so `Ts[i]` folds and the intrinsic accepts it.

ssize
f64
bool

The restriction is on the loop variable's value, not its type. A generic call binds `$T` from the argument's type and works per element, and `#if type_of(it) == string` selects a branch per copy. Only intrinsics and declarations that need the value itself are affected.
break, scope, and defer
A genuinely unrolled `#inline for` produces a list of blocks, not a loop, so there is nothing for `break` or `continue` to leave.
error: break outside loop

The same body is accepted under `#inline for n: 0..6`, because that form was never unrolled and is a real loop with a real exit edge. This is the clearest test of whether a given `#inline for` unrolled: if `break` compiles, it did not.

Each copy is wrapped in its own block, so a local declared in the body does not collide across copies and a `defer` in the body runs at the end of the copy that declared it rather than at the end of the whole expansion.

doubled 2
leaving 1
doubled 4
leaving 2
doubled 6
leaving 3

Assigning to the by-value element variable writes to that copy's local only. `#inline for v: xs { v += 100; }` leaves `xs` unchanged, exactly as the runtime array loop does. A fixed array may instead use `#inline for *v: xs { v.* += 100; }`; each unrolled copy binds the element's address and changes the original array. Tuples do not support pointer binding.
Reverse, and explicit expansions

Both `#inline for <` and runtime `for <` reverse an array walk. Their indices differ: the unroller emits copies in reverse original-index order, so `it_index` descends; the prelude expansion defines `it_index` as a step count, so it still rises from zero.

inline reverse:
  v=3 i=2
  v=2 i=1
  v=1 i=0
runtime reverse:
  v=3 i=0
  v=2 i=1
  v=1 i=2

An explicit expansion selector cannot be combined with `#inline`. The checker consults the `for_expansion` name only on the non-inline path, so `#inline for :looping v: d` skips the macro, falls through to the static path, and reports `error: #inline for expects a compile-time array`. Custom iteration is covered in Custom Iteration with `for_expansion`, and the unrolled `while` in `while` and `#inline while`.

One further position accepts `#inline for`: the case list of a `#code` quote, where it expands into real switch arms instead of statements. That is the mechanism the derive macros use, and it is described in Writing a Derive Macro.

A label marks a position in a procedure body. It is written as a single leading quote followed by an identifier, `'name`, and it is the destination of a `goto`. Neither the label nor `goto` is a keyword: the label is a token kind the lexer produces, and `goto` is a procedure in `std/Jump.glo`.

The lexer decides between a label and an operator name by looking for the closing quote. After `'` it takes an identifier run, and if the character following that run is not another `'` the token is a label. So `'add` is a label and `'add'` is an operator name; the two never collide. Operator names are covered in Reserved Operators and Operator Names.

A label statement is written `'name;`. The terminator is load-bearing: the parser reads a label statement only when the token after the label is a terminator, so the semicolon is what separates defining a label from mentioning one.

'first;      // label statement: defines the label
('third);    // expression statement: evaluates a `label` value

Parentheses force `'third` into expression position; the final `;` then terminates that expression statement, so no label is defined and a later `goto('third)` reports that the procedure has no such label. A bare `'third` followed by another statement is instead missing the required expression terminator and fails at that next statement. A label statement at file scope is not a statement at all and is rejected as a declaration: `error: bad decl name 'here'`.

The parser also accepts a colon, `'name:`, and defines the same label. Nothing in the standard library or the examples uses it, and this manual does not, so treat `'name;` as the spelling. The colon form survives in one visible place: the compiler's own suggestion when a jump names a label the procedure does not declare reads `error: no label 'nowhere' in this procedure (define it with `'nowhere:`)`. Write the semicolon anyway.
Jumping

`goto` requires `#import "Jump";`. Without it the call is `error: unknown function goto`. The declaration takes the target and three optional parameters that only the context-restoring modes use; the one-argument form is the plain jump and keeps the compiler's native local and computed-label lowering.

i=3
right
The label pre-pass

Before a procedure body is checked, a pre-pass walks the whole body and collects every label it finds, recursing into loop bodies, `then` and `else` branches, switch case bodies and bare blocks. Labels are therefore function-scoped, not block-scoped, and a `goto` may name a label that has not been written yet or that sits deeper than the jump. A name the pre-pass never saw is rejected.
error: no label 'nowhere' in this procedure (define it with `'nowhere:`)
The outward jump is the everyday use. `break` and `continue` take no label, so leaving a nested loop from the inside is what `goto` is for.

A forward jump may cross a declaration or enter a nested construct. Execution resumes at the label. A crossed variable still has runtime storage and remains assignable, but its initializer and every other statement skipped on the way to the label do not run.

y=7
inside 0
top 1
inside 1
top 2
inside 2

Labels are collected for the whole procedure before unreachable code is discarded. Lowering reserves storage for a declaration that a jump crosses; only its initializer is dead. A label inside a block or loop also keeps that construct as an entry point. After the first mid-body pass, normal loop control resumes, as the `top 1` line demonstrates.
Duplicate labels
A label may be defined once per procedure. Two procedures in the same file may each define `'entry`; two `'entry` statements in one procedure may not.
error: function 'main' defines label 'U.again' more than once

This is also how a labelled `break` fails. Glosso has no labelled `break` or `continue`; `break 'outer;` parses as a `break` statement followed by a separate label statement `'outer`, which then collides with the real `'outer` the program declared and produces the duplicate-label error rather than a syntax error.
`label` is a type

A label in value position is an expression of the built-in type `label`. It can be stored in a variable, passed to a procedure, held in a struct field, and compared. `#undefined` is the absent label, and `label.is_valid` distinguishes it from a real one. A `goto` through a variable is a computed jump and is not checked against the procedure's label set.

rows: a stable entry point at `'name` inside `proc`
true only for a label in the procedure making the call

blocks.text:
first n=2
second m=4
field valid: 1 name stop
absent is label: 0
stopped

The `,,` operator builds a label value naming a position in another procedure. Such a target is valid but not local, and entering it bypasses the ordinary call sequence, so arguments have to travel another way. That is what the payload mechanism in Explicit Control Transfer with the Jump Library is for.
`goto` and `defer`

A `goto` does not run pending `defer` statements. `defer` is tied to block exit, and a transfer is not a block exit: it abandons the block without unwinding it. This is the one behaviour that separates `goto` from `break`, `continue` and `return`, all of which do run their defers.

before goto
after goto
Targets

A `goto` whose target is a label literal in the same procedure lowers to a plain branch and works on every target the compiler emits, WebAssembly included. A computed target, whether a stored `label` or a `,,` entry point, needs an indirect jump instruction and is rejected where the backend has none: `error: raw label goto is unsupported on portable WASM targets`. Other CPUs report `raw label goto is unsupported for target CPU '<cpu>'`.

sections.title: Explicit Control Transfer with the Jump Library

blocks.text: `std/Jump.glo` builds setjmp and longjmp, exceptions, stackful coroutines, awaitables and a scheduler on a single transfer operation. That operation is `goto`. Everything else in the module is ordinary Glosso written on top of it, which is why the library has one primitive and no privileged internal entry point.

A `label` is only a code address; it carries no machine state. The state lives in `Execution_Context`, which owns a saved register image, a resume address, an inbox for the value a transfer carries, and a pointer to the logical execution-local state that holds the exception stack, the current coroutine and the jump payload.

`Context_Storage` is opaque: the compiler supplies its size and alignment for the target. On `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`, `size_of(Context_Storage)` is 640. A program never reads its fields; it only ever hands the address of the enclosing `Execution_Context` to `Execution_Context.save`, `Execution_Context.prepare` and `goto`.
`Execution_Context.save`

`Execution_Context.save` captures the current continuation into a context and returns `0`. When that context is later restored, the same call returns again, this time with the restoring `goto`'s `return_code`, and the `goto`'s `value` has been written into `ctx.inbox`. The declaration carries `#returns_twice` so the backend keeps the frame in a shape that survives the second return.

Execution_Context ::: #public {
    save :: (*mut #self) -> s32
        #returns_twice #magic "jump_context_save"

    prepare :: (*mut #self, stack: []mut u8,
        local: ?*mut Execution_Local = .None)
        #magic "jump_context_prepare"
}

captured, code=0
restored, code=7 inbox=carried

`save()` records the active execution-local block automatically; the explicit assignment above is redundant. `prepare()` instead uses the block supplied by its `local` argument. Restoring a context publishes its recorded block, including its exception stack and payload storage.
The three modes of `goto`
`goto`'s optional `ctx` parameter is what separates a jump from a context switch, and its `target` selects where the switched-to context resumes. The three combinations are the whole interface.

rows: raw transfer to that label in the current context
restore the context and resume where it was saved
restore the context, overriding its resume address with the label

blocks.text: `value` and `return_code` are only meaningful in the two restoring modes. `value` is stored in the destination context's `inbox` before control arrives, and `return_code` becomes the value the destination's `Execution_Context.save` returns; it defaults to `1` so a restored capture can never be mistaken for the original `0`.
`Execution_Context.prepare`

`Execution_Context.prepare` builds a complete machine image over a stack the caller owns, without transferring control. Entering it with the third mode above runs the named label on that stack. This is the primitive behind coroutines.

running on the fresh stack, inbox=hello
caller resumed: code=9 inbox=and back

The context, its `Execution_Local` and the backing stack must all outlive every transfer that can reach them. A label entered nonlocally has no call arguments and no live caller frame to borrow from, which is why the example keeps all four in one thread-local object rather than in `main`'s locals.
setjmp and longjmp

`Jump_Buffer` aliases `Execution_Context`. Capture with `buffer.save()`; the old free `setjmp` spelling is no longer supplied. `buffer.longjmp(value)` calls `goto(#undefined, .ctx = &buffer, .return_code = value)` with a zero value promoted to `1`.

Context_Storage is 640 bytes
captured
unwound with code 42
Exceptions

`try` is an `#expand` macro taking a `label` and two `#code` blocks. It expands into the caller, pushes an `Exception_Frame`, captures a landing context, and assigns the frame's unique label to the `label` variable passed in. `throw(target, payload)` walks the active frames for the one carrying that label, so an inner body may select an outer handler by name; `throw_current` takes the innermost frame instead. `catch()` reads the payload.

first result 8
before failing call
outer caught division by zero
after try

The inner `try` is skipped entirely: the failing call names `outer`, so the frame walk passes over `inner` and lands in the outer handler, and neither `outer body done` nor the inner handler runs. For code that cannot be expanded inline, `body.try_call(handler, data)` takes two function pointers instead of two quotes and always uses the innermost frame, and `Unhandled_Exception_Handler.set_unhandled_exception_handler` installs a last resort that a `throw_current` with no active frame reaches instead of terminating the process.
Coroutines

A coroutine is a `Execution_Context.prepare`d context with an owned stack, its own `Execution_Local`, and a pointer back to the caller's context. `Coroutine.resume` saves the caller and switches in; `co_yield` saves the coroutine and switches back, carrying a value each way through the inbox. Because the coroutine has a real stack, it may yield from any depth.

rows: runs until the next suspension, returns a `Coroutine_Event`
frees the stack, the payload arrays and the record

blocks.text: `Coroutine_Event` is a tagged union of `Yielded`, `Awaiting`, `Returned` and `Failed`, and `Coroutine_Status` runs `Fresh`, `Running`, `Suspended`, `Waiting`, `Done`, `Failed`. Resuming a coroutine that is already running, done or failed does not return an error: it exits the process with status 1.

yielded 10
coroutine received 100
yielded 20
coroutine received 200
returned 30
status done: 1

The coroutine body never sees `goto`. It returns a value like any procedure, and an internal trampoline wraps it in a `Try_Body.try_call` so a throw that escapes the body arrives at the caller as a `Failed` event rather than unwinding past a stack that no longer has a caller.
Awaitables and the scheduler

`Awaitable.co_await` suspends into the `Waiting` status and links the coroutine onto the awaitable's waiter list. `Awaitable.complete` publishes the result and enqueues every waiter on the scheduler each one was created with. `Scheduler.run` drains the ready queue, re-enqueuing anything that merely yielded and leaving anything that is awaiting.

waiting=1
ready=7
done=1
Nonlocal entry and the payload

Entering a `,,` label bypasses the calling sequence, so arguments cannot ride in registers. `long_goto` is an `#expand` macro that handles both cases: when `label.is_local` says the target is in the same procedure it jumps without evaluating its arguments at all, otherwise it packs the variadic pack into the execution-local payload and then jumps. The destination reads it with `payload()` or the typed `payload_get(T, i)` and calls `clear_payload()`.

local: 0 valid: 1
arrived with 2 arguments
n=40 flag=1
back with returning

`payload_get` checks the recorded type name before it reads, so a mismatched index or type yields `.None` rather than a reinterpretation. A procedure entered this way has no caller to return to, which is why `worker` is `#Never` and why `main` ends with `exit(0)` instead of running off the end of a frame that was never entered normally.

Restoring a context is the one part of the library that is not available everywhere. A plain local `goto` lowers on every target; a computed `goto` needs an indirect jump; a `Execution_Context.save` restore needs a hand-written register switch, and on a CPU without one the build stops with `error: context restore is not yet supported for this target CPU`. Portable programs guard the whole region with `#if OUT.cpu != Target_CPU.X86_64`, which is what the examples in `examples/goto.glo`, `examples/exceptions.glo` and `examples/coroutine.glo` do.

Glosso executes code during compilation with a constant interpreter and a register-based machine. Position decides when an answer is needed, while the body's operations also decide how it executes. Code that needs memory or managed cleanup can use the machine even when the checker needs its result as a constant.

The constant evaluator lives inside the type checker. It walks the syntax tree of the expression it has been asked to fold, at the moment the checker reaches that expression, and interprets the program directly from that tree. Before running a body, it can instead select VM-backed evaluation for pointer writes, view mutation, procedure-value calls, allocator access, or managed owners. Everything it produces is a value the checker then uses immediately: an array length, a branch decision, a spliced constant.

Top-level compile-time work runs later. Each top-level `#comptime` declaration is lowered into an ordinary IR function alongside the rest of the program, and once checking and lowering are finished the machine executes that function as bytecode, before the backend emits anything. The Compilation Pipeline places both against the full sequence of passes.
Which engine runs which construct

A top-level `#comptime` declaration goes to the machine after checking. Constructs that need an answer during checking go through constant evaluation, which can run a checked body in the VM when required. The engine is selected before execution, rather than retrying after a partially executed body and repeating its effects.

rows: `X :: e;` and `X ::= e;` initialisers, and every global initialiser
`#comptime e` and `#comptime { … }` in a value position
During checking; the interpreter or VM is selected for the body.
The condition of `#if`, `#assert`, and `#inline while`, and every `where` clause
The operand of `#insert`, and the argument for a `#comptime` parameter
`#modify` blocks, `#code` materialisation, and derive macro bodies
`#comptime { … }` and `#comptime f();` written as a top-level declaration

blocks.text: How often each one runs

The machine runs each top-level `#comptime` exactly once, in declaration order. Evaluation during checking makes no such execution count or output promise. Bodies can be checked repeatedly, and a VM-backed value evaluation can discard its captured output. Use these forms to compute values, and put observable build steps at top level.

glosso: compile program.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
[ct] top-level block
glosso: link program.exe (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
glosso: done program.exe  (backend=llvm, target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
runtime main

The installed compiler prints the top-level block's output; the in-body blocks produce no visible lines in this example. That is not an execution-count API. A side effect belongs in a top-level `#comptime`, and an in-body block should be used for the value it produces.
What the constant evaluator refuses

The evaluator handles statements and expressions one kind at a time, and a kind it has no case for is refused rather than guessed at. Labels and `goto` are the visible example: an unstructured jump has no meaning in a tree walk, so the evaluator stops at the label. The same body runs without complaint in the machine, because by then the label and the jump have become ordinary IR instructions.

glosso: compile program.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
[vm] counted = 3
glosso: link program.exe (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
glosso: done program.exe  (backend=llvm, target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)

Replacing the `#comptime` block with `X :: #comptime counted();` sends the same body to the constant evaluator instead, and it is `error: statement is not available at compile time`, reported at the label rather than at the constant. An `#asm` block in a folded body gives the same message for the same reason.

Both compile-time engines bound execution so an infinite loop cannot hang a build. The default budget is 2^28 interpreter steps or VM instructions for one evaluation entry. `GLOSSO_COMPTIME_STEP_LIMIT` overrides it; `0` removes the limit. Exhausting it stops compilation with a diagnostic. The budget counts execution steps, not loop iterations.
Managed builders at compile time

The constant evaluator supports managed `String_Builder` values and compile-time formatting. Use the ordinary builder operations to collect text. `to_string()` only borrows the builder's buffer, so returning that view from a local builder would outlive its owner. `into_string()` consumes the builder and transfers the allocation to the result.

glosso: compile program.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
glosso: link program.exe (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
glosso: done program.exe  (backend=llvm, target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
build_text = <hello builder>

Compile-time source generation also supports String_Builder.new(), append(), and finish_source(). The last call consumes the builder and returns its text. Ordinary make_len_cap(), write_string(), and into_string() also work. Use `tprint` or `format` for formatted source and diagnostics; import `Format` to name them directly.
Globals, memory, and foreign calls

Neither engine runs arbitrary target foreign code: a `#foreign` function has no body to interpret. Compile-time code does have its own globals initialized from the program's declarations. Reading or writing them affects that compile-time execution, not the eventual program's runtime storage. Its `context.allocator` can serve VM heap blocks, including typed loads and stores through pointers. Each raw heap block is limited to 4 MiB in the compile-time VM.

rows: `error: 'now_c' is foreign, so its result is not compile-time known`
`error: #comptime stopped: VM cannot call foreign/undeclared function 'now_c'; use the LLVM backend`
Supported through VM-backed compile-time execution; the compiler chooses the required engine.
A raw VM heap block larger than 4 MiB
Compilation stops at the VM's allocation limit.
Observes its compile-time initial value, `5`, independently of later runtime writes.

blocks.text: Reflection is the case that looks as though it should differ and does not. `size_of`, `type_name`, `field_name` and the rest of `std/Meta` are compile-time-only intrinsics with no runtime implementation at all, and the machine has no entry for any of them. They still work in a top-level `#comptime` block, because the checker folds every such call to a constant before lowering; by the time the machine runs, the call is gone and only its answer is left in the instruction stream.

glosso: compile program.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
[vm] describe = Vec3.x
[vm] size_of  = 12
glosso: link program.exe (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
glosso: done program.exe  (backend=llvm, target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
[ceval] describe = Vec3.x
Compile-time output

Both engines send `print` output to the compiler's standard output, while the compiler's own `glosso:` progress lines go to standard error; redirecting one does not capture the other. The machine's output is buffered and flushed in a single block once every top-level `#comptime` has finished, so where it lands relative to the progress lines is not something to depend on.

`#comptime` asks for a piece of the program to run during compilation. There is one spelling and several positions, and the position decides both what the directive leaves behind and which engine runs it.

In a value position `#comptime` produces a constant that is spliced into the program in place of the expression. As a top-level declaration it produces nothing: the block runs for its effects and emits no code. `#run`, the earlier spelling, no longer exists; `X :: #run 1 + 1;` is `error: unexpected directive 'run'`.
The forms

rows: Evaluate `e` during checking and splice the constant in.
Run a block; the returned value is the constant, typed by inference.
The same, with the result typed exactly `T`.
Run the block in the compile-time machine for its effects.
The same, written as one call.
The argument must be compile-time known; see Compile-Time and Type-Only Parameters.

blocks.text:
Inline_Expr=256 Table_Size=256 local=42
Table_Size: ssize (8 bytes)
Byte_Limit: u8 (1 bytes)
Squares = 0 1 4 9
`-> T` and the type of the result

Without the annotation the constant is typed by inference, and an integer literal returned from a block defaults to `ssize`, which is eight bytes. `#comptime -> u8 { return 200; }` is one byte instead. The annotation is checked rather than coerced, so it also refuses a value that does not belong: `#comptime -> u8 { return 500; }` is `error: 500 does not fit u8, whose range is 0..=255`. Compile-Time Numbers and Literal Defaulting explains the defaulting rule the annotation is overriding.

Any type the evaluator can build is accepted, including aggregates. That is what `Squares` above relies on: a lookup table is computed by a loop during checking and ends up in the program as ordinary constant data, with no initialisation code and no way for the two to drift apart.

Nothing of the computation survives into the output. A `#comptime` expression is replaced by its result before the backend sees it, so the emitted function contains a literal where the call used to be.

; ---- #dump typed-ir seed() -> ssize  [4 ins] ----
   0  temp_mark v0
   1  const v1 =6765
   2  temp_restore v0
   3  ret v1
; ---- end seed ----
A top-level `#comptime` is a build step

At file scope `#comptime` is a declaration. It runs once, in declaration order, after checking and before the backend emits anything, and it contributes no code to the program. This is where a build does work that is not part of the program: inspect the target, run an external tool, generate a source file, refuse to proceed.

glosso: compile program.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
[build] targeting Windows
glosso: link program.exe (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
glosso: done program.exe  (backend=llvm, target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)

`exit(status)` called from compile time stops the build where it stands. No binary is written, the remaining top-level `#comptime` declarations do not run, and the compiler itself exits with the requested status, which is what makes the guard above a real gate rather than a warning. Output already produced by the block is still flushed.

The chosen backend makes no difference. `--backend llvm-ir` and `--backend object` run every top-level `#comptime` exactly as the default backend does; the compile-time machine sits before the point where the backends diverge.

A program with a top-level `#comptime` is never restored from the native artifact cache. The cache cannot know what the block did, so a rebuild that skipped it would skip a build step, and the compiler declines to cache the artifact at all. A `#comptime` used only for a constant does not have this effect, which also means its side effects are skipped on a cached rebuild. The Build Cache and Generated Sources covers the cache.

The standard library turns this mechanism into a full build system: a top-level `#comptime` that calls into `std/Compiler` can set build options, add source files, and drive nested compilations. Build Scripts covers that API, and The Compile-Time Command Line and Artifact Cache covers the arguments a build step can read.
Inside a function body

In a body, a `#comptime` block is evaluated while checking. The compiler can use its VM for that value calculation, and output produced there is not a reliable observable effect. What Runs When compares this with top-level compile-time declarations.

The consequence is a rule rather than a number. An in-body `#comptime` is for its value; anything that writes a file, prints, or calls the compiler belongs in a top-level `#comptime` where the count is exactly one.

A bare expression after `#comptime` in statement position is a trap. The parser consumes the directive and then wraps the expression in an ordinary expression statement, dropping the compile-time marking entirely, so `#comptime f();` inside a body runs at run time. Only the block form runs during compilation there.

A `#comptime` fails when the code it names needs something that does not exist in that engine. The eventual program is not running, and arbitrary target foreign calls or runtime locals cannot be evaluated. Compile-time context reads and compiler-provided build, file, and string services are a different matter: they have explicit host implementations. Only such a name can drive `#if`, an array length, an `#inline while` counter, an `#assert #comptime`, or a `#comptime` parameter. `::` asks for immutability, `::=` asks for a compile-time value

`::` declares a constant. The checker tries to evaluate the initialiser: if that succeeds the name becomes a compile-time constant, and if it fails the name becomes a runtime-frozen constant instead, which is still immutable but no longer usable during checking. `::=` inside a body declares a compile-time binding, and there the evaluation is required rather than attempted.

A `::` whose initialiser cannot be folded is not an error. Immutability and compile-time knowledge are separate properties, and `::` asks for only the first of them; refusing the declaration would force a writer to give up immutability for a reason that has nothing to do with it.

`HALF` is derived from a parameter, so the checker cannot know it. The declaration is accepted anyway: the expression is evaluated once, when control reaches the declaration, and the name is bound to that result for the rest of the scope. That is what a reader of `HALF ::` expects, and it is what the loop below it needs.

The price is that a frozen constant is not a compile-time value, and every construct that wanted one says so at the use rather than at the declaration. For a local `FROZEN :: n * 2` over a runtime `n`, `#if FROZEN == 14` is `error: unknown const FROZEN`, `grid: [FROZEN]s64;` is `error: array count 'FROZEN' is not compile-time known`, and `#assert #comptime FROZEN == 14` is `error: #assert #comptime condition is not compile-time evaluable`.

`::=` asks for the other property, so it reports the failure at the declaration: `K ::= n * 2;` over a runtime `n` is `error: comptime variable initializer must be compile-time evaluable`. A later write to a compile-time binding is held to the same standard; `i: s64 := 0; i = n;` is `error: comptime assignment must be compile-time evaluable`.
A compile-time binding is a variable

`::=` binds a name that may be reassigned while the checker runs. That is what makes an unrolled loop possible: `#inline while` re-evaluates its condition in the compile-time environment after each unrolled body, so the body has to move something the condition reads.

`#assert cond` is one statement doing two jobs. When the condition can be evaluated during checking it is a compile-time check that emits no code; when it cannot, the same statement compiles into a runtime check. There is no separate spelling for the runtime one and no flag that turns one into the other.

The decision runs in order. The condition is type-checked first and must be `bool`. Then the constant evaluator is asked for its value. If the answer is `false` the compilation fails; if it is `true` the statement lowers to nothing at all; if there is no answer the statement becomes a runtime assertion.

blocks.text: The compile-time assertion

Anything the constant evaluator can answer is fair game for a compile-time assertion, which in practice means layout facts, reflection results, and target queries. A passing assertion costs nothing, so it can sit permanently next to the declaration whose invariant it guards.
checks passed at compile time

A failing one stops the build and points at the `#assert` keyword. `#assert 1 + 1 == 3;` is `error: assertion failed`, and `#assert #comptime 1 + 1 == 3, "math is broken";` is `error: assertion failed: math is broken`.

A typeclass predicate is an ordinary compile-time `bool`, so an instance requirement can be written as an assertion. For a struct with no instance, `#assert Show(Opaque), "Opaque must be printable";` is `error: assertion failed: Opaque must be printable`. The runtime assertion

When the condition depends on a value the compiler cannot know, the same statement becomes a check in the emitted program. It fires on the way past, prints the source position and the message, and aborts.

…\program.glo:5:5: assertion failed: x must be big
glosso: program exited with status exit code: 134

The runtime form is not removed at any optimisation level: `-O0` through `-O3` all abort here. It exits through the same path as the language's other runtime checks, which Runtime Safety Checks and Panics describes.
What the two lower to
Nothing about the two spellings differs. Only whether the condition folded decides which of them a given `#assert` becomes, and `#dump` shows the difference directly.

`static_ok` has no instruction for its assertion; the statement disappeared during checking, message and all. `dynamic_check` gained a comparison, a branch over the failure, and a call to `assert_failed` with a string that already carries the source position, because the position is known then and not later.
`#assert #comptime`

Writing `#comptime` after `#assert` removes the third outcome. The condition must now be evaluable, and failing to evaluate becomes an error rather than a silent downgrade. That matters for a check that is meant to hold at build time: without the modifier, a change that makes the condition depend on a local quietly turns a compile-time guarantee into a runtime one and nothing reports it.

For `x := 5;` followed by `#assert #comptime x > 0;` the diagnostic is `error: #assert #comptime condition is not compile-time evaluable`, with `note: unknown const x` pointing at the part that could not be folded. The note names the first thing the evaluator gave up on, which is usually enough to find the mistake.
Inside a generic body the assertion is checked once per instantiation, and only for the types that actually reach it.

The message

The message is optional, follows a comma, and must be a compile-time `string`. It need not be a literal: any expression the evaluator folds to a string is accepted, so `tprint` can compose one from the values that made the check fail. A value of the wrong type is `error: #assert message must be a compile-time string`, and a runtime local used as the message is `error: unknown const reason`, pointing at the message rather than the condition.
`#compile_error`

`#compile_error <expr>` evaluates its operand and reports the result as the error message. It has no condition of its own and fires whenever checking reaches it, which makes it the payload for a `#if` guard rather than a check in its own right. The message being a value rather than a fixed string is the point: the failing case can name itself.
That is `error: unsupported backend: widget`. The operand is held to the same standard as an `#assert` message: a runtime local is `error: unknown const reason`.

`#if` prunes the branch it does not select, so a `#compile_error` inside an unselected branch never fires. That pairing is how a generic body rejects an instantiation with a message of the author's choosing instead of whatever the body happens to fail on first.

A `where` clause is the other way to say this, and the two differ in what they do to overload selection: `where Is_Integer(T)` removes the candidate and reports `error: constraint failed for byte_width`, while the `#if` guard keeps the candidate and reports the chosen message. Constraints with `where` covers the first.

Both directives are statements, not declarations. At file scope `#assert 1 == 1;` is `error: bad decl name 'assert'` and `#compile_error "no";` is `error: bad decl name 'compile_error'`. A whole-file invariant goes inside a top-level `#comptime` block, which is a declaration and takes statements.

A directive written in a `#code` quote or `#expand` body keeps that written location after insertion or macro expansion. To report the caller, pass `#source_location` explicitly from the caller, as above.

The parser materializes the three fields before those transformations, so the result is also usable in constants, `#comptime`, and direct member access such as `#source_location.line`. `#code` quotes Glosso syntax and produces a value of the built-in compile-time type `Code`. A quotation is parsed where it is written, but names and types inside it are resolved when `#insert` places it into a program. The same value can therefore be inserted more than once and can acquire a different meaning in each insertion scope.

A `Code` value is compiler-only

`Code` needs no import, has size zero, and never reaches generated machine code. Bind a quotation with `::` or pass it directly to a `#expand` macro. `body := #code print("x");` is rejected with `a 'Code' value is compile-time only; bind it with '::' rather than ':='`, and an ordinary runtime procedure cannot consume one.

Double-backtick substitution

Inside a quotation, two backticks ask the compiler to substitute a compile-time binding while it materialises the syntax. A `string` can supply an identifier, a `type` can supply a type spelling, and another `Code` value can supply syntax. This is distinct from the single backtick used by macros to name the caller's scope.

What quotations can carry

A block quotation uses the statement grammar. Besides executable statements it can carry a nested procedure, type, macro, or typeclass instance declaration, and it can carry quoted `case` fragments for insertion into a switch. A quotation is still not source text: it is already parsed, retains hygiene marks, and is never written to the generated-source cache.
Use `Code` when the generated shape can be expressed as parsed Glosso syntax and only names need to vary.
Use a `string` insertion when the generator must construct tokens or whole declarations that cannot be represented by one fixed quotation.
`#insert` evaluates its operand at compile time and replaces itself with the resulting syntax. Its position selects both the accepted source and the grammar applied to that source.

`scope()` matters inside a macro. It makes the inserted quotation see the hygienically renamed locals established by that expansion. At top level, text is parsed as declarations. That is the general way to synthesize a constant, an aggregate with a computed field list, or several related overloads. A `Code` block can also carry already-parsed procedure, aggregate, macro, and instance declarations.

A subjectless `#pattern P` quotation produces a compiler-only `Pattern` value. In pattern position, `#insert` accepts that value and clones its pattern at every use. `#insert A | #insert B` is an or-pattern because insertion binds tighter than `|`.

Every string insertion is materialised under `<cache>/generated/insert/v1/<sha256>.glo` before parsing. Equal text shares a cache entry. `--show-generated` prints those paths, while `--cache-dir` selects the cache root. `Code` and `Pattern` insertion uses syntax trees directly and creates no file.

`#expand` declares a macro. The checker selects it using the argument types, substitutes argument syntax for parameters, gives declarations fresh hygienic names, and checks the expanded result in the caller. A macro with no value return is invoked as a statement; a macro with an explicit non-`void` return type is a value macro and can contain a full statement body.

An unquoted local declared by a macro is renamed for each expansion, so it cannot collide with a same-named caller local. A single backtick opts an identifier or control-flow keyword into the caller's scope. A backticked declaration can intentionally publish a name to inserted caller code, as when the macro writes a backtick before `it := 0;`, then `#insert body;`. Use that narrowly: ordinary macro locals are hygienic for a reason.

Macros may be declared inside procedures and inside other macros. A nested macro participates in the surrounding expansion and can use the names established there. Recursive value macros are also supported when static branching makes the expansion terminate.

Reflection is the set of compile-time intrinsics that answer questions about a type: its tag, its size, the names and types of its fields, the members of an enum, the variants of a union. They live in `std/Meta` and arrive with `#import "Meta";`. Every one of them is folded to a constant by the checker, so a reflection query costs nothing at run time and is available wherever a constant is: `#comptime`, `#if`, `#assert`, a `where` clause, a constant initialiser, and the argument of `#insert`.

Indices must be compile-time constants

`field_name(T, i)` folds only if `i` folds. An ordinary loop variable does not: an `i := 0` counter driving a `while` gives `unknown const i` at the intrinsic, and so does the loop variable of a plain `for` and of `#inline for`, which unrolls the body but does not record a compile-time value for its variable. A #if branch stops recursion before checking an out-of-range field index, so each live intrinsic call folds at its specialization. It also composes: the helper returns text, which is what `#insert` wants. `#inline while` works because the counter is declared `i ::= 0`, a compile-time binding; declaring it `i := 0` is `#inline while condition must be compile-time evaluable`.
