Matrix      kind 17 rows 2 cols 3 elements 6 transpose Matrix(f32, 3, 2)
names: ?s32 string!s32 Simd(f32, 4)
`?T` has `None: void` at index `0` and `Some: T` at index `1`. `E!T` has `Ok: T` at index `0` and `Err: E` at index `1`, so the variant order is the reverse of the spelling.
`type_name` of an optional or a result gives its source spelling, such as `?s32` and `string!s32`. Nested types include parentheses where needed, as in `?(string!s64)`.

Structural types also use source spellings: `[]s32`, `[*]u8`, `(s64, string)`, and `(s32) -> s32`. Instantiated aggregates include their arguments, such as `Box(s64)`. `Type_Info.name` and the static record carried by `any` agree with `type_name` in native and compile-time execution.

Native and fixed integers retain their identities, so `variant_type` on a `box: s64` variant reports `s64`, while one declared `box: ssize` reports `ssize`. A tuple has tag `Tuple` but `field_count` of a tuple type is `0`; its components are not reachable through the field intrinsics.
Generating code from a type

Reflection pays off when its answers become source. The helper below uses a compile-time index to emit one print per field and splices the result, so a single definition prints any struct without a `Show` instance and without a runtime type table.

`describe` is instantiated once per argument type and each instantiation splices its own generated statements, which --show-generated reports. The inline while index is a compile-time binding. T is a type parameter, so the reflection calls fold inside the generic body; `value` is an ordinary parameter. The generated source spells `value with a backtick to resolve that name in the insertion site rather than the generator.

Generating source is the general answer to a per-field or per-variant job, and it is often the only one. There is no way to index a struct's fields at run time, so a loop over `field_count(T)` has to be unrolled into text or into `#inline while` before it means anything.

Reflection follows the visibility permissions of its defining source file. Inaccessible fields and variants are omitted from reflected member lists, without changing physical layout or discriminants. Generic bodies and default expressions keep the permissions of their defining file after specialization; they do not gain access to caller-private fields.

A `#pattern` written with no `= subject` and no `==` switch after it is a quote: it produces a value instead of performing a match. The value has the built-in type `Pattern`, and it can be stored in a constant, passed to a procedure, returned from one, and spliced back into pattern position with `#insert`. Splicing is covered in Patterns as Compile-Time Values; this chapter covers the intrinsics that ask a quote questions.

`Pattern` is a compiler built-in name and needs no import, as `type` and `Code` do. The six intrinsics that read a quote are declared in `std/Meta/Utilities.glo` and need `#import "Meta";`. Every one of them is compile-time only: the checker folds the call to a constant while it still has the types in hand, so the call may be written in an ordinary runtime expression but nothing of it survives to run time.

binders of NUMBER: 1
  n : f64
uncovered by NUMBER and NAME: 1
  Token.Eof

A quote has no runtime representation, so it must be bound with `::` rather than `:=`. `P := #pattern 1;` is `error: a 'Pattern' value is compile-time only; bind it with '::' rather than ':='`. The same rule governs `Code` and the other compiler-only meta-values, and it is why the pattern parameters of the intrinsics are declared `#comptime`.
The intrinsics

rows: How many names `P` brings into scope when it is matched against `T`.
The name of binder `i`, in the order the pattern was written.
How many witnesses of `T` no pattern in the view `Ps` matches.
Witness `i`, rendered as source-shaped pattern text.
Whether adding `Q` to `Ps` would match anything `Ps` does not.

blocks.text: The subject type comes first in all six because a pattern's meaning is a property of the pattern and the type it is matched against together, not of the pattern alone: `.Some(v)` binds an `s32` against `?s32` and a `string` against `?string`, and a member name is a union variant for one subject and an enum constant for another. `Ps` is an ordinary `[]Pattern` view, so a set of arms can be declared once as `ARMS : []Pattern : .[A, B, C];` and reused; an untyped `.[A, B]` constant has type `[2]Pattern` and does not convert on its own.
A quote carries no type until it is asked about one

The compiler checks a copy of the quote against the requested subject each time it is asked, and discards whatever that check instantiated. The quote itself is never stamped, so one quote serves several subject types and the binder types follow the subject rather than the quote.

?s32    v: s32
?string v: string
?f64    v: f64
uncovered by .Some alone: 1
  Option_s32.None
uncovered by .Some and .None: 0

`Option_s32.None` is the internal name of the compiler-baked option union; `?T` is the whole surface syntax for it, and the witness text is the one place the internal name shows through. Because checking happens at the question and not at the declaration, a quote that cannot be matched against the requested subject reports at the quote's own span: `#pattern 0..=9` asked about `f64` is `error: a range pattern needs an integer subject, got f64`, and an alternative that binds different names from its sibling is `error: or-pattern alternative does not bind 'r', which another alternative does`.
Binders

Binders are reported in source order. `_` is not a binder, a name that appears twice is reported once, and `whole @ P` contributes the outer name followed by everything `P` binds. An or-pattern's alternatives must agree on the names they bind, so a usable or-pattern either binds the same set in every alternative or binds nothing at all.

binders of BOUND: 2
  whole : Shape
  r : f64
binders of EITHER: 0

An index past the end is `error: pattern binder index out of range`, and the witness accessor reports `error: pattern witness index out of range`. Both are compile errors, since both calls are folded.
Coverage

`pattern_missing_count` and `pattern_missing` run the same Maranget usefulness analysis the compiler uses to decide whether a `#pattern` switch is exhaustive, detached from any switch node. The result is a list of witnesses: values of `T` that no pattern in `Ps` matches, rendered as source-shaped pattern text. No more than 32 witnesses are collected, so a count of 32 means "at least 32".

Color after Red, Green: 1 (Color.Blue)
bool after true: 1 (false)
Point after origin: 4 (Point.{ .x = 0, .y = -2147483648..=-1 })
u8 after 0..=9: 1 (10..=255)
u8 after 0..=9, 10..=255: 0
string after "hello": 1 (_)

The witnesses show how each type is taken apart. Union variants, enum constants and booleans are enumerated, so the uncovered ones are named directly. A struct has exactly one constructor, so coverage is decided field by field and the report is a cross product over the fields that were pinned down. An integer domain is not enumerated but split into closed intervals, which is why `0..=9` over `u8` leaves the single witness `10..=255` and why adding `10..=255` leaves none. Floats, strings and pointers have no enumerable structure at all, so only a wildcard covers them and the witness is the bare `_`.

The analysis errs in one direction only. It may report a case missing that a reader can see is covered, and it never reports zero for a set of patterns that is not total. So `pattern_missing_count(T, Ps) == 0` is a genuine proof of totality, and a non-zero answer means "not proved", not "definitely reachable". That is the same contract the compiler's own switches are held to.
Three constructs sit outside the analysis by design, and each of them is a source of witnesses a reader would not have expected.
Where the same analysis runs over a switch, guarded, predicate and `#falling` arms are excluded from the matrix, because every one of them can decline a value after matching its shape.
A raw union carries no tag, so its values cannot be discriminated at all and nothing about it can be proved.

An or-pattern nested inside a constructor is opaque unless one alternative is a wildcard. Over `Shape`, adding `#pattern Shape.Rect(-2147483648..=2147483647)` to the other two variants leaves nothing uncovered, while the equivalent `#pattern Shape.Rect(-2147483648..=-1 | 0..=2147483647)` still reports one witness.
Usefulness, subsumption, and equivalence

`pattern_is_useful(T, Ps, Q)` answers the other half of the same algorithm: does `Q` match anything `Ps` does not? A `false` answer is exactly "`Q` would be a dead arm after `Ps`", which is also "`Ps` subsumes `Q`". Two patterns are equivalent when neither is useful against the other. That relation is what a reader usually means by pattern equality, and it is why `Pattern` has no `==`: whether `A | B` equals `B | A`, or whether `_` equals a binder, has no structural answer, while mutual non-usefulness has one.

A equivalent B = 1
A equivalent C = 0
A subsumes C   = 1
C subsumes A   = 0
W subsumes A   = 1
A subsumes W   = 0
Computing with the answers

The index arguments are ordinary `ssize` parameters, but they must still be compile-time constants, because the whole call is folded during checking. A `while` loop that walks the witnesses with a runtime counter is `error: unknown const i`. The working shape is a recursive compile-time helper that carries the index as an argument, the same idiom type reflection uses and for the same reason; it is described in Reflection.

error: switch is not total; uncovered: Token.Eof
   --> …\total.glo:21:24
   |
21 |     #if REPORT != "" { #compile_error tprint("switch is not total; uncovered: %", REPORT); }
   |                        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

A shorter obligation is `#assert #comptime pattern_missing_count(Token, ARMS) == 0, "the arm list is not total";`, which fails as `error: assertion failed: the arm list is not total`. Once the proof holds, the same constants can drive the switch through `#insert`, so the arms that were proved total are literally the arms that run.

number
name
eof

A build script is an ordinary Glosso file whose work happens in a top-level `#comptime`. `#import "Compiler";` brings in the build API, the `#comptime` declaration runs it once during compilation, and `main :: () {}` is still present because the file is a program like any other. Nothing in the API is available at run time; every operation is a compiler service reached from compile-time execution.

$ glosso build.glo
glosso: compile build.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
[build] nested compilation said:
glosso: compile hello.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
glosso: link hello.exe (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O2)
glosso: done hello.exe  (backend=llvm, target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O2)
$ ./hello.exe
hello from the nested build

`set_build_options_dc(.do_output = false)` suppresses the emit step of the compilation that is running the script, so no `build.exe` appears. Without it the driver would also link the build script itself, which is almost never wanted: the script's `main` is empty and its whole purpose has already been served. The name means "during compile", and it is the only setter that changes the current compilation rather than a nested one.

A nested compilation is a new `glosso` process, taken from `GLOSSO_COMPILER_EXE` if that is set and from the running executable otherwise. `add_build_file` and `add_build_string` wait for that child and return its standard output followed by its standard error instead of passing either stream through. That is why the child's transcript appears under `[build]` above and why discarding the `.Ok` payload discards the child's log. A failed child returns `Compiler_Error`; that type implements `Error`, so `report_error(failure)` prints `compiler error: ` followed by the captured diagnostics.
`Workspace` and `Build_Options`

A `Workspace` is a `distinct s64` handle to one reusable `Build_Options` configuration. Create one with `Workspace.create`, obtain a detached copy of its options with `Workspace.get_build_options`, edit that copy, and install it with `Build_Options.set_build_options`. Nothing is queued: `add_build_file(path, workspace)` and `add_build_string(source, workspace)` each start and await one child compilation immediately. Omitting the workspace argument uses the shared implicit handle `-1`.

rows: Selects the backend when `backend` is `.Default`; `.No_Output` omits `-o` but does not suppress the child's artifact.
`--backend` with the matching name, or derive it from `output_type`.
The name passed through `-o`; empty falls back to the source stem.
Directory joined to the output name; empty uses the working directory.
An all-zero target inherits the caller; raw `compiler_args` may override it, while a nonzero field is appended last and wins.
One optimization flag; see the table below.
Raw child arguments before the flags derived from this record.
One `--module-path` per entry, after the standard library in search order.
Entries after `--`, preserving spaces and empty strings as individual arguments.
`--color always` or `--color never`, resolved against the parent's stderr.

blocks.text: `.Auto` never reaches the child as `auto`. The child's standard error is a capture pipe and can never be a terminal, so the parent resolves `auto` against its own stderr and passes the answer. A script that wants plain text in the captured log sets `.Never` explicitly.

The fields are written through mutators that take a pointer to the record: `Build_Options.set_backend`, `Build_Options.set_target`, `Build_Options.set_optimization`, `Build_Options.set_memory_sanitizer`, `Build_Options.set_thread_sanitizer`, `Build_Options.set_color`, `Build_Options.set_temp_allocator_size`, `Build_Options.set_no_main`, `Build_Options.add_compiler_arg`, `Build_Options.add_linker_arg`, `Build_Options.add_linker_args` and `Build_Options.add_module_path`. They mutate only the detached local record; call `Build_Options.set_build_options` afterwards. Direct field assignment and `array.push` on its dynamic-array fields are equivalent.

`Compiler_Backend` has seven members. `LLVM`, `Object`, `LLVM_IR`, `Static_Lib` and `Shared_Lib` map to `--backend llvm`, `object`, `llvm-ir`, `static-lib` and `shared-lib`. `Default` passes no `--backend` and lets the output type decide. `X64` maps to nothing at all and behaves exactly like `Default`; it is a dead value.

`Build_Output_Type` supplies the default backend independently of the file name: `.Executable`, `.Object_File`, `.LLVM_IR`, `.Static_Library` and `.Shared_Library` select the corresponding artifact. `.No_Output` means "do not pass `-o`"; the child still emits to its own source-derived default path. To suppress the build script's own artifact, use `set_build_options_dc(.do_output = false)` instead.
Optimization levels

`Optimization` is an explicitly numbered enum because its values are part of the compile-time service ABI. `Default` is not a synonym for `Very_Debug`: it passes no optimization flag at all, and the child then applies its own default, which is `-O1`.

rows: `-Os`; LLVM size optimization and dead-section removal
`-Ozz`; reaches the same rejected `default<Oz>` pipeline before stripping

blocks.text: The size modes -Os, -Oz, and -Ozz produce runnable artifacts. They combine LLVM optimization with optsize/minsize attributes and target-specific linker size policies. Runtime checks are disabled in these modes; use -O0 or -O1 for checked builds. -Ozz also strips symbols and metadata.
Named and implicit workspaces

`Workspace.create(name)` returns fresh handles numbered from zero for the life of the compiler process. The name is retained but is otherwise informational; it need not be unique, and there is no destroy operation. Each new handle starts with independent default options. Handle `-1` is reserved for the process-wide implicit workspace used by every call that omits its workspace argument. Reading any other unknown handle materializes it with defaults rather than reporting an error.

output_type=1 backend=0 optimization=7 do_output=1
[ws] built:
glosso: compile hello.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
glosso: link tool.exe (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O2)
glosso: done tool.exe  (backend=llvm, target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O2)

Enum values print as their numbers, so the defaults read as `output_type = Executable`, `backend = Default` and `optimization_level = Default`. The output name comes from `output_executable_name`, joined onto `output_path` when that is set, and falls back to the source's file stem. The whole name is passed through as `-o`, so a fallback name carries no platform extension: a workspace with only `output_path = "outdir"` set produces `glosso: done outdir\hello`. `add_build_string(source, w)` is the same operation over text: the source is written to a temporary file named `glosso_build_string_<pid>_<n>.glo` and that file is compiled and left in place, which is why its diagnostics name a path in the system temporary directory. Give it an explicit output name when the temporary source stem would not be a useful artifact name.

`compile_time_command_line` is active: a nonempty list is appended after `--`, and the child reads exactly those entries through `get_cmdline_args()`. Four other fields are currently reserved: `intermediate_path`, `do_output`, `write_added_strings`, and `text_output_flags`. In particular, changing `Build_Options.do_output` does not suppress either compilation, and `write_added_strings = false` does not stop `add_build_string` from writing its temporary source.
Building C sources

`Native_Compile_Output.compile_c_archive(name, sources)` compiles a list of C files with the compiler's bundled native toolchain and returns `Native_Compile_Output`, whose `artifact` field is the path of the static library it produced and whose `output` field is the tool's log. The archive is written into the native cache, keyed by the archive name, target, parameters, and verified source/header dependencies. If dependency inputs cannot be verified, the archive uses a fresh `uncached-...` directory and is rebuilt. Pass `include_paths`, `preprocessor_definitions`, and `compiler_args` as named `[]mut string` parameters, which default to `.[]`. Their slices and strings are borrowed for the call. `sources` is also `[]mut string`; pass a fixed or dynamic array's `[..]` view. `position_independent` defaults to `false`, and `optimization_level` defaults to `.Optimized`; only `.Debug`, `.Very_Debug`, `.Optimized`, and `.Very_Optimized` are accepted. The input option record and its specialized mutators are no longer public APIs.

glosso: compile archive.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
[c] archive at C:\Users\…\glosso\cache\native\v9\adder\x86_64-windows-msvc\…\adder.lib
glosso: link archive.exe (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
glosso: done archive.exe  (backend=llvm, target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
c_add(3, 4) = 7

The `#library` declaration and the `#foreign` declaration have to be inserted together. A top-level string `#insert` that declares only the library, with the `#foreign` procedure written in the file, is `error: #foreign refers to unknown library 'adder' (declare it with #library)`. Handing `archive.artifact` to Bindgen's `library_spec` and inserting the generated source does the same job for a real header; that route is covered in Generating Bindings with Bindgen. A path inserted into a quoted source literal must escape backslashes and quotes, as above; printing a native Windows path verbatim does not produce a valid Glosso string literal.
Other compiler services

`macro_unit(path, argument)` is the native-code route for a reusable source generator. It builds `path` as a program through a nested compiler, benefits from the native artifact cache, runs the result with `argument` after `--`, and returns the program's standard output as source text. Write `#insert macro_unit("macros/derive_json.glo", "record");` at the use site. A build or run failure is returned as diagnostic text so the following insertion fails with the generator's error visible.
The build-driver idiom

The shape every real build script converges on is a single top-level `#comptime` that turns off its own output, reads a task name from the compile-time command line, and dispatches. This manual is built that way: `glosso first.glo -- build` compiles the manual's `main.glo` for `wasm32-freestanding`, and other task names regenerate its reference data and its syntax highlighting.

$ glosso first.glo
glosso: compile first.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
usage: glosso first.glo -- <command>
commands:
  release   build hello.glo optimized
$ echo $?
1
$ glosso first.glo -- release
glosso: compile first.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
built hello.exe
$ glosso first.glo -- deploy
glosso: compile first.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
unknown task: deploy
usage: glosso first.glo -- <command>
commands:
  release   build hello.glo optimized

`exit(status)` from compile-time execution stops the build with that status and writes no binary, which is what makes a build script usable from a shell script or a continuous-integration job. Because the driver emits nothing, the run above produces `hello.exe` and no `first.exe`. Cross-compiling a nested build is a matter of one more setter: `options.set_target(.{ .os = Target_OS.Wasm, .cpu = Target_CPU.Wasm32, .abi = Target_ABI.Freestanding })` makes the child report `target=wasm32-unknown-unknown`. That changes only children using this workspace. `Native_Compile_Output.compile_c_archive` still uses the build script's active target; compile the script itself for the matching target when its C archive must be link-compatible with the nested Glosso artifact.

sections.title: The Compile-Time Command Line and Artifact Cache

blocks.text: `glosso [options] <file.glo> -- <args...>` hands everything after the `--` separator to compile-time execution rather than to the driver. The separator itself, and the fact that `get_cmdline_args()` returns the process argument vector in the built program, are covered in Using the Compiler. What matters here is the compile-time half: the arguments are how a build script written in Glosso is parameterized, and they are part of the identity of the artifact the build produces.

$ glosso opts.glo -- --release --out dist/tool.exe
glosso: compile opts.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
[ct] output = dist/tool.exe  optimization = 2
$ glosso opts.glo -- --fast
glosso: compile opts.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
unknown option: --fast
$ echo $?
2

A rejected option can end the build immediately because `exit` from compile-time execution aborts the compilation with the requested status and writes no output file. Compile-time `print` output is buffered and flushed to standard output in one block after every top-level `#comptime` has run, while the compiler's own progress lines go to standard error, so the interleaving of the two in a terminal is not something to depend on.
Forwarding arguments to a workspace build

A child started by `add_build_file` or `add_build_string` does not inherit the build script's own `--` arguments automatically. Put the arguments for that child in `Build_Options.compile_time_command_line`, then install the options before starting the build. The service writes one `--` separator followed by the list; each element remains one argument, even when it contains spaces or is empty.

$ glosso parent.glo -- top
glosso: compile parent.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
[parent] 1 argument(s)
[child] 1 argument(s)
[child]   release
glosso: compile child.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
glosso: link child.exe (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
glosso: done child.exe  (backend=llvm, target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
The native artifact cache

When a compilation would produce a native artifact and nothing about it has changed, the driver copies the previous result out of a per-user cache instead of running the pipeline. The restore is announced, and it replaces every phase after argument parsing, so no `compile` or `link` line appears at all.

#import "Io";
main :: () { print("%\n", 6 * 7); }

$ glosso --run sum.glo
glosso: compile sum.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
glosso: link sum.exe (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
glosso: done sum.exe  (backend=llvm, target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
42
$ glosso --run sum.glo
glosso: restored sum.exe from the native artifact cache
42
$ glosso --run sum.glo -- release
glosso: compile sum.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
glosso: link sum.exe (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
glosso: done sum.exe  (backend=llvm, target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
42
$ glosso -O2 --run sum.glo
glosso: compile sum.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
glosso: link sum.exe (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O2)
glosso: done sum.exe  (backend=llvm, target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O2)
42
The key

The key is a hash of an identity string assembled from everything that could change the bytes of the artifact. Adding `-- release` to an otherwise identical command line produced a third cache entry above, because a build script can read those words and emit something different for them.

rows: The canonical input and compiler paths, the working directory, and the resolved standard-library directory.
The LLVM triple, and separately every key and value of `--target`, because the triple collapses distinct maps such as `uefi` and `msvc`.
Backend name, optimization level, size mode, sanitizer selection, and diagnostic color.
The temporary allocator size, `GLOSSO_DEBUG_ALLOCATOR` selection, `--no-main`, and `--use-std`.
Every `--module-path` directory, in order, and explicit `--unit-source` mappings.

blocks.text: The output path is deliberately absent. Building the same source with `-o other.exe` restores the cached artifact and copies it to the new name: `glosso: restored other.exe from the native artifact cache`. The key is 32 hexadecimal characters. An entry holds `<key>.artifact`, `<key>.manifest`, `<key>.stdout`, and `<key>.stderr` under `<cache>/native/artifacts/v1`. A hit replays the stored checker output and diagnostics. Missing output sidecars turn the entry into a miss; new entries use temporary files and publish their manifest last.
The manifest

The key decides which entry to look at; the manifest decides whether it is still valid. It is a small binary file beginning with the magic `GLOART01`, followed by a count and then one record per dependency: the path, the file's length, and its modification time in seconds and nanoseconds. The artifact is restored only if every stamp still matches. The dependency list is the source file, every file reached through `#load` and `#import`, the compiler executable itself, and any `--linker-arg` that names an existing file.

$ glosso --run uses.glo
glosso: compile uses.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
glosso: link uses.exe (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
glosso: done uses.exe  (backend=llvm, target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
one
$ glosso --run uses.glo
glosso: restored uses.exe from the native artifact cache
one
$ # helper.glo edited to return "two"
$ glosso --run uses.glo
glosso: compile uses.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
glosso: link uses.exe (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
glosso: done uses.exe  (backend=llvm, target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
two

Validation is by length and modification time, not by content hash. Restoring a checkout, copying a tree, or any operation that rewrites a file's timestamp without changing its bytes therefore forces a rebuild rather than a stale restore, which is the safe direction. A tool that preserves timestamps while changing content is the unsafe direction and has no defence here.
When caching is skipped
A cache miss costs a compile; a wrong cache hit costs correctness. The driver therefore declines the cache entirely in every case where it cannot account for what the build did.
Only the executable, object and static-library backends are cached. `--backend llvm-ir` and `--backend shared-lib` recompile every time.

A program with any top-level `#comptime` is never stored, because that code can read files, run commands and write outputs that the manifest does not describe. This is why a build script recompiles on every invocation, and why a build script must not be made expensive to check.
`--show-generated` disables the cache for that run, so the generated `#insert` sources it reports are actually produced rather than skipped.
Setting the environment variable `GLOSSO_DISABLE_ARTIFACT_CACHE` to anything turns the cache off for the process.
A build that emitted nothing is not stored: a compile-time `exit`, or `set_build_options_dc(.do_output = false)`, both end the run before the store step.

A failure to write an entry is a warning and not an error: `glosso: warning: could not update artifact cache: <reason>`, after which the build finishes normally. Entries are never removed by the compiler; the cache directory grows until it is deleted by hand.
`--cache-dir` and `--print-cache-dir`

--print-cache-dir prints the resolved root and exits without reading source. --cache-dir overrides that root; a relative path is resolved against the working directory. The override moves generated sources, native C archives, and final-artifact entries together. For example, glosso --cache-dir build/cache --print-cache-dir selects a project cache.
With no override the root is chosen from the host convention, and the environment variable `GLOSSO_CACHE_DIR` overrides that choice without a flag. It too must hold an absolute path.

Every procedure body sees one implicit value named `context`. It takes no import, no parameter and no declaration: the compiler creates the type, creates one instance of it, and makes the name visible everywhere. Allocation, logging and random-number generation all read their policy out of that one value, which is how a caller redirects a library's behaviour without changing a single signature the library declares.
The type is built into the compiler rather than written in a `.glo` file, and its spelling carries the directive sigil to say so: it is `#Context`. The definition is fixed and has six fields.

Reading and writing `context`

`context` is an ordinary lvalue of type `#Context`. Its fields can be read, assigned, copied into a local and passed to a procedure that declares a `#Context` parameter. A bare assignment to a field is permanent: the context is one process-wide global, not a per-call record, so nothing restores it later.
`#push_context`

`#push_context expr body` installs `expr` as the whole context for the duration of `body` and restores the previous value on the way out, including through an early `return`. The restore is scheduled as a `defer`, so it is not skipped by any exit the block has.

Written without an expression, `#push_context body` installs the default context, the same value the process started with. That is the way to run a piece of code under known settings regardless of what an enclosing frame installed. Numeric formatting is selected explicitly with `Formatter` selectors such as `%x`; the former `context.print_style` field no longer exists.

The body may be a brace block or a single statement, so `#push_context saved print("%\n", context.user_index);` is legal and scopes to that one statement.
`#push_allocator`

`#push_allocator(expr);` replaces only `context.allocator`. It is a statement rather than a block form: it takes effect where it is written and is undone at the end of the enclosing block, again through a deferred restore that also runs on `return`.

`#no_context`

A procedure marked `#no_context` may not name `context` in its body. `#c_call` implies the same restriction, because a procedure entered from foreign code cannot assume the context global was ever initialised by Glosso startup.

error: cannot access 'context' in a #c_call / #no_context procedure
  --> ...\bare_fn.glo:2:21
  |
2 |     return n * 31 + context.user_index;
  |                     ^^^^^^^

The restriction is on the name, not on the machinery. A `#no_context` procedure may still call `print` or `alloc`, and those callees read the context as usual, because the context is a global rather than a hidden parameter. `#no_context` is also part of a procedure's overload key, and a `#fn_ptr` type accepts the directive after its return type.
Naming a context field type

`#Context` and its fields are always reachable. The types of those fields are not: they are declared in the `Context` module and stay hidden until a file imports it, so that a program which never spells one out does not have the supporting type names dropped into its global namespace. Naming one without the import reports both the cause and the fix.

  --> ...\field_type.glo:1:13
  |
1 | pool :: (a: Allocator) -> s64 {
  |             ^^^^^^^^^

The gate opens transitively: `#import "Io"` reaches `Context` through `Format`, so a file that prints can also name `Allocator`. Reading and writing `context.allocator` never needs the import; only spelling one of these names as a type does. `Context` written without the sigil is `error: the built-in Context type is written #Context`. This special type-name gate does not re-export the module's procedures: import `Context` directly to call `alloc`, `free`, or allocator helpers.

The compile-time VM has its own readable and writable `context`. Changing it does not initialize the native program's runtime context. VM-backed evaluation supports allocation and typed pointer access; raw heap blocks are limited to 4 MiB each. Arbitrary target foreign calls are still unavailable during compile-time execution. Compile-time evaluation is described in `#comptime`.

Glosso ships no allocation policy in the language. An allocator is a value: a procedure pointer and an opaque data pointer, declared in the `Context` module and stored in `context.allocator`. Every allocation the language performs on a program's behalf goes through that one record, which is what makes an arena, a pool or a tracking wrapper a drop-in replacement rather than a rewrite.

Allocator_Proc :: #fn_ptr(
    data: ?*mut void,
    mode: Allocator_Mode,
    size: ssize,
    alignment: ssize,
    old_memory: ?*mut void,
    old_size: ssize
) -> ?*mut void

Allocator :: struct { procedure: ?Allocator_Proc; data: ?*mut void; }

Four of the slots are optional, and each for a reason. A stateless allocator carries no `data`; `Alloc` and `Free_All` pass no `old_memory`; an unsatisfiable request yields no memory; and `procedure` itself is optional so that a zero-initialised `Allocator` is the "none installed" sentinel. Because `.None` is address zero, that sentinel is still the all-zero bit pattern.
Modes
One procedure serves every operation; `mode` selects which. The enum is closed.

An allocator may implement a subset and return `.None` for the rest; that is what the supplied ones do. `Resize` is not optional in practice, because a dynamic array grown by `array.push` and a `String_Builder` grown by `String_Builder.write_string` both issue it, and an allocator that answers `.None` there hands the caller no memory to write into.
Errors
`Allocator_Error` names the ways a request can fail. Its variants carry explicit values so that the enum is stable across versions, and `Allocator_Error.reason` turns one into a message.

`Allocator_Error` carries an `Error` instance, so a program that propagates one gets the reporting described in `Error`, `Termination`, and `main`. No entry point in the allocation API returns one today: an `Allocator_Proc` signals failure by returning `.None`, and so do `alloc` and `mem_alloc`.
The supplied allocators
The `Context` module supplies four allocators, each behind a constructor that builds the two-field record. All four are stateless and leave `data` empty.

Two layers sit on top of the vtable. `alloc` and `free` route through `context.allocator` and are the everyday pair; the `mem_*` family takes an explicit allocator, defaulting to `context.allocator` when the argument is omitted.

Writing an allocator

An allocator is one procedure with the `Allocator_Proc` shape plus a constructor that packages it. The procedure switches on `mode` and returns `.None` for anything it does not handle. Installing it with `#push_allocator` redirects every allocation in the block, including the ones made inside library code such as `format`.
1-2 after 1 request(s)

The standard library's convention for a routine that allocates is a trailing `allocator: Allocator = context.allocator` parameter, as in `clone`, `String_Builder.make_len_cap` and the `Container` constructors. A caller that wants a different allocator for one call passes it; a caller that wants it for a region uses `#push_allocator`.

`context.temp_allocator` is a growing bump arena. It hands out successive slices of one block, ignores `Free` entirely, and reclaims everything at once when the arena is rewound. It exists for values that are built, used and abandoned inside a bounded region: a formatted line, a path joined for one system call, a line of input.

The initial block is not heap memory. It is a static buffer compiled into the binary, sized by `--temp-allocator-size`, which defaults to 4 MiB, or to 64 KiB on a freestanding target. When a request does not fit, the arena mallocs an overflow block whose capacity is the larger of the request and the initial size, and links it onto the front; rewinding pops and releases those blocks back down to the static one.

`--temp-allocator-size <bytes>` and `--temp-allocator-size=<bytes>` both work. The value must be a positive byte count; anything else, including `0`, is rejected before compilation starts and the driver exits with status 2.

$ glosso --temp-allocator-size 0 report.glo
glosso: --temp-allocator-size must be a positive byte count

Whether each thread gets its own arena is a target decision. The buffer and the three globals that track it are emitted `thread_local` on some targets and shared by every thread on others, Windows among them. The context itself is never thread-local anywhere, so a thread that wants its own settings installs them with `#push_context`.
Frame boundaries

The arena is rewound by the compiler, not by the program. Lowering records the arena's high-water mark on entry to a body and restores it on the way out, so an ordinary block is already a temporary frame. Nothing has to be freed and nothing accumulates.

The marks are emitted only where temporary storage provably cannot leave with the result. A signature is treated as able to carry it out, and therefore gets no marks anywhere in its body, when either of the following holds.
The return type is a `string`, an `any`, a struct, a union, a pointer, a many-pointer, an array or a tuple.
Any parameter is a typed pointer, `*T` or `[*]T`.
A loop body in a procedure that satisfies neither reuses the same arena bytes on every iteration.

row-0 reuses the first block: 1
row-1 reuses the first block: 1
row-2 reuses the first block: 1

The contrast is visible in one program. `scalar` returns an `s64`, so its mark is restored and two consecutive calls hand back the same address. `carrier` takes a `*s64`, so no mark is taken and its two temporaries sit sixteen bytes apart.

scalar reuse 1
carrier delta 16

This is exactly why `tprint` can return arena memory at all. The return type is `string`, so no restore is emitted in `tprint` or in any caller whose own signature also carries storage out, and the result survives until the nearest enclosing frame that does take a mark closes.
A temporary value assigned out of an inner block is stale the moment the block ends. The compiler does not diagnose it; the bytes are handed to the next request that asks for them.

`reset_temporary_storage`

`reset_temporary_storage()` calls `context.temp_allocator.free_all()`, which sends `Free_All` to the arena: overflow blocks are released and the mark returns to the start of the static block. It is the explicit spelling of what the compiler already does at a frame boundary.
What comes from temporary storage
A value backed by the arena does not need individual release and must not be passed to `free` or `string.free`. These are the standard-library entry points that produce one.

blocks.text: `print` and `writef` build their output with `tprint`, and `File.write_int` formats through the arena as well, so a procedure that prints is already using temporary storage even if it never names it. `format` is the owning counterpart: it allocates from `context.allocator` and its result is released with `string.free`.

A temporary value that has to outlive its frame is copied, not retained. `text.clone()` and `format("%", value)` both produce an owned string from `context.allocator`; writing `kept = (tprint(...)).clone()` inside the inner block above makes the earlier example print `kept=inner-1`. Built-in Strings covers the string representation itself.

Every allocation it serves gets a 48-byte header holding the size, the source trace of the request and links into a live list, plus an eight-byte guard written past the end of the user bytes. That bookkeeping is what lets the allocator name the line a leaked block came from, and it is why diagnostic mode must be requested explicitly.

A program can still install `debug_allocator()` explicitly. That routes allocations and releases through the wrapper, but the compiler-wide `GLOSSO_DEBUG_ALLOCATOR` mode additionally instruments pointer uses and requests the automatic report on normal exit, `exit`, failed `#assert`, and `process_abort`.

$ GLOSSO_DEBUG_ALLOCATOR=1 glosso -O1 --run trace.glo
done
glosso debug allocator: leaked 1 allocation(s), 64 byte(s)
  leak: 64 byte(s)
    allocated at:
      ...\trace.glo:5:13

$ glosso -O0 --run trace.glo
done

The report gives one `leak:` entry per block still live at exit, with the byte count and the trace of the call that produced it. A dynamic array is reported at its `array.push`, because that is the call that asked the allocator for storage.
Double free
A second `free` of a block the allocator already reclaimed is reported with all three positions: where the block came from, where it was first released, and where the second release happened.
Use after free

When debug-allocator mode is enabled, the backend inserts a check before every load and store through a pointer at every optimization level. If the address falls inside a block on the freed list, the read or write is reported and then allowed to proceed.
Invalid free and invalid realloc
A pointer the debug allocator never handed out, and that is not on its freed list either, is an invalid free. Only the release site can be named, because there is no header to read a history from.

The same test on the resize path is `invalid realloc`. Its output also shows what a trace is: not one position but the chain of call sites that reached the allocator, innermost first. The single-line traces above are single-line only because `alloc` and `free` lower directly at the point of use.
The tail guard

Eight bytes of `0xa5` are written past the end of every allocation and checked on `Free` and again when the block is walked for the leak report. A write that runs off the end of the requested size damages the guard and is counted.

$ GLOSSO_DEBUG_ALLOCATOR=1 glosso -O1 --run overrun.glo
continued
glosso debug allocator: 1 allocator error(s)

A damaged guard has no message of its own; it raises the error count and nothing else. An error total with no fault report above it is therefore an overrun, and the block that carried it is found by narrowing the writes rather than by reading the output.
When the report runs

The report is emitted at most once per process, guarded by a flag the report itself sets. It runs on a normal return from `main`, and also before `exit`, before a failed `#assert` aborts and before an explicit process abort, so a program that stops deliberately still says what it was holding. It does not run on the safety-check path: a bounds or overflow failure at `-O0` prints its runtime-check category and then terminates without running the allocator report, as Runtime Safety Checks and Panics describes.

`debug_allocator_report_leaks()` forces it early. Because of the once-only flag, forcing it means nothing allocated afterwards is ever reported. The magic behind it, `__debug_report_leaks`, sits in a private section of the `Context` module and naming it directly is `error: unknown function __debug_report_leaks`. The same report is what `context.allocator.free_all()` triggers while the debug allocator is installed, because `Free_All` is the mode it maps to.

$ GLOSSO_DEBUG_ALLOCATOR=1 glosso -O1 --run early.glo
glosso debug allocator: leaked 1 allocation(s), 64 byte(s)
  leak: 64 byte(s)
    allocated at:
      ...\early.glo:5:14
done

The debug allocator sees only what passes through it. Storage from `context.temp_allocator` is never tracked, because the arena serves itself out of a static buffer, and neither is memory taken from a foreign `malloc` or from an allocator installed with `#push_allocator`.

Glosso destroys managed values automatically when their lifetime ends. A type is managed when it implements Drop or contains managed fields. Dynamic arrays and standard containers are owners; primitive strings, pointers, and slices are views.
The Drop contract

The hook releases the value's own resource. The compiler separately destroys its remaining owned fields, including when the hook returns an error. Ordinary code cannot call Drop.drop or take its address. Use a nested scope to end ownership earlier.
Automatic destruction and explicit defer actions share reverse scope order. Cleanup runs on normal exits, return, and error propagation. Process termination and runtime traps do not unwind scopes.
Use Error :: #Never for infallible cleanup. A fallible hook uses its own error type and requires a compatible result boundary or a local #on_drop_error handler.

Binding a new variable, passing a parameter, or returning a managed value by value transfers ownership. The source moves into its destination; the compiler rejects later use of the source, including uses on control-flow paths where it may already have moved.

Use a read-only *T or writable *mut T parameter to operate on an existing owner while leaving ownership with the caller. Receiver methods may automatically take the address of an addressable value. Read-only pointers cannot be passed to writable receiver methods.

A struct, tuple, option, result, or fixed array containing a managed value also needs destruction. Moving the whole aggregate transfers its managed contents. Moving an individual managed field or indexed element directly is rejected; use a typed transfer operation or move the whole owner.

Iterate with for *item: values to visit managed elements through pointers. An ordinary for item: values copies each element and cannot copy a managed owner. Ending a pointer's scope does not destroy its pointee.

Move checking tracks managed values separately from temporal memory analysis. Borrow diagnostics track views through calls, invalidation, escapes, and automatic destruction. They are warnings by default; use --borrow-check=error to reject findings. Keep backing storage valid even when analysis is disabled or cannot prove an origin.
Transfers through existing storage

Import Memory/Ownership or Memory for value_take(slot), value_replace(slot, replacement), and array_pop_last(array_pointer). value_take returns the old owner and leaves its ordinary default in the slot. value_replace moves in the replacement and returns the previous owner without destroying it. array_pop_last moves the last live element out and decreases count; an empty array traps. End retained views before transferring their storage.

Direct assignment into existing managed storage is rejected. These typed operations keep a valid value in that storage and make ownership transfer explicit. The __value_move and __value_init intrinsics are internal tools for manually tracked raw slots; callers must maintain their lifecycle.

A [..]T dynamic array owns both its backing allocation and its live elements. push() and append() move managed arguments into the array. Scope exit destroys the live elements and releases the buffer; a defer array.free() is unnecessary for ordinary ownership.

reserve(capacity) requests total capacity without changing count. reset() retains storage and sets count to zero; it is available only for elements without automatic destruction. free() and deinit() destroy live elements and release storage, leaving a valid empty array. They require infallible element cleanup; use take() with an error handler or result boundary for fallible elements.

Dynamic arrays allocate and release through context.allocator. Keep the allocator used during growth installed until destruction. Their three-word descriptor does not capture an allocator. Standard container structs and String_Builder retain the allocator supplied to their constructor.
Standard containers

Deque, LinkedList, HashMap, HashSet, BTreeMap, BTreeSet, and BinaryHeap are move-only owners. Their Drop instances release elements and storage automatically. clear() destroys elements and may retain capacity; deinit() also releases storage and leaves an empty owner. Removal operations that return an element transfer it to the caller.

These containers require infallible element destruction: Drop_Error(T) == #Never, for both key and value in maps. Use clone_with for managed elements that need an explicit cloning callback. Managed keys need the borrowed _by hashing and comparison operations so comparisons do not consume them.

A pointer or view returned by a container borrows its storage. Structural mutation may invalidate it. A LinkedList element pointer remains stable until its node is removed. Import each Container component explicitly; Container is not an umbrella module.

A *T pointer, []T slice, or primitive string borrows storage without keeping its owner alive. Temporal memory analysis follows the storage origin and diagnoses uses after release, invalidation, or scope exit. This analysis is enabled as warnings by default and can be made an error with --borrow-check=error. It does not insert lifetime tokens or extend storage lifetime.
Read-only and writable access

Writable pointers and slices can be used through read-only forms. The reverse implicit conversion is rejected. volatile marks accesses that must be emitted; *volatile T remains read-only and *mut volatile T permits stores.
Invalidation

Growing a dynamic array or builder may move its allocation. Clearing, freeing, replacing, transferring, or destroying storage can also invalidate retained views. A slice stores its original count; it does not follow later changes to an owner's descriptor.

String_Builder.to_string(), to_bytes(), and to_cstring() borrow the builder. clone(allocator) copies text into an independent allocation. into_string() and into_bytes() transfer the allocation; retain the allocator needed to free the transferred raw result. Import Strings/Memory for string.free(). For arena-backed text, construct the builder with context.temp_allocator and consume it with into_temporary_string(). Alternatively, an owned string allocated from that arena can use string.into_temporary() to hand its release obligation to the arena. Never use this on heap storage. The view expires when the arena is reset or restored.

Returning a builder's to_string() view after that local builder is destroyed creates a dangling view. The current analyzer does not diagnose every builder-backed escape, even in error mode. Return a cloned string or transferred allocation instead. Literal storage lasts for the program's lifetime and must not be freed.

noalias marks unique access during a call. Memory analysis checks conflicting aliases and inferred borrow extents; it is independent of pointer mutability. Runtime bounds checks do not verify aliasing.
Leading memory contracts

Write #memory { ... } immediately before a function declaration. The block belongs to that declaration, and its operands resolve in the following signature: parameters, named results, and #self are available; body locals are not. It can precede foreign and #magic declarations, typeclass and instance methods, and named #fn_ptr types. Visibility prefixes may appear before or after the contract.

A contract on a function with a body is checked against its implementation. A bodyless declaration supplies an external contract. Private functions can omit a contract and use inference. An explicitly written #memory {} asserts an empty contract; unknown(...) records uncertainty instead of silently claiming no effects. Ordinary function directives, such as #inline and #foreign, keep their position after the signature.

A postfix call assertion, call(value) #memory { reads(value), noescape(value) };, supplies trusted effects at that call. For an owned foreign handle, define a local wrapper with a Drop instance. Release that handle in the hook and move the wrapper when transferring ownership. Pass pointers to helpers that should leave ownership with the caller.

This wrapper uses the current context allocator for both acquisition and release. A production wrapper can store its allocator and call memory.mem_free(allocator), or call a foreign library's own release function.

Use defer for a raw resource without a Drop instance. Use #try defer only when cleanup returns a Try carrier and its failure should propagate through the surrounding boundary. Do not schedule a second destructive release for a resource already managed by Drop.

This schematic foreign API gives acquire() a release obligation that release(pointer) discharges. The actual foreign implementation must satisfy those contracts. Wrapping such a handle in a Drop owner makes cleanup automatic; a contract alone does not generate a release call.

Import Memory/ManuallyDrop or Memory to use ManuallyDrop(T). The wrapper has T's size, alignment, and valid values; it adds no allocation or hidden live flag. Wrapping a value transfers ownership and suppresses automatic destruction of the contained value and its fields.

get() returns *T and get_mut() returns *mut T without transferring ownership. into_inner() consumes the whole wrapper and restores automatic destruction. take() extracts through a mutable pointer, including from an enclosing owner's field. drop() runs the full destructor in place and returns Drop_Error(T)!void.

After take() or drop(), the slot must not be used again, including when destruction reports an error. An enclosing Drop hook must account for consumed slots with its own lifecycle state. Use into_inner() when the whole wrapper can be moved.

ManuallyDrop does not make uninitialized storage valid and cannot copy an owner. Leaving an occupied wrapper at scope exit intentionally suppresses cleanup; release or transfer it when that is the intended lifecycle.

A Drop hook returns Error!void. With Error :: #Never, cleanup cannot fail and needs no fallible enclosing function. With a real error type, implicit cleanup propagates as if the generated call used ?. The surrounding result type must accept that error or provide the required Propagate conversion.
Handling a cleanup error locally

Register #on_drop_error(owner, error) immediately after the owning declaration. Its body runs only if implicit cleanup fails. It handles that local owner's cleanup failure without requiring main to return a compatible error carrier.

Without a handler, a cleanup error can replace a successful return with an error. The compiler still destroys remaining owned fields when a hook fails. Dynamic arrays can contain fallible elements; container structs currently require infallible element destruction.
Explicit ManuallyDrop.drop() returns its error to the caller directly. Handle that result or propagate it with ?. The wrapper's slot remains consumed even when cleanup fails.

blocks.text: The old `private_section`, `private_sections`, and `siblings` forms have been removed and report a migration diagnostic. Declarations are private to their source file by default. Use `#public` for an exported API or `#public(unit)` for sharing within an ownership unit; a visibility prefix may apply to one declaration or a braced group. The four feature gates above control static semantics and memory analysis independently of visibility.
Form and placement

A feature directive is a top-level section directive, not a statement. It takes effect at the point it appears and stays in effect until the matching `#disable` or the end of the file. It cannot appear inside a body.

error: unexpected directive 'enable'
  --> ...\f1.glo:6:5
  |
6 |     #enable(allow_union_unwrap);
  |     ^^^^^^^

The reason is that a gate is a property of a declaration, not of a region of statements. The parser stamps the currently-open set onto every declaration it parses, and the checker reads the stamp back when it checks that declaration. A gate opened inside a body would have nothing to attach to, and would have to mean something different from a gate opened outside one.

error: tagged-union payload '.Code' may only be bound by a pattern match
   --> ...\f2.glo:11:39
   |
11 | after :: (t: Token) -> s64 { return t.Code; }
   |                                       ^^^^
note: match on the union and use that arm's payload capture, or enable #enable(allow_union_unwrap) for unsafe access

`inside` compiles and `after` does not, and the split is decided at the declaration, not at the call. Deleting `after` leaves a program in which an ungated `main` calls the gated `inside` and prints `3`. A gate is not contagious in either direction.
The reach of a gate

Every position that carries an expression the checker evaluates is a declaration in this sense, so a gate reaches further than function bodies. It is installed for function bodies, global initialisers, constant initialisers, struct field defaults, and top-level `#comptime` blocks.

This matters because the payload rule is now a default error rather than a relaxation of a permissive default: a gate that could not reach an initialiser would leave that position with no escape hatch at all.

The constant and the gated global are accepted; only `ungated_global` is rejected, with the payload-access error pointing at line 15. Removing that line leaves a program that prints `7 7`. The same holds for a top-level `#comptime` block: gated, it runs and prints; after `#disable`, an identical block is an error.
What each gate actually relaxes

`lossy_numerics` is narrower than its name suggests. The gate is consulted at exactly one place in the checker, inside the branch that compares an integer type against an integer type. Narrowing and sign reinterpretation become implicit; float conversions do not, in either direction and at any width.

Under the same gate, `narrow: f32 = wide;` with `wide: f64` is `error: got f64, expected f32`, and the widening direction is rejected the same way. There are no implicit float conversions in Glosso, gate or no gate; the chapter on conversions gives the full rule and `cast` gives the explicit spelling.

`pointer_punning` relaxes the pointee check and the distinction between a single pointer and a many-pointer. The two assignments below are rejected without it: `error: got *s64, expected [*]s64` and `error: got *s64, expected *u8`. With it, both are accepted and the program prints `65 65`.

What it does not relax is read-only access. The gate is tested inside the branch that has already established the qualifier direction is legal, so adding writable access remains an error under the gate: `writable: *s64 = readonly;` with `readonly: *s64` reports `error: got *s64, expected *s64`.
The gate that tightens
The checks a gate keeps

`allow_union_unwrap` removes a compile-time rule and replaces it with a runtime one; it does not remove the check. A gated payload read compiles to a tag comparison at `-O0` and `-O1`, and reading the wrong variant aborts with the site named.

$ glosso -O1 -o f6.exe f6.glo && ./f6.exe
5
...\f6.glo:14:30: union access: expected .Ok, but the value holds one of .Ok | .Err
$ echo $?
134

$ glosso -O2 -o f6.exe f6.glo && ./f6.exe
5
9

The size modes -Os, -Oz, and -Ozz produce runnable artifacts. They combine LLVM optimization with optsize/minsize attributes and target-specific linker size policies. Runtime checks are disabled in these modes; use -O0 or -O1 for checked builds. -Ozz also strips symbols and metadata.

Glosso compiles a small family of safety checks into the generated code. Each one guards an operation whose failure would otherwise corrupt memory quietly, and each one, when it fails, stops the process on the spot. They are not exceptions: nothing catches them, no `defer` runs. Each check writes a short failure category, and the way the target terminates determines its exit status.

The size modes -Os, -Oz, and -Ozz produce runnable artifacts. They combine LLVM optimization with optsize/minsize attributes and target-specific linker size policies. Runtime checks are disabled in these modes; use -O0 or -O1 for checked builds. -Ozz also strips symbols and metadata.

The flags themselves are covered in the chapter on backends, artifacts, and optimization levels. The debug allocator is selected independently with `GLOSSO_DEBUG_ALLOCATOR` and has its own chapter. This chapter is about what the checks test and what happens when one of them fires.
The check family
There are exactly six checks. They are emitted by the backend, not by a library, so no import turns them on and no call disables an individual one.

rows: overflow in `+`, `-`, `*`, prefix `-`, and division; a zero divisor for `/`, `//`, `%`
indexing a value that carries a count
`<path>:<line>:<column>: runtime check failed: array.bounds` when the site is known; otherwise the category alone
`a[start..end]` on a value that carries a count
`cast(*T)`, `cast([*]T)` and `cast(#fn_ptr)` of an integer or enum
for example, `cast to *s64 of an address that is zero`
names the wanted variant and the ones the type has

blocks.text: All six write a line to stderr before terminating. Array bounds and union-tag failures include the source site when available; the arithmetic and slice labels identify the failed operation but carry no source position. Null-address and formatting-base failures use explanatory prose.
Integer overflow

Addition, subtraction and multiplication on an integer or enum operand lower to the LLVM checked-arithmetic intrinsics, and prefix negation lowers to a checked subtraction from zero. Update assignment goes through the same operators and is checked with them. Integer `/`, `//` and `%` also check a zero divisor, and signed division checks `T.MIN / -1`; `T.MIN % -1` is the defined value zero. The shifts and every floating-point operation are outside the check family. A float-to-integer cast truncates toward zero, saturates out-of-range values, and maps NaN to zero at every optimization level; it does not become unchecked merely because the build uses `-O2`.

before
runtime check failed: arithmetic.overflow

That is the whole output at `-O1`: the second `print` never runs and on Windows the process exits with status 134. WASI uses 125; targets that call `abort()` expose that platform's abort status. At `-O2` the check is not emitted, the addition wraps, and the same program prints `sum = -2147483648` followed by `survived` and exits 0.
The wrapping and saturating operators are different operators, not a mode, and they are never checked at any level. `+%`, `-%`, `*%` and prefix `-%` wrap; `+|`, `-|` and `*|` clamp.

wrapping    = -2147483648
saturating  = 2147483647
negate wrap = -2147483648
survived
Array bounds

An index is checked whenever a count travels with the value being indexed: a fixed array `[N]T`, a view `[]T`, a dynamic array `[..]T`, a pointer to a fixed array, and a `string` or `string16`. The comparison is unsigned, so a negative index fails the same test as one past the end. A compile-time known invalid index is rejected during checking, including an index computed by a folded helper call.

in range: 20
<path>:<line>:<column>: runtime check failed: array.bounds

The size modes -Os, -Oz, and -Ozz produce runnable artifacts. They combine LLVM optimization with optsize/minsize attributes and target-specific linker size policies. Runtime checks are disabled in these modes; use -O0 or -O1 for checked builds. -Ozz also strips symbols and metadata.

A many-pointer `[*]T` carries no count, so indexing one is never checked at any level. Reading far past the end of the storage it points at is a plain hardware fault: on Windows the process ends with status `0xc0000005`.

`cstring` and `cstring16` are outside the family. They are terminated rather than counted, so they carry no bound in their representation. Indexing does not scan for a terminator to check the index; `text[5]` on a three-byte `cstring` reads past the end and the program survives.
The checks that print

Casting an integer or enum to `*T`, `[*]T` or `#fn_ptr` asserts that the address is not zero, because those three types exclude zero so that `?*T`, `?[*]T` and `?#fn_ptr` can use it as the `.None` niche. A zero the checker can fold never reaches run time: `cast(*s64) 0` is `error: cast to *s64 of an address that is zero at compile time`. A zero that only appears at run time reaches the check, which writes `cast to *s64 of an address that is zero` and aborts. The type in both messages is the destination type as the compiler prints it.

The union check exists only because of the escape hatch. A tagged union normally yields its payload through a pattern match; under `#enable(allow_union_unwrap)` a direct payload read is allowed and the backend inserts a tag comparison in its place.

good = 7
...\unwrap.glo:13:28: union access: expected .Ok, but the value holds one of .Ok | .Err

The report is a fixed string built when the access is lowered, which is why it carries a source position. The array-bounds check now does the same; the other checks report a category without a site. At `-O2` the check disappears and the program reads the wrong payload silently: the same build prints `bad = 7` and exits 0. The gate itself is described in the chapter on feature gates.
`#assert` is not one of them

`#assert` is a separate mechanism and survives every working optimization level. A condition the checker can decide is decided at compile time and emits no code at all; a condition it cannot decide becomes a branch that stays in the program.

100/4 = 25
...\guard.glo:4:5: assertion failed: n must not be zero

That output is identical at `-O1` and `-O3`; on Windows the status is 134 at both levels. Without a message the line ends after `assertion failed`. When the condition folds to false the assertion becomes a compile error instead: `#assert 1 > 2, "arithmetic is broken";` is `error: assertion failed: arithmetic is broken`, framed at the `#assert` token. The directive's other uses are covered in the chapter on `#assert` and `#compile_error`.
What nothing checks

Optimized integer division. At `-O2` and `-O3` the zero-divisor and division-overflow guards are omitted with the other runtime checks, so a bad operation reaches target/LLVM behavior. In a checked build both fail through Glosso's checked-failure path. `T.MIN % -1` remains zero at every level because that remainder is representable.

Non-literal shift counts at or beyond the operand width have a defined result on every backend. Left and logical-right shifts produce zero; an arithmetic-right shift produces the sign (`0` or `-1`). A literal overshift is rejected earlier because the checker can see it directly.

Allocator faults. Leaks, double frees and use after free are found by the debug allocator when `GLOSSO_DEBUG_ALLOCATOR` is nonzero. It reports and keeps running rather than aborting. The compile-time memory analysis covers a related static set; both have their own chapters.
How a failing check ends the process

Every check funnels into one termination sequence: write its report line, then take the target's abort path. The debug allocator's report is not part of it, which is why a build that fails a check says nothing about what it was holding even when the debug allocator is enabled; `#assert` and `process_abort` ask an enabled debug allocator to report first. Windows and Linux x86-64 spell out 134, WASI deliberately uses 125, and the remaining targets call the platform `abort()`.

134 is `128 + 6`, the status a POSIX shell reports for a process killed by `SIGABRT`. Picking that number keeps a Glosso panic indistinguishable from a C `abort()` in a build script. Windows spells that value out explicitly. WASI reserves statuses above 125, so its explicit path uses 125 rather than turning the failure into an indistinguishable guest trap.

`process_abort()` from `Process` uses the same target-dependent sequence. `exit(status)` does not: it takes the ordinary exit path and the status reaches the shell unchanged. Under `--run` the compiler prints the target's status — for example, `glosso: program exited with status exit code: 134` on Windows — and returns 1 of its own; the program's status is not propagated, which is covered in the chapter on environment, toolchain, and exit codes.

Two driver flags turn on LLVM's sanitizers: `--memory-sanitizer` and `--thread-sanitizer`. Each one adds a function attribute to every function with a body, runs the matching instrumentation pass over the module, and routes the final link through the Clang driver instead of the raw LLD plan so that the sanitizer runtime is pulled in.
They are mutually exclusive, and the second one is an error rather than a replacement for the first. The message names the mode already in effect, so the order on the command line is visible in it.

$ glosso --memory-sanitizer --thread-sanitizer race.glo
glosso: choose only one sanitizer mode (already using --memory-sanitizer, got --thread-sanitizer)
$ glosso --thread-sanitizer --memory-sanitizer race.glo
glosso: choose only one sanitizer mode (already using --thread-sanitizer, got --memory-sanitizer)
Both exit 2, the driver's status for a rejected command line.
What each flag selects

The flag names describe the class of bug, not the LLVM sanitizer, and the mapping is target-dependent. On x86-64 Windows there is no MemorySanitizer implementation, so `--memory-sanitizer` selects AddressSanitizer there rather than being refused.

The Windows case also disables ASan's ODR indicator globally, because the textual pass syntax cannot pass that constructor argument, and it filters the explicit C-runtime libraries out of the link so the sanitizer's own choice wins.
The supported-target matrix
Support is decided by substring tests on the LLVM triple, before any linking is attempted. An unsupported target is a hard backend error, not a warning and not a silent no-op.

rows: any triple containing `-linux-`, plus x86-64 Windows

blocks.text:
$ glosso --memory-sanitizer --target wasm32-wasi -o m.wasm race.glo
glosso: compile race.glo (target=wasm32-unknown-wasi)
glosso: link m.wasm (target=wasm32-unknown-wasi, -O1)
error: LLVM memory sanitizer is not supported for target 'wasm32-unknown-wasi'

`--thread-sanitizer` on the same target reports `error: LLVM thread sanitizer is not supported for target 'wasm32-unknown-wasi'`, and either flag aimed at `x86_64-freestanding` reports the same sentence with `'x86_64-unknown-none-elf'`. Because the check lives in the backend it fires for every backend, including `--backend object` and `--backend llvm-ir`, where nothing is linked at all. The linker also refuses sanitizers for wasm and for freestanding ELF, but the backend rejects those targets first, so those linker messages are unreachable from the command line.
What each one finds

AddressSanitizer, which is what `--memory-sanitizer` means on Windows, finds out-of-bounds accesses to heap, stack and global storage, use after free, double free, and, because the pass is configured with `use-after-scope`, reads of a stack slot after its scope has ended.

MemorySanitizer, which is what `--memory-sanitizer` means on Linux, finds reads of uninitialized memory. It tracks a shadow bit per byte and reports at the point where an uninitialized value changes control flow or leaves the program.

ThreadSanitizer finds data races between threads, along with a small set of related faults such as unlocking a mutex owned by another thread. It needs the program to actually execute the interleaving, so it reports what a run did, not what a run could do.
Practical caveats

A sanitized build does not use the bundled LLD plan. It shells out to `clang`, found through the usual override chain, and hands it `-fsanitize=address`, `-fsanitize=memory` or `-fsanitize=thread`. Anything that Clang installation refuses, the build refuses.

On Windows the driver tries to copy `clang_rt.asan_dynamic-x86_64.dll` next to the output, looking under `%USERPROFILE%/.local` for an LLVM build tree and then along `PATH`. If it finds none, the link still succeeds and the failure moves to run time: the loader cannot resolve the runtime and the process dies before `main` with `0xC0000135`, `STATUS_DLL_NOT_FOUND`.

> glosso --memory-sanitizer -o race.exe race.glo
glosso: compile race.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
glosso: link race.exe (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
glosso: done race.exe  (backend=llvm, target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
> .\race.exe
> $LASTEXITCODE
-1073741515
`--thread-sanitizer` is accepted by the target matrix on x86-64 Windows but rejected by the Clang driver, so it fails at the link step with the C compiler's own wording.

> glosso --thread-sanitizer -o race.exe race.glo
glosso: compile race.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
glosso: link race.exe (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
error: clang: error: unsupported option '-fsanitize=thread' for target 'x86_64-pc-windows-msvc'

The target matrix and what the platform toolchain actually supports are two separate gates. Passing the first proves only that the compiler will instrument the module; the link is where a missing runtime shows up.

The instrumentation is applied during code generation, so it is present in every artifact and not only in linked executables. A sanitized `--backend llvm-ir` run emits a module carrying `sanitize_address` on each function and the `__asan_` globals the pass introduces, and a sanitized `--backend object` or `--backend static-lib` build produces an instrumented object that some other link step has to supply the runtime for.

The selected sanitizer is part of the native artifact cache's identity string, so a sanitized build and a plain build of the same source never restore each other. Sanitizers are also orthogonal to `-O`: they neither enable nor suppress the `-O0` and `-O1` runtime checks, and combining `-O1` with a sanitizer keeps both.

The compiler reads a fixed set of environment variables. None of them changes the language; they change where the compiler looks for the standard library, its resources and its tools, how much it reports about itself, and which caches it is allowed to use. Wherever a command-line option covers the same ground, the option wins.
Variables that change behaviour
These are read by the driver itself and affect every build.

any value disables the final-artifact cache

the first replaces the default LLVM pass pipeline (`none` disables it); the second enables LLVM module verification when present with a value other than `0`
