blocks.text: The two timing switches are independent and can be set together. The phase names are the compiler's own pipeline stages, and the LLVM line reports the pipeline string in force, which is what makes `GLOSSO_LLVM_OBJECT_PIPELINE` observable. A `GLOSSO_JIT_DUMP` directory must already exist; a failed write is reported as `glosso: could not dump <path>: <error>` and does not stop the build.

$ GLOSSO_TIMINGS=1 GLOSSO_LLVM_TIMING=1 glosso --backend object -o status.obj status.glo
glosso: compile status.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
glosso: timing prepare 227.548 ms
glosso: timing check 616.655 ms
glosso: timing lower 54.163 ms
glosso: llvm object passes=0.025s emit=0.062s pipeline=function(mem2reg,instcombine<no-verify-fixpoint>,early-cse,simplifycfg,adce)
glosso: wrote status.obj  (backend=object, target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
glosso: timing consume 102.922 ms
A warm artifact cache hides both switches, because a restored build never reaches the phases they measure. Set `GLOSSO_DISABLE_ARTIFACT_CACHE=1` alongside them when the numbers matter.
`GLOSSO_NO_PRUNE` is a debugging escape hatch, not a switch with a visible effect: the pruned and unpruned modules are byte-identical for the same program.

`NO_COLOR` is honoured for any value, including the empty string, and it is checked before `--color`, so `--color always` cannot override it. The reverse is not true: `--color never` is honoured regardless of `NO_COLOR`.
Finding the standard library

`--std <dir>` settles the question outright. The directory must contain either `Prelude.glo` or a `Prelude/` subdirectory, and the path is canonicalized. An empty value is `glosso: --std needs a non-empty directory` and a directory without a prelude is `glosso: --std directory must contain Prelude.glo or Prelude/`; both exit 2, because they are rejected while the command line is parsed.
Without `--std` the compiler walks a candidate list and takes the first entry that is a directory holding a prelude. Duplicates are skipped, so the same directory reached two ways is tried once.

Step 3 is why a compiler at `<repo>/build/bin/glosso.exe` finds `<repo>/std` from any working directory: `build/bin` walks up to `build` and then to `<repo>`. `GLOSSO_COMPILER_EXE` replaces the executable path used for that walk, but two further fallbacks derived from the real executable run afterwards, so pointing it somewhere empty does not make the standard library disappear. When nothing matches the compiler stops with `glosso: could not find the project-local or installed Glosso standard library` and exits 1.
Resource, library and toolchain roots

Resources are the non-Glosso material a build may need: the bundled musl sources, the mingw-w64 import libraries, the Clang resource directory, and the third-party C sources behind `Lua`. They are looked up under a list of roots rather than a single prefix.

rows: the project or installed resource root; validated, and a value that is neither is an error
the library root searched as `lib/` and `lib/glosso/`
the musl source tree and a prebuilt musl runtime bundle
the Clang resource directory holding the compiler builtins
`-L` flags harvested from a Nix environment
the LLVM install root searched for tools

blocks.text: The roots are tried in this order: `GLOSSO_RESOURCE_DIR`, `GLOSSO_LIB_DIR`, the parent of `GLOSSO_MUSL_SOURCE_DIR`, the current directory, the compiler's directory, and that directory's parent and grandparent. Under each root a named resource is looked for directly, then under `thirdparty/`, then `lib/`, then `share/glosso/`. A root counts as a project root when it holds either a development tree (`src/lib.rs` and `data/UnicodeData.txt`) or an installed tree (a `lib/` directory next to a `std/` with a prelude).

Library lookup has one development-only candidate ahead of those general roots. When the effective compiler executable (including a `GLOSSO_COMPILER_EXE` override) belongs to a Glosso checkout, that checkout's `build/lib` is searched for staged Clang headers, compiler-rt archives, and other target libraries. The candidate is derived from the compiler path, not the current directory: an installed compiler launched inside an unrelated checkout will not borrow that checkout's possibly stale `build/lib`.
Choosing the LLVM tools

Every external tool is resolved the same way. The tool's own environment names are consulted in order and the first non-empty one wins outright. Failing that, an LLVM root is derived from `GLOSSO_LLVM_ROOT`, then `LLVM_ROOT`, then `$HOME/.local/llvm-project` or its `%USERPROFILE%` equivalent, and the tool is looked for at `<root>/bin/`, at `<root>/<host-bundle>/bin/`, and finally under the `bin/` of each child directory in name order. If none of that finds it, the bare name is used and `PATH` decides.

rows: `GLOSSO_CLANG`, `CLANG`, `CC`, then `cl`, `clang-cl` and `cc`; `#bindgen` itself has no override and runs the in-process Clang

blocks.text: `rust-lld` is the one entry with its own search. When neither variable names an existing file, the compiler looks under `$RUSTUP_HOME` (or `%USERPROFILE%/.rustup`), preferring `$RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN` if it is set. It is reached only by a compiler built without the embedded LLD; an ordinary build links COFF in process, which is why linker diagnostics on Windows are prefixed `lld-link:`.
The compiler's exit codes

The driver uses three statuses of its own, and one borrowed. 2 means the command line was rejected and nothing was compiled; 1 means the compilation or the link failed; 0 means the requested work was done. The borrowed one is compile-time `exit`.

rows: a compile, type, memory-contract or link error
`--run` on a non-host target, or where the built program exits nonzero
an unknown option, or a bad value for one

blocks.text: The program's exit code

A built program's status is its own and is not related to the compiler's. It comes from what `main` returns, through the `Termination` protocol described in the chapter on `Error`, `Termination`, and `main`: an integer result is narrowed to `s32` and used directly, a `void` result is 0, and `exit(status)` leaves immediately with the value given.

`--run` does not pass that status on. It prints what the program exited with and then returns 1 for any nonzero value, so `--run` cannot be used to observe an exact exit code. Build the executable and run it to see one.

$ glosso --run status.glo
glosso: compile status.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
glosso: link status.exe (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
glosso: done status.exe  (backend=llvm, target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
finishing
glosso: program exited with status exit code: 5
Compile-time `exit` is the one path by which an arbitrary status reaches the shell from the compiler. A top-level `#comptime` that calls it stops the build at that point, and no artifact is written.

$ glosso --run ctexit.glo
glosso: compile ctexit.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
[comptime] stopping the build
There is no `link` line and no `ctexit.exe`, and the compiler's own exit status is 7.

Driver messages go to stderr, prefixed `glosso: `. Program output and the output of compile-time execution go to stdout. Redirecting one stream therefore separates the build log from what the program produced, which is what makes a `#comptime` build script usable in a pipeline.
Memory analysis options

--borrow-check=warning is the default. Use --borrow-check=error to reject temporal memory findings, --borrow-check=off to disable body analysis, and --borrow-check-std to include standard-library bodies. --memory-signatures prints inferred body contracts, --memory-axioms prints external contracts, and --memory-report prints the module inventory. #enable(memory_strict); requires written contracts at exported and external memory boundaries. See Memory Contracts and Storage Lifetimes for the effect vocabulary.

Glosso calls C directly. There is no wrapper layer, no generated shim, and no marshalling step: a `#foreign` declaration gives a Glosso signature to a symbol that already exists in a native library, and the call site lowers to an ordinary call in the target's C ABI.

Two declarations are involved. A `#library` declaration names the native artifact the symbols live in, and each `#foreign` function declaration binds one symbol. The library declaration is a compile-time constant like any other, so it is named, scoped, and importable in the usual way. Match the target's C types exactly: `strlen` returns `size_t`, so its Glosso result is `usize`, not a fixed `u64` on 32-bit targets.

strlen = 6
printed by C puts
Declaring a library

A `#library` declaration is `<Name> :: #library[,<kind>] "<file>";`. The string is the library file as the linker should see it, not a Glosso module path. Exactly one link-kind modifier is allowed and the default is `static`.

libc     :: #library "c";                  // static, the default
user32   :: #library,system "user32.lib";  // provided by the platform
kernel32 :: #library,dyn "kernel32.dll";   // resolved at run time

`static` and `system` currently reach the linker through the same path: `#library "yyyprobe"` and `#library,system "yyyprobe"` both fail with `error: lld-link: error: could not open 'yyyprobe.lib'`. The distinction records intent, that a `system` library is expected to be found in the platform's own search path rather than shipped with the program.

`dyn` is different in kind. Each bound symbol gets a lazily initialized pointer slot named `__glo_dynsym_<symbol>`; the first call runs `LoadLibraryA` plus `GetProcAddress` on Windows, or `dlopen` with `RTLD_NOW` plus `dlsym` elsewhere, caches the address, and calls through it. Nothing is passed to the linker, so the library need not exist at build time. It is rejected where there is no dynamic loader: `error: #library,dyn is not supported for target 'wasm32-unknown-unknown'`.

Both malformed spellings are caught at parse time. An unrecognized modifier is `error: #library modifier must be system, dyn, or static`, and `#library,static,system "x"` is `error: #library accepts only one link-kind modifier`.
Binding a function with `#foreign`

`#foreign` is followed by either an identifier, which names a `#library` declaration, or a string, which is the library file itself and needs no `#library` declaration at all. An optional second string gives the C symbol name; without it the Glosso name is used unchanged.

`#foreign` makes the declaration bodyless. At file scope its `;` is required; omitting it, including by attaching a block directly, first reports `error: declaration must end with ';'`. If the terminator is written before that block, the declaration ends and the now-stray brace is `error: bad decl name '{'`. Naming a library that was never declared is `error: #foreign refers to unknown library 'nosuchlib' (declare it with #library)`.
From library name to linker argument

The compiler does not pass `#library` strings through verbatim. Each name is translated into the spelling the target's linker expects, so one source file can name `c` and link against the C runtime on every hosted platform.

A name that already contains `/` or `\` or ends in a known library extension is passed through untouched, which is how a vendored archive is named. A leading `lib` is stripped before the target spelling is applied, so `libpng` and `png` produce the same argument.

# the program declares  zzz :: #library "zzzprobe";
$ glosso -o p08.exe p08_libnames.glo
error: lld-link: error: could not open 'zzzprobe.lib': no such file or directory

$ glosso --target x86_64-linux-musl -o p08l p08_libnames.glo
error: ld.lld: error: unable to find library -lzzzprobe

Where a self-contained MinGW bundle is not available, an `x86_64-windows-gnu` link is re-planned onto the installed Windows SDK and the `lib<base>.a` spelling is rewritten back to `<base>.lib`. The observed failure on such a host names `zzzprobe.lib`, not `libzzzprobe.a`.
If any reachable `#foreign` call uses a `dyn` library, `-ldl` is added on non-Windows, non-wasm targets so that `dlopen` resolves.
The reachability rule

Library arguments are collected by walking the runtime-reachable functions and recording the library of every non-dynamic `#foreign` call found there. A declaration that is never called contributes nothing. The rule exists so that a large bindings file, most of which the program does not use, does not drag its library onto the link line.
linked without the ghost library

Adding one call to `never_called` changes the link, and the library that was invisible a moment ago becomes a hard requirement: `error: lld-link: error: could not open 'no_such_library_at_all.lib': no such file or directory`.

The reachability rule is measured after pruning, not after type checking. A `#foreign` declaration reached only from dead code, or only from a branch a `#if` removed, does not put its library on the link line, and the build succeeds on a machine where that library is not installed.
Passing arguments to the linker directly

`--linker-arg <arg>` appends one raw argument and may be repeated. The final order is the plan's own flags and objects, then the library arguments derived from reachable `#foreign` calls, then every `--linker-arg` in command-line order, then anything a build script added with `add_current_linker_arg`. It is the mechanism for search paths, subsystem selection, and any flag Glosso has no directive for.

$ glosso -o usegreet.exe usegreet.glo
glosso: compile usegreet.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
glosso: link usegreet.exe (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
error: lld-link: error: could not open 'greet.lib': no such file or directory

$ glosso --linker-arg /libpath:vendor -o usegreet.exe usegreet.glo
glosso: compile usegreet.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
glosso: link usegreet.exe (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
glosso: done usegreet.exe  (backend=llvm, target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)

$ ./usegreet.exe
greet_add(19, 23) = 42

The value is not translated between linker flavours. On `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` the linker is `lld-link`, so a POSIX spelling is dropped with `lld-link: warning: ignoring unknown argument '-L.'`. That warning is only visible when the link fails; a successful link does not surface the linker's own output.
A complete link against a system library

The program below binds one symbol from a Windows import library through `#library,system` and one from a DLL through `#library,dyn`, so only the first contributes a linker argument. Constants for the C header's `#define` names are written as ordinary Glosso constants.

glosso: compile f03.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
glosso: link f03.exe (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
glosso: done f03.exe  (backend=llvm, target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
tick count nonzero: 1
screen: 1600 x 1000

`#c_call` selects the target's C calling convention and layout rules for the declaration it is attached to. On a Glosso procedure with a body it turns that procedure into an export a C program can call; on a function-pointer type it describes a callback C will invoke; on a struct it selects C field order.

A `#c_call` procedure is an ordinary Glosso procedure in every other respect. It can be called from Glosso, it participates in overload resolution, and it is type checked normally. The one thing it gives up is the implicit context, which has no place in a C signature.

rows: C ABI, C-callable export, library root
C ABI; part of the pointer's type

blocks.text: `#c_call` does not declare an import. A declaration with no body is only legal with `#foreign` or `#magic`; writing `f :: (a: s32) -> s32 #c_call;` is `error: unexpected token ';'` followed by `error: unknown function f`. Calling into C is `#foreign`, which is handled in Calling C from Glosso; `#c_call` is the outbound direction.
Function pointers carry their convention

The calling convention is part of a `#fn_ptr` type, not a property of the value stored in it. A Glosso procedure without `#c_call` cannot be passed where a `#c_call` pointer is expected; the diagnostic names both sides by kind: `error: arg type fnptr != fnptr in call c_qsort`. This is what makes a callback handed to C safe to invoke.
`#c_call` on a struct

An ordinary Glosso struct is free to reorder its fields, and it does: storage is sorted by descending alignment, then descending size, then declaration order. `#c_call` suppresses that and lays the fields out in the order written, which is what a C declaration of the same type produces. The general rules are in Struct Memory Layout.

Plain    size = 8
C_Layout size = 12

Stable compiler-service records need the same discipline. The `Compiler` and `Bindgen` modules now declare their private service result records with `#c_call`, preserving the service field order on 32-bit output targets as well as the host. Application code should call `Native_Compile_Output.compile_c_archive` and `generate_source` and match their public `Result` values, not copy the private records or redeclare their raw `#magic` entry points.
The implicit context

A C caller has no context to pass, so a `#c_call` procedure may not read one: `error: cannot access 'context' in a #c_call / #no_context procedure`. An export that needs an allocator must take it as a parameter or install one itself. `#no_context` imposes the same restriction without changing the calling convention.
The `glo_` symbol prefix

Glosso does not own the C namespace, so every symbol it defines is prefixed with `glo_`. A `#c_call` export named `add_s32` is the native symbol `glo_add_s32`, and the C header that declares it must say so. The prefix is what lets a Glosso program define `open` or `write` without colliding with the C runtime.

One narrow exception exists: on a non-Windows, non-wasm target that is also the host, a `#c_call` procedure named `main`, or one that lowered to no code at all, keeps its bare name. Everything else, on every target, takes the prefix. WebAssembly exports follow the same rule, which is why the wasm link line reads `--export=glo_main`.
`--no-main` and library roots

Reachability normally starts at `main`. A library has no `main`, so the roots must change: with `--no-main`, or with `--backend static-lib` or `--backend shared-lib`, every defined `#c_call` procedure becomes a root and the hosted entry wrapper and the `argc`/`argv` globals are not emitted. Procedures reachable only from those roots are lowered with internal linkage; procedures reachable from nothing are dropped.

$ glosso --backend static-lib --no-main -o roots.lib roots.glo
glosso: compile roots.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
glosso: link roots.lib (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
glosso: done roots.lib  (backend=static-lib, target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)

$ llvm-nm --defined-only --extern-only --just-symbol-name roots.lib
__real@3fe0000000000000
_fltused
glo_also_exported
glo_exported_root

`not_reached` is gone and `helper` survives only as an internal symbol. The rule cuts the other way too: in a normal executable build, a defined but uncalled `#c_call` procedure is pruned exactly like any other dead code. The same source compiled without `--no-main` contains no `glo_exported` at all.
A static library consumed from C

$ glosso --backend static-lib --no-main -o glomath.lib glomath.glo
glosso: compile glomath.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
glosso: link glomath.lib (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
glosso: done glomath.lib  (backend=static-lib, target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)

$ clang driver.c glomath.lib -o driver.exe
$ ./driver.exe
glo_add_s32(19, 23) = 42
glo_scale_f64(2.5, 4.0) = 10

`--backend shared-lib` produces the same exports in a dynamic library and additionally writes an import library where the platform uses one (`glomath.dll` plus `glomath.dll.lib` on Windows). The artifact names per backend and target are tabulated in Backends, Artifacts, and Optimization Levels.

Linking two separately compiled Glosso objects or archives into one image collides on the floating-point marker symbol: `error: lld-link: error: duplicate symbol: _fltused`, reported against both objects. `--linker-arg /FORCE:MULTIPLE` gets past it, and the shared library route avoids it entirely. Linking one Glosso archive into a C program, as above, does not hit this.

For fixed C parameters and results, the declared type selects the ABI image; the compiler does not repair a mismatched declaration with an implicit numeric conversion. Apart from the string-to-byte-pointer adaptation below and C's default promotions in a variadic tail, the argument is handed to the callee as that image. The checker verifies the Glosso signature that was written down, so a wrong signature becomes a wrong call.

The fixed-width integers, `f32`/`f64`, pointers, an enum with an explicit backing type, and a compatible `#c_call` struct can describe C data directly. A `distinct` type keeps its underlying representation. This is not a promise that every Glosso primitive has a C ABI: complex, SIMD, and matrix values require an explicit boundary representation. Compiling `#c_call` signatures to textual IR shows the lowering directly.

a pointer that may be null

blocks.text: The remaining aggregate types are Glosso descriptors with no automatic C counterpart. A descriptor accepted in a `#c_call` signature passes the record, not the pointed-to data, so the other side must deliberately match its layout. `#c_call` does not turn a `string` into `char *` or a view into a pointer-and-length parameter pair. `word` below is the target's `ssize` width: 32 bits on a 32-bit target and 64 on a 64-bit one.

nullable pointer; length is found by scanning for the terminator
a tagged union, not a null value
