blocks.text: The checker rejects by-value complex primitives at C boundaries, including fields in `struct #c_call`: pass the real and imaginary components separately. `Simd(T, N)` has no portable C ABI; pass scalar memory and use `simd_load`/`simd_store` inside Glosso. Matrices likewise cross through a pointer to scalar storage. `f80` and `f128` must match the exact target's floating format and convention, not merely a C type with the same storage size; `f80` is not a portable alias for C `long double`.
`string` at a pointer parameter

A runtime `string` is a counted view and does not implicitly convert to a C pointer parameter. String literals and `cstring` values can pass to a compatible character pointer. Convert a counted view with `text.c_string()` for a temporary terminated copy, or pass its `.data` explicitly only when the foreign API also accepts a separate length.

String literals are stored NUL-terminated in the image. A substring borrows a byte range and does not add a terminator at its end. A buffer assembled by hand may have no terminator at all: the program below prints its eight bytes and then keeps going into whatever follows them in memory.
The first line prints as written. The second prints `ABCXYZ!?` followed by trailing garbage that changes between runs, which is the whole reason `cstring` exists.
`cstring`

`cstring` is a nullable pointer to zero-terminated bytes. Its `.count` scans to the first zero byte, and a null value has count zero. It has no capacity and does not record ownership. A literal or foreign pointer is borrowed; an explicit allocating conversion carries a release obligation. The conversions live in `std/Strings/Utf8`.

The explicit `c"hello"` literal infers `cstring` and borrows NUL-terminated static storage, so it requires no allocating conversion and must not be freed. An embedded zero ends its visible `.count`. Use `b"..."` for exact byte data: it infers a fixed `u8` array, retains embedded zeros, and adds no terminator. `\xNN` inserts one byte, while ordinary Unicode text contributes its UTF-8 bytes.

rows: a counted view borrowing the same bytes

blocks.text:
atoi = 1234
count = 5 round trip = hello

A `cstring` has pointer representation, so it can also appear directly in a matching C-ABI signature. A counted `string` still passes a pointer-and-count aggregate; declaring it where C expects `char *` does not convert the argument. Match the actual foreign signature.
C varargs

A final `...` parameter marks a C-ABI variadic. It is accepted only on `#foreign` declarations and `#c_call` definitions; anywhere else it is `error: C vararg marker '...' on 'f' is only supported on #foreign declarations or #c_call definitions`. Operators and macros are rejected separately, and a signature with `$T` or compile-time parameters gives `error: C vararg marker '...' on 'f' requires concrete runtime parameters`. Glosso's own variadics are a different feature, described in Variadic Parameters.

sum_s64(10, 20, 12) = 42
printf through C varargs: n=42 flag=1

`std/VarArg` supplies `Va_List`, which is opaque target-ABI storage, plus `start`, `end`, `copy`, and `arg(T, *Va_List)`. It also wraps `vprintf`, `vfprintf`, and `vsnprintf` over an opaque `C_File`. This is a native run's output; WASI skips `printf` but still exercises `sum_s64`. Glosso's `print` and C's `printf` buffer independently, so the output order can vary. Each value consumed by `arg(s64, &ap)` is explicitly `s64`: an unannotated integer otherwise defaults to target-width `ssize`, which is only 32 bits on a 32-bit target. `%lld` matches the 64-bit C `long long`; `%ld` asks for `long`, which is 32 bits even on 64-bit Windows.

C's default argument promotions do happen in the variadic tail: `bool`, `s8`, `u8`, `s16`, and `u16` become `s32`, while `f16` and `f32` become `f64`. A string literal decays to a character pointer, so `c_printf("%s\n", "hello")` is accepted. A runtime counted `string` is rejected in the variadic tail. Pass `text.c_string()` for `%s`, or pass an `s32` precision and `.data` separately for `%.*s`.

`std/Bindgen` turns a C header into Glosso declarations. It runs during compile-time execution, which means bindings can be produced and consumed in the same build, and it reads the header for the target being compiled for rather than the machine running the compiler: `long tgt_long(long a)` generates `(a: s32) -> s32` on `x86_64-windows-msvc` and `(a: s64) -> s64` on `x86_64-linux-musl`.

There are two entry points. Both take the header path, a library descriptor, and optional settings as named parameters, and both return `Bindgen_Error!string`. The library argument must satisfy `Bindgen_Library`: use a `Library_Spec`, a bare library string, or `Libraries` when the header contains functions from several artifacts.

Generated foreign declarations carry leading #memory blocks. C pointer constness determines reads or writes; pointer results use unknown(result: returned) because a C signature does not establish storage origin or ownership. A name such as counter_close does not prove release behavior. Supply the API's actual returns_fresh, released_by, kills, noescape, and escape rules before relying on it as a memory boundary.
The `.Ok` payload of `generate` is a status line, not a path: the run above printed `[bindgen] bindgen: wrote counter_bindings.glo`. The `.Ok` payload of `generate_source` is the source text itself.
Library descriptors

The library argument decides the `#library` declaration at the head of the generated file. The descriptor's name becomes the Glosso identifier every `#foreign` in the file refers to; its file or path becomes the string. `Library_Spec.library_spec(name, .file = "", .kind = .Static)` defaults an empty file to the name for `.Static` and `.System`. `.Dynamic` requires a path.
Direct generation parameters

rows: exact declaration names and their transitive dependencies
empty, generating all supported local declarations

blocks.text: Include paths, definitions, compiler arguments and allowlists are ordinary `[]mut string` parameters, each defaulting to `.[]`. The call borrows these slices and their text only while generating. Pass a fixed array's `[..]` view or a slice; no option record or specialized array mutator is needed. Definitions use `NAME` or `NAME=VALUE` without `-D`, so `SMALL_EXTRA=1` selects the corresponding preprocessor branch. A nonempty allowlist also reaches declarations in external SDK includes, requires Clang even when textual fallback is enabled, and rejects unknown names.

`allow_textual_fallback` is `false` because a clang error is more useful than a plausible-looking guess. With it off, a header clang cannot preprocess fails the call with clang's own message, prefixed `bindgen_generate_source: Clang could not preprocess <path> (status 1):`. With it on, the same header is scanned by a textual parser that understands simple declarations and object-like macros and ignores what it cannot follow.
The banner distinguishes the two parsers: libclang output says `Clang C header bindgen` and ends its summary with `(libclang)`, the textual parser says `C header bindgen` and omits the marker.
What the generated declarations look like
Every record becomes a `struct #c_call`, so field order matches the C declaration. An opaque `typedef struct Counter Counter;` becomes an empty `struct #c_call {}` that exists only to be pointed at.
A C `enum` becomes an integer alias plus one constant per enumerator, not a Glosso `enum`. Enumerators are top-level constants, so `RICH_MODE_ON` is written bare rather than as `.On`.

Function-pointer typedefs become `#fn_ptr … #c_call` with positional parameter names `arg0`, `arg1`, and so on; C parameter names are not carried across. Uses of that typedef in parameters, fields, and return values are optional by default, such as `?Rich_Callback`. A `_Nonnull` annotation makes a C pointer or callback nonoptional.

Bindgen maps C T * to ?[*]mut T and const T * to ?[*]T. These types preserve pointee mutability. Match optional pointers before use; read-only storage cannot be passed to an API that writes through its pointer.

Object-like macros with constant values become constants. Static C functions have no exported symbol and are skipped, as are macros that have no Glosso translation. A `bindgen skipped` note identifies the omission, and the summary counts emitted and skipped declarations.
Ownership at the foreign boundary

Generated declarations describe C layouts and calling conventions. They do not track allocation, retention, or release. Wrap owning foreign handles in a type with Drop, or pair raw acquisitions with their documented release functions using defer.

`#asm` places target instructions directly in a procedure body. The instructions are written as text, but the values they read and write are named Glosso locals and expressions rather than register numbers, so register allocation stays with the compiler. A block declares what it reads, what it writes, and what it destroys; everything it does not declare is assumed untouched.

There are two spellings. The structured form opens a brace block after the directive and is the one to write. An older positional form takes a single string and colon-separated operand lists carrying raw backend constraint strings; it still parses, and it is the escape hatch for a constraint the portable vocabulary cannot spell.
asm add = 42

That block lowers to one LLVM inline-assembly call. `--backend llvm-ir` shows what the compiler built out of the operand list: the placeholders became positional references, and the portable constraints became a single constraint string.
%inline.asm = call i64 asm sideeffect "movq $1, $0\0Aaddq $2, $0", "=r,r,r,~{cc}"(i64 %r0.load, i64 %r1.load)

A structured block has three parts and they must appear in this order: one or more template lines, then the operand bindings, then at most one `clobber:` clause. A block that starts with anything but a template line is `error: structured #asm expects one or more '\\' assembly lines`. An operand written after the clobber clause is `error: structured #asm operands must appear before the clobber clause`, and a second clobber clause is `error: structured #asm may contain only one clobber clause`.
Template lines

Each template line begins with `\\` and contributes exactly one line to the assembly text; the lines are joined with newlines and nothing else is done to them. Escape sequences are not decoded, so the line carries the characters written. Assembler directives and local numeric labels are ordinary text and pass through unchanged, which is how a multi-line sequence branches within itself.

`{name}` refers to the operand called `name`. `{name:modifier}` appends a backend operand modifier, which is how a 64-bit operand is spelled as its byte or word subregister. A literal brace is written `{{` or `}}`; a bare closing brace is `error: unmatched '}' in structured #asm template; write '}}' for a literal brace`. A placeholder naming nothing is `error: unknown structured #asm template operand '{source}'`.

rotate_left(1, 4) = 16
popcount(255)     = 8

`u64.rotate_left` emits `"rolq ${1:b}, $0"` with the constraint string `"=r,{rcx},0,~{cc}"`: the modifier survived, the fixed register became a braced register name, and the `inout` operand became an output plus a tied input. `rolq` needs its shift count in `cl`, and `{shift:b}` is how a `u64` operand is named as that byte register without giving up the type.
Operand directions

rows: `= expression`, or nothing to read the local of the same name
written by the block, previous value dead
`= local` to retarget, or nothing to write the local of the same name

blocks.text: An `out` or `inout` operand names storage, so its target must be a local that already exists; a name nothing declared is `error: #asm out operand needs an existing local, got 'result'`. A parameter counts as a local, so `inout` on a parameter is legal. An `in` operand names a value, so it takes any expression. The placeholder name and the target are independent: `sum: out(.Register) = total;` writes the local `total` through the placeholder `{sum}`.

An operand must have a type a machine register can hold: an integer, a float, a `bool`, a pointer, a many-pointer, or a SIMD vector. A `string` operand is `error: #asm input operand has unsupported type string` on the way in and `error: #asm out operand 'text' has unsupported type string` on the way out. A block with two outputs returns them as one aggregate value, which is why the compiler and not the programmer decides where they land.
The portable constraint vocabulary

Every operand carries either an `Asm_Constraint` member or `fixed(<register>)`. `Asm_Constraint` is declared in `std/Prelude/Assembly.glo` and is therefore always in scope. The members describe allocation semantics, not a backend's constraint letters; the compiler translates each one for the target being compiled, so user code never embeds an LLVM or GCC constraint string.

rows: any direction, the x86 family only
`f`, `w` on aarch64, `t` on the arm family
`x` on the x86 family, `w` on arm and aarch64, `v` on powerpc and s390x, `vr` on riscv64
`Yk` on the x86 family, `Upa` on aarch64
any direction, register must exist on the CPU

blocks.text: The direction column is enforced, because an operand the block writes has to be allocated somewhere the block can write. `result: out(.Memory);` is `error: structured #asm constraint '.Memory' is valid only for input operands`. The availability column is enforced too, and it is checked against `--target`, not the host: `out(.Byte_Register)` compiled for `aarch64-linux-musl` is `error: .Byte_Register is unavailable for the aarch64 target`.

A misspelled member is `error: unknown structured #asm constraint '.Gpr'`, and a bare identifier where a constraint belongs is `error: unknown structured #asm operand placement 'rax'; expected an Asm_Constraint variant or fixed(register)`: a raw register name must go through `fixed`. A misspelled direction is `error: unknown structured #asm direction 'outp'; expected 'in', 'out', or 'inout'`.
Fixed registers

`fixed(<register>)` pins an operand to one machine register, which is what a syscall ABI or a fixed-operand instruction requires. The name is validated against a per-CPU register table, so a wrong-architecture name is caught at compile time rather than by the assembler: `fixed(x0)` on x86_64 is `error: unknown x86_64 register 'x0'`. On MIPS the symbolic names are rewritten to their numbered form, so `fixed(a0)` and `fixed(r4)` denote the same register.
Clobbers and early clobber
The `clobber:` clause lists what the block destroys beyond its declared outputs. Entries are comma-separated and may mix the two `Asm_Clobber` members with bare register names.

rows: the block reads or writes memory the compiler cannot see
the block leaves the flags register in an unspecified state
that register is destroyed; validated exactly like `fixed`

blocks.text: A member outside that pair is `error: unknown structured #asm clobber '.Flags'; expected '.Memory' or '.Condition_Codes'`. Anything comparing an instruction, and every syscall sequence, needs `.Condition_Codes`; a sequence that touches memory the compiler routed through a pointer needs `.Memory`.

`.Early_Clobber` is an optional second argument on an output constraint: `out(.Register, .Early_Clobber)`. It says the operand is written before all inputs have been consumed, which stops the allocator from putting an input and that output in the same register. Two sequential `slt` results computed from the same pair of inputs need it. It is meaningless on an input, and `in(.Register, .Early_Clobber)` is `error: structured #asm '.Early_Clobber' is valid only for out and inout operands`.

The compiler checks the frame, never the instructions. It does not parse the template, so a sequence that writes a register absent from both the operand list and the clobber list is accepted and silently wrong. The declared lists are the whole contract.
One block per CPU

A template is target-specific by construction, so a portable procedure selects its block with `#if OUT.cpu == { … }` and ends the switch with `#compile_error`, which fires only for a target that reaches it. Static branching is covered in Static Branching with `#if`, and `OUT` in Targets and Cross-Compilation.
asm add = 42

That program builds for `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`, `aarch64-linux-musl` and `riscv64-linux-musl`; for `mips-linux-musl` it stops at the guarded `#compile_error`. `examples/inline_asm.glo` is the full version of this pattern: raw Linux syscalls and comparison sequences for every CPU the Linux musl targets cover, using `inout(fixed(rax))`, `out(fixed(r7))`, `.Early_Clobber`, and register clobber lists mixed with `.Memory` and `.Condition_Codes`.
`#bytes`

`#bytes <expression>;` splices pre-assembled machine code into the function body. The expression is const-evaluated and must be a list of compile-time integers in `0..255`, which in practice means an array literal of `16#xx` values bound with `::`. It is the tool for an instruction the assembler in use will not accept, or for a sequence that has already been assembled elsewhere.
spun

Each byte becomes one `.byte` directive in an inline-assembly block with an empty constraint string: the emitted IR for that loop body is `call void asm sideeffect ".byte 0xf3\0A.byte 0x90", ""()`. Nothing else is attached to it.

Because `#bytes` declares no operands and no clobbers, the byte sequence must be self-contained: it cannot name a Glosso value, and it must restore every register the surrounding code and the target ABI rely on. `examples/inline_bytes.glo` does exactly that: each of its thirteen per-CPU stubs saves the non-volatile registers it uses, carries its own message bytes at the end, and branches over them to continue.

The operand must fold. A non-list is `error: #bytes expects a compile-time list of bytes, got 5`; a value outside the range is `error: #bytes value must be a compile-time integer 0..255, got 300`; a runtime array is rejected while evaluating the name, as `error: unknown const code`.
Neither form runs at compile time

Both directives emit machine instructions, and neither compile-time engine executes machine instructions. A procedure containing `#asm` called from a constant is `error: statement is not available at compile time`. The same call from a top-level `#comptime` reaches the compile-time VM instead and is `error: #comptime stopped: #asm (inline assembly) cannot run on the VM; use the LLVM backend`, with the matching `#bytes (inline machine code) cannot run on the VM; use the LLVM backend`. The two engines are described in What Runs When.

`#magic "<name>"` on a declaration binds it to a compiler intrinsic. The declaration has no body: its parameters and result type are the signature the checker sees, and the string picks the implementation out of a registry built into the compiler. This is how the standard library reaches the type system, the host operating system, and the machine. The standard library uses registered intrinsics alongside ordinary Glosso implementations.

`#magic` exists so that these operations stay ordinary declarations. A keyword per intrinsic would sit outside the type system; a `#magic` declaration is a normal procedure, so it participates in overloading, in `where` constraints, in typeclass instances, and in the module system. A program may write its own, and the name may be any registered one.

byte_width(s32) = 4
same_text = 1

The name is not checked when the declaration is read. An unregistered name type-checks, and the program fails only when code generation reaches the call: `weird :: (a: s64) -> s64 #magic "no_such_intrinsic";` produces `error: native LLVM lowering has no classification for #magic 'no_such_intrinsic' [opcode Magic] while lowering 'main' at IR instruction 2`. The check happens where the call is lowered, so a declaration that is never called never produces it.
The four availability classes

Each registry entry carries two independent flags: whether the compile-time VM has an implementation, and whether the checker may evaluate the call while type checking. Their four combinations describe evaluator availability. Native LLVM lowering is classified separately, so an intrinsic available to both compile-time engines can still be deliberately forbidden in a program.

rows: checker evaluation, not the VM; native lowering rejects these queries
both compile-time engines; native availability is decided independently
the VM but not checker evaluation; these representatives also lower natively
neither compile-time engine; compiled code only

blocks.text: Membership follows the nature of the operation. A query about a type has no runtime existence, so it is compile-time only. An operation on a raw address or on the implicit context has no meaning inside an evaluator with neither, so it is native only. Pure value operations generally work everywhere. Host compiler and bindgen services work in the two compile-time engines but are rejected by native lowering: they are services of a build, not of the program that build emits.

rows: so a build script can read the host; the handle-relative sandbox primitives stay native only
VM and compile time, native forbidden
complex numbers, wrapping and saturating integers, indexing, ranges
pointer arithmetic, varargs, jumps, raw memory
terminal query, mode, event, and console control
the `os_*_terminal_query` and `os_*_terminal_set_mode` families, plus Windows native event, clear, cursor, wrapping, and title operations

blocks.text: One entry is special-cased against its class. `get_cmdline_args` is registered native only, but the compile-time runtime answers it anyway, so that a build script can read the arguments after `--`. The two vectors are different: at compile time it returns the trailing arguments, at run time the process argv including `argv[0]`.

$ glosso --run services.glo -- build --release
[ct] compiler = C:\Users\almag\Github\glosso\build\bin\glosso.exe
[ct] 2  compile-time argument(s)
[ct] arg: build
[ct] arg: --release
[rt] 1 argument(s)
What the compile-time engines refuse

Glosso runs compile-time code in two evaluators, described in What Runs When: the constant evaluator, which walks the tree during checking, and the compile-time VM, which executes top-level `#comptime` declarations as bytecode. They reject an unavailable intrinsic differently, and the wording is the fastest way to tell which engine was running.

rows: an intrinsic with no VM implementation, reached while checking
`#magic intrinsic 'ctx_alloc' is not available during compile-time evaluation`
the same intrinsic reached from a top-level `#comptime`
no compile-time evaluator installed at all
a `#foreign` call in a compile-time expression
`'c_strlen' is foreign, so its result is not compile-time known`
a statement neither engine implements, such as `#asm`
`statement is not available at compile time`
any other VM failure inside a top-level `#comptime`

blocks.text:
error: #magic intrinsic 'ctx_alloc' is not available during compile-time evaluation
  --> …\alloc.glo:5:10
  |
5 |     p := alloc(8);
  |          ^^^^^

Neither engine has a context allocator, so `alloc` and `free` are unavailable in both, and so is `temp_alloc`. Dynamic arrays and `tprint` are handled separately and do work. Allocation is covered in Allocators.
What native lowering refuses
The LLVM backend classifies every intrinsic name independently of the registry, and its four answers produce four distinct messages. Each one names the function and the IR instruction being lowered.

rows: `#magic 'size_of' must not reach native LLVM lowering: type introspection query must be folded before native lowering`; compiler services use `compiler service or type query must be folded before native lowering`
`native LLVM lowering rejects #magic 'sb_new': string-builder runtime representation is not lowered`
classified as implemented, but no lowering matched
`native LLVM magic coverage drift: #magic '<name>' is classified as implemented but no lowering matched`
name not in the backend's table
`native LLVM lowering has no classification for #magic '<name>'`

blocks.text: Type queries normally disappear before this classification: a call to a compile-time intrinsic is folded during lowering when the declaration has a `type`-valued parameter. That lets `size_of(Vec3)` and `field_name(Vec3, 1)` stand in a runtime body and become constants. Bind `"size_of"` to a signature with no `type` parameter and the call instead arrives at the backend. Compiler and bindgen services reach the same class when called from ordinary runtime code; use them from `#comptime`, where the VM supplies the service.
error: #magic 'size_of' must not reach native LLVM lowering: type introspection query must be folded before native lowering [opcode Magic] while lowering 'main' at IR instruction 2

String_Builder.new(), append(), and finish_source() support compile-time source generation; finish_source() consumes the builder. The ordinary make_len_cap(), write_string(), and into_string() operations also work in compile-time code. Use a transferred allocation or clone when the resulting text must outlive the builder.
`#magic` on an aggregate

`#magic` also appears on a `union` declaration, where it is a layout marker rather than an intrinsic binding and the string is not looked up in the intrinsic registry. Exactly two markers are recognised, `"option"` and `"result"`, and they select niche layout instead of a tag word. They are carried by the compiler-embedded `Option` and `Result` unions that `?T` and `E!T` resolve to, which is why redeclaring `Option` in a program is `error: type 'Option' is already declared`. Those types are described in The Option Type `?T` and The Result Type `E!T`.

`#import "Lua"` is not a binding file. `std/Lua/module.glo` contains a single statement, `#insert static_bindings_source();`, and importing it therefore runs a build: the bundled Lua 5.5 C sources are compiled for the output target, cached as a static archive, and bindgen is run over the Lua headers so that the resulting declarations are spliced into the program. The mechanism is `#insert` plus the compile-time build API, both described in `#insert` and Build Scripts; this chapter is what that machinery adds up to.
Nothing about the module is Lua-specific. `std/Lua/Build.glo` holds the logic and has no top-level side effects of its own, so it can be imported directly by a program that wants a different linkage.

The work `static_bindings_source` does on a supported target is: check the target against the support matrix, locate the Lua source tree, hand the 32 C files to `Native_Compile_Output.compile_c_archive` with `LUA_USE_POSIX` defined on the Unix family, add `-lm` to the link on Linux, macOS and FreeBSD, and return the bindgen output for `glosso_lua.h` bound to the archive it produced.

<cache>/native/v7/lua55/x86_64-windows-msvc/<key>/lua55.lib
<cache>/native/v7/lua55/x86_64-linux-musl/<key>/liblua55.a
<cache>/generated/insert/v1/<sha256>.glo

The archive path is keyed by the target and by the C compile options, so a host build and a cross build coexist. The bindings themselves are a string-valued `#insert`, so they are also materialised in the generated-source cache and `--show-generated` prints the path. Both caches are described in The Build Cache and Generated Sources.

The cost is paid once. Building `examples/lua/hello.glo` with both caches empty takes about eleven seconds, almost all of it the C archive; with the archive cached but the final-artifact cache disabled, about four seconds; and because the program has no top-level `#comptime`, the finished executable is itself cacheable, so an unchanged rebuild is restored whole.

$ glosso --run lua_hello.glo
glosso: restored lua_hello.exe from the native artifact cache
Lua computed 42
The support matrix

The bundled runtime is compiled from C by the same native compiler the rest of the toolchain uses, so it is available exactly where that compiler has a usable target bundle. Every unmet condition is turned into a generated stub that fails with `#compile_error`, so the diagnostic arrives during checking and no artifact is written.

rows: the host Windows MSVC target with a matching CPU
a Linux non-musl target on a Linux host with a matching CPU
a Linux non-musl target anywhere else
`cross-target static Lua on Linux requires a musl target bundle`
any other Windows target, including `windows-gnu` and a different CPU
`static Lua for Windows currently requires the host Windows MSVC target`
`bundled static Lua currently supports Windows and Linux targets`
sources missing from the resource tree
`Lua sources were not found (expected thirdparty/lua or an installed lib/lua)`

blocks.text: A rejection is reported at the `#insert` in `std/Lua/module.glo`, with a note pointing into the generated stub, so the message itself is visible alongside the location that produced it.

$ glosso --backend object --target wasm32-wasi -o lua.o lua_hello.glo
glosso: compile lua_hello.glo (target=wasm32-unknown-wasi)
error: bundled static Lua currently supports Windows and Linux targets
   --> …\std\Lua\module.glo:44:1
   |
44 | #insert static_bindings_source();
   | ^^^^^^^
note: generated source failed here
  --> …\cache\generated\insert\v1\929f9018….glo:1:49
  |
1 | __lua_unsupported_target :: #comptime -> bool { #compile_error "bundled static Lua currently supports Windows and Linux targets"; return false; }
  |                                                 ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

Two failures are reported through the same stub but print a `[Lua]` line first: `could not compile the bundled Lua 5.5 sources` and `could not generate Lua 5.5 bindings`, each followed by the underlying compiler or bindgen message. Those are toolchain failures rather than target rejections.
What the bindings look like

The spliced source is ordinary bindgen output, about a thousand lines of it: 5 type declarations, 4 aliases, 7 callbacks, 104 constants, 47 macros and 156 functions for this build. The shapes it produces are the general ones, covered in Generating Bindings with Bindgen; three of them matter for everyday Lua code.

`lua_State` is an empty `struct #c_call`, so it is an opaque handle. Every C pointer becomes `?[*]T`, which is why `luaL_newstate` returns an option and the result of `lua_tostring` is matched rather than null-tested.

A C macro that expands to an expression becomes an `#expand,expression` macro with inferred `Bindgen_Macro_T<N>` parameters. `lua_pop`, `lua_pcall`, `lua_tointeger`, `lua_pushcfunction`, `lua_register`, `luaL_openlibs` and `luaL_dostring` are all macros, not foreign functions.
Calling Lua from Glosso
With the bindings in scope the C API is used as it is in C: create a state, open the libraries, run a chunk, read a global off the stack. `defer` is the natural place for `lua_close`.
Lua computed 42

A string literal passed at a `?[*]s8` parameter is lowered to its data pointer, and literals are NUL-terminated in the image, so the chunk text and the global name above reach C correctly. A buffer built at run time is not terminated by anything and needs `cstring`; that boundary is covered in C Data Across the Boundary. Replacing the chunk with a syntax error takes the other branch and prints Lua's own message, `[string "answer = 6 *= 7"]:1: unexpected symbol near '='`.
Calling Glosso from Lua

The reverse direction needs a procedure of the `lua_CFunction` shape: `#c_call`, one `?[*]lua_State` parameter, and an `s32` result giving the number of values it left on the Lua stack. `lua_register` pushes it and binds it to a global name. Because it is `#c_call` it cannot touch the implicit context, which is covered in Being Called from C.
Lua called back into Glosso: 42
Linking an application-owned Lua

A program that ships its own Lua shared library imports `Lua/Build` instead of `Lua` and inserts `dynamic_bindings_source(path)` from its own bindings module. No C is compiled; bindgen runs against the same header and binds a `#library,dyn` descriptor instead of the cached archive. The path is required, so the empty call below is rejected by the same generated-stub mechanism as an unsupported target.

error: dynamic Lua linkage needs a library path
  --> …\lua_dyn.glo:4:1
  |
4 | #insert dynamic_bindings_source("");
  | ^^^^^^^

Its target rule is narrower than the static one, because the running program must be able to load the library: the output target has to equal the host in OS and CPU, must not be musl, and must be Windows MSVC or a dynamically linked Linux. Anything else is `dynamic Lua linkage requires a host Windows MSVC or dynamically linked Linux target`.

The bindings are generated from the bundled Lua 5.5 headers whichever route is taken, so an application-supplied library must match that ABI. A different Lua version will link and then misbehave, because nothing in the build checks the library against the header it was described by.

One compiler binary emits code for every target it supports, and `--target` selects the target for a build. With no `--target` the build is for the host, the machine the compiler process is running on. The choice is settled before checking begins, because the constant `OUT` describes the target and gated code reads it while types are being resolved.

A target is three named fields: `os`, `cpu` and `abi`. The LLVM triple handed to the backend is derived from those fields and is never written directly. The derivation loses information: `x86_64-freestanding-uefi` and `x86_64-windows-msvc` both produce the triple `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`, and only the `abi` field separates the two builds.

$ glosso --target x86_64-linux-musl -o hello hello.glo
glosso: compile hello.glo (target=x86_64-pc-linux-musl)
glosso: link hello (target=x86_64-pc-linux-musl, -O1)
glosso: done hello  (backend=llvm, target=x86_64-pc-linux-musl, -O1)

Every progress line names the resolved triple, so the first line of a build is the confirmation that the spelling was understood. That Linux executable was produced on a Windows host with nothing else installed: the musl runtime for the target is bundled with the compiler, and the result is a static ELF carrying no dynamic interpreter.
Spelling a target

`--target` accepts both `os-cpu-abi` and `cpu-os-abi`. The parser decides which order was written by testing whether the first field is a known CPU name and the second a known operating-system name; there is no table of complete triples to match against. Any field left out is inherited from the host target.
A spec whose first field names a wasm CPU is read wasm first: `os` becomes `wasm`, `cpu` is the wasm word, and `abi` is the following field, defaulting to `freestanding`.
`<cpu>-freestanding` sets `os` and `abi` both to `freestanding`, so the CPU name in the first field is not mistaken for an operating system.

`wasi-wasm32` is accepted for compatibility and normalizes to `os` `wasm` with `abi` `wasi`; WASI is never exposed as an operating system. `host` and `native` name the compiler's own target. An empty spec is tolerated, and so is a trailing hyphen, so `wasm32-` resolves to `wasm32-unknown-unknown`.

Field names are rewritten to a canonical spelling before the triple is formed. For the CPU field, `amd64` becomes `x86_64`, `arm64` becomes `aarch64`, `i686` becomes `i386`, and `ppc` and `ppc32` become `powerpc`. For the operating-system field, `darwin` and `osx` become `macos`, `win32` becomes `windows`, and `webassembly` and `wasi` become `wasm`. Three further rewrites happen only in the emitted triple: `x86` is spelled `i686`, `armv5` is spelled `armv5te`, and `ppc64le` is spelled `powerpc64le`.

A spec with a single field fills the operating-system slot, not the CPU slot. `--target aarch64` therefore resolves to `x86_64-unknown-aarch64-msvc` and dies at the link step with `error: unsupported executable target` naming that triple. For the same reason `--target x86_64-windows` leaves `abi` empty, which triples as `x86_64-w64-windows-gnu` rather than the MSVC ABI of a Windows host. Write the full three-field spelling.
The supported set

`--print-targets` (also accepted as `--targets`) prints each supported target with the triple it expands to and the artifact it produces, then a second list headed `Available LLVM codegen targets:`. That second list is the set of architectures the linked LLVM was built with; it is not the set of Glosso targets, and naming one of its entries does not make a target.

Fourteen further targets share the shape `<cpu>-linux-musl` and link against the bundled static musl runtime: `x86`, `x86_64`, `aarch64`, `armv5`, `armv7`, `loongarch64`, `mips`, `mipsel`, `mips64`, `mips64el`, `powerpc`, `ppc64le`, `riscv64` and `s390x`. Each expands to `<cpu>-unknown-linux-musl` with five exceptions: `linux-x86_64-musl` is `x86_64-pc-linux-musl`, `x86-linux-musl` is `i686-unknown-linux-musl`, `ppc64le-linux-musl` is `powerpc64le-unknown-linux-musl`, `armv5-linux-musl` is `armv5te-unknown-linux-musleabi`, and `armv7-linux-musl` is `armv7-unknown-linux-musleabihf`.
Entry points

A Glosso `main` is lowered under the symbol `glo_main`. What calls it depends on the target family: a hosted target gets a synthesized C entry point that forwards to `glo_main`, and a target with no host runtime has `glo_main` named as the entry or exported directly.

rows: wrapper that calls it, linked with `--export=_start`

blocks.text: `--no-main` and the `static-lib` and `shared-lib` backends suppress the wrapper entirely, along with the `argc` and `argv` globals, and root reachability at every defined `#c_call` function instead. Being Called from C describes that rooting, and Backends, Artifacts, and Optimization Levels describes the backends.
What links from a given host

Emitting an object succeeds for every supported target, because that step needs only LLVM. Linking needs the target's runtime inputs. The compiler bundles the musl runtime, the mingw-w64 import libraries and the wasm builtins, so those targets link from any host; Apple and FreeBSD system libraries are not bundled and must come from an SDK.

Measured on an `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` host, these link with no further setup: both Windows targets, `linux-x86_64-gnu`, all fourteen musl targets, both WASI targets, `wasm32-freestanding` and `x86_64-freestanding`.

These reach the linker and fail there: `x86_64-macos` and `aarch64-macos` on `ld64.lld: error: undefined symbol: _abort`, the two FreeBSD targets on `ld.lld: error: undefined symbol: abort`, and `aarch64-linux-gnu` on `ld.lld: error: undefined symbol: write`.

$ glosso --target aarch64-macos -o hello hello.glo
glosso: compile hello.glo (target=aarch64-apple-darwin)
glosso: link hello (target=aarch64-apple-darwin, -O1)
error: ld64.lld: error: undefined symbol: _abort
>>> referenced by C:\Users\…\Temp\glosso-35100-hello.o:(symbol _glo_write_string+0x248)

$ glosso --backend object --target aarch64-macos -o hello.o hello.glo
glosso: compile hello.glo (target=aarch64-apple-darwin)
glosso: wrote hello.o  (backend=object, target=aarch64-apple-darwin, -O1)

`--backend object` is therefore the portable smoke test: it proves that a program checks and lowers for a target without requiring that target's linker inputs. `x86_64-freestanding-uefi` produces an object by design, and Freestanding, Bare Metal, UEFI, and WebAssembly covers the link step it needs.
The OUT and HOST descriptors

The checker installs two constants into every compilation. `OUT` is an `Output_Target` with the fields `os`, `cpu` and `abi`, describing the target being compiled for. `HOST` is a `Host_Target` with `os` and `cpu`, describing the machine running the compiler. Their field types come from the Prelude and are always in scope, so reading them needs no import.

building for windows
OUT.abi is Msvc: 1
host is the target: 1

`%` prints an enum member as its integer value, which is why the example maps the tag to a string rather than printing `OUT.os` directly. Both the bare `OUT.os == .Windows` and the qualified `OUT.os == Target_OS.Windows` are accepted.

`#if` over `OUT` selects target-specific code, and `#compile_error` rejects a target the program does not support. Static Branching with `#if` covers the construct itself. Both directives are statements, so a gate lives inside a declaration rather than at file scope.

$ glosso --target riscv64-linux-musl gating.glo
glosso: compile gating.glo (target=riscv64-unknown-linux-musl)
error: this program supports x86_64 and aarch64 only
  --> …\gating.glo:5:9
  |
5 |         #compile_error "this program supports x86_64 and aarch64 only";
  |         ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

The LLVM triple is not a unique target key. `x86_64-freestanding-uefi` and `x86_64-windows-msvc` share `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`, so code that must tell them apart tests `OUT.abi`. The artifact cache keys on the `OUT` fields for exactly this reason; The Build Cache and Generated Sources shows the two builds keeping separate entries.

`--run` builds and then executes the result, and is refused for anything but the host: `glosso: --run can only execute the host target (got x86_64-pc-linux-musl)`, exit status 1. Using the Compiler covers the remaining driver options.
Target-width integers and descriptors

`ssize` and `usize` follow the target's pointer width, not the host's: 32 bits on targets such as `x86`, Arm, and `wasm32`, and 64 bits on targets such as `x86_64`, `aarch64`, and `wasm64`. Counts, indices, and the counts inside `string`, `string16`, slices and dynamic arrays use that same width. Only dynamic arrays carry a capacity word; counted strings store a pointer followed by a count, while `cstring` and `cstring16` store one pointer. Consequently a cross-compiled descriptor has the target layout even when the compiler itself is a 64-bit process. Tagged unions use a target-width tag as well, with padding before a more strongly aligned payload. The compile-time VM uses those target offsets when copying or matching unions; the host's word size does not determine a cross-compiled result layout.
Wide floats and target runtimes

A target's scalar alignment and calling convention matter separately from its pointer width. On 32-bit x86 musl, `f64` and `f80` have alignment 4; their complex counterparts inherit that alignment. `f80` keeps sixteen-byte storage but uses x87 on x86 and a binary128 carrier elsewhere. Query `type_info(T).alignment` for the actual output target before designing an ABI or serialized layout.

The driver builds target-keyed compiler-runtime archives for wide floating operations. On PowerPC64 musl it builds the helper archive with IEEE binary128 support and the `kf` helper names expected by LLVM; that private archive setting does not change musl's `long double` ABI. On 32-bit Arm, MIPS, and PowerPC musl, conversion to `f64` uses an integer-word helper instead of assuming a C binary128 type exists. When linking an emitted Glosso object yourself, you must also supply the runtime helpers used by that object's target.

sections.title: Freestanding, Bare Metal, UEFI, and WebAssembly

blocks.text: Three targets run with no hosted operating system underneath them: `x86_64-freestanding`, `x86_64-freestanding-uefi` and `wasm32-freestanding`. What they share is that the backend emits no host entry wrapper and no command-line globals, and that nothing links a C runtime in behind the program's back. The WASI targets are the hosted wasm option and are covered here for contrast.

The predicate the backend uses for bare metal is `os == "freestanding"`. That is true for `x86_64-freestanding` and for the UEFI target, and false for the wasm targets, whose `os` is `wasm`. The families therefore differ in the details below even though they share the same absence of a host.
Bare-metal ELF

`x86_64-freestanding` expands to `x86_64-unknown-none-elf` and sets both `OUT.os` and `OUT.abi` to `Freestanding`. The image is linked with `ld.lld -e glo_main`, so the Glosso `main` is the entry point and there is no `argc`/`argv` pair to receive. When the program has no `main` at all, reachability is rooted at every defined `#c_call` function, the same rule `--no-main` installs.

$ glosso -O2 --target x86_64-freestanding -o bare.elf bare.glo
glosso: compile bare.glo (target=x86_64-unknown-none-elf)
glosso: link bare.elf (target=x86_64-unknown-none-elf, -O2)
glosso: done bare.elf  (backend=llvm, target=x86_64-unknown-none-elf, -O2)

The `-O2` is not decoration. At `-O0` and `-O1` the backend emits runtime safety checks, and a failing check terminates through `abort`, which no freestanding image provides. The default level is `-O1`, so the same command without an explicit level fails at the link step.

$ glosso --target x86_64-freestanding -o bare.elf bare.glo
glosso: compile bare.glo (target=x86_64-unknown-none-elf)
glosso: link bare.elf (target=x86_64-unknown-none-elf, -O1)
error: ld.lld: error: undefined symbol: abort
>>> referenced by bare
>>>               C:\Users\…\Temp\glosso-33852-bare.o:(glo_kernel_add)

The size modes -Os, -Oz, and -Ozz produce runnable artifacts. They combine LLVM optimization with optsize/minsize attributes and target-specific linker size policies. Runtime checks are disabled in these modes; use -O0 or -O1 for checked builds. -Ozz also strips symbols and metadata.
No host entry is emitted: the module defines `glo_main` and no `main` or `wmain` wrapper, and the `__glo_argc` and `__glo_argv` globals are absent.

The default temporary-arena size drops from 4 MiB to 64 KiB on a freestanding target, because the arena is a zero-initialized global in the image. `--temp-allocator-size` overrides it in either direction.
Sanitizers are rejected by the backend before the link is attempted: `error: LLVM memory sanitizer is not supported for target 'x86_64-unknown-none-elf'`.
UEFI

`x86_64-freestanding-uefi` keeps `OUT.os` at `Freestanding`, so no hosted runtime is injected, but maps to the LLVM triple `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`, which selects PE/COFF and the Microsoft x64 C ABI. `OUT.abi` is `Uefi`, and that field is the only way a program can tell a UEFI build from an ordinary Windows one. `x86_64-freestanding-msvc` is the legacy spelling; it produces the same triple and the same calling convention but leaves `OUT.abi` at `Msvc`, so a program that gates on `Target_ABI.Uefi` needs the `-uefi` spelling.

The executable backend cannot finish this target, because the COFF executable plan asks for the Microsoft C startup object and its `wmain`, which a firmware image does not have. The workflow is to emit an object and link it as an EFI application separately.

$ glosso -O2 --no-main --target x86_64-freestanding-uefi -o efi.exe efi.glo
glosso: compile efi.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
glosso: link efi.exe (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O2)
error: lld-link: error: undefined symbol: wmain

$ glosso -O2 --no-main --backend object \
      --target x86_64-freestanding-uefi -o efi.obj efi.glo
glosso: compile efi.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
glosso: wrote efi.obj  (backend=object, target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O2)

$ lld-link /nologo /machine:x64 /subsystem:efi_application \
      /entry:glo_efi_main /nodefaultlib /opt:ref /out:efi.efi efi.obj

The entry is spelled `glo_efi_main` because a `#c_call` definition is exported under `glo_` followed by its Glosso name; Being Called from C gives the full symbol rule. `/nodefaultlib` keeps the Microsoft CRT out, and `--no-main` on the Glosso side keeps the `main` wrapper out and roots reachability at the `#c_call` definitions.

Driving both steps from a build script is the usual arrangement, since the second step is an external command. The compile-time options mirror the flags: backend `Object`, target `os = .Freestanding`, `cpu = .X86_64`, `abi = .Uefi`, and `no_main = true`. Build Scripts covers the API.
WebAssembly

A WASI build synthesizes a `_start` wrapper around `main` and reaches the outside world through the `wasi_snapshot_preview1` import namespace. The module built from a program that prints one line exports `memory` and `_start` and imports `fd_write`.

`wasm32-freestanding` is the other shape entirely. There is no WASI, no C library and no import namespace: the module built from the program below has no import section at all, and its export section holds exactly `memory` and `glo_main`. Everything the program needs is in the module, which is what makes the result loadable by a browser with a bare `WebAssembly.instantiate`.

$ glosso -O2 --target wasm32-freestanding -o wexp.wasm wexp.glo
glosso: compile wexp.glo (target=wasm32-unknown-unknown)
glosso: link wexp.wasm (target=wasm32-unknown-unknown, -O2)
glosso: done wexp.wasm  (backend=llvm, target=wasm32-unknown-unknown, -O2)
# module exports: memory, glo_main

`main` takes a parameter and returns a value there, which no other target allows. On `wasm32-freestanding` a `#c_call main` is exempt from the rule that `main` takes no parameters, because nothing wraps it: the host calls the export directly and passes whatever the signature says. Elsewhere the same declaration is `error: main must not take parameters; use get_cmdline_args() for command-line arguments`.

Anything beyond `glo_main` has to be exported explicitly, and has to be reachable. Reachability is computed before lowering, so an unreferenced `#c_call` function is pruned and the export then names a symbol that does not exist.

$ glosso -O2 --no-main --target wasm32-freestanding \
      --linker-arg "--export=glo_add" -o wexp3.wasm wexp.glo
glosso: compile wexp.glo (target=wasm32-unknown-unknown)
glosso: link wexp3.wasm (target=wasm32-unknown-unknown, -O2)
glosso: done wexp3.wasm  (backend=llvm, target=wasm32-unknown-unknown, -O2)
# module exports: memory, glo_add, glo_main

`--export=glo_main` is passed unconditionally for this target, so `--no-main` on a program that has no `main` breaks the link with `wasm-ld: error: symbol exported via --export not found: glo_main`. A `wasm32-freestanding` program keeps a `main`, `#c_call` or otherwise.
Sanitizers are rejected for wasm: `LLVM memory sanitizer is not supported for target 'wasm32-unknown-wasi'`.

`#library,dyn` is rejected during lowering, with the message `#library,dyn is not supported for target 'wasm32-unknown-unknown'` followed by the instruction it was lowering. There is no dynamic loader to call.

A `#foreign` call names a library file, and the wasm linker resolves that to `-l<name>`, so a host-provided function cannot be declared with `#foreign`. Imports come from undefined symbols admitted by `--linker-arg "--allow-undefined"`.
How this manual is built

The manual being read is a `wasm32-freestanding` module. A build script compiles the manual's entry file for that target, builds the Clay layout library from C sources for the same target, generates bindings for it, and links the result to a single `.wasm` file that the browser host loads.

The size modes -Os, -Oz, and -Ozz produce runnable artifacts. They combine LLVM optimization with optsize/minsize attributes and target-specific linker size policies. Runtime checks are disabled in these modes; use -O0 or -O1 for checked builds. -Ozz also strips symbols and metadata.

The C dependency is built through the same target descriptor. The binding generator checks `OUT.os`, `OUT.cpu` and `OUT.abi` and returns a `#compile_error` string when they are not the wasm32 freestanding triple, so an accidental host build fails during checking instead of producing a module that cannot run. Generating Bindings with Bindgen and Build Scripts cover the two halves.

Every source-level diagnostic is written to stderr in one layout, whatever phase produced it. The layout is a headline naming the level and the message, a location line, a framed excerpt of the offending source with a caret run under the span, and then zero or more notes.

error: unknown function print
  --> …\diag1.glo:2:5
  |
2 |     print("hello from glosso\n");
  |     ^^^^^
help: did you mean 'tprint'?

rows: ` --> ` then the file path, line and column
a bare `|` aligned with the line-number column
the line number, ` | `, and the source line verbatim
a run of `^` under the span, one per character
a label, the note text, and optionally a frame of its own

blocks.text: The gutter width is the width of the line number, so a diagnostic on line 4 indents the frame by one column less than one on line 16. The caret run is the span's length clamped to what remains on the line, and a span with no length still produces one caret. If the source line is empty or the line number is out of range the frame is omitted and only the headline is printed.

Two note labels are produced: `help` for a suggested replacement, and `note` for everything else. A note may carry its own location frame, which is how a diagnostic points at a second place in the program.
A note with no span prints as a bare label and message, with no frame under it. That form carries advice rather than a second location.

error: tagged-union payload '.Ok' may only be bound by a pattern match
  --> …\diag3.glo:7:20
  |
7 |     print("%\n", r.Ok);
  |                    ^^
note: match on the union and use that arm's payload capture, or enable #enable(allow_union_unwrap) for unsafe access
Warnings and errors

Warnings and errors use the identical layout and differ in the headline word and its colour. An error ends the build and the compiler exits 1; a warning is printed and the build continues to completion with exit 0. Multiple diagnostics are separated by a blank line.
When more than one error is rendered, a final summary line closes the group. Warnings never get a summary, however many there are.

error: got f32, expected s32
  --> …\diag8.glo:3:12
  |
3 |     return x;
  |            ^

error: got f64, expected s32
  --> …\diag8.glo:8:12
  |
8 |     return y;
  |            ^

error: aborting due to 2 previous errors

Driver messages are a separate category and are not diagnostics. They are prefixed `glosso: `, carry no frame and no colour, and report command-line and toolchain problems rather than problems in the source. A bad option value exits 2; a build failure exits 1.

$ glosso --color rainbow diag1.glo
glosso: --color must be auto, always, or never
$ echo $?
2
Colour

`--color` takes `auto`, `always` or `never` and defaults to `auto`. Under `auto`, colour is enabled only when stderr is a terminal and either the host is Windows or `TERM` is set to something other than `dumb`. Redirecting stderr to a file or a pipe therefore turns colour off without any flag.

rows: on when stderr is a terminal and the terminal is known to be capable

blocks.text:
$ glosso --color always diag1.glo
^[[1;31merror^[[0m^[[1m: ^[[0m^[[1munknown function print^[[0m
 ^[[1;34m --> ^[[0m…\diag1.glo:2:5

$ NO_COLOR=1 glosso --color always diag1.glo
error: unknown function print
  --> …\diag1.glo:2:5

The escape byte is written `^[` in that transcript. Five escapes are used and nothing else: bold red for `error`, bold yellow for `warning`, bold blue for the arrow and the gutter, bold cyan for a note label and its frame, and plain bold for the message text. Because `NO_COLOR` is checked before the mode, a script can strip colour from a build it does not control.
Diagnostics in generated source

A string-valued `#insert` splices text produced at compile time into the program, and that text has no file of its own in the project. The renderer solves this by retargeting the diagnostic: the primary span is moved to the outermost `#insert` expression, which is a real place in a real file, and the position inside the generated text becomes a note.

error: unbound 'no_such_name'
  --> …\gen_bad.glo:3:1
  |
3 | #insert emit_helper();
  | ^^^^^^^
note: generated source failed here
  --> …\cache\generated\insert\v1\82949d39….glo:1:30
  |
1 | helper :: () -> s64 { return no_such_name; }
  |                              ^^^^^^^^^^^^

Read that from the bottom up. The note names the line that is actually wrong and quotes it, and the path it names is a real file: the cache entry the generated text was written to, which can be opened in an editor. The headline names the `#insert` that produced it, which is the line to change.

When one generated source inserts another, every link in the chain gets its own note labelled `generated by this #insert`, ordered from the failure outwards, and the headline lands on the `#insert` written by hand.

error: unbound 'no_such_name'
  --> …\gen_nest.glo:3:1
  |
3 | #insert outer();
  | ^^^^^^^
note: generated source failed here
  --> …\insert\v1\82949d39….glo:1:30
  |
1 | helper :: () -> s64 { return no_such_name; }
  |                              ^^^^^^^^^^^^
note: generated by this #insert
  --> …\insert\v1\e387a996….glo:1:1
  |
1 | #insert inner();
  | ^^^^^^^

If the cache directory is unavailable the generated text is still rendered, but the note names the virtual path `<generated:#insert/<sha256>.glo>` instead, which cannot be opened. The Build Cache and Generated Sources covers where those files live and how to list them.

sections.title: The Build Cache and Generated Sources

blocks.text: The compiler keeps one per-user cache root holding everything it can reuse between builds: materialized generated sources, finished artifacts, and static archives built from C sources for a target. `--print-cache-dir` resolves the root, prints it, and exits 0 without compiling anything.

$ glosso --print-cache-dir
C:\Users\almag\AppData\Local\glosso\cache
The root is resolved once per process, from the first source in this list that yields an absolute path.

rows: the given directory; relative paths resolve against the working directory
the given directory, which must be absolute

blocks.text: --cache-dir accepts relative paths and resolves them against the working directory. GLOSSO_CACHE_DIR must contain an absolute path. The command-line override takes precedence over the environment. Use --print-cache-dir to inspect the resolved root.

$ glosso --cache-dir "C:/temp/glosso-cache-probe" --print-cache-dir
C:\temp\glosso-cache-probe
$ GLOSSO_CACHE_DIR=C:/temp/env-cache glosso --print-cache-dir
C:\temp\env-cache
$ GLOSSO_CACHE_DIR=C:/temp/env-cache glosso --cache-dir C:/temp/flag-cache --print-cache-dir
C:\temp\flag-cache
The subtrees

rows: static archives built from C sources for a target

blocks.text: The `v1` and `v9` components are format versions: a compiler that changes an entry's meaning changes the version and stops reading the old tree rather than misinterpreting it. `GLOSSO_NATIVE_CACHE_DIR` relocates the `native/v9` subtree alone, leaving the other two under the resolved root, so the C archives can be kept apart from the rest.
The artifact cache

The artifact cache stores the finished output of a build and restores it byte for byte when the same build is asked for again. A hit skips every phase, including checking, so it is reported by a single line and the build takes milliseconds.

$ glosso --run hello.glo
glosso: compile hello.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
glosso: link hello.exe (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
glosso: done hello.exe  (backend=llvm, target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
hello from 3

$ glosso --run hello.glo
glosso: restored hello.exe from the native artifact cache
hello from 3

Only three backends participate: `llvm`, `object` and `static-lib`. `shared-lib` and `llvm-ir` builds are never stored and never restored, and `--show-generated` disables the cache for the run it appears on. `GLOSSO_DISABLE_ARTIFACT_CACHE` set to any value disables it entirely.
A cache entry is keyed by an identity string covering everything that could change the output.
The canonical paths of the source file and compiler executable, the standard-library directory, and the working directory.
The LLVM triple, and separately every field of `OUT`, because the triple collapses distinct targets.

Every `--linker-arg` in command-line order, every compile-time argument written after `--`, every `--module-path` directory, and all explicit `--unit-source` ownership mappings. Backend, optimization, sanitizer, color, temporary-arena size, debug-allocator selection, `--no-main`, and `--use-std` also participate in the identity.

The `OUT` fields in that list are load-bearing. Compiling the same source for `x86_64-windows-msvc` and for `x86_64-freestanding-uefi` produces the same triple in the progress line, and the two builds still keep separate entries.

$ glosso -O2 --no-main --backend object --target x86_64-windows-msvc -o b.obj lib2.glo
glosso: compile lib2.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
glosso: wrote b.obj  (backend=object, target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O2)
$ glosso -O2 --no-main --backend object --target x86_64-windows-msvc -o b.obj lib2.glo
glosso: restored b.obj from the native artifact cache
$ glosso -O2 --no-main --backend object --target x86_64-freestanding-uefi -o b.obj lib2.glo
glosso: compile lib2.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
glosso: wrote b.obj  (backend=object, target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O2)
$ glosso -O2 --no-main --backend object --target x86_64-freestanding-uefi -o b.obj lib2.glo
glosso: restored b.obj from the native artifact cache

Identity decides which entry is consulted; a manifest decides whether that entry is still valid. The manifest records the length and modification time of every source file the build read, of the compiler executable itself, and of any `--linker-arg` value that names an existing file. Touching any one of them turns the next build back into a full compile. A hit also replays saved checker output and diagnostics; entries missing either output sidecar are treated as misses.

A program with a top-level `#comptime` is never stored. Compile-time execution can write files, run commands or print, and restoring an artifact would skip all of it. Build scripts therefore always run, which is the behaviour a build script needs.
Generated sources

At top level, `#insert <expression>` evaluates the expression during checking and splices the resulting text into the program. That text is hashed with SHA-256, written to `generated/insert/v1/<hash>.glo` under the cache root, and the path of that file becomes the source name for every span inside the generated code. Publication is atomic, and an entry that already exists has its contents verified rather than rewritten.

The name is the hash of the text alone, so the same generated source lands on the same file name under every cache root and in every project. That is what makes the entry shareable and makes a diagnostic pointing into it reproducible.

$ glosso --show-generated --run gen_ok.glo
glosso: compile gen_ok.glo (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
glosso: generated source C:\Users\almag\AppData\Local\glosso\cache\generated\insert\v1\74f6963b….glo
glosso: link gen_ok.exe (target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
glosso: done gen_ok.exe  (backend=llvm, target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, -O1)
42

$ cat C:\Users\almag\AppData\Local\glosso\cache\generated\insert\v1\74f6963b….glo
helper :: () -> s64 { return 42; }

`--show-generated` prints one `glosso: generated source <path>` line per materialized `#insert`, plus any cache warning as `glosso: warning: <text>`. It also disables the artifact cache for that run, since a restored artifact would report no generated sources at all.

The lines are printed after checking succeeds and before lowering begins, so a build that fails inside generated code prints no such line. In that case the path arrives through the diagnostic instead: the note under the error names the same cache entry. Diagnostics: Reading and Configuring Them shows the rendered form.
Redirecting the root moves the generated files with it, and the file name does not change, because it is derived from the text and not from the location.

$ glosso --cache-dir C:/probe/mycache --show-generated --backend llvm-ir -o go.ll gen_ok.glo
glosso: generated source C:\probe\mycache\generated\insert\v1\74f6963b….glo

When no cache root can be resolved at all, the text is still compiled and the source name falls back to the virtual form `<generated:#insert/<hash>.glo>`. Nothing is written, so nothing can be opened, and the same build repeats the work every time.

The third subtree is filled by the compile-time C archive builder. Importing a module that builds native code compiles its C sources for the output target. Verified inputs allow archive reuse under `native/v9/<name>/<target>/<key>/`; changed sources or headers rebuild it. When dependencies cannot be verified, each build uses a fresh `uncached-...` directory. Embedding Lua and Generating Bindings with Bindgen cover the modules that use this service.

C:\Users\almag\AppData\Local\glosso\cache
ative\v9\lua55
C:\Users\almag\AppData\Local\glosso\cache
ative\v9\glosso_rgfw
C:\Users\almag\AppData\Local\glosso\cache
ative\v9\glosso_wasm_compiler_rt_builtins
C:\Users\almag\AppData\Local\glosso\cache
ative\v9\glosso_wasm_compiler_rt_builtins\wasm32-wasm-freestanding
C:\Users\almag\AppData\Local\glosso\cache
ative\v9\glosso_wasm_compiler_rt_builtins\wasm32-wasm-wasi

The standard library is a directory of ordinary Glosso source files that ships beside the compiler. Nothing in it is privileged: every module is written in the language the manual describes, and the compiler finds it by searching for a directory that contains `Prelude.glo` or a `Prelude/` subdirectory. Where that search looks, and how `--std` overrides it, is covered in the chapter on the environment and toolchain.

This chapter is the map: what is in the tree, which names can be imported, and how to find the module that owns an operation. The import forms themselves belong to the chapter on source files, imports, and loads.
How a module name resolves
`#import "Name"` is resolved against the standard-library root by one rule, applied to the two candidate paths `std/Name.glo` and `std/Name/module.glo`.
If `std/Name.glo` exists, the module is that one file.

If `std/Name/module.glo` exists, that entry file is the module. It explicitly loads implementation dependencies and uses `#export` to expose its component modules. Other files in the directory are not automatically included.
If both exist the name is ambiguous, and if neither exists the name is unknown. Both outcomes are hard errors.

error: cannot find module "Container" (searched: …\glosso\std)

error: ambiguous module "Ascii": both …\mystd\Ascii.glo and …\mystd\Ascii\module.glo exist

A module name is a relative path with `/` separators, so `Container/HashMap` names the file `std/Container/HashMap.glo` and the same rule applies one level down. The name is validated before the lookup: an absolute path, a backslash, a `..` component, or an empty component is rejected outright.
Namespaces are not modules

Because the rule keys on `module.glo`, a directory that does not have one is a namespace and not a module. Its components are still importable one at a time by path; the directory name itself is not. That is the whole difference between `#import "Memory"`, which works, and `#import "Container"`, which does not.

inserted, len = 1
upper = GLOSSO

One name breaks the rule. `Math` is a namespace directory with no `module.glo`, but the driver rewrites the module name `Math` to `Math/Core` before the lookup runs, so scalar mathematics is reachable under its short name.
`Math` is the only rewritten name. No other namespace directory has a shorthand, and adding one would require a compiler change rather than a library change.
Modules that are one file
These fifteen names resolve to a single `.glo` file at the top of the tree, and each imports on its own.

rows: ASCII byte classification and case folding, all over `u8`.
Compile-time generation of bindings from a C header.
The compile-time build API: nested compiles, C archives, build options.
The allocator procedures and constructors behind the implicit `context`.
Runtime shared-library loading, symbol lookup, and explicit handle release.
Lightweight HTML parsing, crawling, and extraction.
The stream umbrella: `print`, writers, readers, scanning, files.
Explicit control transfer over resumable execution contexts.
Process prelude: ids, executable path, exit status, abort.
Compile-time and runtime string building, with owned buffers, borrowed views, and allocation transfer.
A dependency-free terminal and TUI toolkit.

blocks.text: Terminal sessions and structured events

A `Terminal_Session` returned by `Terminal_Session.terminal_begin` owns every terminal setting it changes. Pair it with `Terminal_Session.end`, normally through `defer`, so input modes, the cursor, and the alternate screen are restored even when the program leaves early.

Call `Terminal_Session.read_event` for a `Terminal_Event` whose nonempty `Terminal_Event_Kind` is `Key`, `Mouse`, `Resize`, or `Focus`. `Terminal_Session.read_key` is the compatibility wrapper: while waiting for a key it consumes and discards mouse, resize, and focus events.

Windows reads `ReadConsoleInputW` records and uses native console controls where they preserve the same behavior; other terminals decode ANSI/UTF-8 keys, SGR mouse reports, and focus reports. Mouse coordinates are zero-based and relative to the current viewport, with horizontal wheel buttons and separate `moved`, `dragged`, and `double_click` flags. A classic Windows console cannot emulate every VT feature: alternate-screen sessions, canvas rendering, styling, and other ANSI-only controls can report `.Unsupported` when VT output is unavailable.
Modules that are a directory

These sixteen directories carry a `module.glo` entry point. An umbrella entry point uses `#export` to expose component modules; implementation fragments can be joined with `#load,embed`. The Lua entry point uses `#insert` to build its native runtime on demand.

rows: ZIP central-directory reading and extraction with path and resource checks.
Native windows, input, 2D drawing, 3D scenes, and an immediate-mode UI on Windows x86_64 MSVC.
Owned RGBA8 images and PNG, JPEG, and WebP codecs written in Glosso.
The Lua 5.5 C API, with a static runtime built from bundled sources.
Airy, Bessel, gamma, hypergeometric, integrals, zeta and polylog.
Raw memory operations, generic slice algorithms, and `ManuallyDrop(T)`.
Compile-time type introspection and folded intrinsics.
The target OS primitive boundary: threads, clocks, syscalls.
Loaded automatically for every program; see the chapter on the implicit prelude.
Deterministic engines, OS entropy, sampling, distributions.
Sorting, ordered search, heaps, deterministic permutations.
UTF-8 and UTF-16 views and conversions, plus owned UTF-8 buffer cleanup; exports `Memory`, `Utf8`, and `Utf16`.
Clocks, durations, civil calendars, text formats, TZif zones.
`Functor`, `Applicative`, `Monad`, `Error`, and `Derive`; `Try` and `Termination` are in the Prelude.
UTF-8 helpers plus the generated character tables.

blocks.text: Images and codecs

`#import "Image"` provides owned, tightly packed RGBA8 pixels and PNG, JPEG, and WebP codecs implemented in Glosso. `Image.image_read` detects the format from the bytes; `image_write` chooses it from the filename extension unless an explicit `Image_Format` is supplied. `Image.resize` takes output dimensions and uses nearest-neighbor sampling. Narrow imports such as `Image/Core` and `Image/Png` are also available.

`Image.image_decode(bytes)` borrows encoded bytes and returns independent pixels; `Image.encode` returns an owned dynamic byte array that cleans up at scope exit. PNG and WebP encoding preserve RGBA losslessly. JPEG encoding is lossy, accepts quality 1 through 100, and discards alpha. Decoding supports progressive JPEG and both lossy and lossless WebP stills; animated WebP is rejected. `Image_Limits` defaults to 67,108,864 pixels and 536,870,912 encoded bytes, with checks on codec working buffers too.

An `Image` owns its dynamic pixel array and moves by value. Scope exit destroys the pixels automatically; `image.destroy()` releases them early. Use `image.clone()` for an independent copy and `*Image` for a borrowed receiver. Keep the creating `context.allocator` installed until cleanup. Pixels allocated from temporary storage expire at the next reset. File writes finish encoding before opening the destination, then create or truncate it; they are not atomic replacements.
Namespace directories
These six directories have no `module.glo` and no sibling file, so the directory name is not importable at all. Every component listed is importable by path, subject to the caveat below.

Filesystem path results can own text too. In `File_System/System`, a successful `weakly_canonical(path)` owns its string and must be released with `string.free`, including the fallback to `absolute` when the path is absent. `relative(path, base)` also returns an owned string, independent of temporary path components; even `"."` is an owned result rather than a borrowed literal.

In `Net/Socket`, `Socket.socket_create` defaults to `kind = .Stream` and `protocol = .Default`. It returns a `Net_Error` with kind `.Unsupported` when the target has no socket ABI or the family is `.Unspecified`. This is not a generic `.System_Error` with a zero native code. On success, the returned socket owns its descriptor and its fallible `Drop` closes it at scope exit. `Socket.close` remains available for an explicit early close.

`Net/Tls` verifies the peer chain and hostname by default. The Linux GNU SDK bundles static OpenSSL archives; other hosted targets resolve an OpenSSL-compatible provider at link time. Unless `ca_file` or `ca_directory` is supplied, Linux supplements the provider's default trust paths with a native CA bundle. `SSL_CERT_FILE` and `SSL_CERT_DIR` retain their provider-defined override behavior.

The `Serialization` components provide `Serialization_Document.json_document_from_string`, `Serialization_Document.toml_document_from_string`, `Serialization_Document.yaml_document_from_string`, and `Serialization_Document.messagepack_document_from_bytes(bytes)` for an owned parsed tree. The resulting `Serialization_Document` captures the current allocator; `document.destroy()` releases its arrays and decoded text. Views into `document.root` expire at destruction, and the allocator's storage must stay valid for the document's lifetime. For a raw model returned by a bundled value parser, `value.destroy(.owned_text = true)` also frees decoded text; the default leaves text borrowed for manually built models.

`text.substring(start, end)` and `text.substring_view(start, end)` from `Strings/Utf8` borrow a clamped byte range without allocating. Their offsets need not be UTF-8 boundaries; both results last only as long as the input storage and must not be freed. Use `view.clone()` for an independent allocation. Trimming and split pieces also borrow the input; `split` owns only its array of views. Filesystem helpers such as `parent_path(path)`, `filename`, and `path_dirname` use borrowed views where their contracts promise to borrow the input.
Two names are both a file and a directory. The file is what `#import` resolves to, because the directory has no `module.glo`; the directory holds the components that the file deliberately leaves out.

A component declares its dependencies explicitly. Importing its umbrella adds the public components selected by `#export`; an ordinary `#load` or `#import` inside that component does not expose those dependency names to the caller. Files intended only as shared source fragments are assembled explicitly with `#load,embed`.
Finding the module that owns an operation

Nothing outside the prelude is in scope until it is imported, so a missing import shows up as an unbound name rather than a link error. The compiler suggests the closest name it can already see, which is a hint about spelling and not about the module.

error: unknown function sqrt
  --> …\miss.glo:4:18
  |
4 |     print("%\n", sqrt(2.0));
  |                  ^^^^
help: did you mean 'seek'?
The direct way to see what a module exports is to ask for a name it does not have. A failed `#import,only` names the module's entire public surface in a note, which makes it a usable index.

error: #import,only names unknown public declaration 'is_ascii_hex' in module "Ascii"
note: public names: is_ascii_alpha, is_ascii_alphanumeric, is_ascii_digit,
      is_ascii_lowercase, is_ascii_uppercase,
      is_ascii_whitespace, to_ascii_lower_byte, to_ascii_upper_byte

Two things that list does not show. A typeclass method is not a module-level declaration, so `sqrt` does not appear in the public names of `Math/Core` even though `#import "Math"` is what brings it into scope. Visibility also matters: private and unit-public declarations are excluded from selective imports by other ownership units. An explicitly `#public` name is exported even when its spelling begins with `_`.
Operations on scalars, including the numeric typeclasses, live in `Math/Core`; bit manipulation in `Math/Bit`; the named constants in `Math/Constants`.
Operations on a borrowed slice live in `Memory`; operations that order or search one live in `Sort`; operations that own storage live under `Container`.

Anything that touches the operating system has a portable face in a top-level module and a raw face in `Os`. Prefer the portable one: `Os` is the boundary the rest of the library is built on, and its shape changes with the target.

read_file(path, max_count) performs one bounded read and may return fewer bytes than requested. Use read_file_up_to(path, max_count) to repeat short reads up to the limit, or File.open(path) followed by file.read() to read through EOF. Raw returned strings need free() with the original allocator.
Default parameters and typed flags

The library uses one entry point when operations differ only by a setting, allocator, or fixed argument. Omit a setting to use its default; select an alternative with `.parameter = value`. Input-only option records have been replaced by direct parameters. Values with their own lifetime, such as a `File`, a `Dns_Resolver_Config`, and workspace `Build_Options`, remain records.

`open` in `File_System/File` takes a path followed by `access = .Read`, `disposition = .Open_Existing`, `permissions = File_Permissions.Default_File`, and `flags = Open_Flags.None`. Its path type must satisfy `AsView(P, Path_View)`. The returned `File` owns its handle, and its fallible `Drop` closes the handle automatically. `file.close()` can finish it early and consumes the handle even if closing reports an error.
